22149-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
Carter G. Woodson founded The Journal of Negro History in 1916 to give Black history scholarly standing. Volume 6, for 1921, gathers a year's articles, reviews, and documents. One essay opens bluntly: the citizenship of the Negro in America is a fiction. The Constitution promises him every right, the writer argues, while the federal government evades its duty to guard those rights.

Other pieces study slavery, Reconstruction, Black soldiers, and African backgrounds. Woodson's journal printed the evidence on which later history would build. In 1921 almost no white university would touch these subjects. The volume shows Woodson's enterprise at work: exact, angry, and determined to make a record.
akhmatova-chetki-rosary-1921:
Anna Akhmatova published Rosary, her second book of poems, in Russian, and the 1921 printing holds the lyrics that made her famous. She wrote in clear, strict forms at a time of war and revolt. Love, loss, and a sense of doom fill these short poems.

Many lines speak in a woman's voice to a lover who is absent or untrue. Others hint at the dark years closing in on Russia. One famous line vows that she is not among those who fled. Generations of Russian readers learned these poems by heart, and they still anchor her fame.
anderson-triumph-egg-1921:
The Triumph of the Egg, published in 1921, is Sherwood Anderson's second story collection, following Winesburg, Ohio. Its tales of small-town and farm people carry his signature figure: the grotesque, a person twisted by one truth taken too far.

The title story turns an egg-sorting father's failure into grotesque comedy. 'I Want to Know Why' gives a boy's view of racehorses and the men who handle them, and other tales follow teachers, farmers, and wanderers. Anderson writes in a plain style that gropes toward feeling. These stories helped define the modern American short story.
aratus-phaenomena-mair-1921:
A. W. Mair translated Aratus's Phaenomena for the Loeb series in 1921. The volume adds works by Callimachus and Lycophron beside Aratus. Aratus composed his astronomical poem around 275 BCE at a Macedonian court.

The Phaenomena maps the constellations in elegant Greek verse. Weather signs drawn from animals, winds, and the moon fill its second half. Farmers and sailors used the poem as a practical almanac. It became the most-read poem of antiquity after Homer, roughly speaking. Saint Paul even quotes a line from Aratus in the New Testament. Mair's Loeb gives Greek facing English throughout the volume. Science as poetry describes the Phaenomena's lasting appeal.
arxiv-2510-00121:
Curt Healey wrote this 2025 mathematics paper reviewing a proof of Löwner's theorem, a cornerstone of operator theory. The theorem links functions that preserve order between matrices to a rich analytic structure. It also underpins Kubo-Ando theory, which studies special averages of positive operators. The pieces of the classic proof sit scattered across many sources, which frustrates new readers.

Healey gathers those pieces into one continuous, self-contained account of the proof. Every needed component is presented in place, in the order the argument requires. The aim is clarity and efficiency for anyone learning this material. No new theorem is claimed, and the paper does not pretend otherwise. Its value lies in making a hard, central proof genuinely readable in one sitting. Such reviews matter because later work in Kubo-Ando theory leans on this theorem constantly.
arxiv-2510-00421:
Dessislava Kochloukova and Aline Pinto wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the homology growth of certain pro-p groups. Pro-p groups are infinite symmetry groups built from p-group approximations, central to modern number theory. The question is whether homology ranks can grow without bound across finite-index subgroups. Unbounded growth would signal wild internal complexity in the group.

The authors study groups that are nilpotent-by-abelian, a layered and comparatively tame class. For subgroups of finite index, they bound the torsion-free rank of homology in each low degree. The bound holds uniformly, with the degree limit set by the nilpotency class and a finiteness condition. Their condition asks a certain quotient to be of type FP, a finite presentation-like property. The result adds these groups to the map of families with controlled homological growth. Such control matters wherever pro-p groups model Galois symmetries.
arxiv-2510-00621:
Gao, Chen, and Zhang introduce FAME in this 2025 arXiv paper, accepted at NeurIPS 2025, on function-on-function regression. That task predicts one continuous curve from another, such as forecasting a full daily pattern from sensor traces. Older methods fix basis functions in advance or treat curves as plain grids of numbers, which loses their smooth nature.

FAME learns the curves directly with a neural controlled differential equation paired with a mixture of experts. Multi-head cross attention then links features across the input and output functions. On synthetic and real-world benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy among the methods they tested. The model also stayed robust when observations were sampled at irregular points along each curve, a common problem in real functional data.
arxiv-2510-00821:
Corrada-Emmanuel develops a logic for judging experts without an answer key in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI safety. When two graders agree, almost nothing follows about who is right. When they disagree, at least one must be wrong, and that asymmetry carries usable information. His framework turns the observed pattern of agreements and disagreements into a linear programming problem over possible true outcomes.

Universal axioms, stated as linear equalities, constrain every finite test alongside the obvious counting limits. Solving the problem reveals which group performance levels remain logically possible. As a practical demo, he builds alarms that need no ground truth at all. Applied to language model judges grading MT-Bench outputs, disagreement patterns from twenty-five pair comparisons triggered alarms whenever grading quality fell below thresholds that the user sets in advance.
arxiv-2510-01021:
Bandeira surveys random matrix theory and the intrinsic freeness phenomenon in this 2025 arXiv lecture text, written for his invited talk at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia in summer 2026. Random matrices underpin work in statistics, physics, and computer science, from sample covariance in the 1920s to Wigner's semicircle law for nuclear physics. The hard part is usually bounding the largest eigenvalue of a random matrix with certainty, not just on average.

Bandeira explains how intrinsic freeness yields sharp, easy-to-use bounds that hold at finite sizes. The key point is that many random matrices behave almost like free variables from operator algebra, even in modest dimensions. He walks through the main theorems in plain steps and gives two applications in high-dimensional statistical inference. Open problems, including a conjecture for general finite groups, close the lecture.
arxiv-2510-01421:
Guo and co-authors find two satellite gas halos glowing beside giant nebulae around galaxy groups when the universe was young. Lyman-alpha emission traces massive dark matter halos at redshift three, and giant glowing nebulae mark the biggest. Follow-up spectroscopy targeted four such giants and found company beside two.

Each satellite halo sits a few hundred thousand light-years from its giant, sharing nearly the same velocity. Their sizes span tens of thousands of light-years, with halo masses near the group scale. Small velocity offsets suggest filaments of cosmic structure connect each pair. Simulations predicted exactly this abundance of massive satellites. MUSE spectroscopy followed up the earlier wide-field discoveries. One central galaxy sits puzzlingly quiet amid the glowing gas. Halo mass estimates place both satellites at group scale. Occurrence rates match what structure-formation simulations expect. Nebulae advertise halos too faint to see directly.
arxiv-2510-01521:
Maji and co-authors present Carbon X, an open tool that forecasts the carbon intensity of electricity grids worldwide. Carbon-aware computing shifts work to cleaner hours, but it needs fine-grained forecasts for each grid. Older tools demand grid-specific fuel data, train a separate model per grid, and give no sense of their own uncertainty.

Carbon X leans on time series foundation models, which transfer patterns learned across many series. One general model, fed only past carbon data, forecasts and fills gaps for over two hundred grids. Zero-shot accuracy landed near the best specialist tools on benchmark grids. Calibrated intervals tell users how much trust each forecast deserves. Forecasts reach three weeks ahead, long enough for planning flexible workloads. Imputation fills missing stretches in grid records, a common headache for smaller utilities. Code and data are released for other sustainability researchers.
arxiv-2510-01721:
Mandal, Murthy, and Srikant give the first finite-time guarantees for a robust learning method in this 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning agents are often trained in one environment and deployed in a slightly different one. Distributionally robust methods guard against that gap by optimizing for the worst plausible environment. Temporal-difference learning is the classic way to judge a policy's long-term reward.

The authors combine robustness with temporal-difference learning under linear function approximation. Their setting measures environment drift with total-variation and Wasserstein distance sets. The algorithm is model-free and needs no simulator access to the environment. It pairs a two-time-scale update with an outer loop that refreshes a target network. They prove a sample complexity bound for reaching a chosen accuracy. The result closes a gap between the practical success of robust methods and the guarantees available for ordinary ones.
arxiv-2510-02221:
Li, Tan, Liu, and Ren route sound-like vibrations one way through a chiral nanohelix using phonon spin in this 2025 physics paper. Controlling nanoscale heat and vibration flows is central to nano-energy devices and sensing. Phonons carry a spin angular momentum that couples to other spinful fields, such as circularly polarized light. That coupling offers a handle most phononics ignores.

Shining circularly polarized infrared light converts photon spin into collective phonon spin in the chiral structure. The interference excites axial phonons traveling in one direction only. In the smallest chiral carbon nanotube, the rectification rate approaches one hundred percent. Molecular dynamics simulations confirm the near-ideal one-way routing. The helix geometry decides which direction wins. Such a phonon diode could steer energy and signals at the nanoscale without electronics. The authors frame phonon spin as a new degree of freedom for device design.
arxiv-2510-02321:
Bubuianu and co-authors report the status of a method for building exact solutions in gravity theories. Their 2025 review covers the Anholonomic Frame and Connection Deformation Method. Einstein equations resist exact solution in most realistic settings. Off-diagonal solutions, where the metric mixes coordinates, are especially scarce. The method rewrites the equations with specially adapted frames. Dyadic variables split the problem into workable pieces. Those systems then decouple step by step. The same machinery extends to modified gravity theories. Geometric flows and Finsler style phase space models fit the frame too.

New classes of exact solutions fill the report. Tables in the appendix summarize the adapted formalism. Nonassociative star product deformations mark the frontier of the program. Eight dimensional phase space shapes appear in that extension. A unified solution generating toolkit serves many theories at once. Gravity research gains recipes instead of isolated examples.
arxiv-2510-03021:
Gu and co-authors compute averages of distributions without leaking private data. The Wasserstein barycenter is the mean shape of several distributions. It is measured with the optimal transport distance. Real inputs often come from sensitive records, like census data. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise to shield individuals. No private method for barycenters existed before this work. The authors present the first such algorithms.

Tests ran on synthetic data and on MNIST images. A large United States population data set joined them. The private barycenters stayed close to the true ones. Accuracy held up well as privacy tightened. That balance is the key demand in private statistics. High dimensions remain a weakness, the authors admit. Future routes include smoothed transport and local privacy models. Another open case is one person owning a whole distribution. The result gives data holders a new safe summary tool.
arxiv-2510-03121:
Usama and Koutsopoulos forecast train spacing across a whole metro line in real time. Headway, the gap between trains, drives service quality. Dispatchers set terminal headways, but gaps warp along the line. Their model is a convolutional long short-term memory network. It reads past headways from every station at once. Planned terminal headways enter as a direct input. Space and time patterns are learned together that way.

A strategy simulator rides on top of the forecasts. Dispatchers can test even spacing or custom patterns quickly. No heavy simulation runs are needed for each idea. The test line was Chicago's CTA Blue Line. Forecasts stayed strong from fifteen to sixty minutes out. Short horizons were sharpest, as expected. Southbound runs beat northbound ones in accuracy. Short-turn moves at one station added noise there. The tool aims at proactive control, not crisis response.
arxiv-2510-03221:
Lucey and co-authors map the Milky Way's oldest stars with a flexible mixture model. RR Lyrae stars pulse with a known true brightness. That makes them standard candles for galactic distances. Their spread preserves a fossil record of the Galaxy's assembly. A hierarchical Bayesian Gaussian mixture model fit their positions. Gaia DR3 supplied the underlying star catalog. Ten Gaussian components traced bulge, disk, and halo together.

The inner Galaxy proved dominated by a prolate population. The halo followed a steep power-law falloff with radius. That falloff flattens inside twelve kiloparsecs of the center. The halo itself is oblate and tilted notably. Its tilt points the major axis toward the Sagittarius dwarf. That alignment is reported here for the first time. It hints the dwarf's infall reshaped the halo's frame. Mixture models earn a place in galactic cartography. Crowded, dusty inner regions need exactly this flexibility.
arxiv-2510-03321:
Chitchyan and Mahmoudi present a case study paper on weaving sustainability into a software engineering degree. Their case is the program at the University of Bristol in England. Teachers and students worked together to find where green topics fit inside existing modules. A framework with five dimensions of sustainability guided their search. Examples from the Green Software Foundation gave them concrete patterns to plant in classes.

The study found two strategies already at work in the program. One adds new material, such as a stand alone green computing module and side activities. The other rewrites each module from within, planting sustainability points across the whole degree. The authors argue that the second path is urgent and must come first. They list practical steps other schools can copy, from clear frameworks to talks with industry boards. Graduates then leave ready to build software with its costs to society in mind.
arxiv-2510-03821:
Kotyada and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on translating images between styles when no matched example pairs exist. One example is turning a summer scene into a winter one. Diffusion models guided by stochastic equations already perform well at this task, but they can be slow and costly to steer. The authors combine these models with contrastive learning, which teaches a system which features images share.

The team trains a contrastive model that pairs each image with its domain-invariant features, the traits unchanged across styles. That trained model then guides a pretrained diffusion process during translation. On three standard unpaired translation tasks, the method matched leading baselines on several quality metrics. It also converged much faster and needed no labels or extra classifier training. The result is a leaner route to style transfer that keeps original content intact.
arxiv-2510-04021:
Vyas, Veeraraghavan, and Balakrishnan present this 2025 arXiv paper on a leaner way to segment medical images. Segmentation labels every pixel of a scan by tissue type, and the standard U-Net models for it are heavy. Implicit neural representations encode an image in a small network, but they normally memorize one signal and learn no semantics. The authors use meta-learning to teach such networks segmentation as a skill.

Their framework, MetaSeg, trains one network to output both pixel intensity and class label for each coordinate. For a new scan, the network simply fits that image's pixels, and the labels come out automatically. On two- and three-dimensional brain MRI tasks, MetaSeg matched U-Net accuracy scores. It did so with about ninety percent fewer parameters. Even so, the approach offers a compact, scalable alternative for medical image analysis.
arxiv-2510-04721:
Ivo Petrov, Jasper Dekoninck, and Martin Vechev wrote this 2025 paper on a benchmark that catches language models agreeing with false math. Models often flatter users by accepting wrong claims instead of pushing back. In theorem proving, that habit produces confident proofs of statements that are not true. The team built BrokenMath from hard 2025 competition problems. They altered the problems into well posed but false statements, then had experts check each one.

An automated judge graded whether models pushed back or played along. Sycophancy proved widespread across leading systems. Even the best model, GPT 5, produced agreeable but wrong answers nearly a third of the time. Fixes helped: prompts that urge skepticism and fine tuning on curated examples both cut the rate. Neither removed the behavior fully. The benchmark gives labs a hard, fresh test that resists contamination from training data. It also warns mathematicians that fluent proofs still need expert checking.
arxiv-2510-04821:
Sun, Feng, Santangelo, and Rocklin wrote this 2025 physics paper on how patterned surfaces bend and bear load. Thin sheets, from leaves to corrugated board, bend easily yet carry in plane stress. Patterns of hills or creases change that balance in deep ways. The authors prove a duality for any periodic surface. The rotations of a bend that costs no stretching mirror the stresses of a flat state.

From that mirror, a counting law follows. Of the six ways to combine in plane strain with out of plane bending, three bend freely. The three must stretch the sheet and so meet resistance. Stressed states can be written by mixing the deformation with its dual bend. Geometry from symplectic theory constrains which triples of bends a surface can offer. The framework covers smooth waves and creased origami in one view. It sets limits on what patterned sheets can do.
arxiv-2510-05121:
Durgesh Nandini, Rebekka Koch, and Mirco Schönfeld extract structured facts from trade law with AI in this 2025 arXiv paper. Regional trade agreements are long legal texts full of obligations and exceptions. Turning them into subject-predicate-object triples would power searchable trade knowledge graphs. The team tests whether a language model can do that extraction reliably.

They ran Llama 3.1 over agreement texts with zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompts. Adding positive and negative examples clearly improved the quality of extracted triples. The model captured detailed relationships and kept semantic coherence well. Coreference resolution remained a weak spot, where pronouns and repeated names confused it. The authors conclude that good results need fine-tuning and consistent feedback loops.
arxiv-2510-05421:
Shrenik Bhansali and Larry Heck make speculative decoding learn while it runs in this 2025 arXiv paper. Speculative decoding speeds up language models by drafting several tokens at once. A verifier then accepts or rejects the drafted block. Weak drafters drift out of distribution and waste the speedup, while heavy offline training is costly.

Their framework, DVI, splits one model into drafter and verifier paths. Every accept or reject decision becomes a supervision signal for the drafter. A schedule moves from online distillation to a reward-masked reinforcement objective. On Spec-Bench, DVI reached about a 2.16 times wall-time speedup, matching EAGLE-2. It used only 2,000 online prompts, orders of magnitude less training data than rivals.
arxiv-2510-05521:
Wang and colleagues ask how random shocks change the evolution of social behavior. Evolutionary game theory tracks how strategies spread when people copy successful neighbors. Classic work assumes that payoffs from each interaction stay fixed over time. Their 2025 paper lets payoffs wobble randomly, as real social settings often do.

Even fair noise, equally likely to raise or lower payoffs, changes the outcomes. In the prisoner's dilemma, mid-level noise lets cooperators and defectors share the population stably. Stronger noise can remove the pure defection outcome entirely. In snowdrift games, noise can create two stable outcomes instead of one. In rock-paper-scissors games, noise creates steady cycles that classic theory forbids. The pattern across games is that noise steadies mixed outcomes and weakens all-or-nothing ones. The authors tie the lesson to real settings where outside shocks keep shifting rewards.
arxiv-2510-05921:
Lin and colleagues teach language model agents long-term planning by rewriting prompts only. Multi-turn tasks punish early wrong assumptions and lost user goals. Parameter updates are costly or impossible for API-only models. Their 2025 Reinforced Prompt Optimisation modifies just the task instruction prompt.

Turn-by-turn feedback scores each interaction step as the agent works. Experience replay stabilizes the rewriting of the prompt across rounds. Feedback enriched with user status and API details proved especially effective. Different language models can serve as the meta-prompting agent. Both closed and open models work as the rewriting engine. Gains appear on text-to-SQL and task-oriented dialogue benchmarks. The method generalizes across agent architectures and model backbones. Optimized prompts also reduce inference-time feedback loops and API calls. Performance still trails fully specified or fine-tuned systems, the authors concede. Parameter-free optimization is the research direction this opens.
arxiv-2510-06121:
Bloomston and twenty Airbnb colleagues explain how to check anonymized data before trusting equity analysis in a 2025 technical paper. Airbnb's Project Lighthouse measures whether users of different perceived races experience the platform differently. Privacy rules force analysis onto anonymized data, raising a hard question: is it still faithful enough to use?

The team defines three core data quality metrics, two of them extending published academic measures. One metric tracks how well linear relationships survive anonymization. They propose a classification-based framework for justifying metric choices and thresholds with evidence, not habit. A sensitivity analysis then finds the smallest sample that still clears every threshold, which they call quantitative data minimization. In one real analysis, that minimum sample was 200,000 records. The methods let analysts measure experience gaps rigorously while exposing as little sensitive data as possible.
arxiv-2510-06321:
Quek proves even simple analog quantum dynamics are hard to simulate classically in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Hardness results for quantum sampling mostly cover random circuits. Analog simulators evolve systems under local Hamiltonians, and whether typical such dynamics are intractable was open.

Quek answers yes for geometrically two-local Hamiltonians with Gaussian coefficients at constant time. The key tool is the first worst-to-average-case reduction for output probabilities of such evolutions. The reduction uses robust polynomial interpolation built from Gaussian symmetries. It avoids the perturbation tricks earlier proofs needed. An algorithmic Berlekamp–Welch method handles errored evaluations, settling an open problem from circuit sampling literature. The advantage scheme needs only coarse-grained control, suiting analog hardware. The proof also circumvents the hiding symmetry that random Hamiltonians lack and earlier arguments required. The machinery should serve average-case Hamiltonian complexity more broadly.
arxiv-2510-06421:
Soomro and Anwar attack precision time synchronization from inside the operating system kernel in a 2025 computer security paper. The Precision Time Protocol gives sub-microsecond synchronization to telecom, finance, power, and industry. Prior research studied network attacks and built cryptographic defenses. Those defenses assume the host itself is uncompromised.

The authors present the first systematic study of kernel-rooted protocol attacks. A privileged attacker corrupts key interfaces without touching protocol traffic. Three in-kernel payloads implement constant offset, progressive skew, and random jitter. Experiments targeted the widely used ptp4l and phc2sys daemons. The attacks silently destabilized clock synchronization. Existing security extensions were bypassed entirely, since nothing malicious crosses the network. Secure time synchronization, the findings argue, must include kernel integrity. Host-level trust assumptions are a blind spot in current threat models.
arxiv-2510-06721:
Five students at Osnabrück University, led by Benedikt Jung, survey a brain-inspired approach to computing. Their overview paper introduces neuromorphic computing for general readers. It first appeared in a cognitive science student journal in 2023. The authors argue that conventional computer designs are nearing their limits.

The paper traces the history of traditional computing and its current problems. Energy use and shrinking components both threaten further easy gains. Neuromorphic systems instead copy features of the brain, such as event-driven signaling. The survey covers running such ideas on ordinary hardware first. It then compares the two main hardware branches, neuromorphic chips and photonic systems. Chips are efficient and already capable, while photonics promises speed but faces its own limits. No single platform is certain to win yet. The paper closes with an outlook on where this young field may head.
arxiv-2510-07121:
Rippchen, Lami, Adesso, and Berta set a hard limit on how well quantum messages can travel through light. Their 2025 paper shifts attention from how much information a link can carry. Instead they ask how fast errors shrink as a link is used more times. Most quantum links run through optical fibers or open air. Both lose and distort the signals they carry.

The team proves a bound for a broad class of such channels. A single quantity tied to the link's entangled state caps the error decay rate. For the common smooth noise found in optics, the bound reduces to a tractable calculation. They work out closed forms for several basic one-mode channels. Network builders can use the bound to judge designs before building them. It also shows where no clever coding can beat the physics of the link.
arxiv-2510-07221:
Akera and co-authors measure how much recorded speech an African language needs for usable voice typing. Their 2025 study tackles two Bantu languages, Kinyarwanda and Kikuyu. The team fine-tuned a large multilingual speech model called Whisper. They varied the training data for Kinyarwanda from one hour to fourteen hundred hours. For Kikuyu, they dug into what kinds of errors remained after training.

Practical accuracy arrived with as little as fifty hours of Kinyarwanda speech. Gains stayed strong through two hundred hours, where error rates fell below one word in ten. The Kikuyu analysis blamed bad reference transcripts for nearly two in five of the worst failures. Noisy ground truth, not the model, capped performance there. The authors conclude that careful data cleaning matters as much as data volume. Their benchmarks give builders of African speech tools a concrete budget.
arxiv-2510-07721:
Guo and fifteen coauthors wrote this 2025 computer vision paper on cleaning product images for online stores. Watermarks, price tags, and promotional text clutter many listings. Diffusion inpainting can erase such elements, but it often invents unwanted objects instead. Commercial images also differ from the data those models learned on. The authors build a remover tuned for e-commerce using reinforcement learning.

Their system, RePainter, steers attention toward background context during the editing process. A composite reward balances global structure, local pixel accuracy, and semantic sense. That reward design reduces artifacts and blocks cheap reward hacking. The team also built EcomPaint-100K, a dataset of e-commerce inpainting cases, plus a benchmark. Across tests and human judgments, RePainter beat rival methods, especially in busy scenes. Sellers could reuse supplier photos without the clutter they arrived with. Cleaner automated editing could save sellers large amounts of manual retouching.
arxiv-2510-08021:
Alendouro Pinho, Amorim, and Viana Parente Lopes wrote this 2025 condensed matter theory paper solving exactly how driven crystals carry current while losing energy. Modelers add dissipation through a relaxation-time approximation, estimated perturbatively, and exact results covered steady states. The authors instead solve the dissipative master equation analytically for a general single-band tight-binding system. The driving field can vary in time in any way.

Two limits showcase the solution. Under a monochromatic field, the formulas show how dissipation shapes high harmonic generation. Under a constant field, they generalize the classic Esaki-Tsu current relation to any single-band lattice. A two-dimensional nearest-neighbor lattice illustrates how competing length scales enter. Transient even harmonics decay away, leaving stable odd harmonics with plateau regions, and dissipation enforces that symmetry. Comparing against perturbation theory exposes where it misleads. Such benchmarks anchor simulations of materials under strong laser fields.
arxiv-2510-08221:
Yu Zeng and co-authors classify a special family of finite groups in a 2025 arXiv paper on character theory. A character is a function that records how a group acts through matrices. Its codegree is a number built from the size of the group, the character kernel, and its degree. The team studies groups whose size is not a pure prime power. They ask which such groups have exactly four distinct codegrees.

The authors give a detailed description of all groups that meet this strict count. Their result pins down the group structure that forces the codegree set to stay at four values. Work like this extends a long program that reads group structure from character data. Small sets of character values often force strong limits on how a group can look. The classification adds one more complete case to that broader effort in finite group theory.
arxiv-2510-08421:
Kaustav Mitra and Frank van den Bosch stress-test a standard model of how galaxies inhabit dark matter haloes in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Conditional Luminosity Function describes how galaxy brightness is distributed within haloes of each mass. Most studies use one standard formula shape for it, rarely questioning that choice. That fixed shape acts as a hidden prior on every result drawn from the model.

Using their Bayesian tool Basilisk, the pair fit satellite galaxy motions and counts from the SDSS survey. They first validated the pipeline on realistic mock data with known answers. Then they tried more flexible variants of the standard formula, adding or removing degrees of freedom. Some long-ignored freedoms improved the fit drastically and shifted the inferred galaxy-halo connection. Others added nothing the data demanded, marking where the standard model suffices.
arxiv-2510-08521:
Yusong Hu and co-authors build FlowSearch in a 2025 arXiv paper, a multi-agent system for deep research tasks. Deep research demands breadth and depth at once: agents must roam wide knowledge spaces and chain multi-step reasoning. Static plans fail when early findings should reshape later steps. FlowSearch instead grows a dynamic structured knowledge flow as it works.

Agents plan and expand this knowledge flow to explore branches in parallel and split tasks hierarchically. Feedback from intermediate reasoning adjusts the flow in real time, redirecting effort where it pays. The system reached state-of-the-art results on general and scientific benchmarks alike. Named benchmarks include GAIA, HLE, GPQA, and TRQA, covering assistant tasks and hard science questions. The authors argue the design suits multi-disciplinary research and scientific discovery. Their code is publicly released.
arxiv-2510-08721:
Guillermo García-Segura and co-authors simulate planetary nebula formation across star masses, hunting for neutral spikes in a 2025 arXiv paper. Planetary nebulae are glowing shells shed by dying low- and intermediate-mass stars. The James Webb Space Telescope recently observed spike-like neutral structures in some of them. The team ran two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations for six stellar models from one to five solar masses.

Stellar evolution calculations set the inner boundary conditions, with updated counts of ionizing photons driving the nebula's glow. Simulations follow each nebula from formation through late evolution in full. Neutral spikes can appear either at formation or during decline, they find. At formation, the detection window shrinks with stellar mass, from three thousand years for one solar mass to zero for five. In decline, only the 1.5, 2.0, and 2.5 solar mass models show spikes for most of the remaining time.
arxiv-2510-08821:
Kobin and Zureick-Brown compute algebraic structures attached to a wild class of curves, in this 2025 arXiv paper in pure mathematics. Their objects are stacky curves, curves with extra symmetry data at special points, studied over fields where arithmetic wraps around a prime. The goal is a ring, a structured set of functions, that encodes the curve's overall shape. Computing it also unlocks rings of modular forms, symmetric functions central to number theory, reduced modulo that prime.

The pair extend earlier work by Voight and the second author to cover the wild cases, where the symmetry interacts badly with the prime. A surprise emerges in the smallest cases. In characteristics two and three, there are infinitely many levels at which a certain family of forms exists modulo the prime but cannot be lifted to ordinary numbers. The result maps a genuine gap between the modular world and its classical shadow.
arxiv-2510-09021:
Mahdavi and a large team test whether language models can grade olympiad-style proof problems fairly, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Top models have leapt from failing such problems to solving most of them, which raises a natural next question about judging. Grading a proof means spotting errors, weighing their severity, and awarding partial credit, not just checking the final answer. The authors built a corpus of ninety model-written solutions with detailed expert error annotations, plus official contest solution sets.

Their analysis found that models reliably flag wrong solutions, even subtly wrong ones, but their partial credit drifted out of calibration. To fix that, they built grader workflows in which agents first study the reference solution, derive a problem-specific rubric, and then grade in steps. Across both collections, the workflows agreed with human grades more closely and handled partial credit more consistently. All code, data, and logs are released.
arxiv-2510-09121:
Winter and colleagues generate fake pathology images, complete with perfect labels, to train cell-counting software, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Segmenting cells and nuclei in microscope slides is vital for diagnosis, yet annotated examples are scarce, especially for rare cell shapes. Their diffusion model builds an image and its exact segmentation mask together. It takes direction from several signals at once: maps describing cell shape and orientation, color characteristics, and text metadata about the assay and disease context, encoded by a language model.

An attention mechanism weaves those signals together, giving fine control over what grows in the image. Statistical checks showed the fake images sit close to real ones under matching conditions. Adding made-up examples of a neglected cell type, tall columnar cells, clearly improved a segmenter's accuracy on exactly that type. They present the method as a way to aim synthetic data at a model's known weaknesses.
arxiv-2510-09321:
T Cridge, L A Harland-Lang, and R S Thorne present updates to the MSHT parton distribution functions in a 2025 arXiv paper. These functions describe how momentum is shared inside the proton, and collider predictions depend on them. The update uses an approximate third-order theory, the level known as aN3LO, and folds in fresh calculations made since the earlier public set appeared.

The new calculations cover splitting functions, which govern how partons branch, and transition matrix elements, which link different quark counts. The authors find only small changes in the resulting functions. The shifts are at most about as large as the stated uncertainties, and usually well below them. Effects on predicted collision rates, called luminosities, are smaller still, which the team reads as a sign that the earlier set was already stable.
arxiv-2510-09421:
Victor Morand, Josiane Mothe, and Benjamin Piwowarski probe how language models represent named entities in a 2025 arXiv paper. Entities such as people, places, and organisations anchor factual knowledge in text. Earlier work mostly studied explicit relationships between entities, leaving open how the entities themselves are encoded inside the model.

The authors introduce entity mention reconstruction, a test that asks whether an entity's name can be regenerated from the model's internal states. Using task vectors, a tool that steers hidden states, they consistently produced multi-token mentions from many different internal representations. They also extend the logit lens, a method that reads predictions from inner layers, into an Entity Lens for whole mentions. The results suggest models build entity-specific mechanisms for representing and manipulating entities, including entities never seen in training.
arxiv-2510-09521:
Anthony Brady, Zihao Gong, Alexey Gorshkov, and Saikat Guha design a quantum imaging method in a 2025 arXiv paper. Incoherent imaging, used in fluorescence and absorption microscopy, suffers weak signals and a classic resolution limit known as Rayleigh's curse. The authors ask whether probes made of structured quantum light, paired with quantum detection, can beat those limits.

Their protocol uses twin-beam echoes to split the general imaging problem into separate passive channels. One channel carries the absorption signature and the other the fluorescence signature, so both can be imaged at once with quantum-enhanced sensitivity. The same setup can reconstruct displacement fields, such as the positions of tiny oscillators, and it works for ordinary and sub-diffraction imaging alike. The authors also examine Fock states, light with a fixed photon count, in a structured mode basis, and find comparable performance in principle.
arxiv-2510-09621:
Krishno Dey, Diogo Barradas, and Saqib Hakak survey the tech and the security risks of the Metaverse in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Metaverse mixes extended reality, AI, blockchain, and digital twins into shared virtual worlds that feel present. Its growth brings risks for identity, for data rules, and for user safety that older platforms never faced at this scale.

The authors run a systematic review of past work to list the core tech, the main weak points, and the published fixes. They argue the Metaverse gives attackers a far larger surface than older platforms. Its immersive, spread-out, and lasting nature creates new kinds of weak points. Most published defences are still theory, untested in real use. The review maps what exists, shows the gaps in the work so far, and points to next steps for a Metaverse that is safe and governed fairly.
arxiv-2510-09721:
Jiale Guo and ten co-authors survey how language models are reshaping software engineering in a 2025 arXiv paper. Development is shifting from rule-based tools toward autonomous agentic systems that plan, remember, and use tools to solve complex tasks. Progress is hard to track because benchmarks and solutions have mostly been studied apart from each other.

Reviewing over one hundred fifty recent papers, the authors build a taxonomy with two dimensions. Solutions fall into three paradigms, built on prompts, on fine-tuning, and on agents, while benchmarks cover tasks like code generation, translation, and repair. The survey connects more than fifty benchmarks to the strategies used on them and sketches a unified pipeline from task specification to deliverable. It traces the evolution from prompt engineering to agentic systems with planning, reasoning, memory, and tool use. Critical gaps are identified, with future directions including multi-agent collaboration.
arxiv-2510-10021:
The Euclid Collaboration prepares for its galaxy survey in this 2025 arXiv paper in cosmology. To extract cosmic facts from the Euclid data, the team must model many systematic effects, the biases that the telescope and the data pipeline add. Each effect brings free parameters that must be varied and then averaged out before the cosmic values can be stated.

That averaging step is the focus of this groundwork paper. With so many free parameters in play, the inference must stay both exact and cheap enough to run. Small mishandled biases could shift key results, such as the values tied to dark energy and the growth of cosmic structure. The paper sets up the modeling chain the survey will use.
arxiv-2510-10121:
Miah and co-authors detect Parkinson's disease severity from finger tapping in this 2025 arXiv paper on medical machine learning. Rating Parkinson's severity accurately guides treatment, and finger tapping is a standard clinical test of motor decline. Earlier gesture-based systems have not reached satisfactory accuracy.

The team proposes a multi-class detection system using an attention-enhanced CNN-BiLSTM. The convolutional part reads spatial patterns in each frame, the bidirectional recurrent part reads motion over time, and attention highlights the most telling moments. Multi-class output grades severity rather than giving a yes or no. A camera-based test could support remote assessment, sparing patients repeated clinic visits for routine checks.
arxiv-2510-11821:
Matěj Moravík computes explicit formulas for a special kernel attached to hyperbolic harmonic functions. These functions live on the unit ball, the sphere's higher-dimensional cousin, and are annihilated by the hyperbolic Laplacian, a curved-space version of the usual smoothing operator. The Szegő kernel reproduces such functions from their boundary values. Moravík's 2025 arXiv paper gives that kernel in closed series form.

The main expansion writes the kernel through a triple hypergeometric function introduced by Exton. Such functions generalize the familiar hypergeometric series to several variables. Moravík also shows the kernel can be written as a finite sum of ordinary hypergeometric functions, a much simpler form. For the special case of linearly dependent arguments, the kernel reduces to the first Appell hypergeometric function. The paper further expands the weighted Bergman kernels, close relatives in harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2510-11921:
Yongbin Du, Jia-Rui Sun, and Xiangdong Zhang test whether quantum black holes still lose information. The information paradox asks how a black hole can evaporate without destroying information. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies two well-motivated black hole solutions from loop quantum gravity that respect covariance, the demand that physics not depend on slicing choices.

For both solutions, radiation entropy first grows linearly at late times, as the paradox demands. The endings diverge sharply. In the first solution, the quantum parameter raises the barrier near the horizon and speeds evaporation as mass shrinks, leaving temperature untouched. The second evaporates ever more slowly at small mass and continues smoothly, suggesting a remnant or a bounce into a white hole. Applying the island prescription to the first solution, the authors find quantum extremal surfaces that cap the entropy growth, preserving unitarity. Their moral: such black holes show no universal late-time behavior.
arxiv-2510-12021:
Leili Barekatain and Ben Glocker ask which vision transformers explain themselves best to doctors. Transformers now lead diagnostic imaging, but doctors will not trust a model that cannot show its reasons. Their 2025 arXiv paper compares four designs, ViT, DeiT, DINO, and Swin, under two explanation methods: Gradient Attention Rollout and Grad-CAM, which paint heatmaps over the image regions driving a decision.

Two tasks anchor the tests, sorting peripheral blood cells and breast ultrasound scans, scored both by numbers and by eye. DINO paired with Grad-CAM gave the most faithful and tightly localized explanations on both datasets. Grad-CAM steadily produced class-discriminative, tightly placed heatmaps, while attention rollout scattered its focus. Even when the model erred, DINO with Grad-CAM highlighted shapes with real medical meaning that likely misled it, turning errors into checkable events. The authors argue such openness is a must before transformers enter diagnostic work.
arxiv-2510-12221:
Li and Ren study a stochastic wave equation driven by noise rougher than white noise, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. The equation describes waves on a two dimensional torus, the surface of a donut shape, with a cubic nonlinearity that makes waves interact. The forcing is a Matérn type Gaussian noise, built by smoothing white noise with a Fourier multiplier of some order.

The authors prove local well posedness, meaning solutions exist and depend sensibly on their starting data, for a range of roughness below a threshold of three eighths in their parameter. This extends an earlier white noise result and strengthens a quadratic case result that allowed roughness up to one half. Their argument develops new trilinear estimates, which bound interactions of three waves at once, inside Bourgain spaces. It also uses counting estimates tailored to the cubic terms.
arxiv-2510-12421:
Boone, Sánchez Cuartielles, and Lizy-Destrez catalogue the orbit options for a future spacecraft around Saturn's moon Enceladus, in a 2025 arXiv astrodynamics paper. Enceladus attracts mission planners because of the geyser region at its south pole, where plumes vent material from a subsurface ocean. Choosing a science orbit there is tricky because Saturn's gravity strongly perturbs close orbits.

The authors compile the orbit configurations proposed across the literature. They present numerical methods to compute each within the circular restricted three body problem, a standard model of a spacecraft moving under two gravitating bodies. They also explore higher period dynamical structures that this model reveals. For each orbit family they report figures of merit covering observational properties and geometry, such as how well the orbit views the polar region. Analyzing all candidates consistently, the work aims to serve as a baseline reference for future mission designs.
arxiv-2510-12621:
Lacunza and a large team release a parallel dataset of academic texts in twelve languages to improve machine translation of scholarly writing, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Academic translation has specialized vocabulary and long documents that general systems handle poorly. ACAData contains about one and a half million human generated paragraph pairs for training. It adds a curated benchmark of nearly six thousand translations covering twelve directions.

To validate the resource, the authors fine tuned two large language models and benchmarked them. Competitors included specialized translation systems, open weight general models, and large proprietary models. Fine tuning improved academic translation quality greatly on average for both model sizes. It also improved long context translation in a general domain, when translating out of English. The top fine tuned model surpassed the best proprietary and open weight systems on the academic benchmark. The dataset, benchmark, and fine tuned models are all public.
arxiv-2510-12721:
Gou and co-authors compress the embedding layer of large language models to under two bits per value, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Token embeddings consume a large share of a model's memory, which dominates on edge devices where memory is the bottleneck. Shrinking embeddings frees bandwidth and speeds inference, but aggressive quantization usually damages quality.

Their method, CARVQ, partitions the embedding matrix into groups and compresses each with residual vector quantization, storing the results in a lookup table. At inference time each token retrieves its quantized vectors. A lightweight corrective adaptor network, a small multilayer perceptron, repairs the error by mimicking the original embedding. The mix of linear and nonlinear maps reaches roughly one point six bits per parameter without specialized hardware. Tested across LLaMA, Qwen, and Phi models on generative, math, and reasoning tasks, CARVQ kept perplexity and accuracy reasonable. It reached lower average bitwidth than scalar quantization.
arxiv-2510-12921:
Richards pays tribute to Richard Askey in this 2025 arXiv article, mixing memories with new results on beta integrals. Askey was a leading figure in special functions. The Cauchy beta integral dates from 1974. It survives, in the same form, in projects like MathOverflow and in work on Macdonald symmetric functions.

Acting on a colleague's suggestion at one of the Askey conferences, Richards surfaced several obscure hypergeometric results. They had never appeared in one place together. Among the integrals he recovers are matrix cases over real symmetric and complex Hermitian matrices. He also derives formulas for non-symmetric cases and for the Gamma distribution. He proves integral identities for a one-factor term. He also answers, with a conjecture and partial work, a question about how often multinomial coefficients depart from favorites.
arxiv-2510-13021:
Marazzato and Venkataramani compute stresses inside jammed packings in this 2025 arXiv paper. Jammed systems such as granular materials and masonry are rigid assemblies of cells or grains whose contacts carry the load. Predicting their internal stress fields is essential for understanding failure, but standard discrete element simulations can be heavy and opaque.

The authors model rigid polygonal cells obeying a Tresca friction law, a rule capping shear stress at contacts. They first pose a constrained minimization of friction energy subject to cells never interpenetrating, then derive the dual maximization problem, whose solution directly gives normal stresses at the interfaces between cells. Finally they reconstruct a consistent full stress field with low-order Raviart-Thomas finite elements through local problems. Numerical results demonstrate the method's consistency and robustness on jammed configurations.
arxiv-2510-13121:
Son and colleagues argue that supernova cosmology carries a strong progenitor age bias in this 2025 arXiv paper. Type Ia supernovae are standardizable candles only if their corrected brightness does not depend on the age of the stellar population that produced them. Direct age data of host galaxies instead show a clear link. Standardized supernova magnitude tracks progenitor age.

Because progenitor age and host mass evolve very differently with distance, the usual mass-step correction cannot remove this bias. After correcting for age bias with redshift, the supernova data moved closer to the evolving dark energy model suggested by the DESI baryon oscillation project. A test using only supernovae from young hosts supported the shift. Combining supernovae with microwave background data, the authors find strong tension with the standard cosmological model. They point to time-varying dark energy in a non-accelerating universe.
arxiv-2510-13421:
Lassalle and co-authors build a fault identification pipeline for the SPIRAL2 accelerator in France. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses data from the machine's low-level radio frequency systems. SPIRAL2 is a superconducting linear accelerator that produces beams of heavy ions. Radio frequency anomalies can disrupt runs and cut the machine's availability. Expert reading of these events is slow, and some behaviours stay obscure.

The team works with fast, multivariate time series recorded after each incident. They adopt the Time2Feat pipeline, which selects informative features from these signals. Dashboards let users run several clustering algorithms and inspect the groupings visually. A case study separates true electronic quenches from false quench alarms in the records. For that task they propose a fast K-nearest neighbours classifier, judged reliable in tests. The approach moves anomaly reading from pure expert judgement toward data support.
arxiv-2510-13621:
Hao and a large team of co-authors measure how computing resources shape foundation model research output. Their 2025 arXiv paper reviews over six thousand foundation model papers from 2022 to 2024. They also survey more than two hundred first authors about their access to computing. The study asks whether more graphics processors simply buy more scientific impact.

More computing tracked with national funding levels and with citation counts, they find. It did not track strongly with research setting, domain, or method, though. Academic and industrial authors showed no simple resource-driven split in outcomes. The authors advise funders and institutions to build shared, affordable computing pools. Such pools would lower the entry barrier for under-resourced researchers. Wider access, they argue, sustains diverse ideas and steady innovation in the field.
arxiv-2510-13721:
Luo and co-authors present NExT-OMNI, an open omnimodal model that both understands and generates across media types. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets any-to-any models, which take in and produce text, images, video, and audio freely. Most unified models lean on autoregressive designs that unbalance understanding against generation. Hybrid fixes bolt the two halves together without truly integrating them.

NExT-OMNI instead builds on discrete flow matching, a generative scheme with metric-shaped probability paths. A kinetic optimal velocity guides samples along those paths efficiently. One shared representation then serves generation, understanding, and even cross-modal retrieval tasks. Training mixes large interleaved streams of text, image, video, and audio data. Benchmarks show competitive results on both generation and understanding suites. The model beats earlier unified systems at multi-turn multimodal chat and at retrieval, the authors report. Code, checkpoints, and training details are released openly.
arxiv-2510-13921:
Levy Chaves, Eduardo Valle, and Sandra Avila address model merging, a way to combine several specialized neural networks into one without retraining, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Merging methods blend model weights using scaling factors that set each model's contribution, but principled ways to choose those factors without data are scarce, so researchers often tune them on test data.

Their technique, Weight Weaving, pools model weights across the range of scaling values using a pooling rule the user picks, such as averaging or random selection. It plugs into existing merging methods and needs no evaluation data at all. Across three vision transformer variants, Weight Weaving improved merging methods consistently. The settings covered multi-task learning, continual learning, and domain generalization. Average accuracy gains reached nearly sixteen percentage points in the fully data-free setting.
arxiv-2510-14021:
Wen-Cong Gan and co-authors report a prediction from loop quantum cosmology. The early universe's shear, its uneven expansion in different directions, gets damped away by quantum effects, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They study the Bianchi I universe, the simplest model that expands at uneven rates along its axes. It sits inside a modified loop quantum cosmology, where the Big Bang is replaced by a bounce.

The team finds an isotropization mechanism, meaning the universe smooths itself into expansion in all directions. After the bounce, shear is suppressed dynamically and decays in the quantum post-bounce regime. This happens regardless of the equation of state, the relation between pressure and density, of matter. The universe heads toward a homogeneous, isotropic expanding phase without fine-tuned starting conditions. The authors stress this smoothing is absent in other bounce models. It is a distinctive prediction of their framework.
arxiv-2510-14521:
Akutagawa, Imada, and Shoda present a 2025 arXiv study of magnetic reconnection, where magnetic field lines in a plasma break and join again in a new pattern. Their problem is one of scale. Particle-level physics controls how fast reconnection runs. Yet particle simulations cost too much computing power to cover large events such as solar flares.

The team built a code named KAMMUY that runs two models side by side. A fluid model covers a wide region, and a particle model covers a smaller one, with each feeding results to the other. Tests with waves and a shock tube problem behaved as hoped. Fine, fast waves stayed inside the particle region, while broad structures crossed the boundary smoothly. When the authors changed the particle region's size, the reconnection rate did not change. That result suggests how far the Hall magnetic field reaches does not set the rate.
arxiv-2510-15221:
Xiao Sun releases a rare kind of dataset: facial emotion records gathered from real employees across more than two and a half years at work. This 2025 arXiv paper introduces WELD, with about 734 thousand expression records from a small team of thirty-eight people, collected between late 2021 and mid-2024. Each record carries scores for seven emotions plus job and personality details.

Because the window spans the COVID-19 pandemic, the data capture mood shifts around events like the Shanghai lockdown. Sun adds thirty-two derived measures, covering mood level, swings, and how emotions spread between coworkers. Checks reproduced known effects, such as a sharp weekend lift in positive mood, and baseline models classified emotions with about 91 percent accuracy. Sun reports that one model even predicted which staff would quit without error in testing, and the dataset is free under an open license.
arxiv-2510-15321:
Saeed Salehi gives new proofs of three classic results by Georg Cantor about sizes of infinity, in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. Cantor showed that the infinite binary sequences cannot be counted. He showed the same for the real numbers, and that any set is strictly smaller than its powerset, the set of all its subsets. His diagonal argument is famous, but Salehi pursues a different route.

The proofs here proceed by induction, building the needed object step by step so that each finite stage already escapes the corresponding entry of any proposed list. For binary sequences, the construction fixes one digit at a time, choosing it so the growing sequence can never match the list's sequence at that position. The same inductive idea carries through to real numbers and then to the powerset theorem. Salehi notes the powerset proof assumes the axiom of choice.
arxiv-2510-15521:
Fei Wu and Chen Wu ask whether exotic matter can appear inside neutron stars threaded by strong magnetic fields. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies antikaon condensation, a state where antikaons, antimatter cousins of kaons, pile into the star's dense matter once it passes a threshold density. Such exotic phases soften the star's equation of state, the rule linking pressure and density, which threatens the observed two-solar-mass stars.

Working with an extended FSUGold model and a sigma-cut scheme, the authors find strong magnetic fields push the condensation threshold to higher densities. The field also stiffens the equation of state compared with the field-free case. By tuning the sigma-cut parameter carefully, they can still support a maximum neutron star mass above two suns even with antikaons present. The study maps how magnetism and exotic matter interact inside the densest stable objects known.
arxiv-2510-15721:
Complexity theory links hard worst cases to hard average cases through reductions. Divesh Aggarwal and Dexter Kwan build such a reduction for quantum computing in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their problem is matrix-vector multiplication, basic yet central to quantum fine-grained complexity. Recent classical reductions lean on deep additive combinatorics and carry heavy overheads. The authors adapt hardness self-amplification, a technique that boosts a weak solver into a strong one.

Their quantum reduction is more efficient and conceptually simpler than previous constructions. It improves how the success probability enters the overhead of the reduction. The authors present it as groundwork for broader results in quantum fine-grained complexity.
arxiv-2511-00521:
Bao Nguyen, Hieu Trung Nguyen, Ruifeng She, Xiaojin Fu, and Viet Anh Nguyen tackle a meta-problem: for each new query, which reasoning method should a language model use? Common practice samples many candidate answers and aggregates them, assuming more candidates means more accuracy. The authors test that assumption with a rigorous analysis and derive accuracy bounds for standard aggregation under fixed generation settings.

On that foundation they build EPIC, a planning framework that learns a shared space linking queries, reasoning methods, and model abilities through contrastive learning. Their probability bounds enter as a regularizer, balancing accuracy against computing cost. Across varied math reasoning tasks, EPIC consistently picked the best method for each query, improving accuracy while cutting overhead. Smart selection, the work suggests, beats brute sampling.
arxiv-2511-00721:
Thanh Nha To and four co-authors design fair, secure links for systems that sense and communicate at once. Integrated sensing and communication shares spectrum between radar-like sensing and data service. Their design adds two tools: surfaces that transmit and reflect signals simultaneously, and rate-splitting access that divides messages into common and private parts. Each sensing target doubles as a potential eavesdropper, a realistic threat.

The team jointly optimizes base station beamforming and the surface coefficients to maximize the minimum secrecy rate across users, fairness built into the objective, while holding a floor under sensing beam quality. The non-convex problem yields to alternating optimization with a majorization-minimization method. Simulations verify fast convergence and significant gains in secure communication performance.
arxiv-2511-01021:
Sainik Karak and Tanmoy Paul study extension problems for p-compact operators between Banach spaces. The question is when an operator defined on a smaller space can be extended to a larger domain. It must keep its special compactness property. A second question asks the same for the operator's adjoint.

Much of the analysis assumes the spaces involved are projection friendly spaces of a standard type. The authors ask whether extensions, when they exist, can be chosen to almost preserve the norm. Often an operator can be extended to a larger domain if the codomain is enlarged as well, and under extra assumptions the range can be kept the same. They also derive necessary and sufficient conditions for a Banach space to be an L1-predual.
arxiv-2511-01221:
Kazuki Hiroe and Daisuke Yamakawa study wild character varieties, spaces that parametrize certain equations with irregular singularities on compact Riemann surfaces. The tame cousins, with only regular singularities, are far better understood, and bridging the two has been an open problem in the geometry of these moduli spaces.

The authors construct Poisson maps from wild to tame character varieties by unfolding each irregular singularity into regular ones. They then show these unfolding maps are Poisson birational equivalences, meaning the wild and tame spaces match up at the level of their Poisson geometry away from small excluded sets. The result answers yes to a conjecture posed by Klimes, Paul, and Ramis.
arxiv-2511-01421:
Arda Kosay and colleagues steer city traffic without charging tolls. Connected and automated vehicles make intersections programmable, and their framework uses that: roadside units adjust timestamp based scheduling, in effect delaying or advancing vehicles on particular paths. That nudges drivers' routing choices toward flows that are better for everyone.

A hierarchical design separates real time intersection control from network level coordination, and the model becomes a congestion game with path dependent node costs. The authors prove equilibrium flows exist and are essentially unique, removing ambiguity and making a tractable two level optimization for designing the incentives. On the standard Sioux Falls test network, the scheme cut the gap between selfish user equilibrium and the system optimum by up to about seventy one percent.
arxiv-2511-01721:
Thierry Goudon and Antoine Mellet analyze flocks in the extreme where attraction and repulsion between individuals become very strong. Their starting point is a mean-field kinetic model of a population, organisms or particles. The population is pushed around by mutual interactions and an external velocity field. They study the singular limit as the interaction forces grow.

For well-prepared initial data, the population piles up inside a moving domain. The domain's shape is fixed by minimizing the interaction energy, while its center of mass rides the external field. Inside the domain, the organisms' flow obeys a classical hydrodynamic model, the lake equation. That result needs only existence and uniqueness of energy minimizers. It holds for general interaction kernels. The internal-flow part uses a modulated energy method, under stricter assumptions.
arxiv-2511-01821:
Soham Chanda and Amanda Hirschi build a new algebraic structure for contact geometry, a branch of math that studies spaces with a special twisting structure at each point. Their starting point is contact homology, a tool that counts closed orbits of a flow on such a space to tell spaces apart. The paper adapts a method called global Kuranishi charts to this contact setting.

For any closed contact manifold with no degenerate orbits, the pair build what they call a flow category. Its building blocks are the Reeb orbits of the manifold and the spaces of pseudo-holomorphic buildings that link them. The construction lifts contact homology, so it keeps that older tool's information in a richer form. It is also natural: an exact symplectic cobordism between two manifolds yields a matching flow bimodule between their flow categories.
arxiv-2511-01921:
Roberta Fiandaca and Manil Dev Gomony shrink neural radio receivers so they can run on constrained hardware. Neural receivers beat classic designs but carry heavy compute cost. The authors attack the cost from two sides, quantization and compression, both keyed to the Fibonacci coding scheme.

They introduce uniform and non-uniform quantization schemes. One is Fibonacci code word quantization. Another is a refined, fine-grained version of incremental network quantization. It recovers accuracy lost in the process. Two new lossless squeezing algorithms then exploit the patterns in sequences of Fibonacci-quantized weights. Quantizing alone cut multiplier power by about 45 percent. It cut area by about 44 percent. Squeezing reduced the memory footprint by about 63 percent. The receiver still outperformed a standard one.
arxiv-2511-02021:
Daniel Klocke and a large international team report a landmark climate computation: the first global simulation of the full Earth system at kilometer scale. Their model resolves the planet at a grid spacing of 1.25 kilometers, coupling atmosphere, ocean, and land so that energy, water, and carbon flow through all three at a resolution where storms and ocean eddies appear explicitly.

The run harnessed two of the world's largest GPU installations. One had 8,192 graphics processors on the Alps system. The other had 20,480 on JUPITER. The team used the ICON code base, its components balanced across Grace CPUs and Hopper GPUs. A separation-of-concerns redesign halved the code's complexity while raising performance and portability. The machine sustained about 146 simulated days per real day. That time compression beats even earlier atmosphere-only simulations at similar resolution. It opens long, fully coupled Earth system studies.
arxiv-2511-02121:
Anastasia Matveeva studies when sequences defined by recurrences with polynomial coefficients consist only of whole numbers. These are tied to their generating functions, which satisfy differential equations. Whether they stay bounded decides much of their arithmetic nature. Classical work gave an integrality test for Motzkin-type sequences, but elsewhere ad hoc methods ruled.

Matveeva revisits that test with tools from differential algebra and builds a unified approach to boundedness and algebraicity across a wider holonomic class. The central product is an algorithm that decides whether all, none, or a one-parameter family of cases for certain second-order recurrences stay bounded. It succeeds on several well-known cases listed in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences.
arxiv-2511-02221:
Lei Tan and six co-authors trawl a major Chinese spectroscopic survey for a distinctive class of stars. Be stars are fast-spinning B-type stars whose spectra show hydrogen emission lines from material they have flung into a disk, and they matter for understanding how stars evolve and form disks. The team built a labelled dataset from the eleventh data release of LAMOST, a telescope that records spectra in bulk.

A classifier combining convolutional and memory networks reached 97.86 percent accuracy on held-out spectra. Applied broadly, then cross-checked with an automated classification tool and by hand, the pipeline confirmed over forty thousand B-type spectra. Matching against published emission-line catalogues produced a sample of 8,298 Be stars, more than half of them new discoveries, which the team further split into classical and Herbig types using colour information.
arxiv-2511-02521:
Romy Peled, Daniel Kroening, Michael Tautschnig, and Yakir Vizel put language models to work on one of hardware verification's most manual chores: finding the inductive invariant that proves a chip design correct. Their system, a neurosymbolic pipeline, has the model propose candidate lemmas and invariants through two prompting frameworks. A formal symbolic tool checks every proposal, so nothing unverified slips through.

With enough reprompting, the models produced provably correct inductive arguments for mid-size open-source register-transfer-level designs. At least one of the two prompting setups succeeded on eighty-four percent of the problem set. The authors frame the result as practical relief for formal verification engineers. The creative search for lemmas can be partly automated, while the guarantee of correctness still comes from the symbolic checker, not from the language model's confidence.
arxiv-2511-02721:
Translators often add small explanations so readers in another culture can follow a text. Doreen Osmelak and four colleagues built PETra, a multilingual corpus for that habit, called pragmatic explicitation, and describe it in a 2025 paper. It spans eight language pairs drawn from TED talks and European Parliament records.

The corpus tags additions like short entity descriptions, converted measurements, and translator remarks. The team found candidates where words had no direct match in the source, then refined them with active learning and human checks. Entity and system-level additions proved most common. Active learning lifted classifier accuracy by seven to eight points, reaching 0.88 accuracy in the best cases. The resource makes a slippery habit measurable.
arxiv-2511-03421:
Shihai Wang and Tao Chen present LQPR, a light tool that turns written performance demands into checkable numbers automatically. Engineers must quantify such demands for tuning and testing, yet hand quantification is slow and error prone because wording stays vague. LQPR reframes the job as classification under a new theoretical frame.

Rather than lean on large language models, the tool exploits the short, patterned phrasing that performance demands tend to use. A linguistically induced matcher reads those patterns directly. Trials against nine rivals test speed and accuracy on real requirement sets. Fast, cheap quantification could let teams check far more demands than manual review ever allows.
arxiv-2511-03521:
Mohamed Swailem and Alastair M Rucklidge add seasons to the classic predator-prey model and watch order give way to chaos. Carrying capacity now pulses with time, standing in for seasonal swings in food or nutrients. Steady coexistence disappears under that pulsing, though letting the predation rate pulse as well can restore a balance point.

That balance can still break through parametric resonance into slower or matched cycles, even when predation stays constant. Period-doubling steps and outright chaotic swings appear across the parameter map. Letting numbers vary across space, with diffusion added, yields spatial patterns on top of the timing chaos. Seasonal forcing, the work shows, is not a small wiggle on the classic model but a driver of rich behavior.
arxiv-2511-20421:
Cota, Matos, and Vieira classify a family of algebras by how fast their identities grow. Their 2025 paper works in PI theory, the study of polynomial identities. Every algebra obeys certain polynomial equations for all inputs. The codimension sequence counts how many such rules are independent at each degree. Its growth rate is a key fingerprint of the algebra. Graded algebras with a matching symmetry operation are the focus here.

The authors classify unitary algebras whose growth is quadratic. Their method links minimal varieties to character decompositions. Nonzero multiplicities in the proper cocharacters carry the key data. A complete classification up to sameness is achieved. Every variety of at most quadratic growth decomposes nicely. It is generated by a direct sum of minimal pieces. Each piece itself has at most quadratic growth. The funding came from Brazilian agencies FAPESP, CAPES, and CNPq. Such classifications organize a sprawling landscape of structures.
arxiv-2511-20621:
Karvonen, Reuter, Rinberg, Marks, Garriga-Alonso, and Warr check whether AI providers run models honestly. Their 2025 paper tackles inference verification for large language models. Re-running a model gives slightly different outputs each time. Numerical noise blurs honest variation and cheating. Customers need proof the advertised model actually ran.

Token-DiFR compares generated tokens against a trusted reference implementation. Syncing the sampling seed tightly constrains what outputs are valid. The output tokens themselves then serve as free audit evidence. Simulated bugs, sampling errors, and quantization all get caught. Four-bit quantization shows up within three hundred output tokens. Detection quality there reaches near-perfect scores above 0.999 AUC. A second scheme compresses activations into compact fingerprints. Random orthogonal projections make those fingerprints cheap to send. Activation-DiFR spots quantization from just two output tokens. Communication costs fall by a quarter to three quarters. An open-source vLLM integration ships alongside.
arxiv-2511-20821:
Samuele Dell'Erba and Andrew D. Bagdanov ask in 2025 whether text-to-image generators really need a trained prior, the costly network that translates a text prompt's embedding into a visual one before decoding. Such priors demand big training sets. Their alternative, Optimisation-based Visual Inversion, starts from random pseudo-tokens and reshapes a latent visual representation until it matches the prompt embedding, with no training.

Two added constraints keep the optimisation realistic. One uses Mahalanobis distance, which measures how unusual a point is relative to a distribution. Another uses nearest neighbours in image data. Tested on the Kandinsky 2.2 generator, the constrained methods beat a raw text-embedding baseline on visual fidelity. The nearest-neighbour version matched or beat the data-efficient trained prior on scores. The study also exposes a flaw in the T2I-CompBench++ benchmark, where the raw text embedding scores surprisingly high despite worse images.
arxiv-2511-20921:
Mitzi Urquiza-González and a large collaboration report in 2025 precision laser measurements on fermium-255, one of the heaviest nuclides reactors can breed. The isotope lives just 20 hours, and fermium, element 100, is the heaviest element available in weighable amounts. At the RISIKO separator in Mainz, the team probed hyperfine structure in two ground-state transitions, at 398.4 and 398.2 nanometres, using a high-resolution ion source. Atomic theory calculations supplied the hyperfine fields needed to read off nuclear moments.

The magnetic dipole moment came out at minus 0.75 nuclear magnetons, with an uncertainty of 0.05 in the final digit. The electric quadrupole moment measured plus 5.84 electron-barns, plus or minus 0.13 at the same precision. The magnetic value points to the neutron occupying the 7/2 Nilsson orbital, and the hefty quadrupole moment confirms a stable, strongly prolate shape. The results revise earlier data and benchmark nuclear theory for the heavy actinides.
arxiv-2511-21121:
Document search systems usually start by running optical character recognition over every page, then fight brittle rules for chunking, tables, and layout. Anup Roy and three colleagues present VisionRAG in 2025, a retrieval system that skips text extraction and indexes pages as images. A three-pass pyramid builds compact semantic vectors from page-wide summaries, fact-level cues, visual hotspots, and section headers. At query time, ranked fusion merges the pyramid levels, and the winning page images go straight to a multimodal model for the final answer.
