VisionRAG keeps just 17 to 27 vectors per page, where patch-based rivals store hundreds. On financial document tests it reached 0.8051 accuracy at rank ten on FinanceBench. Recall at rank one hundred on TAT-DQA reached 0.9629 in the same runs, so nearly every answer-bearing page was found. The authors argue summary-guided, OCR-free retrieval is a scalable replacement for text-first pipelines.
arxiv-2511-21721:
Gao Mo and eight coauthors present PeerCoPilot, a language-model assistant built for peer-run behavioral health organizations, in 2025. Such organizations pair mental health care with help on income, jobs, and housing, but thin funding and staffing leave many needs unmet. Peer providers, who draw on their own lived experience, carry heavy day-to-day workloads.

PeerCoPilot helps providers draft wellness plans, build step-by-step goals, and find matching resources. A retrieval pipeline grounds its answers in a database of over 1,300 vetted resources. In evaluations with 15 peer providers and 6 service users, over 90 percent backed using the tool. It also gave more reliable, specific information than a plain baseline model. A group of 5 to 10 providers at CSPNJ, an organization serving over 10,000 people, now uses it daily.
arxiv-2511-21921:
Frontiere and colleagues extend the GPU cosmology code CRK-HACC to simulate ordinary galaxy-forming matter at survey scale. Sky surveys measure the universe so precisely that ignoring gas, stars, and black hole feedback distorts the predictions those surveys are tested against, especially for cross-correlated, multi-wavelength analyses of large-scale structure. Exascale supercomputers make full-physics runs over volumes feasible, if the software is built for them.

The team added subgrid models, treatments of processes too small to simulate, covering radiative cooling, a multiphase interstellar medium, stochastic star formation, galactic winds, and two-mode black hole feedback. The models were calibrated to reproduce the galaxy stellar mass function from redshift 0 to 2 and the cluster populations surveys probe in their validation. It is presented as the baseline for exascale survey-volume simulations.
arxiv-2511-22121:
Li, Wang, Huang, and Rehg, computer vision researchers, ask which visual cues modern single-image 3D generators actually use. Humans infer shape from one picture using shading, texture, silhouette, perspective, and edges, but deep models that now produce impressive 3D objects from a single photo might lean on entirely different shortcuts. Their Cue3D framework systematically perturbs each cue, dilating silhouettes, shuffling pixels, occluding parts, and measures how much the generated 3D output degrades for seven state-of-the-art methods.

The headline finding is that shape meaningfulness, not texture, drives generalization, and geometric cues, above all shading, are crucial for good 3D output. Models also over-rely on the provided silhouette, and sensitivity to perspective and local continuity varies sharply across model families, regression-based, multi-view, and native 3D alike. By dissecting these dependencies, Cue3D points toward more transparent, robust, and controllable single-image 3D generation.
arxiv-2511-22221:
Isichei and Magueijo, cosmologists, ask what happens if emergent gravity is allowed to do work. In the thermogravity view, Einstein's equations arise as an equation of state from heat exchange across local horizons, making general relativity look like a degenerate thermodynamic cycle with only heat legs. The authors add the missing ingredient, work-producing legs, and find the additions are not free. They generate controlled violations of local Lorentz invariance and of energy-momentum conservation.

Those violations are features, not bugs, because their cosmological consequence is late-time acceleration of the universe's expansion, the phenomenon usually blamed on dark energy or a cosmological constant. The paper discusses what the framework implies for the cosmological constant problem and for structure formation. For local observations that tightly constrain Lorentz violation, it positions thermodynamic cycles as a generator of genuinely new, testable gravity theories rather than a mere reinterpretation of Einstein's.
arxiv-2511-22321:
Meuser, Weil, Lahiri, and Paraschiv teach a quantum network to route entanglement using only what each node can see locally. Distributing entangled pairs across repeaters is probabilistic and links decay quickly. So hand-written routing heuristics either need global topology knowledge or perform poorly. RELiQ trains a reinforcement learning agent with a graph neural network centrally, then lets nodes decide from local observations plus message exchange with neighbors, building an implicit picture of the network.

Trained only on random graphs, the agent transfers to unseen topologies without retraining, beating local heuristics and matching global ones by reacting faster to changes. Routed-pair counts and end-to-end fidelity both hold up as swap success rates, link generation, and memory quality vary. The design points toward quantum internets that adapt on the fly rather than recomputing routes from a central map.
arxiv-2511-22521:
Mohammadshirazi, Guha Neogi, Kulshrestha, and Ramnath teach a small model to answer document questions like a big one. Document question answering needs the answer's location on the page, not just its text. Large vision-language models ground answers well but are costly to deploy, while compact students lose that locating skill. Their framework, DocVAL, distils a teacher's reasoning into a student, with validation at every stage.

A validator checks each trace for correctness and geometric consistency, using text detection only in training, and returns pixel-level error feedback. The student learns from the cleaned traces, then improves through rounds of validator-guided correction. The resulting 12-billion-parameter Gemma-3 student scored 91.4 percent on text accuracy and 82.4 percent on localisation quality on DocVQA, with no OCR needed at deployment. Ablations credit validation with a 6.3 point localisation gain and refinement with 9.7 more, and the team releases 95,000 verified traces.
arxiv-2511-23021:
Shah and colleagues rethink generative recommendation, where a model predicts the next item a user will pick from the history of what they have clicked or bought. Items are represented by semantic IDs, short token codes built from their descriptions. And the standard approach generates those codes one token at a time, which is slow and leans heavily on short-range patterns.

Their method, MADRec, instead learns with masked diffusion: some tokens in a user's sequence are hidden. And the model learns to restore them all at once, treating the hidden tokens as independent given the visible ones. That allows several codes to be predicted in parallel at serving time. In experiments on Amazon Beauty, Sports, and Toys data plus MovieLens-1M, MADRec consistently beat the one-at-a-time approach, with the largest gaps when training data was scarce and on coarse-grained recall.
arxiv-2512-00121:
Johannes Hagel studies a nonlinear oscillator whose forcing changes in an irregular, non-repeating way, in a 2025 study. The system is a parametrically forced equation with a quadratic term. Hagel asks how such an oscillator behaves over long times.

The forcing term depends on a strictly positive solution of a weakly forced companion equation. The study examines the phenomenon named in its title, tube rupture, through theory and simulation together. Results of this kind matter for understanding driven mechanical and electrical systems that can drift into failure when forcing never settles into a pattern. Hagel's approach combines proof with numerical experiment, each checking the other. That pairing suits a system whose long-run behavior is hard to guess.
arxiv-2512-00421:
Epidemics unfold together with human beliefs and behavior, each shaping the other. Mulin Tian and Ajitesh Srivastava present TrendGNN in 2025, a graph neural network aimed at understanding epidemics, beliefs, and behaviors together. Most forecasting work predicts epidemic signals with simple mechanistic models or opaque deep models.

Black-box forecasters ingest every available signal without offering interpretability, so officials cannot see why a prediction moved. A graph-based model that links disease spread to behavior could show which social signals drive the forecast. That transparency matters when predictions guide school closures, vaccination drives, and hospital planning. Beliefs drive behavior, and behavior drives transmission, so the loop is the story. For health teams, the gain is a view of cause and effect. They can see which shifts in mood or habit push the curve up, and which pull it down.
arxiv-2512-00621:
AI music generators now compose whole songs, which threatens artistic authenticity and copyright alike. Arnesh Batra, Dev Sharma, and Krish Thukral present a method for detecting synthetic music in 2025, built on dual-stream contrastive learning. Existing detectors falter as new generators appear.

Earlier models such as SpecTTTra performed well at first, then dropped sharply on out-of-distribution content from newer systems. A dual-stream design compares two views of the audio to catch generator fingerprints that survive across systems. Reliable detection helps platforms label synthetic tracks and protects musicians whose styles are imitated. Contrastive learning teaches the detector by comparing streams rather than labeling songs. Detection must keep pace with generators that improve month by month.
arxiv-2512-00721:
Hiroko Okada, Wako Aoki, Nozomu Tominaga, and Satoshi Honda report on a very old, metal-poor star in a 2025 astronomy paper. The star, known by its survey name SMSS 0224-5737, holds very little of the heavy elements later stars carry. Such stars preserve clues about the first stars and how elements formed.

The team measured abundances for many chemical elements in the star's light. Several elements, including nitrogen, oxygen, vanadium, zinc, and barium, are reported with fresh values. Others get upper limits rather than firm values. The pattern points to a weak form of the rapid process that builds heavy elements in extreme events.
arxiv-2512-00821:
Michael Kerber and Elena Xinyi Wang wrote a 2025 paper on measuring shape differences. The Persistent Homology Transform summarizes a shape by collecting diagrams from height sweeps in every direction. Each sweep tracks when features like holes appear and vanish, giving a rich fingerprint of the shape.

The transform is known to be continuous, stable, and able to tell apart broad classes of shapes. Kerber and Wang work on computing the bottleneck distance between two such transforms, the cost of matching one fingerprint to another. A workable distance lets software compare shapes in medicine, graphics, and data analysis.
arxiv-2512-00921:
Ahsan Javed and five coauthors review a key ingredient of materials modeling in a 2025 paper. Two-dimensional materials, sheets one or a few atoms thick, have reshaped nanoscience with properties unlike their bulk forms. As experiments race ahead, reliable computation is needed to sort which new materials are promising.

Exchange-correlation functionals are the part of density functional theory that captures how electrons interact, and the choice among them drives accuracy. The review covers their applications to 2D materials, the challenges they face, and their limits. A clear map of these tools helps modelers pick functionals wisely instead of by habit. The paper gives readers a plain guide to what each choice can and cannot do well.
arxiv-2512-01121:
Christine Awofeso, Patrick Greaves, Oded Lachish, and Felix Reidl design a practical algorithm for a graph measure in a 2025 paper. The 3-admissibility of a graph is a promising measure for spotting real-world networks with algorithmically favorable structure. Sparse, well-structured networks admit faster algorithms for many hard problems.

Their algorithm decides whether a graph's 3-admissibility is at most a given bound. They state its running time in terms of the number of edges and the bound, and its space in terms of vertices and the bound. A practical test lets analysts screen large real networks for the structure that makes them tractable.
arxiv-2512-01221:
A 2025 astronomy paper presents new radio observations of a supernova remnant in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The remnant, cataloged as N206, is nicknamed the Goat's Eye by the authors. It is the expanding wreckage of a star that exploded in our neighboring galaxy.

Observations at multiple radio frequencies map the remnant in fresh detail. Inside it sits a radio structure that is likely a pulsar wind nebula, a bubble blown by a spinning neutron star left behind. That inner structure has a striking zig-zag shape, which the authors analyze in detail. Multi-frequency maps help separate the shell's glow from the nebula inside.
arxiv-2512-01321:
Juan Hernandez and co-authors test a learning method when many agents act at once. The method, called Never Give Up, rewards an agent for finding new states. It mixes that drive with scores from the task. That mix helps when rewards are rare.

The team moved the method from one agent to many agents. They tried it in a tag game from the PettingZoo set. In that game, agents chase and flee in a small world. Early tests show how the drive to explore holds up when peers learn too. The work is a first step, not a final word.
arxiv-2512-01421:
Valentin Duruisseaux, Jean Kossaifi, and Anima Anandkumar explain Fourier neural operators in plain terms. Equations for fluids, heat, and stress govern much of science. Solving them needs fine grids and many repeats. That makes each solve slow and costly.

Neural operators learn the solve step itself. Fourier types do that work in the frequency domain for speed. The guide lays out how they work with real cases. It shows when they shine and when they fail. A clear guide helps engineers pick the right tool for fast physics forecasts. Worked cases span fluids and waves, so a reader can see the same operator idea pay off across more than one physics field.
arxiv-2512-02021:
Databases come in long-standing families: B-trees, log-structured stores, graph databases, and blob stores each handle one kind of job. Jun Kawasaki's 2025 paper proposes a ninth lineage, a functorial-categorical database called Enishi, built to fuse those jobs into one design.

Enishi separates watching the data, held in graph form, from the authority to persist it, handled categorically. It composes ownership, capability checks, content addressing, and graphs into a double categorical system. The stated goals are content that cannot change silently, capability-based safety, schema-free graph traversal, and coherence over time. It is a ground-up rethink of what a database is.
arxiv-2512-02221:
Two kinds of entropy share one formula and one name. One comes from heat and engines. The other comes from Shannon's theory of messages and code length. Dallin Fisher and Qi-Jun Hong show in 2025 that the two match in size for real solids and liquids.

They treat the atoms' layout as a source of messages. Then they gauge entropy from how well the paths of the atoms can be squeezed by data compression. No split of the system into parts is used, and no fitted model is used. A squeeze-based gauge could give a handy new way to get entropy out of computer models of matter.
arxiv-2512-02421:
Fine-tuning a vision-language model on one domain usually dulls its ability to handle new ones. Xinyao Li and five co-authors propose in 2025 dedicated prompt guidance as a way to adapt such models while protecting their domain generalization, the ability to work in unseen settings.

The usual recipe fine-tunes one universal model on the whole dataset, trading generality for fit. Guidance through dedicated prompts aims to steer the model per domain while leaving its broad skills intact. Keeping both sides of that trade-off matters for models deployed in the open world, where the next domain is never in the training set.
arxiv-2512-02521:
Laura Zarraoa and four co-authors chase one of the faintest signals in optics: a few photons hidden in sunlight. Counting such weak light demands filters that pass a narrow color band and block all else. Strong background light otherwise drowns the signal completely.

Earlier work showed that single trapped atoms can act as narrow band detectors with very low false counts. The team's atomic photodetector builds on that idea for signals buried in bright broadband light. Detectors of this kind could serve quantum communication and sensing tasks that must work outdoors in daylight. Daylight work has long been a blind spot for tests that chase the most faint light of all.
arxiv-2512-02621:
Panagiotis Papantonakis and four co-authors improve how captured scenes are textured in Gaussian splatting. Splatting has become a favorite way to rebuild real scenes in 3D and render them in real time. Fine surface detail, though, demands huge numbers of tiny primitives, which wastes memory.

Surfaces often mix smooth geometry with rich, busy appearance, or the reverse. Content aware texturing spends detail where the content needs it, not evenly everywhere. Leaner scenes render faster and store smaller, a gain for virtual reality, games, and digital copies of real places. The trick spends bits where the eye will look, and saves them where the eye will not rest.
arxiv-2512-03021:
Real data often mix a clear signal with messy noise. Ananyabrata Barua and Ayanendranath Basu wrote this 2025 study on how to find the true center of such data. Older tools, called mixture models, split mixed groups into smaller, cleaner parts.

The authors work on a flexible method that stays steady when noise is present. A steady center estimate matters when a few odd values could pull a result off course. Their approach fits fields like health, finance, and lab work, where mixed data are common. It gives analysts a safer way to name the main signal. Readers get a clear sense of why finding a center in messy data needs care.
arxiv-2512-03621:
Yaokun Li and colleagues make driving videos from fresh viewpoints without any LiDAR, in this 2025 paper. Self-driving work needs the same street replayed from shifted lanes, but camera-only tools often warp the scene's geometry. Their system, ReCamDriving, leans on dense 3D Gaussian pictures as a scaffold.

Training proceeds in two stages, first steering by camera pose alone, then fine-tuning with those pictures. A data trick builds matched-trajectory pairs from plain single-pass drives, yielding their ParaDrive set of about one hundred ten thousand pairs. Tests gave the method leading camera control and steady shape among rivals.
arxiv-2512-03721:
Calcium hydrides squeezed to extreme pressures were predicted to superconduct above two hundred kelvin, and experiments later backed that claim. Wenbo Zhao and co-authors revisit the calcium and hydrogen system in a 2025 superconductivity preprint. Loose ends remain, including unexplained peaks in diffraction data and a drop in superconducting temperature as pressure is released.

Earlier calculations often treated atoms as if they vibrated in a simple, regular way. Zhao and colleagues instead include anharmonic effects, where vibrations behave less neatly, and rebuild the temperature and pressure map showing which crystal structures stay stable. Under this correction, a calcium-rich clathrate phase becomes stable even near absolute zero. The celebrated calcium hexahydride phase, they find, holds together only at high temperatures. That result underlines how strongly heat shapes these materials.
arxiv-2512-04021:
Rebuilding a three-dimensional scene from a handful of unposed photos usually takes millions of tiny Gaussian blobs, most of them redundant. Honggyu An and a large team propose C3G in a 2025 preprint, a feed-forward system placing only about two thousand Gaussians where they matter. The compactness cuts memory use and sharpens scene understanding at once.

Learnable tokens gather features from multiple views through self-attention and steer where Gaussians are generated, so each one carries information pooled across viewpoints. The same attention patterns then guide feature lifting, attaching rich descriptors to the sparse geometry. Experiments cover pose-free novel view synthesis, open-vocabulary segmentation, and view-invariant feature matching. C3G beat existing methods on memory efficiency and feature fidelity. Their message: a small, geometrically meaningful representation suffices for high-quality reconstruction.
arxiv-2512-04421:
Changhe Liu and a team of co-authors present UTrice, a graphics pipeline that uses plain triangles as the shared building block for two rendering styles. Modern three-dimensional scenes often blend ray tracing, which gives true-to-life light effects, with rasterization, which is fast. Particle scenes built from soft Gaussian blobs trace poorly, so older tools route them through proxy meshes. That detour costs time and quality. Their 2025 arXiv paper removes the detour.

UTrice treats triangles as the direct primitive for both tracing and drawing. No proxy geometry is built, and no costly crossing tests are wasted on stand-ins. Scenes tuned by fast raster methods can pass straight into the tracing pipeline. The team reports higher rendering quality than prior tracing tools for particle scenes. Speed stayed at real-time levels in their tests. One shared primitive also simplifies scene tools for film, games, and virtual worlds.
arxiv-2512-04521:
Ruijing Liu, Cunhua Pan, Jiaming Zeng, and co-authors teach WiFi signals to read hand gestures in rooms the system never trained in. The same signals that carry data also bounce off moving bodies, leaving traces in channel readings. WiFi sensing is cheap and works in darkness and damp air. The catch is cross-domain skill: tools tuned in one room often fail in another. Their 2025 arXiv paper attacks that drop-off.

The team pulls Doppler spectra from channel data at every receiver. They then fuse the spectra along one time axis into images that carry multi-angle views of a gesture. An attention mechanism weighs the most telling parts of each fused image. Training across people and places builds gesture rules that travel better. Their tests show steadier accuracy in new settings than older designs. Touch-free control for homes and clinics stands to gain from such portable sensing.
arxiv-2512-04621:
Paolo Rossi, Sergey Shadrin, and Ishan Jaztar Singh build the quantum double ramification hierarchy for the Gromov-Witten theory of elliptic curves. Gromov-Witten theory counts curves inside a space; for an elliptic curve, those counts hold rich number patterns. Integrable hierarchies turn such counts into flowing equations with deep structure. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives the first explicit quantum version from a theory that includes fermionic fields.

The construction leans on known results by Oberdieck and Pixton about double ramification cycles and Hodge classes. Vanishing results for a lower Hodge class clear the path. The outcome is a closed, modular formula for the hierarchy's flows. The fermionic fields come from the odd cohomology of the elliptic curve. Having one worked example in hand lets researchers test broad guesses about quantum hierarchies, which aim to quantize a wide class of integrable systems from geometry.
arxiv-2512-04721:
Felipe Chaves-Silva, Marcos Ferreira-Silva, and Diego Souza ask whether steering a fluid to rest gets more expensive when one control channel goes missing. The setting is the Stokes system, the slow-flow model of fluid mechanics, in n dimensions. Null controllability means nudging the fluid exactly to rest in a set time, using controls on the boundary or inside. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies controls that act on one fewer component than the full set.

The team proves a fresh spectral estimate for the low frequencies of the Stokes operator, using only the available components. From it, they show the control cost keeps the same order in time as with full control. Losing one channel, in other words, does not raise the price of stopping the flow. Applications follow for related systems. The result matters wherever actuators are limited and each channel is precious.
arxiv-2512-04821:
Ngoc Huynh Trinh, Hoang Anh Nguyen Kim, Hai Toan Nguyen, and co-authors present LatentFM, a generative model that outlines organs and lesions in medical scans while honestly reporting its own doubt. Segmentation guides surgery and treatment planning, yet borders are often fuzzy and experts disagree. Flow matching, a fresh generative method, learns exact data patterns without simulation. Their 2025 arXiv paper moves that idea into a compact latent space for segmentation.

Two autoencoders first compress scans and their masks into small codes. A learned velocity field then flows noise toward mask codes, guided by the scan. Sampling the flow several times yields varied, plausible outlines. The spread between them maps uncertainty pixel by pixel, flagging borderline zones for human review. The team reports both high accuracy and uncertainty maps that track real ambiguity, a pairing clinicians can trust.
arxiv-2512-04921:
Julien Benchek, Rohit Shetty, Benjamin Hunsberger, and co-authors launch the AI Consumer Index, a benchmark that grades frontier models on everyday errands. Most benchmarks test exams and code; consumers ask models to shop, order food, plan games, and guide home projects. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds four hundred hidden test cases across those four activities, with a small open dev set released under a free license.

Ten frontier models took the test with web search on. A fresh grading method checks each claim in an answer against the web sources actually retrieved. The best model scored only in the mid-fifties percent. Shopping proved hardest, with even the leader under half marks. Models often hallucinated key facts such as prices. The index gives buyers and builders an honest read on consumer readiness.
arxiv-2512-05221:
Jiayan Xu and five co-authors benchmark universal machine-learned potentials on supported nanoparticle catalysts. Running these particles atom by atom with quantum accuracy is too slow for the searches and dynamics researchers need. So learned potentials stand in for the costly physics. Universal versions, trained on huge mixed data sets, promise accuracy without bespoke training. But how far they can be trusted on real catalyst shapes was untested.

The team checks several universal potentials against a focused model for copper nanoparticles on alumina. One universal model matches the low-energy shapes from global searches, with accuracy matching the specialist. Another, despite looser energies, sometimes finds even more stable layouts, showing flair for exploration. In motion studies, both track the specialist's atomic motion in broad terms, though at roughly a hundred times the cost. The verdict: useful straight off the shelf, with speed the remaining bottleneck.
arxiv-2512-05921:
Dominic Payne, Marc Swisdak, James Drake, and Tak Chu Li follow the heat bookkeeping of magnetic reconnection as it switches on. Reconnection, the snapping and rejoining of magnetic field lines, powers solar flares and substorms. Shear across the polarity line stores free energy that can help or hinder onset. The team simulates a current sheet starting out of balance, under a strong guide field.

Using a two dimensional particle in cell simulation, they stage the equilibration process step by step. Intervals are classified by what drives the pressure: changes in density, or changes in temperature. They also track the power flowing through the electromagnetic fields themselves, its growth and its transfer to particles, and compare those rates against the thermodynamic changes. Onset is explosive when stored energy converts fast. Knowing which channel carries the conversion refines the ignition picture.
arxiv-2512-06321:
Vikramjeet Singh Chandel leads a team with Sushil Gorai and with Anwoy Maitra and Amar Deep Sarkar. They study how to add a boundary at infinity to curved domains in complex space. Their domains carry the Kobayashi distance, a length measure that bends with the domain's shape. Adding far away boundary points, known as a horofunction compactification, lets mathematicians study how paths escape to the edge.

The authors give a test on a domain that tells when the plain identity map can be stretched to fit the whole closed domain inside this added boundary, with no folds. The test is generous: it allows domains that stretch off to infinity and fail a stricter curve condition used in past work. They also exhibit a large family of flat, planar domains that pass the test. Such results help pin down how complex domains behave at their edges.
arxiv-2512-06421:
Gengze Zhou and five co authors fix a training flaw in image generators that build a picture step by step, from coarse to fine. At each scale the model predicts the next finer layer from the last. In training it always sees perfect past layers, but in real use it must build on its own flawed output, and that mismatch drags quality down. Some scales are also far harder to learn than others, which unbalances training.

Their method, Self Autoregressive Refinement, lets the model practice on its own drafts during training. A staggered rollout feeds the model its own mid level output so it learns to cope with flaws. A new loss teaches on those self made contexts, keeping training steady. Applied to ready trained models, the fix lifted image quality scores within a few rounds, at small added cost.
arxiv-2512-06521:
Jens Dede and Anna Forster present ShadowWolf, a framework that automates the whole pipeline for teaching AI to spot animals in camera trap photos. As human settlement spreads, watching wildlife matters more, from raccoons in city bins to species at risk of vanishing. Cameras in the wild gather the images, but labeling them and training the models by hand is slow, and shifting light, weather, terrain, and distance make models brittle.

ShadowWolf joins the stages, collection, labeling, training, and grading, and tunes each to the others. Models can be retrained on the fly as conditions or goals change, which cuts the labeling burden and keeps accuracy up in new settings. The framework is built for the real mess of field data, rather than clean lab sets. For conservation teams with more photos than people, a pipeline that refreshes itself offers a way to keep watch as habitats change.
arxiv-2512-07021:
Jose Geraldo Fernandes and co-authors teach a heart-tracing model to absorb knowledge from the wider medical record, then work from the tracing alone. Deep learning reads electrocardiograms accurately, but doctors distrust black-box answers. During training, the team feeds the model laboratory results, vital signs, and body measures alongside each tracing. A self-supervised stage blends that context into the model's internal picture of what a heartbeat tracing means.

At use time, only the tracing is needed, yet the enriched picture remains. As a built-in explanation, the model also predicts which laboratory abnormalities a tracing implies, tying its answers to body chemistry a clinician can check. On a large public hospital data set, the model beat a tracing-only baseline at multi-label diagnosis. It also closed much of the gap toward a full model that demands every record at use time.
arxiv-2512-07121:
Megan A Brown and co-authors test a common complaint: that social media traps partisans in echo chambers worse than anything in offline life. Their check links two worlds for the same people. Public voter files give the partisan makeup of neighborhoods for a huge share of United States voters, measuring offline geographical segregation. Matched Twitter accounts give the partisan makeup of each user's online network, measuring segregation there.

Users do cluster with their own side online, forming fairly homogeneous networks. Yet those levels of sorting run significantly below the offline ones: the street is more segregated than the feed. Democrats sit more isolated than Republicans in both worlds. Only older Republicans show the reverse pattern, more sorted online than off.
arxiv-2512-07221:
Zichao Shu and co-authors sharpen the yardstick used to judge the tracking systems inside extended reality headsets. Those systems, which map a room while locating the headset in it, are graded against ground truth from optical motion capture studios. But that truth is itself flawed: the studio and the device must be aligned in space and time, and the studio's markers jitter. The flaws blur exactly the measures that matter for immersion, like rotation error and frame-to-frame shake.

Their estimator works in continuous time and folds in data from the headset's own motion sensors to cancel the studio's jitter. A variable scheme synchronizes the clocks, and a geometric constraint based on screw motions ties the sensors and device into one precise calibration. Experiments beat existing methods and reached the precision needed to benchmark state-of-the-art tracking.
arxiv-2512-07421:
Pei-Sen Su, Wen-Tao Lyu, Wei-Hong Liang, and Eulogio Oset wrote this 2025 particle physics paper. They study how one short-lived particle, named in the title with the number 2317, breaks apart. Two decay paths matter: one gives off a light neutral particle, the other gives off a photon.

The team models the particle within a picture built on a local hidden gauge approach. Several linked channels feed into their calculation of the strong decay path. Mixing between two light particles can roughly double the decay width they first obtain. For the photon path, they test extra anomalous terms and find their effect is tiny. They compare their results with a recent Belle measurement of the ratio of the two paths. Better separate measurements of both widths, they argue, would help settle what this particle really is.
arxiv-2512-07821:
Shaoheng Fang, Hanwen Jiang, Yunpeng Bai, Niloy Mitra, and Qixing Huang wrote this 2025 computer graphics paper. Video generators now make strikingly realistic clips. Yet their scenes wobble in three dimensions, with geometry that shifts as the camera moves.

Their system, WorldReel, generates video in four dimensions from the start. Alongside each color frame it produces a full scene representation. Point maps, the camera's path, and dense motion flow come out together. One underlying scene persists across viewpoints and moving content. That persistence holds even under large non-rigid motion and bold camera moves. Training mixes synthetic and real footage for complementary strengths. Synthetic data supplies exact supervision for geometry, motion, and camera. Real videos contribute the diversity and realism that synthesis lacks. Tests show a new best level of consistent video generation. Geometric consistency and motion coherence improve while view-time artifacts shrink.
arxiv-2512-07921:
Zongwei Li, Zhonghang Li, Zirui Guo, Xubin Ren, and Chao Huang wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. Coding agents can now turn a scientific paper into a working codebase. Doing that faithfully is hard: papers overload the model's limited context.

Their framework, DeepCode, treats the overload as a channel problem. Repository synthesis becomes a matter of managing information flow on purpose. Four operations are orchestrated to maximize signal under a fixed budget. Source compression distills the paper into a lean blueprint first. A stateful code memory then indexes the growing repository in structure. Retrieval injects outside knowledge only when a step actually needs it. A closed loop corrects errors as the build proceeds. On the PaperBench benchmark, DeepCode sets a new state of the art. It beats leading commercial agents, including Cursor and Claude Code. On key reproduction scores it surpasses even doctoral-level human experts.
arxiv-2512-08521:
Jing yi Wu and Yong Tang, gravitational wave physicists in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Future space detectors such as LISA and Taiji will listen for a stochastic background of gravitational waves, a sea of faint signals mixed with instrument noise. Telling the two apart depends on the template used, and real missions complicate matters because their triangle arms slowly change length as they orbit.

Using simulated signals and the dominant noise sources, the authors compare three template strategies. One averages over time segments, one pretends the arms are equal, and one lets the arm length float. Under realistic, time varying geometry, the time averaged template gave the most accurate parameter estimates. Letting the length float instead added uncertainty. The message is practical: templates must respect the true, breathing geometry of the detector, or the measurement suffers.
arxiv-2512-08621:
Xue Mei Li, Colin Piernot, Szymon Sobczak, and Kexing Ying, probabilists, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. They study multiscale stochastic systems whose slow component is pushed by fractional Brownian motion, a noise with memory, rougher and more persistent than ordinary random walks. Averaging principles say the slow motion follows a simpler random limit as the time scales separate. The question here is the next term: how large are the fluctuations around that limit.

They prove the deviation, scaled by a precise power of the scale gap, converges to a new stochastic equation. That limit is driven by fractional Brownian motion together with an extra space time Gaussian field. The proof is delicate, and standard tools do not apply directly. The authors combine cumulant methods with a residue lemma, recasting the enlarged system as a rough differential equation.
arxiv-2512-08721:
Christos Tyrpenou and coauthors search by computer for new lead free materials for solar and indoor light harvesting. They start from a known silver bismuth iodide double salt and replace bismuth with indium to design a new compound. First principles calculations suggest that compound is stable and has a direct band gap close to its bismuth cousin.

Even so, its predicted solar performance is lower, under both sunlight and indoor light. The authors trace that gap to forbidden optical transitions and to the loss of bismuth lone pair states at the band edge. A broader screen of the silver indium iodine space finds other stable compounds in two structural families, with wider band gaps. Lab attempts could not make the target phase, showing how hard these indium salts are to stabilize. Uses in charge transport may suit them better.
arxiv-2512-08921:
Tharon Morrison and coauthors demonstrate an optical atomic clock that runs on its own using several trapped ions and on chip light delivery. Integrated photonics are key for portable clocks and scalable quantum computers, but putting all needed functions into one system has been a major challenge. Their clock uses an ensemble of four ytterbium ions in a surface electrode trap at room temperature.

All clock operations use light delivered through waveguides built into the chip. The system shows strong short term frequency stability and keeps running autonomously for extended periods. Automated shuttling and reloading of ions handle ion loss during interleaved measurements, adding resilience. The work moves beyond single component demonstrations. It establishes a robust architecture for the next generation of portable multi ion quantum sensors and computers that can operate with little human intervention.
arxiv-2512-09021:
Daniele Sorini and coauthors use interpretable machine learning to study how feedback shapes the gas density profile in halos. Feedback from stars and active galactic nuclei moves gas from inside galaxies far into intergalactic space. How it sets the host gas profile was unclear.

The team trains a random forest on suites of three major cosmological simulations that span different feedback models. Inputs are halo mass plus five central galaxy properties. The model reproduces simulated profiles with high average accuracy across a wide mass and redshift range. A global sensitivity analysis, applied for the first time to such simulations, ranks each input by radius. Halo mass and central galaxy gas mass matter most, while stellar and black hole traits matter less. Exact rankings depend on feedback model and redshift.
arxiv-2512-09521:
Ö. Adebali and colleagues disentangle the blended light of HR 7275, a double-lined spectroscopic binary of the RS CVn type. Its two cool stars sit close enough that both contribute to every observed spectrum. Both stars are magnetically active and variable, which corrupts measurements of the orbit. The team separates the two component spectra so the primary star's activity can be studied on its own.

Their Doppler image of the primary shows two large cool spots covering about a fifth of the visible hemisphere each, plus three smaller ones. Total spottedness nears forty percent of the surface in mid-2022. Those spots make the radial velocities wobble, with two modulation behaviors over the observing run. Removing that activity jitter sharpened the orbital solution roughly tenfold. Snapshot magnetic measurements show fields changing with rotation phase, and lithium abundances for both stars point to internal mixing, with the secondary's value low.
arxiv-2512-09721:
Spyridon Kakaroumpas and Stefanos Lappas prove an extrapolation result for bilinear operators in a variable exponent setting. Extrapolation lets mathematicians carry a property known in one family of function spaces over to many others. Here the property is compactness, which means an operator squeezes sets into a form with strong convergence behavior. The spaces are weighted Lebesgue spaces whose exponent can vary from point to point. The authors first prove a general principle built on a theorem by Cobos, Fernández-Cabrera, and Martínez.

They then apply it to get new compactness results for several standard objects. These include commutators of bilinear Calderón-Zygmund operators, bilinear fractional integrals, and bilinear Fourier multipliers, all acting on the weighted variable exponent spaces. The work extends and unifies results, placing findings under one roof. Such results feed into the analysis of partial differential equations, where compactness helps prove solutions exist.
arxiv-2512-09921:
A team led by A. Yu. Murtazin asks whether twisted particles keep their twist while being accelerated. Vortex particles carry orbital angular momentum, a helical twist in their wave. The worry is that shedding photons during acceleration would bleed that twist away. Working within scalar quantum electrodynamics, the authors model charged spinless vortex particles in the axial electric and magnetic fields of an accelerator. A real wave packet locally feels a nearly constant field, which makes a workable model possible.

For field strengths typical of accelerator facilities, the useful lifetime of the vortex state far exceeds the acceleration time. Photon emission therefore drains almost no angular momentum in practice. The conclusion is encouraging for accelerator physics: vortex electrons, ions, and muons can be pushed to relativistic energies in ordinary linear accelerators. The same robustness holds for wakefield accelerators with steeper field gradients. The study appeared in Physical Review D.
arxiv-2512-10121:
Zhongjie Jiang proposes that workflow, not a bigger model, is what long form expert writing needs. The paper names an impossible trinity for language models in specialized domains: low hallucination, deep logical coherence, and personal expression cannot yet be had together. The cause, Jiang argues, is a statistical smoothing trap: models average away the high entropy information gathering and structured thinking that expert writers actually do. His DeepNews framework models the cognitive process of seasoned financial journalists with three modules.

Schema guided planning builds a logical skeleton from expert narrative schemas and atomic content blocks. Adversarial constraint prompting then disrupts the model's smoothness with tactics meant to restore rhythm and tension. Experiments locate a knowledge cliff where truthfulness collapses below a context threshold. In a blind test, the workflow beat a leading model's zero shot output decisively.
arxiv-2512-10221:
A large collaboration reports a search for a halo of axions bound to the Sun, using a worldwide network of precision magnetometers. Axions are hypothetical ultralight particles proposed as dark matter. Theory suggests self interacting axions could be captured by the Sun's gravity, thermalize, and settle into a dense ground state cloud. Such a halo would generate faint pseudo magnetic fields through its coupling to protons, oscillating at a single frequency. The GNOME network, shielded atomic magnetometers on several continents built to catch exotic spin effects, is the right instrument to look.

The team analyzed a sixty nine day run, matching data against daily modulation templates. No significant signal appeared. The null result becomes upper limits on the halo's field amplitude across a wide frequency band. For one form of the axion proton coupling, those limits beat existing astrophysical bounds by more than a hundredfold over much of the range.
arxiv-2512-10521:
Pasquale De Marinis, Gennaro Vessio, and Giovanna Castellano attack few-shot semantic segmentation, where a model must outline a brand-new class in images after seeing only a handful of labelled examples. Most earlier work polished the decoder, but the authors argue the real bottleneck is the encoder, which extracts weak features for classes it has never met.

Their method, Take a Peek, nudges the encoder with a light touch. Using low-rank adaptation, a cheap fine-tuning trick, it shifts the encoder's feature space based on the support examples, adapting quickly to new classes while limiting forgetting of old ones. The method is model-agnostic and drops into existing pipelines. Across COCO, Pascal, and cross-domain sets spanning satellite, skin, and chest X-ray images, it improved results consistently, with low ranks already giving strong gains.
arxiv-2512-10821:
Leijie Wang and a large team start from how content moderators actually work. Vision classifiers sort images into concepts, but builders of these systems usually assume the user arrives with a crisp, stable definition of the concept. Interviews with moderation experts showed the opposite: people begin vague and sharpen their idea by deliberating over hard cases. The team turned that practice into a system called Agile Deliberation.

The system first scopes a concept, breaking it into a structured hierarchy of sub-concepts, then iterates by surfacing borderline images for the user to judge, aligning the classifier with their evolving intent. Because the process is subjective and interactive, the authors evaluated it through eighteen long user sessions rather than a static benchmark. Agile Deliberation beat automated decomposition baselines on F1 score by a clear margin and edged out manual deliberation too. While participants reported clearer understanding and lower mental effort.
arxiv-2512-10921:
V Mylnikov, S Potashin, and Alex Kamenev analyse a cavity that cannot make up its mind. Their system is a single bosonic resonator. It is driven and drained two photons at a time, with a finite detuning. Its steady state has two attracting points. Those points are visible through the Wigner function in phase space. Quantum fluctuations make each attractor metastable, so the system occasionally jumps between them, and any qubit stored there decoheres accordingly.

Exploiting a hidden time-reversal symmetry, the authors build an effective phase-space potential for the steady state. They then compute, inside the Keldysh real-time path integral formalism, the instanton trajectory that governs the quantum activation jump between attractors. And tie it back to the Wigner picture, unifying the static and dynamical descriptions. An analytical formula for the decoherence rate follows. The framework speaks directly to designing bosonic qubits in driven, dissipative nonlinear resonators.
arxiv-2512-12121:
Ahmad Chamma, Omar El Herraoui, and Guokan Shang release MixtureKit, a toolkit for building Mixture-of-Experts models from models that already exist. Mixture models route each token to a few specialist sub networks, gaining capacity at low cost. Assembling them by hand from pretrained parts is fiddly work.

MixtureKit supports three recipes: classic routing per block, BTX with a router per sub layer, and BTS which keeps experts whole and adds trainable stitch layers between them. It rewrites configs, patches model classes, and saves one ready checkpoint. A visual tool shows routing per token and per layer. On multilingual code switched data, a BTX model built with the kit beat dense baselines.
arxiv-2512-12221:
Jakob Vanhoefer and four co-authors speed up model selection in a 2025 paper. Scientists pick among many models using scores like AIC, BIC, and Mallows's Cp. Checking every model by brute force grows too fast as models gain parts, so many use step by step rules that may miss the best model.

A common belief said branch and bound search fails when scores do not rise in a steady way. The authors give a new bound that makes such search work for these scores. It guarantees the best model across many classes and sizes. In one past task with about 4 billion models, their speedup topped 6,000 times.
arxiv-2512-12621:
Haizhong Li and Bo Yang study a nonlocal isoperimetric problem in hyperbolic space in a 2025 math paper. Isoperimetric problems ask which shape gives least perimeter for a fixed volume. Here a nonlocal term, built from a negative power of distance, competes with perimeter, and such problems are well studied in flat Euclidean space but not in curved hyperbolic space.

They prove geodesic balls are the unique minimizers, up to hyperbolic isometries, for small volumes. For large volumes, they prove no minimizer exists under certain ranges of the exponent in the nonlocal term. The contrast shows how volume size and curvature together decide whether an optimal shape exists at all.
arxiv-2512-12921:
Amy Chang and co-authors at Cisco present a unified framework for the security and safety of AI systems. As AI spreads into consumer, business, and agent based tools, the ways it can fail or be attacked have grown. Threats range from harmful outputs to poisoned data and prompt injection.

Older frameworks each cover only part of this space. Cisco's framework spans the full life cycle and ties security and safety together in one taxonomy. It is meant for finding threats, red team testing, and ranking risks. The report also reviews gaps in older frameworks and shows how the new one structures modern AI failures and defenses.
arxiv-2512-13021:
Mo Yang, Jing Yu, and Necmiye Ozay design controllers for groups of agents, such as robots or vehicles, that must stay safe while talking to each other as little as possible. Links between agents are limited by bandwidth, delay, and energy. Less chatter makes systems easier to scale.

They frame the design task as a rank minimization problem and solve a relaxed version with system level synthesis. The method respects safety and coordination demands plus delay limits. In simulations covering tracking tasks with mixed sensing setups, it cut inter-agent transmission sharply compared with baseline methods. The result is a principled route to quiet, safe multi-agent control.
arxiv-2512-13421:
Qingyu Shi and co-authors present RecTok, a visual tokenizer designed to escape a trade-off in diffusion image generation. Tokenizers compress images into latent codes; richer, higher-dimensional codes rebuild images better but usually generate worse. Prior fixes borrowed features from vision foundation models, yet high-dimensional tokenizers still lagged.

RecTok distills semantic knowledge into the forward flow paths of flow matching, rather than only into the latent space. A masked feature reconstruction loss enriches the semantics further. It achieved state-of-the-art generation scores with and without classifier-free guidance, plus strong reconstruction. Notably, raising the latent dimensionality improved results instead of hurting them.
arxiv-2512-13521:
Alberto Canali and co-authors study how long ultracold molecules of dysprosium and potassium survive in a light trap. Each molecule joins two fermionic atoms, a pairing of interest for work on superfluids with unequal masses. The team holds a dense sample in traps made with near-infrared light at four wavelength ranges.

They find that light from the trap is the main cause of loss in most ranges. Near 2000 nanometers, that loss is much weaker, and near 1550 nanometers they find a low-loss plateau. For weakly bound molecules near a Feshbach resonance, they also show a Pauli block that cuts clash losses by about tenfold.
arxiv-2512-13721:
John Homer launches a series on Spectral-Operator Calculus with a study of the self-adjoint setting. The calculus aims to assign scalar values to spectral quantities built from operators. In this first part, quantities are bounded Borel transforms, and locality is imposed by additivity across spectral partitions.

Under premises of unitary invariance, extensivity on orthogonal sums, projector locality, and a smooth-limit condition, Homer proves a rigidity theorem. Every admissible evaluator must agree with a weighted trace of one Borel profile applied through functional calculus. He then builds a sorting of spectral growth from eigenvalue counting. The polynomial growth regime stays stable under the basic builds, giving later parts an analytic base.
arxiv-2512-13821:
Subramanyam Sahoo presents a framework to catch harmful behavior in code written by language models. Models now generate code with little human review, which raises fears of backdoor injection. His Cross-Trace Verification method checks an untrusted model without running its possibly harmful code directly.

Instead, the protocol uses the model's own predicted execution traces across matching program rewrites. Matching patterns in those traces reveal anomalies that signal backdoors, an approach he calls semantic orbit analysis. He defines an Adversarial Robustness Quotient for the cost of verification, which grows very fast with orbit size. Theory gives information-theoretic bounds meant to show adversaries cannot game the check through training. High false positive rates in early tests remain a practical barrier.
arxiv-2512-14221:
Jiarong Fan, Juhyun Park, Thi Phuong Thuy Vo, and Nicolas Brunel tackle missing data in conformal prediction in a 2025 paper. Conformal prediction builds prediction sets with a promised coverage rate, but missing input values can break that promise.

Their frame first imputes missing values, keeps the mask that records which values were missing, then corrects the sets with a weighted method. They prove valid marginal coverage and mask conditional validity for general missing data mechanisms. Two algorithms follow, both close to the target guarantees in tests. On synthetic and real data, their sets are much narrower than standard mask conditional methods while keeping the promised coverage.
arxiv-2512-14421:
Mischa Dombrowski, Felix Nützel, and Bernhard Kainz build a detector for a privacy risk in image-generating AI: models sometimes reproduce training images, including private ones. Checking for that memorization has been unreliable, and earlier audit tools worked poorly outside their home domain. The authors treat detection as one problem joining identity matching and copy detection.

Their model, LCMem, trains in two stages, first learning to match identities, then learning to spot altered copies. Across six benchmark datasets it gained up to sixteen points on re-identification and thirty points on copy detection over prior methods. Current privacy filters, they found, catch far less than users might assume.
arxiv-2512-14521:
Riccardo Grazi and three colleagues model a quantum battery, a chain of interacting qubits in the transverse-field Ising setup, and ask how the charging style changes what noise does to it. Sudden charging and non-interacting batteries are the baselines. Charging gradually over a finite time, with interactions active, turned out smoother and easier to control.

Noise then split the results by protocol. Gentle charging gained stored energy from noise but kept less of it usable as work. Strong charging lost stored energy yet grew more efficient, meaning a larger usable share. The lesson for battery design is that the best protocol depends on which loss matters.
arxiv-2512-14621:
Dataset distillation squeezes a big data set into a small synthetic one that trains models almost as well. The trick works nicely for images, but extending it to video has proven hard, and earlier attempts often performed poorly.

The response here is to distill video data sets into images: compact image sets that carry the training value of the original videos. Keeping the distilled form as images makes it cheap to store and quick to train on. The work tests how much of a video data set's training value an image set can retain. Success would help labs that cannot keep or process full video collections.
arxiv-2512-14721:
Synthetic patient data promises a privacy-compliant way to share medical information for secondary use. A popular generator, Synthea, builds realistic patients from rules that describe a synthetic lifetime, so the quality of its output depends on the quality of its rules.

A large team works on extracting those rules automatically from real-world population data, using glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor, as the test case. Automatic rule extraction could spare the slow manual authoring that now limits such generators. Better synthetic cohorts would help researchers develop and test health software without exposing real patients to new risks.
arxiv-2512-14821:
Ping He and three coauthors look for the best quantum probes to sense fields of wave like dark matter. Dark matter of this kind acts like a faint wave that fills space, with random phases and a limited span of coherence. A network of sensors must catch that weak signal together.

The team shows that symmetric Dicke states, shared states of many sensors, beat other choices. They squeeze the most information from the field, and their edge grows with the square of the sensor count. Unlike fragile GHZ type states, they keep that edge when noise damps the signal. The framework also covers fields like gravitational waves, and the probes could be built from superconducting qubits, atoms, or diamond centers.
arxiv-2512-14921:
Miguel Megevand studies a class of exotic stars made not of atoms, but of boson fields. Standard boson stars are steady balls of such fields held up by their own gravity. In earlier work he helped define l-boson stars, a broader family labeled by an angular momentum number l, which still keep a round shape.

Here he moves these stars into anti de Sitter spacetime, a universe with a negative cosmological constant that bends space inward at large scales. The study presents the solutions and works through their main traits in that setting. It extends the boson star family into a backdrop widely used in gravity and holography research.
arxiv-2512-15321:
Stanislav Dubnička and three coauthors compute a batch of decays of the Bs meson, a particle made of a bottom antiquark and a strange quark. The decays include hadronic and semileptonic final states with varied spins and diagram shapes. A covariant confined quark model handles the hadronic effects inside the Standard Model.

Agreement with experiment varies by channel. It is good for two semileptonic decays into Ds or K mesons with a muon and neutrino. It is acceptable for two hadronic modes, and marginal for three more, including the phi J/psi channel. Two channels, into phi with an anti D0 or an eta c, disagree significantly. The authors blame the breakdown of naive factorization and missing long distance effects. Two of the troubled channels are in theory among the cleanest, yet other groups see the same gaps, hinting at shared missing physics.
arxiv-2512-15521:
Guillermo Rodriguez Llorente and co authors train an autonomous pressure controller for a fusion test facility prototype in a 2025 paper. IFMIF DONES will test materials under extreme conditions for nuclear fusion, and its MuVacAS prototype copies the final beamline segment. Keeping argon pressure steady in its vacuum chamber is vital and hard to do by hand.

The team trains a deep learning surrogate model on real operating data to act as a digital twin of the gas injection system. A reinforcement learning agent then practices inside that twin. The learned policy holds pressure within strict limits despite changing disturbances. The work points toward self running control for future accelerators.
arxiv-2512-16021:
Marek Jankola and three co-authors study how opinions flip in a paper that appeared on arXiv in 2025. Their model is majority dynamics on a large random network. Each node holds a plus or minus state. At each step, it copies the majority of its neighbors. The question is stark. How small a starting minority can still take over the whole network?

The team uses a cavity method that tracks histories backward. It predicts a clear threshold. When each node has at least four neighbors, an initial minority of plus nodes can drive full consensus fast. They then built an algorithm to find such starting setups for a given network. It is called history-passing reinforcement. It beat simulated annealing in their tests. It could not reach the lowest densities theory allows, though. It stopped near a predicted phase boundary.
arxiv-2512-16221:
Lorenzo Nava, Ye Chen, and Maximillian Van Wyk de Vries speed up hazard forecasts in an arXiv paper made public in 2025. Landslides and avalanches kill several thousand people a year and can run for kilometers from their start. Predicting how far they will flow is vital, but physics solvers are slow while simple models miss key behavior.

The team trained a neural network to emulate the solvers. Training used more than 100,000 simulations across more than 10,000 real terrain tiles. The emulator predicts flow extent and deposit thickness with high accuracy, running 100 to 10,000 times faster than the numerical codes. It reproduces channel switching and deposition patterns and generalizes across flow types, sizes, and landscapes. Fast, realistic runout maps could feed large-scale early warning systems.
arxiv-2512-16321:
Aryan Esmailpour and three co-authors solve a sampling problem in an arXiv paper uploaded in 2025. Subset sampling includes each data item in a sample independently with its own probability, a basic tool for fast approximate analytics. Trouble starts when the data is not a plain list but the result of a database join, which can be vastly larger than its inputs.

Materializing the join just to sample it is hopeless, so the authors design the first efficient algorithms for acyclic joins. A static index produces many independent samples, a one-shot algorithm produces a single sample, and a dynamic index keeps working as tuples are inserted. Sampling probabilities can come from tuple weights combined by product, sum, min, or max rules. All three methods run in near-optimal time and space relative to input and expected sample size.
arxiv-2512-16621:
Vijay H. Mahatma, Andrew C. Fabian, and Leah K. Morabito report the first radio detection tied to the odd hourglass X-ray glow around 3C 294, a radio galaxy at redshift 1.8. Data came from LOFAR at 144 megahertz and Chandra in X-rays.

The matched radio and X-ray glow is well fit by one electron pool acting two ways, shining by synchrotron in radio and boosting cosmic background light into X-rays. The electrons have strikingly low energies, so deep low-tone radio views are vital at high redshift. The glow holds more energy than the hot cluster gas suggests, making 3C 294 one of the strongest radio systems in a dense young cluster. Inner hot spots look restarted while outer ones stay strong.
arxiv-2512-17221:
Brandon Huang and five co-authors present DAVE, a vision encoder built for vision-language models used on documents and web pages. Standard encoders, they argue, miss the fine layout and position cues those tasks need. DAVE is trained in two stages to fix that gap without huge labeled sets.

First the encoder learns on its own from unlabeled images. Then it trains on a smaller set of high quality examples for tasks like parsing and finding items on a page. The team also merges encoders trained with different text decoders, and blends DAVE with a general encoder called SigLIP2. On document tests, visual questions, and web agent tasks, the combined system performs strongly.
arxiv-2512-17421:
Sourav Banerjee and Neel Kanth Kundu model a radar with an unusual antenna. The antenna is a cloud of atoms pushed into a Rydberg state. In that state, outer electrons orbit far from the core and react strongly to radio waves. Instead of wires and circuits, lasers and light detectors read out what the atoms feel. The pair ask whether such a quantum radar can beat a classic set.

They build the math for the system, work out its signal-to-noise ratio, and add a method for reading a target's speed from the Doppler shift. In simulations, the atomic radar posted a stronger signal ratio and smaller speed errors than the classic design. The study is a design analysis, pointing builders toward a new kind of receiver.
arxiv-2512-17521:
Nanna Berre and three co-authors ease a hard simulation problem: squishy, fluid-soaked solids such as brain tissue, soil, and bone. The Biot system couples a porous solid's bending with fluid seeping through it. Real organs have wiggly shapes that are painful to mesh, the step of filling a shape with neat little blocks before any math can run.

Their cut finite element method lays a plain background grid over the shape and lets the true border cut through blocks wherever it falls. A total-pressure form of the equations keeps the method steady across material settings. They prove stability and best-possible accuracy, then show the method working on a realistic brain shape. Surgeons and engineers who model soft, wet materials gain a simpler path.
arxiv-2512-17721:
David Kolenatý and eight co-authors coat hydrogen electrolyzer parts with a film so thin it slashes the platinum bill by up to a hundredfold. Inside a PEM electrolyzer, acid and voltage eat steel plates alive, so makers armor them with precious platinum. The team's titanium-niobium-oxygen film, just 200 nanometers thick, is sputtered onto stainless steel in two layers.

By tuning oxygen levels and the niobium-titanium mix, they dial in both low electrical resistance and near-zero corrosion currents, far under the United States DOE 2026 target. After harsh aging tests, parts met the contact resistance goal with a platinum skin only 5 nanometers thick. Cheaper coatings could cut the cost of green hydrogen hardware.
arxiv-2512-18021:
Fabian Kreppel, Reza Salkhordeh, Ferdinand Schmidt-Kaler, and André Brinkmann teach language models to route ions in a quantum computer. In trapped ion machines, charged atoms must be shuttled between zones to meet and interact. Writing that traffic plan by hand for each new chip layout is slow work.

Five language models were fine tuned on plans from hand coded rules for two layouts. For circuits up to 16 qubits, the models produced valid plans on both layouts they knew. In 12 percent of good runs, the best plan used up to 21 percent fewer moves than the rule based plans. One model even planned a valid run on a new four way layout, a first hint of transfer.
arxiv-2512-18121:
Ce Xu, a mathematician at Anhui Normal University, studies Apéry like series, the infinite sums tied to famous constants such as values of the Riemann zeta function. The paper treats a wider family of these series that carries both a parameter and a cyclotomic twist.

The main tool is contour integration, applied to series whose terms rest on a parametric central binomial coefficient defined through the Gamma function. With it, Xu writes a whole family of the series in terms of multiple polylogarithms, cyclotomic Hurwitz zeta values, Riemann zeta values, and log 2. Worked examples recover several known results. Integrals of the generating function for Fuss Catalan numbers yield a fresh form for one classical series, plus new identities among polylogarithms. Two questions are left open.
arxiv-2512-18221:
Shiguang Ma and Jie Qing carry potential theory into Carnot groups, spaces where motion is allowed only along certain directions. Potentials measure how a spread mass pulls on its surroundings, and polar sets are the spots where a potential blows up. In flat space their size is well known, but these bent spaces break the usual tools.

The pair use a completeness trait of the space to bound how large polar sets can be, leaning on bent versions of classic integral bounds. Their path also imports pieces of geometric measure theory into this setting. The payoff reaches into three cousin fields built on such spaces: CR geometry and its quaternion and octonion forms.
arxiv-2512-18521:
Bella Finkel and Jose Israel Rodriguez work on multiview geometry, the math behind reconstructing 3D scenes from camera images. A multiview variety models every set of matching image features a camera setup can produce. Its Euclidean distance degree counts how complex it is to find the 3D points that best fit the images. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, proves a formula for that degree.

The formula covers curves described by rational functions, under mild genericity assumptions. Applying it, the authors settle conjectures about one-dimensional line multiview varieties that Duff and Rydell had proposed from computer vision. Knowing the distance degree tells vision engineers how hard a triangulation problem really is before they run it. The work links pure algebraic geometry to a daily problem in 3D reconstruction.
arxiv-2512-18621:
Neelanjan Chakraborti, Snehasish Nandy, and Sudeep Kumar Ghosh seek a fingerprint of unconventional magnetism, the exotic orders whose spin split bands vary with momentum. Their 2025 study examines transport at the junction of a magnetic topological insulator and an unconventional magnet. An insulating magnetic layer ensures the response comes only from the proximity induced exchange field.

The probe is the intrinsic gyrotropic response, split into conduction and displacement currents set by Zeeman Berry curvature and the quantum metric. A fixed pattern appears: the transverse displacement response shows even fold angular harmonics for orders from p-wave to i-wave. The longitudinal response reveals parity through sign reversal patterns. The conduction part barely notices the symmetry, so the displacement current is the true tell. For values drawn from real heterostructures, the signals sit well within reach. The framework gives labs a general way to pin down unconventional magnetic insulators.
arxiv-2512-18721:
Yunji Ha uses hypothetical particles, magnetic monopoles, as a probe of the Standard Model's hidden global structure. Monopoles arise in heavier theories that complete the Standard Model at high energies, and their allowed magnetic charges depend on the exact shape of the gauge group. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, works out which monopoles can survive to low energies.

After electroweak symmetry breaking, only monopoles with magnetic charges 3g_D and 6g_D can persist as isolated, color-neutral states. Ha traces this selection rule to the interplay of the symmetry structure with magnetic 1-form symmetry, and notes the breaking scale can naturally suppress their leftover abundance. Using CORSIKA simulations, he also shows such monopoles with Lorentz factor up to 10^4 lose energy in matter at a rate scaling with the square of the charge. The results guide searches for real monopoles.
arxiv-2512-18921:
Andrew Polar and Michael Poluektov parallelize the training of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, a neural architecture whose Newton-Kaczmarz training beats classic perceptrons on accuracy and speed. The catch has been sequence: each Newton-Kaczmarz update depends on the last, blocking parallel hardware. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, attacks that bottleneck from three directions at once.

First, a pre-training procedure shaped to the updates' structure. Second, training separate models on disjoint data subsets and merging them afterward. Third, a division-free rewrite of the algorithm for field-programmable gate arrays, implemented and benchmarked on the device itself. Experiments compare their implementation against popular MLP packages for scalability, and all code is public for full reproducibility. The work moves KANs toward the parallel hardware modern machine learning actually runs on.
arxiv-2512-19021:
Sihao Lin and twelve co-authors built VLNVerse, a large benchmark for robots that follow spoken directions using vision. Older benchmarks, they argue, use small fixed sets and weak physics, so results say little about real rooms. Split task formats also slow shared progress in the field.

VLNVerse joins the split tasks in one framework with tools for adding more. Its agents have full bodies that move under a real physics engine, rather than teleporting between views. The team tested methods from classic models to large multimodal agents, and added a single model that handles all tasks. The goal is to close the gap between simulation and real-world movement.
arxiv-2512-19521:
Santhoshini Velusamy improves a streaming algorithm for Max-DICUT, a canonical problem about cutting directed graphs well. In the streaming world, data flows past once and memory is scarce. A famous lower bound says beating a one-half approximation in one pass and sublinear space is impossible, and recent work matched it for bounded-degree graphs.

Arbitrary graphs of unbounded degree resisted that single-pass result. Velusamy's two-pass algorithm reaches the same near-one-half guarantee in sublinear space, for every fixed error slack. The extra pass is the price of generality. The problem doubles as a testbed for streaming methods across constraint satisfaction, so the advance may travel.
arxiv-2512-19621:
Jherek Healy opens a two-part set of warnings for traders in foreign exchange options. Prices and volatilities are filled in between quoted points by interpolation. That step sits under the risk work on plain FX option books. It counts even more for exotic trades. Those are priced with local volatility models fed by the filled-in surface.

The article does not sell a new scheme. It collects cases where some well-liked interpolation choices break down. Each case is a concrete failure, not a vague worry. For traders and quants, the worth is in the check it prompts. A method that behaves on standard quotes may still give nonsense in odd corners of the surface. These cases mark where to look before trusting it.
arxiv-2512-19821:
Fabien Le Floc'h reviews a down-to-earth question in derivatives pricing. How should one pick the parameters of a stochastic volatility model? In such models, volatility itself moves at random. The prices a desk quotes hinge on the values picked. Traders face several rival ways to pick them. Each way has its own effects on the prices that come out.

The article draws on the past literature. It surveys the ways the choice is made, in the broad setting of pricing contracts. The survey also covers the use of such models inside stochastic local volatility models. There, a leverage function scales the random volatility. For quants who keep pricing code, the review pulls a scattered field into one place.
arxiv-2512-19921:
María Isabel Cortez, Jamal Drewlo, Jaime Gómez, and Tobias Jäger link two constructions of aperiodic order. Toeplitz arrays are symbolic patterns built by filling positions in stages, leaving a hierarchical, almost-periodic structure, while model sets arise from cut-and-project schemes that slice higher-dimensional lattices. The paper proves a one-to-one correspondence between Toeplitz arrays over residually finite groups and model sets from specific schemes built on the array's own odometer.

That dictionary is then put to work. The authors construct irregular Toeplitz arrays that extend their maximal equicontinuous factor, the odometer, with maximal rank k while carrying exactly k distinct ergodic measures. A modified construction keeps the same measure-theoretic profile but pushes the maximal rank to infinity, separating two notions that tamer examples keep together.
arxiv-2512-20021:
Anna Flowers and three co-authors ask where a vision model is weakest, before paying to teach it more. Realistic training data are costly. Detectors for rare objects fail most in the conditions least covered. Their meta-learning method treats the facts of data collection as variables. Season, time of day, and location are the examples. The learner is tested as the training data vary along those axes.

A Gaussian process surrogate is fit to that response surface. It can then predict which new data would help most. Acquisition is steered by that map. The method improved the learner, versus data picked at random. It was shown on classic learning cases. A live use case hunted airplanes in aerial images.
arxiv-2512-20421:
Nino Dekkers and Klaas Landsman give the old idea of molecular chaos a precise meaning. Physicists invoke chaos at the smallest level to explain why large-scale laws, like Boltzmann's, run one way in time. The authors instead demand that individual microscopic paths be algorithmically random.

That sharpening pays three dividends. It gives a test for single paths, not just typical ones, to produce one-way behaviour. An effective ergodic theorem then makes the large-scale laws self-contained in their toy models. And the one-way flow traces to time-reversal asymmetry in the randomness test itself. The scenario is realized in the Ehrenfest urn and Kac ring models. A closing discussion weighs Chaitin's incompleteness results, which say random paths can never be displayed in full.
arxiv-2512-20521:
Amedeo M Favitta's doctoral thesis studies axions where two hard approaches meet: non-equilibrium quantum field theory and quantum field theory in curved spacetime. Axions were invented to solve the strong CP problem and also appear in string theory wrappings. Being extremely weakly coupled, they remain leading dark matter candidates.

The thesis reviews curved-spacetime field theory, then develops the Peccei-Quinn mechanism and its high-energy completions. A large part treats axion electrodynamics, where a classic axion background rewrites Maxwell's equations and shifts what can be measured. Out-of-balance dynamics of self-interacting axion fields, handled with the two-particle-irreducible effective action, are applied to the cosmos before and after inflation. The results yield new insights and early constraints on axion scenarios.
arxiv-2512-20621:
Isabel Neto and co-authors test whether robots can earn cooperation from children the way people do: by reputation.
