bailey-english-dictionary-1721:
Nathan Bailey issued his Universal Etymological English Dictionary in 1721, the most complete English word book of its day. Bailey was a schoolmaster who gathered some 40,000 entries, giving each word's origin along with its meaning. Earlier English dictionaries had been small lists of hard words; Bailey aimed at the whole language.

The entries trace words to Greek, Latin, French, and other roots, and add notes on grammar and usage. The book sold through many editions and served writers and readers for decades. Samuel Johnson borrowed heavily from it when he built his own famous dictionary a generation later. Bailey's work marks the point where English lexicography became a serious, full-scale trade.
basden-among-the-ibos-of-nigeria-1921:
George Thomas Basden lived thirty-five years in Nigeria and wrote Among the Ibos of Nigeria in 1921, late in that long stay. Basden, an Anglican missionary and school builder, records the Igbo world he knew at close range and loved. Chi, the personal god of each person, ancestors, dibia diviners, and the village republic of elders fill his chapters.

Markets, marriages, funerals, and the rules of a stateless, democratic people come through in practiced, concrete detail. Basden writes as a friend of his subject within a missionary's frame, and both sides of him show on the page. His ethnography remains a first source on Igbo religion and society in the early colonial years.
berzelius-emploi-chalumeau-1821:
Jons Jacob Berzelius teaches the blowpipe's use in chemical trials in this manual, in its 1821 French version. A flame, a tube, and a steady breath reveal what a mineral hides. Prospectors and mineralogists learned the craft from the great Swedish chemist's clear, patient pages of instruction.

Tiny beads of melted ore tell their tale by color and change. Berzelius turns a camp skill into a exact field science for travelers. His methods traveled to mines and surveys on every continent in time. The little guide helped build mineralogy as a practical art, putting a laboratory, in effect, in a coat pocket.
bryant-poems-1821:
William Cullen Bryant published his first book, Poems, in 1821, when American poetry still had few names of note. Bryant had written its best-known piece, 'Thanatopsis,' while still in his teens. The slim volume gathered that poem with other early work on nature, death, and faith.

'Thanatopsis' urges readers to face death calmly, since all people return to the earth together. Other poems praise wild woods, open skies, and the quiet of country places. Bryant wrote in smooth, grave verse shaped by British models yet rooted in American scenes. The book was praised abroad and helped start a lasting American tradition of nature poetry.
carbonari-memoirs-1821:
Secret groups in the south of Italy drew wide fear after revolts shook Naples in 1820. An English book of 1821, turned from a French text, gave British readers their first full report on them. Its main subject is the Carbonari, a network of lodges with oaths, grades, and signs. No author is named on the title page.

Pages describe how the Carbonari met, how new men joined, and what their rites meant. Reports of trials from 1820 show how the state struck back at the groups. The book still serves as a first-hand source on the secret groups that fought kings in Italy.
cardozo-nature-judicial-process-1921:
The Nature of the Judicial Process, published in 1921, prints Benjamin N. Cardozo's Storrs Lectures at Yale, the most famous lectures ever given by an American judge. Cardozo, then on New York's highest court, answers a simple question: how do judges actually decide cases?

He names four methods: logic, history, custom, and sociology, and shows judges moving among them, often without knowing which is in command. Precedent guides but does not bind absolutely; the judge legislates in the gaps. Cardozo's candor and grace made the lectures a classic of legal writing. Lawyers still assign them to every beginner.
chahar-maqala-browne-1921:
E. G. Browne revised his translation of the Chahar Maqala in 1921 for the Gibb Memorial series. Nizami-i-Arudi wrote the Four Discourses in the twelfth century, treating the four men a king needs near him. The secretary, the poet, the astrologer, and the physician each get a discourse, salted with tales of courts and their servants.

Anecdotes carry the teaching: how a verse saved a life, how a doctor read a pulse and a fate. Browne, the great Cambridge Persianist, loved the book's lively mix of counsel and gossip. The work remains a window on Persian court life and letters at their most humane.
chekhov-cooks-wedding-1921:
The Cook's Wedding and Other Stories appeared in English in 1921, in Constance Garnett's translation. The title story is seen through the eyes of Grisha, a boy of seven. Grisha watches the household plot to marry off the cook Pelageya to a cabman she has barely met.

The Dependents shows an old peasant begging care for his starving horse, and finding none. The Orator mocks a pompous speaker hired to praise a man he barely knew. Chekhov moves easily here between comedy and quiet sorrow. Several tales take a child's view of adult dealings, with sharp results. The volume rounds out Garnett's long Englishing of his shorter fiction.
chekhov-horse-stealers-1921:
The Horse-Stealers and Other Stories reached English in 1921 through Constance Garnett's translation. The title tale follows a hospital watchman drawn into the company of horse thieves at a lonely inn. Drink, boasting, and a rising wind build the night toward theft and flight.

The Privy Councillor draws gentle comedy from a grand official's visit to a modest country estate. Other pieces in the volume range across the steppe, the road, and the village. Chekhov knew the open southern plains from travel and wrote them with love. Wind, grass, and distance shape the moods of these tales. The volume favors his stories of travel and open country.
chekhov-schoolmaster-1921:
Garnett's Schoolmaster volume of Chekhov stories appeared in English in 1921. The title story shows a worn schoolmaster honored at a dinner after twenty-five years of service. Praise rings hollow for a man spent by routine, and he dies soon after, little noticed.

The Man in a Case gives Belikov, a teacher so afraid of life that he wraps himself in rules and galoshes. His fear poisons a whole town until his sudden death frees it. The volume also reprints The Horse-Stealers, among other tales of school, town, and country. Chekhov's portraits of small, fearful lives remain painfully fresh. Few writers have matched his mix of pity and precision.
cia-0000009921:
American prisoners and their detention cells, north of Chavane in Saravane province, were sighted in a January 1971 report. Saravane sits in southern Laos, astride trail routes into Vietnam's center. Seeing the cells as well as the men gave the report unusual physical detail.

Cells describe a prison better than claims do: size, bars, and guards can be checked later. Such detail helped judge whether a site was a true camp or a stopping point. It also told planners what rescue would face. This file preserves the observed cells and captives together, a ground-level view of Laotian detention.
cia-0000012321:
Helms to the Director of Central Intelligence, January 1962: the summit correspondence on the Penkovsky case continues without pause. The subject, cut short in the file, concerns military matters in the colonel's channel. Principals traded these memos back and forth even as the year's crisis deepened. Berlin's tension and Cuba's approach formed the backdrop to every page.

The files keep the dialogue at the peak intact for readers today. Case management at this level balanced a spy's safety against a nation's hunger for his product. For readers, the memo shows the operation steered from the very top, month after month.
cia-0000013121:
How the Viet Cong used American prisoners, as policy rather than chance, is studied in a CIA paper from February 1967. In the south, captives were held in jungle camps. They answered to the southern movement's own command, not to Hanoi. The paper examines the doctrine behind their treatment. Prisoners served as sources of information and as labor. Above all, they served as propaganda, exhibits in a war for world opinion.

The study shows how systematic that use was. Captivity in the south followed rules written far from the camps. For readers, the paper is the enemy's prison theory read from inside, by the side that feared it most.
cia-0000013221:
Forty-two American prisoners were held by the Viet Cong in the border country, and a CIA report from November 1966 confirms the detention. The camps sat along the South Vietnam and Cambodia border area named in the title. Forty-two captives in one report made the southern system's scale plain. It was larger, and better organized, than Washington liked to admit in public.

The report counts and places the men as sources then knew them. Each number in it was a name to someone waiting at home. For readers, the page shows the southern captivity measured whole, years before its survivors came home.
cia-0000013621:
Brazil, titled with one word, gets a CIA country brief from February 1968. The brief sketches the giant's Cold War face at a hard season. The generals ruled with full force and full pride that year. Students and workers were filling the streets against them in protest. The regime was months away from the decree that closed congress. That decree opened the dictatorship's harshest years of rule.

Such briefs caught a country at a glance for busy readers above. This one catches Brazil at the hard-liners' peak, before the iron years deepened. For readers, it is the giant in brief: vast, rich, and governed by decree.
cia-0000013921: Policy toward American prisoners and a secret hospital for their care fill a CIA report dated November 2, 1967. A hidden hospital for wounded prisoners is a striking detail. It suggests the north set apart medical care for captives, away from public view. Reports like this fed debate over how the north really treated the men it held.
cia-0000014721: USSR intelligence activities are the broad subject of a CIA file dated March 5, 1954. The title names the whole field rather than one operation. Files at this level summed up Soviet spy work as the agency saw it. Such surveys helped set the watch lists and budgets of the early Cold War security state.
cia-0000014821: Major consequences of certain U.S. courses of action on Cuba fill a CIA paper dated September 6, 1962. The paper weighed the big results that might follow American steps. Like its twin of the day before, it came just ahead of the missile crisis. The pair show estimate work at full stretch on the eve of the Cold War's sharpest hour.
cia-0000049121: A trace reply on former members of El Salvador's revolutionary junta and their contacts survives in a CIA item from 1987. The junta had ruled at the war's start, and its scattered members still drew the file system's interest. Traces on yesterday's rulers show how long the paperwork of power follows the men who held it.
cia-0000049221: A draft letter to a Mr. Hamilton survives in a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. Drafts preserve what officials almost said: the argument as first framed, before it was softened or sharpened. Who Hamilton was, and whether the letter was ever sent, sits inside the document and its file.
cia-0000049321: Terrorism Review is the short title of declassified CIA document 0000049321, dated July 4, 1990, and marked for the Truth Commission. The file presents itself as a review of terrorism rather than a report on one event. Readers get a dated agency survey item, preserved under a general heading that does not name a country or a single incident.
cia-0000098721: A Red Sea Security System: Political, Military, and Economic Issues is the title of declassified CIA document 0000098721, dated November 2, 1981. The subtitle sorts the study into three kinds of issues. Readers get a short declassified study whose heading promises a system examined from political, military, and economic angles at once. The record survives in the CIA Reading Room mirror collection.
cia-0000102921: Colony Settlement Prison Ya 38/10, Baku, with dates of information 1976 to December 1977, is declassified CIA document 0000102921, dated February 5, 1981. A coded designation and a city share the heading. Readers get a short single-prison record from Baku, companion to the Arkhangelsk colony settlement item in the same labor cluster. The heading and date are the firm facts the catalog gives.
cia-0000109821: Dr. a. Von Miorini is the whole heading on declassified CIA document 0000109821, dated September 1, 1945. The title is a name and nothing else: no topic, place, or charge is stated. A name-only heading leaves the file's subject to the pages inside. The brief record is a name file from the first month after the war in Europe ended.
cia-0000112821: Shanghai - Counter-espionage Summary is the short heading on declassified CIA document 0000112821, dated July 2, 1945. The title names a city and a form: a counter-espionage summary for Shanghai. Summary is the heading's own word for what the file holds. The brief record is a city summary item from the summer of 1945 in the China files.
cia-0000119721: A September 1956 CIA item notes a Hungarian newspaper backing Tito's position on ties with Moscow. Each such editorial marked Budapest's drift from the Soviet line, weeks before the revolution made that drift impossible to ignore. Praise for Tito in print was itself a political act, since his break with Stalin made his path a standing challenge to Moscow's rule.
cia-0000124321: A January 1952 CIA document covers preparations for exchanging United Nations prisoners in central and south China. Prisoner swaps were being arranged long before any armistice in Korea. The paper records those preparations as the agency tracked them during the war. Exchange planning began while fighting still raged, since both sides held men the other wanted back and lists had to be built long before any signing.
cia-0000132421: Control of the Cuban labor movement is the subject of item 16 in a CIA series, dated January 1, 1960. The item reports that the struggle for that control was still going on. Whoever held the unions held power in the streets of Havana. Castro's government was steadily bringing organized labor under its own direction, and the item tracks that fight.
cia-0000132621: A Castro-sponsored news agency drawing hostility across the region fills a CIA item dated June 2, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the word Lat, short for Latin America. A Havana-run agency meant Havana-shaped news reaching papers across the hemisphere. Governments and editors pushed back against the service that year. The short item reports the meeting behind the agency and the reaction it met.
cia-0000136221: 2 May 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about the Calligeris situation and WSBURNT interest in Arbenz, the coded names circling the target. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136321: Majority ADAM troops are en route to the HANK complex for a major showdown, LINCOLN tells CADICK in this June 1954 cable. The movement runs toward Ipala and then Chiquimula, and troops bombed on the rail line are now walking the roads. Every indication, the station says, is that they fear strafing and will break each time. If the HANK fight goes badly that night, CALLIGERIS should prepare at once for strong counterattacks from Ipala.
cia-0000136621: Written in Spanish and dated March 1961, this Brigade 2506 document is a forwarded complaint and extract from Cuban records. A man reports being caught taking a box of orange juice; the official who questioned him said it was for the Americans and threatened punishment for stealing. The writer respectfully passes the account to a brigade adjutant for knowledge and appropriate effects. Preserved among the brigade files weeks before the Bay of Pigs landing, it shows internal discipline paperwork, not combat orders.
cia-0000136721: A Spanish document dated 1 February 1961, filed in the 2506 Brigade papers released by the CIA. It shares its date with a companion brigade record in the same stretch of the file. The brigade was in final training for the April invasion. The catalog gives neither item a subject. This document is kept in Spanish as released, a primary source from the brigade's last winter.
cia-0000136921: Physical details of the Alfhem fill this April 1954 cable to LINCOLN, describing the Swedish arms ship for officers who might have to find, board, or attack her. She is diesel-powered, 386 feet long with a 51-foot beam and 25-foot draft, 4,900 gross tons and 8,100 deadweight. Her hull has a split superstructure placed in the center of the ship, divided into two parts. The dry specifications turn a diplomatic crisis into a target folder.
cia-0000137321: Cuba's revolutionary government is a dictatorship under Fidel Castro, the CIA briefing for the 398th National Security Council meeting of 26 March 1959 states flatly. Castro has absolute power and is sole arbiter of all policies; he has had no administrative experience and resorts to demagogy to whip up support. His economic policies, agrarian reform and cutting rents and utility rates, have alienated most sound business groups, and capricious statements calling for a one-class society caused apprehension. The briefing also weighed his April visit to address newspaper editors in Washington.
cia-03150421: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/05/23, a CIA publication. The May briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Its place in history is secure. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06235321: AR 6-2 AGENCY PREPUBLICATION REVIEW OF CERTAIN MATERIAL PREPARED FOR PUBLIC DI, a CIA regulation. The review rule. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
cia-06240321: MESSAGE FROM THE DIRECTOR, a CIA document. The director's message. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
commons-industrial-government-1921:
Commons published Industrial Government in 1921, setting out his plan for democracy inside the workplace. He had spent years in Wisconsin helping to write labor laws and run the state's industrial commission. The book distills that practice into a theory of how firms and unions should govern work together.

Commons argues that collective bargaining works like a form of self-rule for industry. Workers, through unions, gain a voice in the rules that govern their days, much as citizens gain a voice in a state. He backs the claim with studies of real firms and unions he had watched at close range. The ideas here fed directly into the labor laws of the New Deal a decade later, before that program had a name.
conrad-notes-life-letters-1921:
Notes on Life and Letters, published in 1921, gathers Conrad's essays and occasional pieces from across his career. The sailor turned novelist writes here as a public man of letters on war, Poland, and the craft of fiction.

'The Crime of Partition' pleads Poland's cause after the First World War, and 'Poland Revisited' recalls his return to his homeland in 1914. Other pieces assess Henry James and Turgenev, masters he honored, and reflect on books and the sea. The essays show Conrad's mind at work without the mask of fiction. They remain essential reading for his admirers.
constitution-botswana-2021: Botswana's Constitution, from 1966 with amendments, frames its stable democracy. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It anchored Africa's gem. Diamonds funded. Votes held. Peace stayed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-ecuador-2021: Ecuador's 2008 Constitution, amended through 2021, grants nature itself rights. It is a world first. The Tower library holds the full text. It crowned Pachamama. Rivers gained. Forests stood. Law greened. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-slovenia-2021: Slovenia's 1991 Constitution, amended through 2021, frames its republic. It left Yugoslavia first. The Tower library holds the full text. It slipped away. Ten days warred. Alps voted. Europe embraced. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-zimbabwe-2021: Zimbabwe's 2013 Constitution, amended through 2021, frames its republic. It guards land reform. The Tower library holds the full text. It ended white rule. Farms seized. Voters came. Struggle stayed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cooper-spy-1821:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Spy in 1821, his second novel and his first real success. Cooper, a New York landowner turned writer, set it in Westchester County during the Revolutionary War, a neutral ground crawling with informers. It proved American fiction could outsell British imports at home.

Harvey Birch, a humble peddler, seems to be a British spy despised by both sides. In truth he serves Washington, who watches the action disguised as a mysterious traveler. Families split between king and Congress, and loyalties stay hidden until the end. Cooper mixes battle scenes, escapes, and secret missions into a new kind of American romance. The Spy launched the historical novel in the United States.
dequincey-confessions-1821:
Thomas De Quincey published his Confessions in the London Magazine in September 1821, and fame came at once. He calls the piece an extract from the life of a scholar. In opening pages he explains why a sane man would bind himself to opium, the drug sold then as laudanum.

Early chapters trace the lonely youth and pain that led him to the drug for relief. Later pages turn to the grand and dreadful dreams that opium brought him at night. Part life story and part prose poetry, the book made addiction a subject for serious writing in English for the first time.
digha-nikaya-rhys-davids-1921: Volume three of the Dialogues of the Buddha, completing the Digha Nikaya set. The final long discourses of the Pali canon. This edition preserves those venerable Buddhist scriptures. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
dospassos-three-soldiers-1921:
Three Soldiers divides into six parts with blunt titles: Making the Mould, The Metal Cools, and Machines. Rust, The World Outside, and Under the Wheels close the plan. Dos Passos printed the novel in 1921, fresh from the First World War.

Part one opens with a company at attention on a parade ground at evening. Men stare ahead, tired from drilling, while cooks' smells drift on the wind. Three young Americans move from hope through disgust toward revolt and desertion. The army itself becomes the foe that crushes the human spirit, in one of the first great antiwar novels in English.
europmc-pmc10203321:
Yang and colleagues review epigenetic regulation in the tumor microenvironment in a 2023 paper. Epigenetics covers changes that switch genes on or off without altering the DNA code itself. Such switches, from chemical marks on DNA and histones to reshaped packaging and RNA changes, help control how cancers start and grow.

The review explains how these switches act not just in tumor cells but in the immune and support cells around them. It shows how they shape response to immune therapy. It also surveys drugs that reset faulty switches, a growing front in cancer care.
europmc-pmc10480221:
Xie and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how drug hunters now chase proteins once deemed undruggable. Such proteins have shapes or jobs that defy the usual drug design playbook. Their size and smooth surfaces leave no snug pocket for a drug to grip. Yet many drive major diseases, so the prize for success is large.

Fresh tactics fill the review by Xie. Some drugs bind for good to a target, while others grip a side pocket to shut it down. Other routes break the protein, silence its gene, or block its talks with partners. RNA-based drugs and immune therapy add more angles. The team tracks which of these have reached patient trials.
europmc-pmc10484921:
Leguia and colleagues traced a bird flu strain in Peru in 2023 as it killed sea life in bulk. The strain is H5N1, a highly harmful form of avian flu. It reached Peru in November 2022 and sparked huge die-offs of pelicans and sea lions. The team read the virus genome from five kinds of wild animal.

Samples came from dolphins, sea lions, sanderlings, pelicans, and cormorants. The Peru viruses mixed parts from two lines, one from Eurasia and one from North America. Four genome parts came from each line, Leguia reports. The viruses were also gaining changes fast, some of concern. The team urges close local watch to curb spread to other species, humans included.
europmc-pmc10515021:
Sun, Rao, Zhou, and Li reviewed plant carotenoids in 2022, the pigments that colour many fruits and leaves. Plants make these compounds from scratch in light-using tissues. In plants they aid light capture, guard against light harm, and give colour to petals and fruit. They also feed into plant hormones and signals.

For humans, carotenoids are the raw stock for vitamin A. Sun notes that they also act as antioxidants in the diet, soaking up cell-damaging bits. New regulators of their build-up keep turning up in lab work. The review sums up how plants control their levels at many steps. Farm uses include richer crops with more of these healthy pigments.
europmc-pmc10564921:
Clusmann and co-authors mapped the future of large language models in medicine in 2023. Such models are AI tools trained to write and process text. ChatGPT's public launch in November 2022 drew world notice. The models can answer, sum up, and translate text at near-human level.

That skill tempts clinics, schools, and labs, Clusmann notes. Wider access to medical facts could help patients and staff. The same tools could spread false claims just as fast. Weak openness about how they work adds risk for fraud and error. The review sorts gains and caps for care, research, and teaching. It urges clear rules on blame when a model errs.
europmc-pmc11080421:
Rahimi and Khatooni clarify a key quality concept in interview-based nursing research in this 2024 paper. Saturation is the point where new interviews stop adding fresh insight. Judging it well is essential for rigorous qualitative research, meaning research based on words rather than numbers. The authors used an evolutionary concept analysis, a method that traces how a concept's meaning shifts over time.

They analysed 33 articles and books from 2005 to 2023. Saturation proved to be context-dependent and subjective, needing detailed systematic work, they found. It is used in four senses: theoretical, data, code or theme, and meaning saturation. Causes split into study factors and researcher factors. Reaching it secures credibility and quality while saving time, energy, and budget. Two independent researchers checked the analysis for validity.
europmc-pmc11121021:
GBD 2021 Forecasting Collaborators project disease burden to 2050 for 204 countries and territories in this 2024 analysis. Policy makers need future trends in disease and its drivers to plan long-term health spending. The team built a reference forecast, meaning the most likely future, plus what-if scenarios. Those scenarios ask what changes if chosen risk factors were eliminated by 2050.

Forecasts cover deaths, years of life lost, years lived with disability, and a combined measure, split by age and sex. Drivers include a socio-demographic index built from income, schooling, and fertility. Only risk factors judged causal in the parent study shape each cause's path. Results are given for 21 regions, seven super-regions, and the world. The work expands earlier Global Burden of Disease forecasts with improved methods.
europmc-pmc11392821:
Dimitrov and colleagues present an all-in-one framework for inferring cell-to-cell communication in this 2024 paper. Cells signal to each other, and new methods read gene activity in single cells or in tissue spots to guess those signals. Each past tool caught only part of the picture. The team set out to unify them.

Their framework, LIANA+, rests on a rich base of known signal pairs. It works on single-cell data and on spatial data, where each spot on a tissue slice is read in place. It also handles data that mixes several conditions or several measurement types at once. Rather than replace past methods, it extends and unifies them, the authors say. The code is shared openly, with many worked examples. They present it as a scalable answer for decoding signals within and between cells.
europmc-pmc11802921:
Zheng and co-authors published a 2025 review on the most common form of liver cancer. That form is called hepatocellular carcinoma, or HCC for short. It makes up about nine in ten liver cancer cases. The review links it to hepatitis B and C, to a food toxin, and to metabolic disease.

Readers get a map of the cell signals that drive growth, spread, and return of these tumors. Some signals guide cell growth, while others shape cell identity and stress response. Zheng also surveys drugs that block those signals. The work helps doctors match treatments to tumor biology.
europmc-pmc11889221:
Guan and co-authors reviewed tissue macrophages in a 2025 survey. Macrophages are immune cells that patrol tissues across the body. They eat dead cells and germs, and they present alarms to other cells. They also help repair damage and keep tissues in balance.

Origins vary more than once thought, and the review sorts them out. Some macrophages arise early in development, others from blood stem cells. In tumors they can help or hinder cancer growth. Guan links their states to heart, immune, and cancer disease. That link makes them targets for new drugs.
europmc-pmc1257421:
van der Helm-van Mil and colleagues compared two forms of rheumatoid arthritis in 2005. Antibodies to citrullinated proteins mark one form of the disease. They appear before symptoms and are highly specific. Genetic risks differ between antibody-positive and antibody-negative patients.

The cohort held 454 new patients, split near evenly by antibody status. Early symptoms and joint counts were recorded at entry. Blood inflammation levels were also compared. Disease course over time was tracked for both groups. The study tests whether the two forms behave as distinct diseases. Separate mechanisms would call for separate care logic.
europmc-pmc1334221:
Parikh and co-authors linked a vessel protein to lung leak in sepsis in 2006. Sepsis can trigger acute respiratory distress syndrome, a deadly lung failure. Vessel leak drives that failure, but its mediators were unclear. Angiopoietin-2 blocks a vessel-stabilizing receptor and was the suspect.

Blood levels of angiopoietin-2 ran significantly higher in sepsis patients. The elevation was clearest in patients with impaired oxygenation. Serum from those patients disrupted vessel cell architecture in dishes. Mouse and cell studies backed the human pattern. Parikh names angiopoietin-2 as a contributor to septic leak.
europmc-pmc1665421:
Lead harms the developing mind most at a specific stage of pregnancy. Hu and co-authors pinpointed that stage in 2006, following 146 pregnant women in Mexico City. They measured lead in blood and plasma each trimester, then tested the children at 12 and 24 months.

Only first-trimester lead predicted lower mental development scores. A one standard deviation rise in first-trimester plasma lead cost 3.5 points on the index. Later pregnancy lead, and the child's own later blood lead, mattered less. Plasma lead, the fraction that can cross to the fetus, beat whole blood lead as a predictor. Hu urges prevention aimed at early pregnancy.
europmc-pmc1831521:
Kärrman and co-authors measured man-made perfluorinated chemicals in Swedish mothers' milk and blood in 2007. These persistent chemicals, used in coatings and foams, build up in the body. Little was known about how much reaches a nursing infant or how levels changed over time.

Matched milk and blood samples came from 12 first-time mothers, plus pooled milk samples from 1996 to 2004. Eight such chemicals appeared in blood, and five of them also showed in milk. Two, named PFOS and PFHxS, appeared in every milk sample, at mean levels of 0.201 and 0.085 nanograms per milliliter. Total levels in milk were about one percent of blood levels for PFOS, yet milk levels rose tightly with blood levels. The pooled samples let the team track the trend across nine years.
europmc-pmc2072821:
Calafat and colleagues measured fluorinated chemicals in blood from a national United States survey in 2007. These polyfluoroalkyl chemicals, used since the 1950s in many products, spread widely through the population. Production methods changed sharply after 2002. The team analysed 2,094 serum samples from the 2003-2004 national survey of people aged 12 and older, and compared results with 1999-2000.

Four chemicals, including PFOS and PFOA, were detected in over 98 percent of samples. Levels differed by race, ethnicity and sex. Average levels fell about 32 percent for PFOS and 25 percent for PFOA since the earlier survey. PFHxS fell about 10 percent, while PFNA doubled. The authors link the drops to the 2002 halt in one major production process.
europmc-pmc2124821: A medical paper concerning compensatory hyperplasia of the intima. The thickened lining. This article preserves that vascular pathology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2126321: A medical paper on effect of exposure to the sun on the circulating lymphocytes in man. The sunlit white cells. This article preserves that hematology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128321: A medical paper with a further inquiry into the source of the virus in turkey blackhead. The turkey virus. This article preserves that veterinary virology. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2140521: A biology paper with studies on the regulation of osmotic pressure, the effect of increasing concentration. The salty balance. This article preserves that physiology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140821: A biology paper on the combination of salts and proteins, a method for determination. The salty measure. This article preserves that biochemistry. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2267221:
Wang and co-workers systematically assessed computer predictions of MHC class II peptide binding in 2008. These molecules present protein fragments to helper T cells, and predicting binding helps find immune epitopes. Unlike class I, the class II groove is open at both ends, so peptides vary in length and their binding core must be located correctly. The team assembled over 10,000 previously unpublished binding measurements, 29 crystal structures and 664 peptides tested for T-cell responses.

Public prediction tools were benchmarked against that data. The best tools reached accuracy scores up to 0.86 in selected cases. Class II predictions generally lagged behind class I performance. The variable peptide length and core assignment emerged as the critical limiting factor in this large systematic evaluation. A consensus approach combining top methods performed best overall. The data sets were released publicly as a benchmark.
europmc-pmc2275221:
Wang and co-workers compared chloroplast genome junctions in 2008 across 123 flowering plant representatives. Chloroplast genomes contain two inverted repeats separated by single-copy regions, and the repeats expand or shrink over evolution, shifting their junctions. The team classified gene arrangements around the junctions between the inverted repeat and the large single-copy region. They focused on a gene cluster, trnH-rps19, found in most monocots but not other flowering plants.

Junction arrangements fell into three types, and monocot repeats had expanded more progressively than those of other plants. Junctions commonly sat at A-rich DNA stretches. Lab tests showed the cluster in one repeat is controlled by two opposing promoters. The authors propose two successive DNA break events expanded the repeats before monocot lineages diversified. Duplicated trnH copies in different lineages then had distinct fates.
europmc-pmc2292821:
Izcue and colleagues reported in 2008 on interleukin-23, a signal protein that drives gut inflammation, and its role in colitis in mice. Colitis is inflammation of the colon. The team used a model where T cells, a type of immune cell, are transferred into mice that lack their own immune cells.

They found that this colitis did not need T cells to release interleukin-17, a related signal. When interleukin-23 was absent, more protective cells called regulatory T cells formed in the colon. Those cells carry a marker named Foxp3, and they calm immune attack. If the transferred cells lacked Foxp3, colitis still developed without interleukin-23. So the signal drives disease largely by holding back these protective cells.
europmc-pmc2323621:
Yang and colleagues reported a new research tool for plant guard cells in 2008. Guard cells are pairs of cells that open and close stomata, the tiny pores leaves use for gas exchange. Studying their signals was hard because known gene switches gave weak or uneven activity in these cells of Arabidopsis, a model plant.

The team screened activity data for 23,000 genes and picked a strong switch, named pGC1. It drove marker genes strongly and mostly only in guard cells, in both Arabidopsis and tobacco. With a calcium sensor under its control, they filmed calcium pulses inside guard cells of living plants. The switch also shut a target gene down in guard cells while leaving leaf skin cells untouched.
europmc-pmc2327221:
Amiel and colleagues reviewed low blood sugar in type 2 diabetes in 2008. The medical name is hypoglycaemia, and in these patients it is caused mainly by diabetes drugs. Drugs that raise insulin no matter what the blood sugar is, such as sulphonylureas and injected insulin, carry the most risk.

The review found the highest rates in people on insulin, with 25% of long-term users reporting a severe episode. Severe means the person needed outside help to recover. Sulphonylureas caused fewer events per person, yet over 5,000 UK patients a year were estimated to need emergency care for one. Risk rose with age, longer illness, and tight sugar targets. Each hospital stay for a severe episode cost about 1,000 pounds.
europmc-pmc2375021:
Huang and co-authors described a free tool for making sense of long gene lists in 2007. Gene chips can flag thousands of genes at once, leaving researchers with lists too long to read. Their tool sits inside the DAVID database, a public web resource for gene function notes.

The tool, called the Gene Functional Classification Tool, groups a gene list into biological modules, clusters of genes that share a job. It uses a fuzzy clustering method, meaning a gene can sit partly in more than one group, as real genes often work in several processes. The same grouping can be run on the plain-language terms attached to genes. The authors said condensing thousands of genes into a short set of modules shows the main biology at work far faster than reading entries one by one.
europmc-pmc2440421:
Scholl and a large team tested whether a defence system runs hot throughout the body in eye disease in 2008. The disease is age-related macular degeneration, the leading cause of blindness in older people. It damages the macula, the centre of the retina. Gene studies had blamed poor control of the complement system, an immune cascade that attacks microbes.

They measured complement activation products in blood from 112 patients and 67 controls. All activation markers were higher in patients, especially Ba and C3d, which signal chronic activation, with significance below 0.001 for both. A model using just three blood markers, Ba, C3d, and factor D, separated patients from controls better than a model using the known risk genes. Marker levels also tracked the risk-gene variants in patients and controls alike. The authors called the eye disease a body-wide condition showing up in the ageing macula.
europmc-pmc2518121:
Levina and colleagues asked in 2008 whether chemotherapy itself can leave behind lung cancer stem cells. These rare cells are blamed for tumours regrowing after treatment, because they resist drugs and can rebuild the tumour. The team treated human lung cancer cells with three standard drugs and studied the survivors.

The surviving cells carried stem cell markers such as CD133 and Oct-4 and could grow as spheres, renew themselves, and mature into ordinary cancer cells that regained drug sensitivity. In mice they formed tumours readily and spread widely. Their tumours held two to three times more growth and blood-vessel factors, such as VEGF and IL-6, than ordinary tumours did. The authors suggest blocking this factor network could improve therapy.
europmc-pmc2602721:
Laskowski and colleagues showed in this PLoS Biology paper how a root's bending shapes where its side roots form. Where lateral roots emerge largely sets a plant's architecture, and the pattern is governed by the hormone auxin. Experiments and computer modelling in the model plant Arabidopsis traced the chain from physical shape to hormone distribution.

Curvature changes cell sizes in the root, and on the outside of a bend the pericycle cells, the layer that spawns lateral roots, end up with higher auxin levels. Transporter proteins restrict this response to the zone able to form roots. One importer, AUX1, is itself switched on by auxin, pulling in still more and creating a peak that triggers a new organ. PIN proteins, which export auxin, set the spacing between roots along the organ.
europmc-pmc2637921:
Sandgren and colleagues announced in 2009 a free online database that collects gene changes linked to drug-resistant tuberculosis. Resistant TB was spreading worldwide, and fast lab tests that spot resistance from a strain's genes were badly needed. The facts about which gene changes cause resistance sat scattered across many separate papers.

The team gathered those published findings into one searchable resource, open to anyone on the web. For each drug, it lists the gene changes found in resistant strains and how often the common ones occur. Drug makers can map the changes onto the germ's proteins to see how resistance works. Test makers can use the lists to design quick checks that read a patient's strain and guide treatment choices.
europmc-pmc2646321:
de Jonge and co-authors asked in 2008 whether the oxygen given to intensive care patients on breathing machines affects their chance of dying. Too little oxygen harms the body, but too much may also do damage. The team reviewed records from 36,307 patients treated in 50 Dutch intensive care units.

They focused on oxygen levels in the first day after admission. Death rates rose in a straight line with the share of oxygen in the air patients were given. Blood oxygen showed a U-shaped pattern: both low and high values came with more deaths. The links held after the team accounted for how sick each patient was on arrival. A closer look at five units showed the same pattern across the whole stay. Dutch units, they note, ran oxygen higher than guides suggest.
europmc-pmc2722021:
Ponjavic, Oliver, Lunter, and Ponting catalogued in 2009 long non-coding RNAs, RNA copies that do not make proteins, that sit between genes in the genome. Thousands of such RNAs exist, but most have no known job. Copies that have changed little over evolution are likely functional, since useless parts drift freely.

They found six hundred fifty-nine constrained long non-coding RNAs, and those active in the brain were conserved more often and folded into stable shapes more often. Brain copies tended to sit beside protein-coding genes also active in brain, many guiding development or gene control. Staining in mouse brain confirmed that many pairs switch on together in place and time.
europmc-pmc2746121:
Terwilliger and Berendzen presented in 1999 a fully automated procedure for solving protein crystal structures from MAD and MIR X-ray data. Those methods use heavy or anomalous atoms to recover phase information. Solving that partial heavy-atom structure is often the slowest, most decision-heavy stage of crystallography. Structure output was rising fast, and genomic projects promised demand at a far larger scale.

Their procedure turns structure solution into an optimization problem with a scoring scheme that judges candidate solutions. Each step, normally run by hand across several programs, is carried out and verified automatically. Automation could cut the time from data collection to solved structure sharply, a step toward determining structures of broad protein groups at genomic scale.
europmc-pmc2806521:
Carmena, Ruchaud, and Earnshaw reviewed in 2009 how partner proteins steer two cell-division enzymes, Aurora A and Aurora B. Kinases are enzymes that switch other proteins on or off. The two Auroras are close cousins in sequence, yet they work at different places and times while a cell divides.

Aurora A gathers at the spindle poles, the hubs that organize the ropes pulling chromosomes apart, and drives entry into division. Aurora B rides a moving protein team called the chromosomal passenger complex, shifting from chromosomes to the cell middle as division ends. Partner proteins deliver each kinase to its post and tune its activity, and that targeting explains how near-identical enzymes run distinct jobs.
europmc-pmc2831921:
Bartell and colleagues measured in 2010 how fast blood levels of the industrial chemical PFOA fell once two Ohio Valley water systems filtered it out. A nearby DuPont plant had tainted drinking water in several districts, and two of them started carbon filtration in 2007. The team drew up to six blood samples from two hundred residents over the following year.

Blood PFOA dropped in both districts, for bottled-water drinkers as well as tap-water drinkers. After adjustment, levels fell by about twenty-six percent per year, which lines up with a median half-life of roughly two and a third years in the body. The decline followed the smooth curve expected if the body clears the chemical at a steady proportional rate.
europmc-pmc2850921:
Diancourt, Passet, Nemec, Dijkshoorn, and Brisse mapped the family tree in 2010 of Acinetobacter baumannii, a hospital bacterium notorious for drug-resistant outbreaks. Sequencing seven housekeeping genes in more than one hundred fifty strains from around the world, they measured how diverse the species is and how its outbreak clones relate.

The species proved genetically compact, with a star-shaped tree pointing to a severe population bottleneck in its recent past. The known international clones I to III formed tight clusters, each a dominant genotype with a few close variants, the signature of recent rapid expansion. Resistance to antibiotics was nearly universal inside these clones and a new one, ST15, while other genotypes stayed mostly drug-sensitive, fingering resistance as the engine of their spread.
europmc-pmc2854721:
Ruzzin and colleagues demonstrated in 2010 that persistent organic pollutants, the long-lived industrial chemicals that build up in food chains, can directly cause insulin resistance. Human studies had linked diabetes to body burdens of these pollutants, but no experiment had shown cause. Rats ate high-fat diets made with either purified salmon oil or crude oil carrying its natural pollutant load for twenty-eight days, and fat cells in dishes faced pollutant mixtures.

Only the crude-oil rats developed insulin resistance, belly obesity, and fatty liver. In the dish studies the pollutants, especially old-style organochlorine pesticides, bluntly blocked insulin's action on fat cells. They also switched down two master regulators of fat handling, Insig-1 and Lpin1, giving a molecular handle on the effect.
europmc-pmc2871121:
Hanhineva and colleagues reviewed in 2010 how polyphenols, plant compounds in tea, coffee, cocoa, wine, berries, and grains, affect the handling of carbohydrates. Diets rich in these compounds track with better blood sugar in population studies. The review gathers lab, animal, and early human evidence on how the compounds act at each step of sugar control.

In animals and a few human studies, polyphenol-rich foods blunted the sugar spike after meals and lowered fasting sugar levels. They also sharpened insulin release and the body's response to it. Likely routes include slowing starch digestion and sugar uptake in the gut, prompting insulin release from the pancreas, and easing sugar release from the liver. The authors call for solid human trials before prevention claims can be made.
europmc-pmc2874221:
Muñoz-López and García-Pérez reviewed in 2010 DNA transposons, the jumping genes that move by cutting themselves out and pasting into a new spot. Repeated DNA fills much of the mammalian genome, and these movers have reshaped genomes over evolution. Because they need few host helpers, scientists have turned them into delivery tools across many species.

Famous tool versions include Sleeping Beauty, a jumper rebuilt from fish remains, plus piggyBac and Tol2. They serve to add genes to cells, to break genes at random so their jobs can be read, and to probe the control regions of the genome. Uses now reach embryonic development studies, disease gene hunts in pathogens and hosts, and early gene therapy designs.
europmc-pmc2905321:
Johnson and co-authors reviewed in 2010 how shingles and its lingering nerve pain erode quality of life, arguing both are underestimated. One in four people develop shingles in a lifetime, rising to one in two among the elderly. Pain dominates every phase and is reported by up to ninety percent of patients, often rated worse than surgical or labor pain.

Up to a fifth of patients develop post-herpetic neuralgia, moderate to severe pain lasting months or years after the rash heals. The review documents harm across physical, psychological, functional, and social domains, with worse pain tracking greater interference in daily activities. Eye involvement can threaten sight, and some elderly patients never regain independence after an attack. Prevention by vaccination frames the authors' closing challenge.
europmc-pmc2908021:
Richard and colleagues reviewed in 2009 L-tryptophan, an essential dietary amino acid best known as the sole raw material for serotonin, the brain's mood-linked messenger. The brain's serotonin output rises and falls with tryptophan supply. Researchers can therefore dial the system up with supplements. Or they can crash it briefly with a tryptophan-free drink, a tool called depletion. The review covers its basic metabolic jobs first.

Depletion studies have mapped serotonin's hand in mood, aggression, appetite, sleep, and cognition by watching what falters when synthesis pauses. Supplementation trials show early promise for psychiatric disorders, mainly as an add-on that strengthens standard drugs rather than a stand-alone treatment. The authors call for better trials while noting the approach's unusual power to test a brain chemical directly.
europmc-pmc2935121:
Power reviewed how farming both depends on and shapes ecosystem services in a 2010 article. Farms supply food, forage, fuel crops, and plant medicines, yet they lean on wild nature for pollination, pest control, fertile soil, and water flows.

Well-run farms can also guard water quality, store carbon, and shelter wildlife, while poor practice brings habitat loss, runoff, and pesticide harm. Judging these trade-offs means weighing scale, timing, and whether damage can be undone. Better ways to value services raise the odds of outcomes where farms and nature both gain, provided management improves.
europmc-pmc2949821:
Laugsand and co-authors compared symptom ratings from advanced cancer patients with ratings by their care providers across eleven European countries in a 2010 study. Patients depend on staff to notice suffering, so gaps in judgement matter.

Nearly two thousand patient and provider pairs rated symptoms on matching four-point scales. Providers consistently scored symptoms lower. Moderate or severe pain, for example, was reported by about two thirds of patients but under half of providers. Similar gaps appeared for tiredness, weakness, and appetite loss. Agreement varied with patient and disease traits. The pattern warns clinics to ask patients directly rather than guess.
europmc-pmc3016421:
Wang and co-authors sequenced the active genes of sweet potato roots in a 2010 study, building the first large transcript catalogue for this staple crop. The swollen root is the harvested organ, yet public data on its genes were scarce.

From tens of millions of paired reads they assembled over fifty thousand gene units and matched most to known proteins, pathways, and function groups. Sugar handling and plant chemical defence pathways were well covered. They also mined several thousand simple repeat markers from the sequences and validated a hundred primer sets, giving breeders fresh tools for tracking traits.
europmc-pmc3017121:
Huang and co-authors mapped how a family of interferon-induced membrane proteins blocks different viruses in a 2011 study. The IFITM proteins were known to stop flu entry, and the team tested Ebola, Marburg, and SARS viruses alongside.

All three IFITM types restricted the filoviruses and the SARS coronavirus, but with distinct fingerprints: Ebola and Marburg entry resisted IFITM3 more than flu did, while IFITM1 hit them harder. Two mouse relatives blocked filoviruses but not flu. Treating SARS particles with an enzyme that bypasses a cell compartment also bypassed the block, locating the defence late in entry.
europmc-pmc3033821:
Lässer and colleagues reported in 2011 that tiny parcels shed by human cells, called exosomes, carry RNA in saliva, blood plasma, and breast milk. Exosomes are small bubbles released by many cell types into body fluids. Earlier work had found RNA inside parcels from lab grown cells, raising the question of whether this also happens in the body.

The team purified parcels from the three fluids and confirmed RNA inside all of them, including message RNA in plasma parcels. Breast milk parcels carrying RNA were reported here for the first time. Labeled parcels from saliva and milk were readily taken up by macrophages, a type of immune cell. The findings support the idea that cells can pass working RNA messages to each other through these parcels.
europmc-pmc3046121:
Chen and colleagues benchmarked in 2011 six software methods that clean up gene chip data collected in separate batches. Gene chips measure thousands of genes at once, but samples processed on different days carry systematic offsets called batch effects. These offsets can swamp real biology unless they are removed before analysis. The team compared the six tools on precision, accuracy, and overall results.

One method, an empirical Bayes tool called ComBat, beat the other five on most measures. The study also showed that scaling the data probe by probe before comparing samples matters a great deal. Without that step, a sizable probe level effect inflates how similar samples look. The authors give practical guidance for the thousands of chip studies published each year. Clean batch handling, they show, is not optional polish but a core step.
europmc-pmc3053321:
Speliotes and a large consortium hunted in 2011 for common gene variants that raise the risk of fatty liver disease not caused by alcohol. Fat in the liver runs in families, yet only one gene region was firmly known. The team measured liver fat by scanning in more than seven thousand people from several population studies, then checked top hits in patients with biopsy proven disease.

Beyond confirming the known region, they tied variants near three other genes to liver fat and to disease in patients. Each variant behaved differently on blood fats, blood sugar traits, and body measures, so there is no single pattern. That split suggests fatty liver arises through several distinct biological routes. Knowing which route a patient carries could one day shape treatment. The study also validates scan based fat measurement as a stand in for biopsy in gene hunts.
europmc-pmc3059221:
Mukherjee and colleagues showed in 2011 how a common childhood virus disarms the cell's antiviral alarm by cutting two key adaptor proteins. Coxsackievirus B3 carries a scissor enzyme that the team found snipping both adaptors in infected cells. Those adaptors normally pass danger signals onward to trigger interferon, the cell's main antiviral messenger, and to order infected cells to self destruct.

Cutting one adaptor tore it away from the cell power stations where it must sit to work, silencing its signal. Cutting the second adaptor at both ends scrambled the signaling hub it assembles. Both cuts depended on the enzyme's scissor activity and hit precise sites. The result is a virus that muffles two alarm routes with one tool. Such tricks help explain how this virus establishes infection, and they name targets for future antiviral design.
europmc-pmc3072921:
Grammas made the case in 2011 that blood vessel damage and inflammation sit near the heart of Alzheimer disease, not at its edges. Alzheimer disease affects millions in the United States, its numbers are set to climb steeply, and no treatment yet slows its course. The review gathers evidence that vessel risk factors overlap heavily with Alzheimer risk factors, and that the vessel lining itself changes in the disease.

The lining of brain vessels acts like a chemical factory, releasing signals that can calm or inflame nearby tissue. In Alzheimer disease that lining appears to malfunction and release inflammatory and toxic products into the brain. Chronic inflammation links vessel disease and brain degeneration in both directions. The author argues this vessel and neuron partnership deserves the attention drug hunters have lavished on plaques. New treatments may come from fixing the vessel side of the disease.
europmc-pmc3094421:
Power and coauthors linked in 2011 long term exposure to traffic pollution with weaker thinking in older men. They studied close to seven hundred veterans in a long running aging study who took a battery of thinking tests over a decade. Exposure was estimated from a validated model of black carbon, the sooty marker of traffic exhaust, at each man's home.

For each doubling of exposure, the odds of scoring poorly on a standard mental screening test rose by about a third. Scores on a combined measure of the other tests also fell, by an amount similar to the effect of roughly two extra years of age. The screening result held after accounting for past lead exposure, while the combined score link weakened slightly. The authors add cognition to the list of harms tied to traffic air, and note the exposure is one cities can actually reduce.
europmc-pmc3116821:
Ole Vang and many co-authors issued recommendations on a grape and wine compound in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The compound had won fame for possible benefits against cancer, heart disease, and diabetes, and people were buying it as a supplement. Experts meeting in Denmark in 2010 asked what the published evidence actually supports.

Their verdict was cautious: results in animals look hopeful for several diseases, but human evidence is too weak to advise taking the compound beyond normal food amounts. Open questions include the right dose, side effects, and how the compound acts in the body. The group calls for proper human trials and clearer safety work before any health advice can be given.
europmc-pmc3128121:
Brett Williams and colleagues uncovered a two-stage chemical trick used by a crop fungus in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The fungus attacks an unusually wide range of plants and kills tissue to feed, relying on an acid it secretes as its main weapon. That acid seemed to both block and trigger plant defence chemistry, a puzzle the team set out to solve.

Using plants engineered to glow as their cell chemistry shifted, they showed the acid first makes host cells more chemically reduced, muting alarm signals and wall defences. Once settled, the fungus flips the setting, sparking harmful oxygen chemicals that drive host cell death, which feeds it. A mutant unable to make the acid failed entirely, unless researchers chemically reduced the tissue for it.
europmc-pmc3130021:
Maria Van Kerkhove and colleagues pooled hospital data from nineteen countries to find who fared worst in the 2009 flu pandemic, in a 2011 paper in PLoS Medicine. The new virus spread worldwide within months, and early reports disagreed on which patients were most at risk of severe illness. Their dataset covered roughly seventy thousand hospitalised patients.

Severe outcomes clustered in people with long-term illness, especially heart disease, chronic lung disease, and diabetes, echoing the risk pattern of seasonal flu. Newer signals, including obesity and pregnancy, appeared often in some countries, and indigenous communities were over-represented among severe cases in places. The authors aim the findings at vaccination and drug planning, so the highest-risk groups get protection first in future pandemics.
europmc-pmc3143121:
George Rogers and colleagues adapted a plate-based oxygen meter for isolated cell power stations in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. New machines can track breathing in many tiny wells at once, but they were built for whole cells stuck to the plate. Isolated mitochondria, the cell's energy engines, allow tighter control of fuel and demand, so the team rebuilt the method around them.

Working with mouse liver mitochondria, they found assay conditions quite unlike classic single-chamber methods. Only a few micrograms of material per well gave clean readings of resting, working, resting-again, and fully driven breathing, added step by step through injection ports. The protocol turns a cell tool into a fast screening platform for drugs and proteins that tune metabolism.
europmc-pmc3170621:
Andy Dickens and colleagues reviewed programmes tackling loneliness and isolation in older people in a 2011 paper in BMC Public Health. Isolation harms health and well-being, and a quarter of the population will soon be over sixty. Thirty-two trials and comparison studies of social interventions, published before mid 2009, met their criteria.

Group-based programmes improved at least one health outcome far more often than one-to-one schemes. Programmes where older people take an active part, rather than passively receiving visits, also did better, as did those built on a stated theory. Activity and support groups beat home visiting, and internet training fared worst. Oddly, programmes aimed squarely at isolated people did worse than open ones. Study quality was shaky overall, so the authors demand better trials.
europmc-pmc3210621:
Marcel Ale, Jørn Mikkelsen, and Anne Meyer wrote this 2011 critical review in Marine Drugs on fucoidan, a sulfated sugar chain found in brown seaweeds. Fucoidans have attracted interest for possible benefits such as fighting tumors and preventing blood clots. But batches differ widely, and the authors argue that how a fucoidan is extracted shapes what it can do.

They explain how the source seaweed, the chain's composition, and the number and placement of sulfate groups all influence biological activity. Extraction methods can preserve or damage those features, yet this step is often overlooked when results are compared. The review connects structure to function, giving researchers a guide for producing fucoidan with the properties a given application actually needs.
europmc-pmc3216421:
Val Jenkins and colleagues followed women with early breast cancer for three years. They tested whether additional treatments harm thinking and memory. The study appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. They assessed eighty-five women scheduled for chemotherapy, forty-three receiving hormone therapy or radiotherapy, and forty-nine healthy controls, before treatment and at later points.

On group averages, the treated women performed no worse than controls once age and intelligence were taken into account. Looking person by person, a minority in every group showed reliable decline on several tasks shortly after treatment, and fewer did later. Women whose treatment triggered menopause were more prone to early decline. Self-reported mental failures tracked distress and quality of life, not test scores. The authors conclude most women are unaffected or improve.
europmc-pmc3234221:
Michael Ziller and colleagues charted an understudied form of DNA methylation across human cell types in this 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Most methylation research concerns one sequence context, CpG. Methylation at other cytosines, called non-CpG methylation, was poorly mapped. The team analyzed seventy-six genome-scale methylation maps from stem cells and differentiated cells.

Non-CpG methylation proved to be largely a feature of pluripotent cells. It faded as cells specialized and nearly vanished in adult cell types. Then it reappeared when cells were reprogrammed back to stem cells. Its patterns varied a lot between stem cell lines and tracked the levels of the DNMT3 enzymes; reducing those enzymes cut it sharply. The mark also clustered near ordinary CpG methylation. The study clarifies where this extra layer of marking exists and what controls it.
europmc-pmc3245621:
Tao Liu and colleagues built Cistrome, a web platform for studying how gene activity is regulated, in this 2011 paper in Genome Biology. Experiments that map where regulatory proteins bind DNA, known as ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq, were generating data faster than labs could analyze them in a standard, reproducible way. Cistrome was designed to close that gap.

Built on the open-source Galaxy framework, the platform adds twenty-nine tools specific to these binding experiments. They span the whole workflow. The tools run from first-pass peak calling and correlation checks to linking binding sites with genome features. They also compare sites with gene expression and hunt for the short DNA motifs proteins recognize. The authors offer Cistrome as a shared, integrative workspace for transcriptional regulation studies.
europmc-pmc3295821:
Ramirez and co-authors examined how gut bacteria shape dengue infection in mosquitoes, in work published in 2012. Dengue virus spreads between people through Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and puts billions at daily risk. The mosquito gut hosts microbes that it needs to develop, and those microbes also interact with its immune defenses.

Mosquitoes carrying certain bacteria taken from wild mosquitoes were much less likely to become infected with dengue. The bacteria seemed to switch on a low level immune activity that worked against the virus. Infection itself then changed how many bacteria the gut carried. The results point to the gut community as a possible lever for breaking dengue transmission.
europmc-pmc3311621:
Lam and a large team linked leaky gut walls and changed gut bacteria to fat inflammation in obese mice, reporting in 2012. Belly fat in obesity becomes inflamed and drives insulin problems, but what starts that inflammation is unclear. The team fed mice a diet rich in saturated fat and measured gut barrier strength, gut bacteria, and inflammation in several fat depots and organs.

Fat fed mice developed weaker colon barriers, with looser seals between gut cells and more inflammatory signals in the colon wall. Their gut bacteria shifted too, with one helpful genus falling and another rising, and both shifts tracked the barrier weakness. Fat hugging the gut became packed with immune cells and inflammatory signals, while fat under the skin stayed quiet. The authors argue that gut trouble helps ignite the metabolic problems of obesity.
europmc-pmc3334621:
Cloonan and colleagues investigated whether variant forms of tiny gene regulating RNAs do real work or are mere noise, in a 2011 study. Deep sequencing often finds these variants, called isomiRs, which differ slightly from the standard form of a microRNA. Their patterns are too orderly to be random, hinting at a function, but none had been proven.

Sequencing ten adult human tissues with a custom analysis pipeline, the team found variants behaving much like the standard molecules and tracking their levels closely. Variants were found riding the cell's protein making machinery just as often as standard forms. When the team fed both kinds into cells and measured the effects, they suppressed heavily overlapping sets of genes and pathways. The verdict is that variants are working partners, which helps explain how such short molecules achieve precise control.
europmc-pmc3338721:
Sikweyiya and Jewkes asked people who had answered a survey about gender based violence how the experience felt, reporting in 2012. Ethics boards worry that asking about abuse and trauma may distress participants or put them in danger at home. The study was nested inside a South African household survey on violence, and the team interviewed thirteen men and ten women in depth afterward.

Most participants valued the interview as a rare safe chance to tell their story, and nobody said the questions caused lasting emotional or physical harm. Some did relive painful events and felt temporary sadness. A gender split appeared around risk: some women feared a partner's anger if the survey's full contents came out, and a few received threats, though none were assaulted. Men reported no such reactions. The authors urge protocols that build in support and protection for this minority.
europmc-pmc3410521:
Ngugi, Bottomley, Kleinschmidt, Sander, and Newton pooled epilepsy surveys in 2010 to size the world's burden of the condition. Epilepsy is among the most common brain disorders, yet world estimates were rough and rarely separated active cases needing treatment. Their meta-analysis sorted studies into developed countries and urban or rural areas of developing ones.

Lifetime epilepsy ran several times more common in rural developing areas than in rich countries. Active epilepsy in rich countries affected roughly five people per thousand, amounting to millions of cases, while developing-country totals ran far higher. Small studies and rural settings reported the largest rates, and adult studies outscored child ones. The numbers, they argue, should guide treatment planning.
europmc-pmc3444121:
Liu and colleagues surveyed gas sensing technology in 2012, the instruments that sniff out gases for industry, safety, and research. Each sensing principle suits some jobs and fails others, so engineers keep refining calibration and design. The review sorts the field by the physical change each sensor exploits.

Methods that read electrical changes get the fullest treatment, split by sensing material. The roster runs from polymers and carbon nanotubes to metal oxide semiconductors and moisture-absorbing films. Optical, heat-based, sound-based, and chromatography approaches are sketched more briefly. The authors compare technologies on sensitivity and selectivity, the two scores that matter most, and dissect what drives each. Several routes to better scores are listed, along with directions for future development.
europmc-pmc3460821:
Yang and a large team reported in 2012 that small molecules switching on the protein SIRT1 can cool inflammation by stripping tags from a master immune switch. Chronic inflammation feeds many diseases of aging, and the switch, NF-kB, sits at its center. SIRT1 was already known to quiet the switch by removing an acetyl tag from its p65 part.

The team built a cell assay to measure that tag directly. Their activator compounds sped tag removal, blunted the switch's response to an inflammatory trigger, and cut release of a key cytokine from stimulated cells, all dependent on SIRT1. In mice given a bacterial toxin, one compound lowered two inflammatory cytokines. The work validates a fresh class of anti-inflammatory drugs.
europmc-pmc3566921: miR-125 got a family review. This 2013 paper reviews the many jobs of the miR-125 family. The authors map the functions. Their review guides genetics. Sun's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3580721: Drugs got a blood-level bible. This 2012 paper lists safe and toxic blood levels of nearly 1,000 drugs. The authors reveal the levels. Their work guides toxicology. Schulz's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3585121: Fungi got an alkaloid genome study. This 2013 paper maps alkaloid gene spots in plant-friendly fungi. The authors reveal the dynamics. Their work guides agriculture. Schardl's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped fungal chemistry.
europmc-pmc3615021: Cirrhosis got a rifaximin study. This 2013 paper tests rifaximin's effect on gut germs. The authors reveal the shift. Their work guides liver doctors. Bajaj's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped liver care.
europmc-pmc3618321: Gene sets got GSVA. This 2013 paper introduces GSVA for gene-set scoring. The authors reveal the method. Their work spread through labs. Hänzelmann's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide.
europmc-pmc3652521: Leaf pores got a drought-action review. This 2013 paper reviews leaf-pore action in drought. The authors map the control. Their review guides agriculture. Daszkowska-Golec's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped crop science. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3669621: Cancer got a nitric-oxide review. This 2013 paper reviews nitric oxide's role in cancer. The authors map the links. Their review guides oncology. Choudhari's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer drugs. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3679821: Air pollution got a heart-lung review. This 2013 paper reviews dirty air and heart-lung deaths. The authors weigh the evidence. Their review guides policy. Hoek's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped clean-air rules. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3682121: Brains got a tACS review. This 2013 paper reviews tACS brain stimulation. The authors map the mechanisms. Their review guides neuroscience. Herrmann's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped brain-stimulation science. The review is widely taught. Labs rely on it.
europmc-pmc3781321: Spines got a CYFIP1 study. This 2013 paper finds CYFIP1 builds dendritic spines. The authors reveal the building. Their work guides neuroscience. De Rubeis's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped brain development.
europmc-pmc3820521: Care got a family-doctor review. This 2012 paper reviews the impact of family doctors. The author maps the gains. Their review guides policy. Shi's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped health systems. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3823921: Cancer got a red-wine-compound study. This 2013 paper finds a red-wine compound blocks colon invasion. The authors reveal the block. Their work guides oncology. Ji's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped nutrition science.
europmc-pmc3876121: Brains got a rust-and-rot review. This 2013 paper reviews cell rust in brain decay. The authors map the rust. Their review guides neurology. Li's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped dementia research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3885521: Therapy got a which-treatment-wins demo. This 2014 paper demos matching patients to treatments. The authors reveal the method. Their work guides psychiatry. DeRubeis's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped therapy science.

flammarion-death-and-its-mystery-before-:
Camille Flammarion was a French star man with a love of the strange. His Death and Its Mystery ran to three books from 1921. Book one, Before Death, came out in the dress of E. S. Brooks. It deals with signs of the soul at work while men still live.

Dreams that come true, views at a range, and deaths felt far off fill the text. Flammarion stacks tale on tale from his vast post bag of years. He holds the count too great to brush off as chance. The set is the great store of the field in its late prime.
fontenelle-histoire-des-oracles-french-1:
Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle, the French man of letters, wrote his Histoire des oracles from the learning of the Dutch scholar Van Dale. This edition of 1721 kept the work before French readers. Fontenelle treats the pagan oracles of Greece and Rome, once thought to speak with the voices of gods or demons.

His verdict is elegant and deadly. The oracles were priestly frauds, kept up for profit and power, and they faded when politics changed. Wit does the work of demolition in graceful French prose. The book became the Enlightenment's classic doubting account of pagan divination. Oracles, one might say, were laughed out of court by the politest executioner in Paris.
frus-1861-d121:
Charles Faulkner wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 April 1861. The dispatch is document 121 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Faulkner stayed at the Paris post until Dayton could arrive. His April report came three days after Fort Sumter, from a capital full of war talk. It shows an outgoing envoy still serving the new chief through the handover. His service bridged two parties and two cabinets in the space of a few weeks. Bridging two cabinets in weeks was a strain few envoys of the age could match.
frus-1861-d21:
Henry Sanford, the American minister to Belgium, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 May 1861. The dispatch is document 21 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Brussels sat close to both Paris and London, and Sanford prized news from each. His reports mixed court talk with press and market word. For Washington, such letters were a cheap way to keep eyes on Europe's mood in the war's first spring. Belgium's king, Leopold, had wide family ties in Europe, which made Brussels talk worth hearing. Talk in Brussels often reached Seward before the same news came by formal note.
frus-1861-d221:
