By the date of 22 November 1861, Seward had new word ready for Mr. Marsh. Congress received it as Document 221 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the autumn of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d121:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, dated 7 August 1862. Congress received it as Document 121 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d21:
By the date of 11 February 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 21 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d221:
On 1 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart of the British legation, in a letter printed as Document 221 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter opened the month's run of Seward-Stuart exchanges.

July began with McClellan's army pulling back from Richmond, a retreat that looked like defeat abroad. Foreign governments read Union weakness as a reason to push for a truce. Against that mood, Seward kept his tone even and his letters frequent. This one belongs to the effort to steady nerves in the first days of a bad month. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d321:
Two Dayton reports are dated 3 September 1862, and the first stands as Document 321 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went from William L. Dayton in Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Dayton wrote three days after Bull Run, before the defeat's full weight had reached Paris. The French government was then drafting its proposal for a joint truce, the fall's central danger. Reports from these days show the envoy gathering the court's mood while the ground shifted under his information, a fair picture of his craft. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d421:
On 30 May 1862 Horace J. Perry reported from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward, five days after his last letter home. The report is Document 421 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Frequent short reports kept Washington current in an age when mail moved by steamer. Perry covered the Spanish court's view of the war, its Cuban concerns, and its part in the Mexican affair. In the last days of May 1862, French forces had just been checked at Puebla, news that changed the tone in Madrid. Perry's dispatches let a reader follow that shift as the legation saw it, week by week.
frus-1862-d521:
On 24 September 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His report is Document 521 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Pike's letter was dated two days after Lincoln issued the preliminary emancipation order, but the news had not yet reached the Netherlands. He wrote instead of the Dutch scene as it stood: cautious, commercial, and waiting on American battle news. The gap between the date on the page and the facts on the ground is the story of all these letters. Seward, reading in October, could correct for it; the modern reader should too, and will find the Hague file a clear window on that lag.
frus-1862-d621:
On 10 January 1862 Jacob S. Haldeman reported from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 621 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Haldeman opened the year reporting Swedish goodwill and the north's reading of the war after the Trent settlement. Sweden and Norway sent the Union settlers and sailors rather than trouble, and their government's neutrality was never in question. Still, Seward wanted every post reporting, and Stockholm's letters fixed the friendly north in his survey of Europe. The report is part of the early-1862 round of the Department's work. In that round it confirmed, capital by capital, where it stood. The crisis with Britain had by then passed.
frus-1863p1-d121:
Third in its set comes this letter of 16 March 1863 from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 121 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By the third sheet, a batch turns from the great heads to the finer ones. Seward's file for Britain held many small claims and talks, each worth its own page. This letter is the third of the 16 March set. It shows the depth of the brief that one envoy carried, and the care with which Washington stocked him for it.
frus-1863p1-d21:
For the last time in 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 29 December. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 21 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, Seward's last to London in the old year.

Seward wrote days before the freedom edict for the enslaved took force on New Year's Day. That act would change the war's face abroad, and his envoys had to be ready to speak for it. This letter belongs to that hinge in time. It shows Washington briefing its London man at the close of a year that had tested the Union and its foreign ties alike.
frus-1863p1-d221:
The mail from London dated 25 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 221 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d321:
A formal note dated 13 November 1862 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 321 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d421:
From the British legation in Washington on 23 March 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 421 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada bordered the Union along a long, thinly guarded line. British worries about that frontier, and American worries about plots hatched there, fed part of this mail. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d521:
Under the date 21 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d621:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 22 September 1863 and wrote to William Stuart, Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863. With Lyons away from Washington, Stuart kept the British side of the correspondence going through the autumn of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d121: A second message from Stalin to Roosevelt dated November 12, 1943 stands as Document 121 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It pairs with the Stalin letter just before it, in the last exchange before the Tehran meeting sixteen days later. The catalog record gives the date and the two names and nothing narrower. The letter is kept in the Foreign Relations series, in the voyage run of papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d21: After a gap of more than three weeks, Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on August 8, 1943, and the message became Document 21 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The pause and the return both matter in this correspondence, which rose and fell with the war's turns. The record gives the date and the two leaders' names only. Printed in the Foreign Relations series, the letter resumes the thread that led to Tehran in November.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d221:
Minutes record President Roosevelt's meeting with the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 15 November 1943. It was held at two in the afternoon in his cabin aboard the battleship Iowa, as he sailed toward the Cairo conference. The printed excerpts cover French forces, Balkan strategy, and high command.

On rearming France, the chiefs note a plan to equip eleven or twelve French divisions. Admiral Leahy warns that de Gaulle would use such divisions as a lever for power in France itself. Roosevelt orders the present plan to proceed, with no new commitments. He also approves the chiefs' Balkan and eastern Mediterranean policy paper as it stands, and states his wish that General Marshall command the whole effort against Germany.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d321:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 407, in revised form, at Cairo on 26 November 1943, setting the broad lines to follow at the coming conference with the Soviets at Tehran. It is the Anglo-American playbook for their first staff talks with Stalin's officers.

The Western chiefs should first agree their own strategy in Europe. They should win their leaders' approval before facing the Soviets. They should consult each other before answering any Soviet proposal. And they should hold an agreed line on Balkan or Aegean operations. On Turkey they will back the Soviet wish to force her into the war, but refuse any diversion of forces that harms approved operations. The paper also reverses the Moscow pattern: this time the West should make specific requests of the Soviets, from bombing coordination to Siberian ports and air bases against Japan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d421:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, telegraphed Secretary of State Hull from Tehran on 3 December 1943, number 1086, reporting the Declaration on Iran signed there on 1 December. The message gives the declaration's contents in four numbered points for Washington's record.

The three powers recognize Iran's contribution to the war against the common enemy. They see that the war has caused Iran special economic difficulties, and state their intent to go on providing such economic help as they can. Iran's postwar economic problems are to receive full consideration from the international conferences and agencies dealing with such matters. And the three powers reaffirm their desire for Iran's sovereign independence and territorial integrity, under the Atlantic Charter. Dreyfus notes the declaration was issued at the Iranian prime minister's request, and judges it has strengthened the American position in Iran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d521:
Marshal Stalin wrote to President Roosevelt on December 20, 1943, less than three weeks after the two men met for the first time at Tehran. The message passed between the Soviet leader and the President in their direct wartime correspondence. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Stalin's messages to Roosevelt were usually brief, formal, and carefully weighed, and each one mattered out of proportion to its length. A December letter belongs to the season when the alliance was converting Tehran's promises into the campaigns of 1944. For readers, it is the Soviet voice in a record often told from Washington and London, speaking for itself.
frus-1944-quebec-d121:
Roosevelt answered Churchill's Warsaw telegrams on September 5, 1944, in a personal and secret message sent from Hyde Park. It is short, and it closes the urgent exchange that had run through the previous day. The president relied on a report from his Office of Military Intelligence about the fighting in the Polish capital.

That report claimed the fighting Poles had left Warsaw and the Germans held full control. On that basis Roosevelt said the relief problem had been solved by delay and German action, and nothing more could be done. He added that he had long been distressed by the failure to help Warsaw's defenders. He hoped Poland would still end the war among the victors.
frus-1944-quebec-d21:
Prime Minister Churchill sent this message to President Roosevelt on August 8, 1944, one of two from him bearing that date in the volume. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume's pre-conference papers.

Churchill's August correspondence pressed British concerns as American power grew: the Mediterranean, the future of Italy and Greece, and Britain's shrinking share of the common effort. Two messages in a day show him working several fronts at once. For readers, the message captures a prime minister determined that victory should not leave his country a spectator at its own alliance's table.
frus-1944-quebec-d221:
Hull pressed the Argentine meat question again on September 12, 1944, in a memorandum for Roosevelt's talks with Churchill. Effective implementation of American Argentine policy, he wrote, depended on British economic cooperation, and London had so far given only tentative, highly qualified promises. Rumor held that Britain intended to sign a four-year meat contract.

Hull argued the food situation made a long contract unnecessary. Judge Byrnes had reported production in Allied areas a third above normal, with war reserves becoming surplus at peace. Beef could reach Britain from America, Canada, Australia, and other South American suppliers, including America's surplus utility beef. He proposed more lend-lease beef in exchange for reduced British purchases in Argentina, and spot buying instead of any long agreement.
frus-1945-50-intel-d121:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark on 8 August 1946, the same day the National Intelligence Authority wrote to Clark. The FBI director's letter answers the board's move from inside the Justice Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Hoover rarely accepted a ruling against the bureau without putting his objection in writing to his own chief. His letter of 8 August belongs to the peak of the Latin American fight, when the board's decision on the field was being delivered. Readers can read the day whole: the authority's letter and Hoover's response, claim and counter-claim, preserved side by side. The volume's fairness in printing both is what makes it history rather than a victor's tale.
frus-1945-50-intel-d21:
General John Magruder, who now ran the Strategic Services Unit in the War Department, wrote to three intelligence chiefs at once on 1 October 1945. His unit was the surviving core of the dissolved OSS. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Magruder's letter went to the Army's intelligence chief, the Navy's, and the State Department's new research and intelligence head. That mailing list is the post-OSS world in miniature: three services and one department, each holding a piece. Readers meet here the man trying to keep the remnant alive while the pieces were argued over. His papers through the autumn form the volume's thread of survival, written from inside a unit that everyone expected to vanish.
frus-1945-50-intel-d221:
Dated 18 September 1947, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) to the Intelligence Advisory Board. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 221, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Congress was then debating the National Security Act, the law that would soon create the CIA and the National Security Council.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d321:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Group (Houston) addressed a memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) on 29 July 1947. The State Department prints it as document 321 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d421:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to the Army's assistant chief of staff for military intelligence, Bissell, on 8 May 1950. The memo is document 421 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Within weeks, war in Korea would test every part of the system these men ran. In May the work was still one of charts, duties, and shared reports. The memo shows the CIA chief dealing with Army intelligence at staff level, where the real links were made. Bissell's office linked the Army's field reports to the joint picture the CIA tried to build.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d121:
The Cabinet Committee could not agree on Germany, the Secretary of State told the President on 29 September 1944. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, sets the State Department's thinking against the Treasury's. It answers the Quebec paper of 15 September.

That Quebec paper, with its talk of the Ruhr, the Saar, and turning Germany into a farming and pastoral country, reflects mainly Secretary Morgenthau's views. The Treasury memorandum, Hull writes, is decidedly at odds with the line worked out in the State Department. He reports the practical ground already won: the surrender instrument has been approved in Washington, and the American and British zones were settled at Quebec.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d21: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on 18 November 1944, raising the Soviet channel again after a run of Churchill letters. The message is document 21 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Any summit needed Stalin's agreement on timing and place, so presidential letters to Moscow carried weight that staff messages to the Soviet government could not match.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d221:
Leo Crowley, head of the Foreign Economic Administration, wrote to Stettinius on 13 January 1945 about Moscow's credit request. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, suggests the two men take the matter to the President together. Harriman's cables of 4 and 6 January had raised questions fit for the coming conference.

Enclosed is a rough draft of the points Crowley wants in Washington's reply, both to Molotov's proposal and to Gromyko's note on the Fourth Protocol. The first point draws a bright line. Projects under the Lend-Lease Act belong to the war supply program. They must be kept wholly apart from any projects financed by long-term credits for postwar needs. The study of those credits, the draft says, is now under way.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d321:
A group photograph and a famous memoir help the editors pin down one Malta meeting in this short note. The session's substance survives only in Secretary Stettinius's book. A few words more appear in Churchill's history and Admiral Leahy's memoir. Times and names come from the official trip log.

The note even prints the caption of an Army photo of the Combined Chiefs at Montgomery House on January 31. Marshall, King, Brooke, and Portal are all named in the frame. Small notes like this one let readers check the main record against pictures and later books. They anchor names and faces to a single crowded week.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d421:
Antonov came back with answers, and Kuter's minutes of February 9, 1945, record them. The Soviet general opened by saying he had laid every point before Stalin. His first day's comments had been personal views only. Now he could give definite and official replies to each question.

On Far East operations, he reported no change of intent and only minor changes of plan since October. Units meant to move east early in 1945 were now fighting in the center of the Russian front. Their transfer would wait. The minutes catch the moment the Pacific bargain moved from asking to terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d121:
Churchill proposed announcing the press ban in advance in telegram number 103 to President Truman, sent July 4, 1945. The message is document 121 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The three leaders had already agreed that reporters would not be allowed at Terminal, while photographers would.

A public announcement now, Churchill argues, will avoid disappointment and stop newspapers from sending their best people to Berlin. Each government should let it be known that no press will be admitted and that only official communiqués, issued as agreed from time to time, will come out of the meeting. He says he is sending a similar telegram to Stalin, who, a note adds, accepted the idea on July 6.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d21: Stalin accepted at once in this reply to Truman, dated May 20, 1945, and given here in translation. He had received the President's message about the arrival of Hopkins and Harriman in Moscow by May 26. He readily accepted the proposal to meet them. The date — May 26 — was quite convenient for him. The short letter, transmitted through the Soviet Embassy in Washington, opened the door the Hopkins mission would walk through six days later.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d221:
Joseph Davies set out his creed on foreign policy in a memorandum dated July 3, 1945. The paper is document 221 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Davies, who chaired the President's War Relief Control Board and had been ambassador to Moscow, sent it to Truman along with his survey of the conference agenda.

Foreign policy, Davies writes, is nothing more than rules governing a country's relations with peoples outside its borders. Its first purpose is protection from invasion and attack, freedom from fear. Its next is to preserve the people's standard of living and way of life, freedom from want. He urges clear statements of American policy, defense of the western hemisphere as a neighborhood of friends, and grounding in justice, liberty, and the Four Freedoms.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d321:
Censorship is the point Melbourne adds in his Bucharest cable of July 15, 1945. He first notes General Schuyler's two messages of July 14, which set out the least changes needed in how the Rumanian armistice was run. Melbourne then turns to Article 16 of that armistice, which covered censorship.

Control of censorship, he wrote, was a great political and cultural weapon held by Soviet officials alone. With the war over, he argued, three-power control of censorship could no longer be put off on military grounds. While the armistice lasted, Washington should claim a right to help decide what Rumanians could print and read.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d421:
German coal is the subject of Murphy's despatch No. 539 from supreme headquarters, dated June 28, 1945. He transmits a staff memorandum on the present coal situation, written by his economic officer Rainey. With it goes the Potter-Hyndley report on coal in northwest Europe, dated June 1945.

Murphy points Washington above all to three paragraphs of that report's summary. The coal supply problem in western Europe, he stresses, is extremely critical. Everything touching the production and movement of German coal must take the highest priority. Shortages in France, Belgium, Holland, Denmark, and Norway demand export of all available western German coal if civil order is to survive the winter.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d521:
Reconstruction aid for Poland is urged in a briefing book extract dated June 29, 1945, from the paper on suggested American policy toward Poland. To carry out the policy of a truly independent, democratic Polish state, it argues, America should be ready to help. Subject to legislative authority, it would assist through credits or otherwise. The help would rebuild Polish agriculture and industry.

Immediate action to supply urgently needed equipment and relief materials, it says, will promote a healthy American influence in Poland in an enduring way. That influence bears especially on the holding of free elections, the final step in the Yalta program. The efforts, the extract adds, should be national rather than international in form.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d621:
Ambassador Harriman sent extracts of a study of Soviet oil output from Moscow on June 29, 1945. The secret report is document 621 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It was prepared for U.S. talks on oil and reparations that summer.

The study puts Soviet crude output at about 21.5 million tons in 1945. That is down from 31.1 million tons in 1940. Baku's fields faded for lack of new drilling during the war. German forces wrecked the Maikop field and much of Grozny, and the big Bashkiria field also fell off. The study concludes that the Soviet Union cannot export oil in the early postwar years, save in small amounts for set ends. It also expects Moscow to keep its grip on oil output in the parts of Eastern Europe it holds.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1021:
American staff drafted this undated working paper on separating the Ruhr and Rhineland from Germany. It argues that disarmament alone cannot guarantee Germany will never attack again. So long as the Ruhr and Rhineland stay under German rule, the paper says, Germany keeps the means to wage a major war.

The paper proposes five rulings. The two regions would be permanently detached from Germany. Before occupation ends, they would form an international protectorate under the United Nations Security Council. Belgium, France, and the Netherlands would run it for the council. Its output would serve all Europe without favor. Truman's own note on the copy reads: not presented, but discussed; decided they should remain in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1121:
London's team tabled this proposal on 19 July 1945, the third day of the Potsdam Conference. Like the Soviet paper of the day before, it set down an opening stand for the three-way talks. Each team wanted its terms on paper before the trading grew hard.

Britain had fought the war for six years and was worn down in men, money, and ships. Its team sought a peace that guarded British interests without taking on new burdens. A formal proposal from the first week fixes that starting offer in the team's own words. The final terms can be read against it to see what London held and what it gave up.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1221:
A second Hurley dispatch to the Secretary of State bears the same date, 29 July 1945. Two cables in a day from the China post signal a file moving too fast for one report. Hurley's embassy dealt with a government, an army, and a rival party all at once.

Back-to-back dispatches let an envoy split subjects: one for the urgent, one for the standing picture. Together they kept Washington's China brief full during the summit's close. This one is the day's companion piece. Read as a pair, the two cables show the tempo of a post where the next war was already taking shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1321:
Parten, chief of staff of the American reparations team, wrote to Pauley, its head, on 21 July 1945. The note ran inside the mission that judged Germany's capacity to pay. Parten ran its staff work; Pauley carried its findings to the summit.

Internal notes of a mission fix facts, assign tasks, and ready the chief's brief. This one dates from the heart of the reparations fight at Potsdam. It shows the mission's machine at work behind its famous head. The figures that leaders quoted in the great rooms began in staff traffic of exactly this kind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1421:
The Soviet delegation at Potsdam submitted a text on 14 July 1945, in the volume's closing run of conference papers. The date falls just before the conference formally opened, when delegations were tabling their opening positions.

Early texts at a summit stake out ground. A paper tabled before the leaders even sat down shows a delegation arriving with its asks already drafted. Readers can follow this Soviet text forward through the talks: which of its points the final protocol kept, and which the other powers bargained away. The closing run of the volume gathers many such texts, letting the drafting fight be read whole.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-121:
State Department minutes record a meeting held on July 27, 1945, late in the Potsdam Conference. By then Attlee had returned as Britain's new prime minister, and the talks pushed toward their close. Formal minutes like these anchor the second Potsdam volume. They state the business done in a sober, ordered form.

The worth of minutes grows with time. Memories fade and claims conflict, but the written record holds. Readers find who spoke, what was proposed, and what was left for the final text. Set beside the note-takers' rougher sets, these minutes give the day's work its official shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-21:
Thompson's minutes record the foreign ministers' meeting of July 19, 1945, with Eden in the chair. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The day's agenda held German political questions, Poland, and German economic problems.

Before the agenda, Byrnes asked to reopen one point in the Council of Foreign Ministers paper. Its third section limited council duties to governments that had signed surrender terms. Some governments, Byrnes noted, were at war but had not signed armistice terms. France, for example, was at war with Italy without being such a signatory. He asked that the drafting committee reconcile the rival views on the wording. Molotov said the question was not quite clear to him. The exchange shows the council's membership rules still unsettled three days into the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d721:
Hurley wrote once more to the Secretary of State on August 1, 1945, in document 721. It is the last of his letters in this run of the second Potsdam volume. The pair of August 1 letters bookend the conference's closing day. From Chungking, Hurley kept Washington's China policy tied to the talks in Germany.

A closing letter in a series has summary force. The ambassador states where his mission stands as the ground shifts. Readers gain a sense of China as the conference left it: ally, problem, and prize at once. The document ends the Byrnes-Hurley thread on the day Potsdam itself ended.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d821:
Schoenfeld reported from Hungary on July 26, 1945, in document 821. The representative in Budapest wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His letters, with Barnes's and Melbourne's, build the volume's Balkan wall. This one entered the second Potsdam volume as the conference neared its end.

Three missions reporting in parallel give readers a regional picture. Hungary's path can be set beside Bulgaria's and Rumania's. Schoenfeld's part of the wall is steady and detailed. The document shows a professional doing his duty in a post the maps were leaving behind. His reports remain a prime source for Hungary's first postwar summer.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d921:
Soviet delegates proposed this plan for advance deliveries from Germany, circulated at Potsdam in late July 1945. Until a permanent agency for reparations exists, urgent removals would go to nations that suffered, to help them rebuild. Each delivery would later be booked as reparations, restitution, or a purchase.

A Berlin sub-commission of the Allied Commission on Reparations would run the system. It would list the industries open for removals and approve deliveries from them. Raw materials from current output or stocks would need its approval too. The plan also demands uniform records of account. Each occupying power must report all property removed from Germany within six months.
frus-1969-1976-chile-vol-21:
Volume twenty-one of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1969 to 1976 covers Chile from 1969 to 1973. The State Department's Office of the Historian compiled the volume from declassified records. It documents one of the darkest chapters of Cold War policy in Latin America.

The papers follow Washington's alarm at Salvador Allende's election in 1970. They record the order to make the economy scream, the Track I pressure to block Allende's confirmation, and the Track II covert action run beside it. Aid cuts, coup plotting, and contacts with Chilean officers fill the file. The record ends with the September 1973 coup that brought Pinochet to power.
galsworthy-to-let-1921:
John Galsworthy published To Let in 1921 as the closing novel of The Forsyte Saga proper. The title comes from the empty Forsyte houses standing to let after the First World War. Galsworthy set the story in 1920, with a new generation in charge.

Fleur Forsyte, Soames's daughter, falls in love with Jon, the son of Irene and Jolyon. Neither knows at first why their families hate the match. The old scandal of Soames and Irene rises again to crush the young lovers. Beneath the romance, Galsworthy records an age passing: the solid Forsyte world dissolving into a looser, sadder England.
gao-gaoreports-b-293105-21: Greenleaf Construction tripled its April 2007 protest — three case numbers, one building fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three claims. The firm challenged the awards as unfair; the call weighs each claim with care. Builders get the same careful hearing as everyone else.
gao-gaoreports-b-295421: Gray Graphics disputed a February 2005 print contract award, and GAO's ruling is the final word. The printer's protest went through the full review process. The ink dried on the verdict at last. The verdict stood. The process was fair. The word was final.
gao-gaoreports-b-296221: Linguistic Systems took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297121: Cartographics took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297321: Laerdal Medical doubled its December 2005 protest — two case numbers, one medical-supply fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297421: STR took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-311321: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Guam Shipyard. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-400321: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Delex Systems, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-221: Means-tested program access data got a GAO nudge in 2005, and the report says the information could be a management tool. The review makes the case. The poor deserved the reachable aid. The tool had to be used. The poor deserved the reachable aid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-421: Special gasoline blends got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the fuels cut emissions but complicated supply. The findings balance the clean air and the costs. The report warns that the drivers deserved honest fuel. The blends had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-521: DOD's problem disbursements kept coming in 2005, and GAO's report says long-standing accounting weaknesses caused inaccurate records. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the defense dollars deserved honest books. The weaknesses had to be resolved. The defense dollars deserved honest books.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-621: Storefront banks' boom got a GAO look in 2005, and the report sizes up the growth and the rule gaps. The findings do the math. The report warns that the lenders deserved consistent rules. The lenders deserved consistent rules. The growth had to be sized.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-721: Clean Water Act planning needed better resources in 2005, and GAO's report says improved planning would help EPA respond to changing needs. The findings demand the foresight. The report warns that the waterways deserved prepared protection. The planning had to be improved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-821: Welfare work counts needed one yardstick in 2005, and GAO's report says HHS had to watch the states' math. The findings demand the uniformity. The report warns that the welfare-to-work numbers deserved honesty. The welfare-to-work numbers deserved honesty.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1021: Exotic mortgages got a second GAO look in 2006, and the report again says the default impact was unclear, though disclosures could improve. The findings repeat the warning. The report cautions that the housing boom's loans needed sunlight. The borrowers had to be warned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-21: Small-town air service projects had mixed results in 2006, and GAO's report says initial development efforts achieved uneven outcomes. The findings balance the wins and misses. The report warns that the rural runways deserved honest assessment. The results had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-421: Data sellers' privacy habits got graded in 2006, and GAO's report checks how agencies and brokers kept the key rules. The findings grade the habits. The report warns that the personal files deserved careful hands. The dossiers deserved principled handling. The rules had to be kept.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-521: Military absentee voting improved for 2004, and GAO's 2006 report says assistance to troops and overseas citizens increased. The findings give the credit. The report warns that the ballots from the front deserved a fair fight. The assistance had to continue. The front's ballots deserved a fair fight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-821: Rail transit safety oversight needed leadership in 2006, and GAO's report says more federal direction would enhance the state safety program. The findings demand the guidance. The report warns that the subway riders deserved a strong watchdog. The oversight had to be firm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-121: Federal law enforcement got a GAO census in 2007, and the report surveys the civilian functions and authorities. The findings map the badges. The report shows who carried a federal gun and why. The count brought clarity. The badge count brought clarity.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-21: Retirement savers needed clearer fee disclosures in 2007, and GAO's report says 401(k) participants and the Labor Department deserved better information. The findings demand the transparency. The report warns that the do-it-yourself pension had hidden costs. The fees had to be visible.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-221: Other countries handled nuclear trash better in 2007, and GAO's report says foreign approaches to low-level waste held lessons for America. The findings look abroad with real humility. The report's point is sobering: the glow lasts millennia, so borrow the best ideas you can.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-321: The war memorials' books got audited in 2007, and GAO's report grades the Battle Monuments Commission's finances for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The report shows the graves of the fallen get honest books. The honored dead got honest accounting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-521: Job rehab for the disabled needed better report cards in 2007 — GAO's report says improved data and methods could lift state earnings results. The findings target the vocational system's blind spots. The report's goal is plain: jobs that pay, proven with real numbers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-921: Thirstier cars, tighter rules? GAO's 2007 report says reworking fuel-economy standards could meaningfully cut the oil burned by cars and light trucks. The findings give Congress the efficiency math behind the mileage debate. The report frames the pump as a policy lever, not just a price.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-21: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report arguing that U.S. efforts to combat nuclear smuggling networks need better data. Programs to stop the spread of nuclear weapons materials suffered from weak information on proliferation risks and on whether countermeasures were working. GAO's findings call for sharper measurement so policymakers can tell which nonproliferation dollars are actually making the world safer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-221: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at head Start: A More Comprehensive Risk Management Strategy and Data Improvements Could Further Strengthen Program Oversight. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-321: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on federal User Fees: Substantive Reviews Needed to Align Port-Related Fees with the Programs They Support. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
garland-daughter-middle-border-1921:
Garland's Daughter of the Middle Border won the 1922 Pulitzer Prize for biography, a note in this printing stresses. Pictures show his mother Isabel and his wife Zulime Taft, called the new daughter. Book one opens with his first winter in Chicago.

The sequel carries his life from the pioneer boy of the first volume into manhood. Marriage to Zulime Taft and years as a striving writer fill the middle chapters. A return East and a backward look at the frontier close the arc. Issued in 1921, the book crowned the career of the great chronicler of the Middle Border in fitting style.
geley-unconscious-conscious-1921:
Gustave Geley sought the root of strange feats in From the Unconscious to the Conscious, his book of 1921. Geley ran the chief lab for such study in Paris. He holds that man is not a fixed self, but a stream that flows from a deep hid source. That source, pressed, can push out the stuff that forms shapes in the dark room.

His scheme tries to join mind science to the seance. Death, to him, is a shift of the stream, not its end. The book is the creed back of his lab. Its bold reach still draws fans.
graves-truth-about-the-protocols-1921:
Philip Graves, a Times writer in Constantinople, blew the Protocols hoax wide open in three pieces in August 1921. The Times put them in book form in London the same year. The Protocols claimed to be a secret Jewish plan to rule the world, and had spread far.

Graves sets the Protocols side by side with Joly's talk in hell of 1864. Line by line, the fake is shown to be a copy, with names swapped and the rest near word for word. His proof is the key work that named the Protocols a fake for all to see.
hamsun-pan-worster-1921:
Knut Hamsun published Pan in Norway in 1894, and W. W. Worster Englished it for Knopf in 1921. Lieutenant Thomas Glahn spends a summer in a hut in Nordland, hunting and fishing with his dog Aesop. At the trading post he meets Edvarda, the merchant's daughter, and falls into a proud, halting love.

Glahn tells the tale himself, two years later, and his telling keeps slipping. Pride, jealousy, and wild joy in the northern summer drive him to strange acts. Hamsun builds the novel from Glahn's senses: light, scent, blood, and weather. Worster's translation became the classic English Pan. The book stands apart from Hunger and Growth of the Soil as his lyric peak.
hd-hymen-1921:
Hymen, published in 1921, is a collection of poems by H. D., the pen name of Hilda Doolittle, the imagist poet Ezra Pound had launched in London. The title poem is a ritual piece for voices, built like a Greek chorus.

The poems take up marriage, myth, and the gods of Greece, retelling old stories through women's eyes. H. D.'s early imagism, with its hard, clear images, here grows more ceremonial and strange. Sea, heat, and white light run through the verse. The book shows a poet moving from imagist precision toward the mythic scale of her later epics.
heike-monogatari-sadler-1921:
A. L. Sadler translated the whole Heike Monogatari into English in two parts, in 1918 and 1921. The Tale of the Heike is Japan's great medieval war epic, telling the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185. The Taira clan, called the Heike, rises to glittering power, then falls to the Minamoto in five years of civil war.

Blind lute priests first spread the tale, chanting its battles and deaths across Japan. Its opening lines on the bell of impermanence set the Buddhist tone of the whole. Sadler's version, from the Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan, first gave English the complete epic. Pride, loyalty, and the fall of the mighty fill its pages.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: The last volume of Carlyle's life of Frederick the Great brings the huge work to its close. Thirteen years of toil end here, in a tribute to the hero-king. The crown of Carlyle's life work, and of Victorian life-writing at its grandest.
hobhouse-rational-good-1921:
The Rational Good, published in 1921, is Hobhouse's study in the logic of practice, his fullest statement in ethics. The liberal philosopher asks what makes a good rational: not appetite, not command, but harmony realized through reason.

He defines the good as a harmony of feelings, purposes, and relations that can grow without internal war, and tests pleasure, duty, and perfection against it. Social ethics follows: a rational society is one whose order lets each part develop. The argument is systematic and humane. The book crowns the philosophical side of the New Liberalism Hobhouse had helped to build.
howard-bury-mount-everest-reconnaissance:
The first Everest reconnaissance of 1921 came home with more than maps in 1922. Mount Everest: The Reconnaissance, 1921, the official account led by Charles Howard-Bury, tells the march to the great peak. His party crossed Tibet and probed the routes to the top.

On the high snows they found tracks they could not name, and the report prints the find in plain words. Porters called the maker of the tracks a wild man of the snows. From that report grew the Abominable Snowman of world fame. The book is thus both climbing history and the start of a mystery.
husserl-logische-untersuchungen-1921:
Husserl issued a second edition of his Logical Investigations in the years around 1921, revising the work that had made him famous in 1900. By then he was the master of a movement, and his own thought had moved on through the Ideas of 1913. The new edition let him bring the young breakthrough closer to the mature system.

He rewrote passages, added clarifications, and rethought parts of the sixth investigation in light of his later work. Some sections he left standing, judging them still sound. The result is phenomenology's classic in its definitive form, with the founder's second thoughts visible on the page. Comparing the two editions shows a philosopher arguing with his younger self. The volume is thus a document in the history of his thought, as well as a work of philosophy.
hutton-the-angami-nagas-1921:
John Henry Hutton worked as a colonial administrator in the Naga Hills of Assam, and he wrote about the peoples he governed. His 1921 book studies the Angami Nagas, one of the major groups of those hills, drawing on years of direct contact and local testimony.

Hutton describes village government, kinship, farming, and the great feasts of merit by which men gained honor and standing. He also covers the ancestor cult, omens, and the customs that shaped birth, marriage, and death. The book became a standard source on the Angami and a model of the administrator-ethnography of its period.
hutton-the-sema-nagas-1921:
Hutton wrote this 1921 volume as a companion to his book on the Angami Nagas, turning here to their neighbors the Sema, now often called Sumi. Like its partner, the study grew out of his years as an administrator in the Assam hills.

The account centers on the morung, the bachelors' hall where young men lived and learned tribal custom. Hutton also describes headhunting, warfare, farming, and the feasts that marked rank and wealth. Sema religion, with its spirits, omens, and rites, fills much of the book. Together the two volumes preserve a detailed picture of Naga life in the early twentieth century.
iamblichus-on-the-mysteries-taylor-1821:
Iamblichus wrote On the Mysteries in reply to a sharp foe of rite. Thomas Taylor gave the work English dress in 1821. Iamblichus was a Greek sage of the late Roman age. The book defends theurgy, the work of rites that lift the soul to the gods.

Porphyry had asked how mere rites could move high gods. Iamblichus holds that the gods gave the rites and work through them by their own will. Signs, names, and gifts all take their place in his scheme. The book is the base text for all rite magic of the West since.
il-proteo-metallico-o-sia-delle-trasform: Il proteo metallico, 1721. The metallic Proteus. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
j-p-jacobsen-mogens-and-other-stories-19:
Short tales by Jacobsen fill Mogens and Other Stories, given here in the 1921 English version. The title tale tells of young love, fresh and brief as spring. Other tales turn darker, with plague, fear, and death stalking their pages.

Jacobsen polished every sentence until it shone like a cut gem. Few writers in Danish have matched his care for sound, color, and mood. Love and plague sit side by side, beauty and dread in one hand. The book gathers the full range of his short fiction and shows why later writers held his craft in awe.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-21:
Isaac Jogues and his captivity dominate Volume 21, published in 1898. Thwaites covers Quebec and the Hurons in the years of Jogues's ordeal. Mohawk captors seized the priest, tortured him, and held him as a slave for months.

Jogues writes of his pain with a restraint that deepens its horror. Fingers crushed, body scarred, he still seeks chances to teach and baptize. Fellow priests report his calm faith under cruel, daily abuse. Many readers rank his letters the most famous captivity account in the set. A saint's suffering, told in his own quiet and steady words, fills this volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-ali-ibn-hiba:
Abu al-Ma'ali ibn Hibat Allah, an Egyptian Jewish physician, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He lived at Fustat, or old Cairo, at the end of the twelfth century. He served as physician to Saladin himself. After Saladin's death he attended the sultan's brother, al-Malik al-Adil.

The article draws on Ibn Abi Usaibi'ah, the Arabic historian of physicians. That source praises Abu al-Ma'ali's learning, generosity, and great influence at court. It also reports that almost all his children embraced Islam. He wrote many works and essays on medicine, but none has survived. One titled work on medicine is named in the entry. Steinschneider suggested he may have been Maimonides' brother-in-law, a link the article leaves as a guess. The entry preserves the outline of a court doctor's lost career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malachi-book-of:
Malachi, the last book of the Old Testament prophets, is analyzed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The Hebrew text has three chapters, while the Greek and Latin versions divide it into four. The King James Version follows the longer count. The entry notes that the final verse repeats the one before it, as in several other Bible books.

The article describes a book argued like a school debate. Its style is plainer and more prosaic than the other prophets'. The writer states a claim, voices the objections of his hearers, then presses his claim again. The contents fall into three parts. First, God rebukes priests who offer blemished animals on the altar. Next come men who left Jewish wives for heathen women. Last, a messenger is promised who will purify the people before judgment. The entry gives readers both the book's shape and its stern message.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mazliah-ben-eli:
Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn profile Mazliah ben Elijah ibn al-Bazak, an Italian Talmudist of the eleventh century, in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His surname, whose meaning is unknown, marks a family of Eastern Jews, and he knew Arabic well. He served as a dayyan, a religious judge, in Sicily. Then he crossed the world of Jewish learning to Pumbedita in Babylonia. There he heard the lectures of Hai Gaon, the last great head of the Babylonian academies.

Before returning to Europe after the death of Hai, Mazliah wrote an Arabic life of his teacher. It is the “Sirat R. Hai Gaon,” and he presented it to Samuel ha-Nagid. Later authors quoted it. Its sharpest observation was the friendship between Hai and the Christian Catholicos, whom Hai freely consulted on interpretation. The entry closes with the guess that this Mazliah taught Nathan ben Jehiel, author of the Aruk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-migration-10821:
Migration, the movement of Jews from country to country since the Exile, is treated in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 as nearly the whole of Jewish history in another form. Joseph Jacobs heads a team of four contributors on the article. Its boldest device tracks the center of Jewish population across the centuries, from Tarsus in the first century to Troyes in the twelfth.

By the mid-sixteenth century that center sat in Poland, pushed east by the expulsions from western Europe. The article puts numbers where it can: England's expulsion removed 16,000 Jews, and Spain's scattered more than 300,000 around the Mediterranean. German Jewish history in the Middle Ages, the writers say, is mostly whole communities moving from town to town, and hard figures are frustratingly rare.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morosini-giulio:
Giulio Morosini, born Samuel ben Nahmias in Venice in 1612, was an Italian Jew who converted to Christianity. Crawford Howell Toy and Ignatz Goldziher wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Samuel studied under Leon of Modena, the rabbi of Venice, and came from a wealthy family with roots in Spain.

In 1649, after a public disputation in Venice on the seventy weeks of Daniel, Samuel chose baptism. He took the name Morosini from his godfather, and his wife refused to follow him into the new faith. In Rome he became Hebrew scrittore of the Vatican Library under Clement the Ninth, and he taught Hebrew at the Propaganda. His book Derek Emunah appeared in Rome in 1683, when he was past seventy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ha-levi-a: Moses ha-Levi Alkabiz was a prominent rabbi of the first half of the sixteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, notes that he was the father of Solomon Alkabiz. About 1530 he served as dayyan, a judge, at Safed. He also studied the Cabala, for Isaac ibn Shoshan of Safed wrote a cabalistic work for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muhr-abraham-10:
Abraham Muhr was a German Jewish philanthropist born in Berlin on April 7, 1781. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He settled at Plesse in Silesia in 1806, first as a family teacher, then as a bookkeeper. In time he built a business of his own and prospered.

Muhr worked for the emancipation of the Jews in Germany, writing for the press and winning the ear of officials. He is credited with gaining Jews the right to trade as apothecaries. In 1847 he went to Berlin to press the deputies of the Landtag in person. He died that June, before the session ended, honored as president of Plesse's city council.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munk-salomon-11:
Salomon Munk was a French Orientalist born at Gross Glogau on May 14, 1803, and dead at Paris in 1867. Isidore Singer and Moïse Schwab wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Barred as a Jew from Prussian office, he left Berlin without a degree and settled in Paris in 1828. There he catalogued the Hebrew and Arabic manuscripts of the national library.

His life's work was an edition of the Arabic text of Maimonides' Guide, with translation and notes, in three volumes. He finished it after losing his sight in 1850. Munk also went to Egypt with Montefiore in the Damascus Affair. His Arabic helped win the word justice, not mercy, in the firman that cleared the accused. Paris made him professor of Hebrew at the Collège de France, in succession to Renan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naquet-alfred-j:
Alfred Joseph Naquet was a French chemist and politician born at Carpentras in 1834. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia biography. He took his medical degree in 1859 and taught chemistry at Paris and Palermo. Opposition to the empire cost him prison and his civil rights, twice over.

After the amnesty of 1870 Naquet sat in the Assembly with the Extreme Left, then in the Senate. He followed Boulanger past the general's fall and survived the Panama scandal with an acquittal. His lasting monument is the divorce law of 1884, fought for through eight years of defeats. It went into French law under his own name, the Loi Naquet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehardea-nearda:
Nehardea was an early center of Babylonian Judaism. Richard Gottheil and Wilhelm Bacher wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city stood near the Euphrates and the King's Canal. As the exilarch's seat, it traced its start to Jehoiachin. Its Shaf we-Yatib synagogue was called the Shekinah's Babylonian home.

Josephus calls Nehardea thickly peopled, fertile, and impregnable. Eastern Jews kept their Temple taxes there for forwarding. Samuel made its academy famous across the Jewish world. Rab, who taught there too, raised rival Sura instead. Papa b. Neser destroyed Nehardea in 259. Pumbedita then took its place as second academy. Nahman and Amemar later restored much of its standing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nice-11521:
Nice is a city of southern France on the Mediterranean. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there as early as the fourth century. They linked Levant trade with Gaul as middlemen. Statutes of 1341 forced them to wear a badge.

Duke Amédée let them lend money in 1430, for tribute. Payments in 1613 and 1614 bought tax relief. Foreign Jews gained trade rights in 1650 and 1673. The ghetto, assigned in 1430, bound them at night. In 1750 they could at last discard the badge. Kneeling oaths ended for them in 1789. Their present synagogue was dedicated in 1886. Some 500 Jews lived there in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-numismatics-116:
Numismatics here means the study of Jewish coinage. Joseph Jacobs and Théodore Reinach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. True Jewish coinage begins with the Maccabees. Before that, weighed metal did money's work. Lydia's kings invented coining only shortly before Judah fell.

Tales of coins of Abraham or David earn no belief. David's gift of darics is plain anachronism. Darics were struck under Darius, centuries after David. Silver was the common medium of exchange. Its Hebrew name, kesef, came to mean money itself. Balances and stone weights ruled every large bargain. The talent held sixty minas of sixty shekels. Standard weights lay in the Temple for fairness. That Temple weight is Scripture's holy shekel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ophrah-11721:
Ophrah is a name borne by towns and a man in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One Ophrah was a town in the land of Benjamin. It lay five miles north east of Beth-el. Men link it to the town now called Al-Taiyyibah.

A Philistine band marched on that town in Saul's days. A second Ophrah was the home seat of Gideon's kin. An angel came to Gideon there, by the old tales. Gideon built an altar there for a gift of thanks. He made a gold ephod there from rings of the foe. That ephod became a snare to him and his house. He died and was laid to rest at Ophrah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolengo-samue:
Samuel David ben Jehiel Ottolengo was an Italian rabbi. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was of the school of the Cabala, the mystic path. He was born at Casale-Monferrato, in Italy. He died on the twenty-fifth day of Ab, 1718.

Samuel was chief rabbi of Padua and of Venice in turn. His books drew on great works of the Cabala school. One book took parts from the Ma'abar Yabbok of Modena. That work, from 1701, was called Kiryah Ne'emanah. One took parts from the Shene Luhot ha-Berit of Horwitz. He wrote replies to points of law as well. He wrote hymns and laments, some in print, some by hand. He left notes on tracts of the Talmud in hand script.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pereira-jonatha:
Jonathan Pereira was an English physician and medical writer. He was born in London in 1804 and died there in 1853. Joseph Jacobs and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He trained at St. Bartholomew's Hospital in London.

Pereira taught chemistry, then materia medica, in London schools. He held chairs at the London Hospital and the Pharmaceutical Society. His Elements of Materia Medica became a lasting standard text. He also wrote a treatise on food and diet. The Pharmaceutical Society later struck a medal in his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phinehas-ben-ja:
Phinehas ben Jair was a sage famed for piety, not learning. He lived at Lydda in the late second century. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was son-in-law to Simeon ben Yohai.

One tale shows his scrupulous honesty in full. Two men left two measures of wheat with him. For seven years he sowed that wheat and saved the harvest. When the men returned, he gave back every grain grown. He would not eat at any man's table. He said the times shamed all who kept the Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poverty-12321:
Poverty among the Jews is the subject of an article by Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The writers note a strange clash of facts. The wealth of the Jews has passed into a proverb. Yet all who study the matter agree on one point. Jews have more poor, in share, than their neighbors.

In Prussia in 1861 the count bore this out. Of grown Jewish workers, more than six in a hundred were fully dependent. In the whole people the share was near four in a hundred. Italy in 1871 showed the reverse case. There Jewish paupers were far fewer, in share, than others. The article weighs such counts land by land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-procedure-in-ci:
Procedure in civil causes means how a court hears claims over goods and debts. The Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jewish law set great store by property law, they say. It asked judges to run such suits with care. The Pentateuch gives few hints on method, though.

One verse tells judges to hear between your brethren. One more says both men in a dispute shall stand before the Lord. The Talmud built a firm rule on such verses. A judge may rule only when the accused man stands before him. No judgment can be given in his absence. The article sets out the steps of a suit from claim to ruling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-ii-surn:
Ptolemy the Second, surnamed Philadelphus, was king of Egypt. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He reigned from 285 to 247 B.C. He fought on for Coele-Syria and Palestine. By about 274 he held those lands for good.

Like the other heirs of Alexander, he loved to build cities. Philadelphia rose on Palestinian soil in his reign. Philoteria rose near Lake Tiberias as well. Ptolemais was founded on that coast too. Of late, men think a found statue shows the king. A second statue is thought to show his wife Arsinoe. The entry weighs his wars and his works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rachel-a-ewe-12:
Rachel was the younger daughter of Laban and a wife of Jacob. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, and the Editorial Board wrote her article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jacob first met her at a well near Haran. She had brought her father's flocks there for water. She was fair and bright in form, Genesis says. Jacob fell in love with her at that first meeting.

Jacob struck a bargain with Laban for her hand. He would serve seven years for the right to wed her. Through a fraud of Laban, the match was delayed. Jacob was wed to her elder sister first by that trick. The article follows Rachel through the Genesis tale. It weighs her sons, her idols, and her early death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-red-heifer-1262:
The red heifer was a flawless animal used for purification. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Numbers chapter 19 gives the rules for it. The heifer must never have worn a yoke.

The article walks through the rite step by step. Priests slew the heifer outside the camp. Eleazar sprinkled its blood seven times toward the tabernacle. Cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet went onto the fire. A clean man gathered the ashes outside the camp. Mixed with fresh water, the ashes cleansed corpse impurity. Everyone who handled the rite washed and waited till sunset. The entry explains a strange rite in plain sequence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revue-orientale:
The Revue Orientale was a periodical issued in Brussels at uneven intervals. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It was published in French. It was devoted to Jewish science.

The article says Eliakim Carmoly founded and edited it. He also wrote most of its articles himself. Three volumes appeared from 1841 to 1844. Its prospectus claims success beyond all expectations. Articles were reprinted in German, English, and Dutch. They appeared in journals and even in books. Carmoly's history of Jewish physicians first ran there. So did his work on rabbinical geography in France. Essays treated Jews in Belgium, Italy, and Poland. The entry honors a one man journal with wide reach.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rona-samuel-128:
Samuel Róna was a Hungarian dermatologist born on April 1, 1857. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Halas. He was educated at Budapest.

The article says he assisted Professor Kaposi at Vienna in 1881. He then assisted at Budapest's Rukós Hospital until 1885. In 1886 he helped found a public dispensary for the sick. He kept the section for syphilitic diseases for himself. He traveled through Europe studying leading clinics. In 1889 he became a lecturer in Budapest. He rose to professor six years after 1893. His works treat pityriasis, dermatitis, lichen, and prurigo. Most titles are in Hungarian in the entry. A Pallas lexicon supports the whole record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubinstein-anto:
Anton Grigoryevich Rubinstein was a Russian pianist and composer born on November 28, 1829. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His parents were Jews who embraced the Greek Orthodox faith in his childhood.

Raised in Moscow, Rubinstein took his first piano lessons from his mother. The teacher Villoing then trained him for years without pay. He gave his first public concert at Moscow in 1839, aged nine. Tours through Germany, Holland, Scandinavia, and France followed in 1841. In Paris, Chopin left a deep mark on the boy, and Liszt praised him highly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-kalo:
Samuel ben Kalonymus ha-Hazzan, also called Samuel Dewlin, led the congregation at Erfurt. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He lived in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, in Germany.

Samuel wrote a number of piyyutim, the liturgical poems of the synagogue. Five were made for Sabbath weddings, and others for Friday evening services. One serves the Sabbath of Hukkat, another the Sabbath after Sukkot. A Purim poem credited to him is usually given to Samuel of Magdeburg instead. On June 16, 1221, Samuel and his wife Hannah died as martyrs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-satire-13221:
Joseph Jacobs and Israel Davidson wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on satire. Satire is an ironic, often veiled attack, mostly in verse. Among the Hebrews it appeared early. Jotham hurled his fable of the trees and the bramble at Abimelech from Mount Gerizim. Nathan trapped David with the parable of the poor man's lamb. Isaiah's song over Babylon's fallen king ranks among the strongest satires anywhere.

Ben Sira's satire takes the form of pointed sayings. He strikes at faithless friends and arrogant rich men alike. The Talmud and Midrash overflow with puns, parables, and epigrams. The rabbis used satire against the Sadducees. Against Caesar and Rome they spoke in veiled metaphors. One famous tale shows a widow crushed by rule after rule. Each new demand robs her of a little more. The article gathers such cases across the centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schul-13321:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the word schul. It is the Judæo-German name for the synagogue. Jews used it as early as the thirteenth century. In most of Europe, building synagogues was then forbidden. Jews held services in private buildings instead. They used the schools they were allowed to run.

So people said simply, I go to school. The article weighs another view. Güdemann held that schul first meant assembly. Christians would not call the place a church, so the name stuck. Forms of the word spread across Europe. Italy has scuola, England had schola, and Poland has szkola. Jacobs warns that English records may mean real schools. At Norwich and London the school stood apart from the synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seneca-lucius-a:
Seneca was a Roman Stoic thinker, born about 6 B.C. and dead by 65 C.E. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Seneca taught the young Nero and wrote widely in Latin. His remarks on Jews survive only in fragments quoted by others.

Those fragments are harsh, above all on the Sabbath. Seneca mocked Jews for resting one day in seven, yet admitted their customs had spread worldwide. He did grant that Jews at least knew why they kept their rites. The entry helps readers see how a famed Roman mind viewed Jewish practice from outside, with respect and scorn mixed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shebu-ot-oaths-:
Shebu'ot, meaning Oaths, is a treatise of the Mishnah, Tosefta, and both Talmuds. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The treatise deals chiefly with the many forms an oath can take. It usually stands sixth in the order Nezikin, on damages.

Its eight chapters hold sixty-two paragraphs in all. The first chapter sorts oaths into two classes, then four. It links them to other things sorted the same way. Those include uncleanness, Sabbath carrying, and kinds of leprosy. Later parts explain how atonement works for sins done in uncleanness. The entry maps a legal text where oaths open doors into much wider law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shushan-susa-he:
Shushan, or Susa, was the ancient capital of Elam and Persia's winter royal seat. Emil G. Hirsch, Louis H. Gray, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the city. It stood between two rivers southeast of Dizful. Babylonian inscriptions name it as early as 2400 B.C.

In 640 B.C. the city passed under Babylonian control. Cyrus the Great later captured it for Persia. He made Shushan his seat of government. Alexander's rise lifted Babylon and shrank Susa's importance. After a revolt the city was razed, then rebuilt by Sapor. It resisted Arab invasion stubbornly in the year 645. In its prime the city spanned six or seven miles around. Bible readers know it as the stage of Esther and Daniel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-of-teman:
Simeon of Teman was a tanna of the second generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He argued with Akiba over a legal point drawn from Exodus. He also worked closely with Judah ben Baba. Some of his legal sayings appear in the Mishnah.

One tale-like saying of his has also been kept. He taught that God split the sea at the Exodus for a reason. Israel had earned that help through the covenant of circumcision. The entry lists the Mishnah passages where his views appear. It gives readers a compact sketch of a working second generation sage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sonnenfels-1392:
Sonnenfels was an Austrian family of scholars and writers of note. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The family descended from Wurzbach Lipmann of Brandenburg. Its members rose to prominence during the eighteenth century. Perlin Lipmann moved to Austria as an agent for Dietrichstein.

Perlin and his children embraced the Catholic faith in time. He took the name Aloys Wiener, then Sonnenfels by patent. He taught Semitic languages at the University of Vienna. His son Joseph became a jurist and novelist of fame. Joseph taught political science at Vienna from 1763. He later presided over the Academy of Sciences until 1817.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinthal-morit:
Moritz Steinthal was a German physician born at Stendal on October 22, 1798. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at the University of Berlin and earned his medical degree in 1821. After two years of travel he set up practice in Berlin. He stayed there until his death in 1892.

Steinthal built a large medical practice in Berlin. In 1847 he became the first Prussian Jew to receive a senior medical title. He wrote on spinal disease and on brain disorders in children. Other works cover nerve fever, cancer, and mental illness. In 1870 he published a new edition of Hufeland's book on long life. The entry honors a doctor who served Berlin for fifty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tamar-14221: Tamar is a city named in Ezekiel's vision of the land's borders. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Ezekiel sets it as one end of Canaan's southern line. That line runs from Tamar through Meriboth-kadesh to the sea. The district was assigned to the tribe of Gad. Comparing Numbers suggests a site near the Dead Sea. The name likely matches Hazazon-Tamar, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-te-omim-hezekia: Hezekiah Feiwel Te'omim was rabbi at Przemysl in Poland. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He lived across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. His one known book grew out of a bitter dispute. It preserves the papers of his fight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tripoli-ancient:
Tripoli, a North African seaport and the ancient Oea, held Jews from early times. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Local tradition brings its first Jews from a Fatimid-era oasis. Benjamin of Tudela never mentions the city, though. Spanish exiles of 1492 avoided it under Ferdinand's rule.

Jews settled in numbers only after Ottoman rule began in 1551. Family names there are not Spanish in character. A Shabbethaian preacher was expelled by local Jews in 1667. Tripoli's Jews kept two special Purims of their own. One marked escape from a Tunisian invasion in 1705. The other marked deliverance from a corsair in the 1790s. About 1,000 Jewish families lived there in 1850.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uzza-uzzah-1462:
