Uzza, son of Abinadab, died for touching the Ark of the Covenant. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He and his brother Ahio drove the Ark's new cart. David and all Israel escorted it toward Jerusalem. At Nachon's threshing floor the oxen stumbled badly.

Uzza reached out to steady the Ark and was slain. David named the place Perezuzzah in memory of it. Rabbis labored to explain and soften his death. The Ark bore its bearers, they argued, so it bore itself. Uzza failed to grasp that truth, they said. Yet dying by the Ark won him a share in eternity. The name also marks a Benjaminite, a temple servant, and a royal garden.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vizhainy-vizhun:
Vizhainy is a Russian town in the government of Suwalki. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article centers on a royal charter for its Jews. King Michael granted the charter at Warsaw in 1670. King John III confirmed it at Cracow in 1676.

The charter protected Jewish homes, stores, and meat markets. It covered their synagogue, cemeteries, and baths as well. Jews could sell liquor and trade goods by weight. They could rebuild after any fire. Taxes on slaughtered cattle still applied. The entry shows how Polish kings secured a small community's daily life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-jules-150:
Jules Worms (born 1832) was a French painter of gay genre scenes. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Paris, he trained with two masters of the craft. His first Salon piece came in 1859. It showed a dragoon wooing a nurse on a bench.

That first work marked his gift for light scenes. In 1861 his Arrest for Debt drew more note. He then toured Spain for a long stay. There he sketched the dress and ways of the folk. Medals came to him at four Paris Salons in a row. In 1876 France gave him the Legion of Honor. Rich buyers in America paid high sums for his works. The entry lists them town by town and year by year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yoma-15121:
Yoma is the tract on the rite of the Day of Atonement. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in the Mishnah, the Tosefta, and both Talmuds. In some books its name is Kippurim, or Atonement in short.

The day was known as Yoma Rabba, the Great Day. That name was cut short to Yoma, the Day, in time. The tract is the fifth in the order of feast days. It has eight parts with sixty-one short rules in all. Part one treats the high priest and his week of prep. It tells how the rite order was read to him. Elders warned him to hold to that set order. They warned him not to heed the Sadducee way at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeissl-hermann-:
Hermann von Zeissl (1817-1884) was an Austrian doctor of skin ills. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Moravia, he took his degree at Vienna in 1846. That year he joined the staff of three town hospitals.

Those were the eye, the knife, and the skin wards of Vienna. In 1850 he set up his own work and taught as well. He soon stood as a chief voice on skin ills. His fame in the cure of sex ills grew with the years. In 1869 he rose to chief of the second ward for such ills. He held that post till he quit work in 1883. The emperor made him a knight for his long service. His books treat the late stage of that dread ill in full.
journal-of-discourses-vol-21:
Volume Twenty-One, from 1881, braces for the hardest law yet. The Edmunds Act draws near, set to jail hundreds of polygamists. Votes and offices will be stripped from men who keep the doctrine.

Sermons ready the Saints for prison, fines, and public scorn ahead. Speakers call the coming storm a trial sent to sift the faithful. Old unbroken spirit answers new threats in the familiar pulpit voice. Families weigh flight, hiding, and open defiance in the talks' shadow. The volume stands on the storm's edge, and every page knows it well. Its warnings read as both prophecy and plain, practical counsel.
keith-fossil-remains-java-1921:
Arthur Keith gave this round up of new fossil finds to the journal Nature in 1921. Three far flung finds fill his page: Wadjak in Java, Talgai in Australia, and Boskop in South Africa. Each had come to light in the past few years of work.

Keith sets the three frames in one world map of man's deep past. He tells what each skull shows and how it shifts the tale of the races of man. The short paper is a fine snap shot of a field in fast change at that hour.
keynes-treatise-probability-1921:
Before Keynes remade economics, he wrote a deep book on the logic of uncertain belief. His Treatise on Probability, published in 1921, began as a Cambridge fellowship thesis before the First World War. It treats probability as a logical relation between evidence and claim.

Keynes argues that some probabilities can be numbered, but many sound judgments rest on evidence that resists exact measure. He also weighs the strength of evidence itself, apart from the balance it strikes. The book's doubts about neat numbers quietly underlie his later economics of uncertainty. He had set the book aside when war came, then finished it in the peace.
king-henry-v-pg1521:
William Shakespeare's Henry the Fifth, in this edition, lays out its five acts scene by scene. Choruses open each act, carrying the audience from England to France. The contents name the Southampton plot, where traitors are unmasked before the fleet sails. Harfleur's siege follows, with Henry's speech at the breach.

At Agincourt the plan shows the English and French camps on the night before battle. Henry's disguised walk among his soldiers stands at the act's heart. The field of battle, the lists of the slain, and the peace talks close act five. An epilogue looks ahead to Henry the Sixth and England's losses in France. The contents alone trace Shakespeare's arc: claim, voyage, siege, battle, and hard-won peace.
knight-risk-uncertainty-1921:
Frank Knight was an American economist whose 1921 book Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit began as his doctoral thesis. He asks a simple question with a hard answer: why do business owners earn profit at all? Perfect competition, on paper, should grind profit down to nothing.

Knight splits risk, which can be measured and insured, from true uncertainty, which cannot be measured at all. Profit, he argues, is the pay for bearing that unmeasurable uncertainty with judgment. His split still anchors how economists think about enterprise, insurance, and the founder's role. His distinction is taught to first-year students to this day. It rewards slow reading.
lawrence-psychoanalysis-unconscious-1921:
Lawrence wrote this 1921 book as a direct attack on Freud and the psychoanalytic movement then sweeping Europe. He knew the theory well enough to respect its power, and he rejected its picture of the unconscious entirely.

For Lawrence, the unconscious is not a clinic of buried wishes but a living mystery, the source of spontaneity and growth. He argues that modern people think too much and feel too little, and that analysis makes the sickness worse. The prose is combative, funny, and deliberately unscientific. It stands as modernism's anti-Freudian manifesto, written by its most bodily thinker.
lawrence-sea-sardinia-1921:
In January 1921 Lawrence and Frieda sailed from Sicily to Sardinia for a ten-day trip, and this book is the record of it. Sea and Sardinia, published that year, is often called his finest travel writing.

Lawrence describes Cagliari, mountain villages, buses crawling through snow, and peasants whose lives seem older than history. He writes of the island as a place the modern world forgot, and he half envies it. The Mediterranean itself becomes a living presence, almost a god. Every scene is sharp with hunger, cold, color, and irritation at bad inns. Few travel books feel this awake.
machen-origin-of-pauls-religion-1921:
John Gresham Machen taught New Testament at Princeton and defended orthodox Christianity against the liberal theology of his day. His Origin of Paul's Religion, published in 1921, asks where the apostle Paul's teaching came from. Machen answers with detailed scholarship rather than pulpit slogans.

He argues that Paul's religion grew from the facts of Jesus's life, death, and resurrection, not from Greek mystery cults or Jewish legend. The target is the history-of-religions school, which traced Christian ideas to pagan sources around the Mediterranean. The book won respect even from scholars who rejected Machen's conclusions.
mctaggart-nature-existence-vol-1-1921:
J. M. E. McTaggart published The Nature of Existence, Volume 1, in 1921. McTaggart was a Cambridge philosopher known for rigorous idealist argument. This volume lays out the general features any existing thing must have. Substances, qualities, and relations are defined and tested step by step.

His famous claim that time is unreal comes in the second volume's groundwork and an earlier essay. Here he builds the system that supports such bold claims. The prose is dry, exact, and hard to skim. Philosophers of the Cambridge school debated it intensely. The work remains a peak of systematic metaphysics in English. It rewards readers who enjoy pure argument.
menander-principal-fragments-allinson-lo:
Francis G. Allinson translated the principal fragments of Menander for the Loeb series in 1921, with the Greek text facing his English. Menander, master of Greek New Comedy, wrote over a hundred plays in Athens around 300 BCE. None survives whole; his work comes down in fragments and in lines quoted by later writers.

The fragments give sharp scenes of fathers, sons, slaves, and lovers in everyday trouble. Roman playwrights copied Menander closely, and through them his plots shaped European comedy for good. Allinson labels the book honestly as fragments, since that is all the evidence allows. Readers meet a great writer the way scholars do: in bright shards. The facing Greek keeps the original within sight.
millay-second-april-1921:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published Second April in 1921, a year after A Few Figs from Thistles made her notorious. The title nods to Chaucer's April opening and to her own second spring as a poet. Millay was by then the best-known young poet in America.

The volume holds sonnets and lyrics of her Greenwich Village maturity: love poems, elegies, and city pieces. The famous sonnet sequence beginning Euclid alone has looked on Beauty bare stands among them. Millay's tone deepens here, trading some early sparkle for grief and reflection. Wild swans, childhood memories, and lost lovers move through the pages. Second April showed that Millay was far more than a Jazz Age sensation.
mining-laws-of-ohio-1921:
Ohio's Department of Industrial Relations compiled this pamphlet of the state's mining laws in 1921. The F. J. Heer Printing Company printed it at Columbus, and the state bindery bound it. A foreword explains the new administrative code of the Eighty-fourth General Assembly. That law took effect on July 1, 1921.

The code moved all duties over mines and mining from the Industrial Commission to the new department. The pamphlet collects every General Code provision on operating, controlling, and managing mines. It was put into convenient form for employers, employees, and the general public. The laws were meant, the foreword says, for their benefit and observance.
moore-poems-1921:
Marianne Moore's first book, Poems, appeared in London in 1921, published by friends, H. D. and Bryher, largely without Moore's own direction. She was famously displeased, yet the slim volume fixed her standing among the modernists of two continents.

The poems show her manner already formed: precise syllabic stanzas, quotations woven into argument, and armored animals as emblems of conduct. Her subjects range from critics and poets to the pangolin-like exactitude of things well made. Moore writes with a fencer's care, every word placed. The book began one of the most exact careers in American poetry.
murray-witch-cult-in-western-europe-1921:
Margaret Murray read the witch trials and saw a church where others saw a crime. The Witch-Cult in Western Europe, printed in 1921, argues the accused were heirs of an old pagan faith. Murray was a trained scholar of Egypt and of folk rite.

She holds that covens of thirteen met at sabbats to serve a horned god, age after age, under the Church's nose. Her proof is drawn from the trial records themselves, read in her own bold way. The thesis swept the field, then drew fire from later scholars. No witchcraft book of its century stirred more debate.
nicholson-studies-in-islamic-mysticism-1:
Reynold A. Nicholson, the Cambridge scholar who translated Rumi and Hujviri, gathered his Studies in Islamic Mysticism in 1921. The essays treat the early masters of Sufism and the ideas that rule their teaching. Nicholson wrote for students who wanted the sources read with care, not the legends repeated.

He traces the growth of the doctrine that the self must pass away in God, and the lives of saints who embodied it. His method joins Arabic and Persian texts to a clear English style. The book became a foundation stone of Sufi studies in English. Readers who meet Rumi through Nicholson start here for the world that made him.
no-plays-of-japan-waley-1921:
Arthur Waley translated sixteen Noh plays into English in The Noh Plays of Japan, published in 1921. Noh, Japan's masked theater of chant, dance, and flute, had been closed to Western readers until Waley's work. His introduction explains the stages, roles, and ghost-haunted plots that English readers were meeting for the first time.

Most Noh heroes are spirits who return to relive one binding sorrow or joy. Warriors, women, and demons appear in turn, played with stately slowness and sudden fire. Waley's plain, musical English caught the plays' strange calm. Yeats and Pound felt the influence at once in their own theater work. The volume founded the Western study of Noh.
o-henry-memorial-award-prize-stories-of-:
Prize Stories of 1921, issued in 1922, holds the third year of O. Henry Memorial Award winners. The Society of Arts and Sciences chose them, and Blanche Colton Williams introduced the book. A note credits John F. Tucker, the Society's late directing manager, with founding the memorial committee in 1918.

Edison Marshall opens with The Heart of Little Shikara. Thomas Beer's Mummery, Mildred Cram's Stranger Things, and Sophie Kerr's Wild Earth follow. Wilbur Daniel Steele places again, with The Marriage in Kairwan. Fifty-Two Weeks for Florette and Mr Downey Sits Down add lighter notes. The award had settled, by 1921, into a yearly survey of the form.
oe-physiologus-cook-1921:
The Old English Physiologus survives only as a fragment, three beast poems in Anglo-Saxon verse. Albert Cook edited what remains in 1921, with modern English translations beside the old text. The Panther, the Whale, and a lost Partridge piece are all that time has left of the English version.

The Panther's sweet breath draws all beasts, a figure of Christ drawing the world. The Whale tricks sailors who camp on its back, a warning against the devil's false ground. Each poem joins close description to moral meaning. Cook's edition presents text, translation, and notes together. Three beasts and three morals survive, in the tongue of Beowulf's scribes.
openalex-w1867913521:
Sarah Moxon, Joy Lawn, and many co-authors wrote this roadmap. It appeared in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth in 2015. The Every Newborn Action Plan launched in 2014. Its goal is to stop newborn deaths and stillbirths that can be prevented. National targets were set for the year 2030.

Good data on care at birth is needed to track progress. The team assessed a matrix of seventy indicators. Ten core and ten added indicators were published, they report. Three impact measures are well defined already. Several care coverage measures lack clear definitions or data. Task teams now lead the hardest measurement work.
openalex-w2019595721:
Roel Aaij and colleagues in the LHCb Collaboration reported signs of pentaquark particles. Their paper appeared in Physical Review Letters in 2015. Pentaquarks would contain five quarks, more than normal particles. Theorists had proposed such states decades earlier. Clear evidence had been lacking.

The team studied a rare decay recorded by the LHCb detector. They used proton collision data from two energy runs. Their analysis found two unusual structures in the debris. Each structure matched a resonant particle state. Both signals were far too strong to be chance. The two states had different masses and spins. The finding opened a new class of matter for study. Later work would test and refine the claim.
openalex-w2032080021:
Livia de Figueiredo Diniz, Julio Urbina, Isabel Mayer de Andrade and colleagues tested two drugs together against Chagas disease. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. Current Chagas treatment works poorly in the long phase. Side effects often make patients stop treatment. Combining drugs might work better.

The team infected mice with the Chagas parasite. They gave benznidazole and posaconazole alone and together. Combined treatment cut parasite levels more than single drugs. In longer tests, cure effects exceeded the sum of single effects. Giving one drug after the other also worked well. One sequence matched full single-drug courses in cures. The results support combined therapy trials in people.
openalex-w2057889321:
Ernesto Cuevasanta, Ana Denicola, Beatriz Alvarez and Matias Moller measured how hydrogen sulfide moves through fat membranes. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. The gas is known as a poison. The body also makes small amounts of it. Those small amounts help regulate body functions.

The team measured how the gas splits between water and membranes. They used lab-made membrane bubbles and simple solvents. The gas gathered about twice as strongly in membranes. That made membrane crossing very fast. A computer model then tracked spread in tissue. Sulfide from one cell could reach hundreds of neighbours. Membranes still slowed its overall travel notably. The work clarifies how the gas acts in the body.
openalex-w2077334721:
Myrielle Dupont-Rouzeyrol, Olivia O'Connor, Elodie Calvez and colleagues reported two patients infected with Zika and dengue at once. Their letter appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2015. Both viruses spread through Aedes mosquitoes. New Caledonia faced outbreaks of both in 2014. The cases show the viruses can overlap in one person.

Dengue had circulated in New Caledonia for decades. Zika arrived from French Polynesia in late 2013. Local Zika spread began soon after. Over a thousand confirmed Zika cases followed. Dengue cases also continued during the same months. Lab tests confirmed both viruses in the two patients. Joint infection complicates diagnosis, since symptoms overlap. The letter alerts clinicians in outbreak regions.
openalex-w2089584121:
Mehdi Moussaid, Niriaska Perozo, Simon Garnier and colleagues filmed how social groups walk in crowds. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2010. Most crowd studies treat people as lone walkers. In reality, most pedestrians move in small groups. Friends and families try to stay together while walking.

The team analysed about fifteen hundred walking groups. At low density, members walked side by side. That line faces across the walking direction. As crowds thickened, the line bent forward. The bent shape formed a V-like pattern. It kept conversation easy within the group. It also slowed the wider crowd flow. Group shape trades speed against social contact. Crowd models should include social behaviour, they argue.
openalex-w2089968521:
Martin Llewellyn, Michael Lewis, Nidia Acosta and colleagues traced one lineage of the Chagas parasite. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. The parasite has six stable genetic lineages. The lineage studied here lives mostly in wild cycles. It is increasingly linked to human infections.

The team applied dozens of variable DNA markers. They typed over fifty isolates of the lineage. Sequence data added deeper family history. The lineage showed clear geographic structure. Its history hints at a distinct origin and spread. Wild mammals maintain it in nature. Spillover into homes could seed new Chagas cases. Knowing its range helps target surveillance.
openalex-w2108565421:
Massimo Sartelli, Fausto Catena, Luca Ansaloni and colleagues reported a worldwide study of severe belly infections. Their paper appeared in World Journal of Emergency Surgery in 2014. Complicated abdominal infections can kill without fast care. Data across countries were scarce and patchy. The CIAOW study gathered them in one design.

Sixty-eight hospitals worldwide joined the study. It ran for six months in 2012 and 2013. Adults with complicated abdominal infections were enrolled. Teams recorded sources, treatments and outcomes. Antibiotic resistance patterns were tracked too. The dataset allows fair comparison between regions. It also highlights where outcomes lag behind. Surgeons can use it to benchmark their own results.
openalex-w2440323021:
Hana Chaïr, Renan Traoré, M. Duval, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2016. Taro, a starchy root crop feeding millions across the tropics, spread worldwide with human migrations, but its origin and routes stayed murky. The team used genetics to retrace how taro diversified and traveled.

Eleven DNA markers profiled taro samples from nineteen countries across four continents. Asian samples, mainly from India, held the richest diversity and the most unique variants. Asia-Pacific taro diversified largely through sexual reproduction. In Africa and the Americas, plants spread mostly as clones, changing by mutation. Clustering split taro into two great genetic groups, with mixed cultivars between them. West African taro traced mostly to India.
openalex-w2627092521:
Glenn R. Gibson, Robert W. Hutkins, and Mary Ellen Sanders lead an expert panel behind this 2017 statement in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology. The panel, called together by the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics, met in December 2016. Their task was to update the meaning and scope of the word prebiotic. Research and medical practice had moved since the term was first coined.

The updated meaning calls a prebiotic a substance that host microbes use selectively, bringing a health benefit. The wording now allows substances beyond carbohydrates, and uses beyond the gut and food. Selective action through gut microbes remains required, and health gains must be documented. The statement covers prebiotics for animals as well as humans. The authors hope shared language will bring consistency to research, marketing, and rules. Their review also covers the science, health effects, and laws in this area.
openalex-w2769372721:
Judith Bakker, Owen S. Wangensteen, and Demian D. Chapman, with colleagues, piloted a DNA-based way to count sharks, in the paper whose title begins Environmental DNA reveals tropical shark diversity. Sharks anchor marine food webs but are hard to survey without catching them. The team tested water samples from Caribbean and Pacific Coral Sea habitats. DNA shed by animals into water can betray who lives there.

Using targeted DNA metabarcoding, they identified at least twenty-one shark species from water alone. Diversity patterns matched known differences in human pressure and conservation effort between regions. Places with heavier exploitation showed the expected poorer shark variety. The method is rapid, non-invasive, and needs no fishing gear or divers. The authors conclude such sampling can effectively track elusive ocean predators. Wider use could transform how shark populations are monitored and protected.
openalex-w2788689621:
Amelie Driemel, John Augustine, and Klaus Behrens lead a large team describing the Baseline Surface Radiation Network in Earth System Science Data in 2018. Tiny shifts in Earth's surface radiation budget can drive large climate responses over time. In the 1980s, existing networks lacked the accuracy to track those shifts. The World Meteorological Organization therefore proposed a new baseline network in 1988.

The network began in 1992 with nine stations collecting one-minute radiation measurements. By 2018 it had grown to fifty-nine active stations plus nine candidates, across all continents and ocean environments. Data flow into a central archive, the World Radiation Monitoring Center. The paper explains the network's structure and describes its data in detail. These records anchor satellite checks and climate model tests. They give climate science its most trusted ground truth on sunlight and heat at the surface.
openalex-w3123817721:
Sergei Põlme, Kessy Abarenkov, R. Henrik Nilsson, and colleagues introduced this database in Fungal Diversity in 2020. FungalTraits gathers the traits and habits of fungi and fungus-like organisms called stramenopiles. It is built to be friendly for working scientists, at genus and species level.

Most fungi live hidden lives and must be identified by DNA in field studies. Gene tools have revealed fungal diversity everywhere, but what each kind actually does stayed vague. Without traits, ecological readings of those DNA surveys remain shallow. The database assigns jobs such as decay, parasitism, or partnership with plants, drawn from expert knowledge. It lets researchers turn lists of names into statements about how an ecosystem works.
openalex-w3177419021:
Salomé Aubert, Javier Brazo-Sayavera, Silvia González, and colleagues review global data on physical activity in children and teens. Their narrative review appeared in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2021. World health plans call for better tracking of how much young people move. Yet national surveys measure activity in very different ways.

The team compared eight large global tracking efforts and checked their methods and quality. Definitions differed so much that figures for active youth clashed between surveys, even for one country. A few patterns held everywhere, including low activity overall. The authors list research gaps and urge standard measures, so countries can be compared fairly.
openalex-w4401815221:
John Deanfield, Subodh Verma, Benjamin Scirica, and colleagues report a planned analysis of the SELECT trial. Their paper appeared in The Lancet in 2024. The weight-loss drug semaglutide lowers major heart events in people with obesity. Whether it helps patients who also have heart failure was unknown.

SELECT was a large randomised trial run in forty-one countries. Adults aged forty-five or older with excess weight and heart disease received weekly semaglutide or a placebo. The analysis asks whether patients with a history of heart failure benefited. It also compares two forms of heart failure, with preserved and with reduced pumping strength.
openalex-w7204532421:
Marcelo de Vargas Estrella led a Portuguese-language legal paper, in Brazil in 2026, on river piracy in Amazonas and the mental health of inland navigation workers. Boats are the Amazon's roads, and attacks on them threaten the crews who work the rivers. Using a deductive method across constitutional, labor, health. Waterway law plus official records and studies on fluvial violence, the authors treat piracy as a psychosocial risk in the work environment and identify legal duties of prevention and response.

The threat of violence must enter companies' risk inventories and action plans, they find, with worker participation, communication protocols, training, post-event support, and coordination with public authorities. Raising penalties alone is insufficient; effective protection needs prevention and full health care adapted to Amazonian distances.
openalex-w7204576321:
Marcos Rodrigo Barreto and Ruben Alexandre Boelter released a Portuguese-language review in Brazil in 2026 on paleontology in science teaching. The study read six Brazilian dissertations on teaching paleontology in basic education, asking what role fossils and deep time play in building research knowledge. Content analysis focused on inquiry sequences as the plan for promoting research literacy in the final years of elementary school.

Paleontology is widely recognized in these works as a driver of research literacy and inquiry-based learning, the authors find, and investigative sequences are the key plan for making that happen. The studies converge on practical, contextual, investigative approaches, with paleontology as a structuring theme that also builds respect for natural heritage.
openalex-w7204914121:
Beatriz da Cunha Crespo led a Portuguese-language evidence review, in Brazil in 2026, distinguishing physiological gastroesophageal reflux from reflux disease in infants. Ordinary reflux is frequent in babies because the lower esophageal sphincter is immature, and it is mostly benign and self-limited, resolving by age two. The disease form brings persistent symptoms, harms quality of life, and can cause problems. The review searched five sources for post-2020 work on how reflux is defined, diagnosed, and managed.

Physiological reflux resolves on its own in the great majority by age two, while disease shows irritability, food refusal, poor weight gain, and respiratory or digestive problems. Diagnosis is mostly medical, helped by validated forms, with invasive tests reserved for refractory cases. Non-drug measures come first; acid-suppressing drugs suit refractory cases, and surgery is reserved for the severe.
openalex-w7208819721:
Bernardo Rubim Clavijo and Jose Ricardo Paintner Torres profile patients with rheumatoid arthritis who take synthetic medicines in the Brazilian state of Parana. Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease that attacks the joints, causing pain, deformity, and loss of function. Synthetic disease-modifying drugs, including methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and leflunomide, are central to holding it back. The authors work from health system data for the state, and they state plainly that the data used are simulated.

Women over fifty predominated in the profile, and hospital admissions showed a rising trend across the years examined. The authors use the exercise to stress two things that hold beyond the simulation: patients must stick with their drug treatment, and care works best when several professions follow the patient together. The study reads as a training-ground analysis of how such patient profiles are built and read.
openalex-w7211871221:
Elaine Christina da Silva Sanches Bueno, writing alone, argues that overprotective parenting can violate the rights of children and teenagers. Her legal and narrative study looks at overparenting: parenting that controls excessively, even from love. Under Brazil's rule of full protection for the young, she asks whether constant shielding crosses from care into a quiet offense against a child's dignity and personality rights.

Too much control, she finds, can stunt the growth of independence, self-esteem, and identity in the young. As a cultural mirror she uses a famous television pair, the overindulgent mother Dona Florinda and her pampered son Kiko from the series Chaves, to show the pattern in popular form. Her conclusion is a plea for balance: children need care and room to act, and only both together let their rights and their development flourish.
openalex-w7212251821:
Georgia Santana da Silva Mansur leads a team that sorts the new words the pandemic forced on schools. When COVID-19 shut schools round the world, teaching had to be rebuilt in weeks. New terms rose fast, and not all staff used them the same way. Remote teaching was the chief of them. The team read past work to set the terms side by side and pin what each one means.

Clear terms, they argue, are not a small thing. A school that names its modes well can plan, train, and judge its work with less fog. The piece walks through the chief forms that rose in the health crisis. It shows where they match and where they split. For staff who lived that shift, the value is a shared tongue. For new staff, it is a map of a hard time that reshaped the field.
openalex-w7213513821:
Luane Costa Menezes leads a review on artificial intelligence and children's psychic and brain development. Their 2026 exploratory, qualitative review uses academic work and institutional documents. Childhood is a period of high brain plasticity, when thinking, emotional, and social skills are still forming.

Artificial intelligence can personalize learning, support inclusion, and widen access to knowledge, the review finds. It can also help produce teaching materials. Risks include heavy digital use, fewer face-to-face interactions, and effects on emotional control and autonomy. Children's mental integrity in the face of new neurotechnology is raised as a rights issue. Balanced, guided use is the direction the authors favour, rather than rejection or unchecked adoption.
openalex-w7214086521:
Maria Eduarda dos Santos Sacks and Laryssa Karas review cognitive behavioural therapy for anxiety in adolescence. Their 2026 library review starts from psychic suffering today, including social media, comparing lives online, and family and school pressure. The teen years bring intense body, mind, and social change.

Techniques fitted to the young person's growth are discussed in turn. Teaching about the mind, reshaping unhelpful thoughts, spotting the thoughts that pop up, and gradual exposure all feature, plus a unified transdiagnostic plan. Family and school settings can hold anxiety in place or help reduce it, they argue. Therapy builds self-control skills and lasting freedom, the authors conclude, beyond symptom relief alone.
openalex-w7218417721: Scarlett Pujols Melendez led a 2026 case report on a rare, dangerous complication: a gastrostomy feeding tube migrated and tore the duodenum. The patient was a woman aged forty-three with cancer spread along the lungs, pressure on the esophagus, trouble swallowing, and malnutrition. She received a feeding tube made from a urinary catheter. Two months later the catheter was replaced without incident. The next day she got abdominal pain, and imaging followed. The sample ends during the workup, before management and outcome, so those are not described here.
openalex-w7220899221:
Maria Eduarda Rodrigues Guadagnini led a 2026 cross-sectional mixed-methods study of how older people with cancer in palliative care perceive nursing assistance, and how that perception relates to their quality of life. Patients averaging seventy-four years, mostly men, answered an abbreviated quality of life instrument and the Palliative Outcome Scale, and spoke about their care. Quantitative answers received descriptive statistics, and the spoken material content analysis.

The environment domain scored highest and the social domain lowest, while the items quality of care and feeling of peace scored highest of all. Qualitative categories were continuous presence, empathy, and gratitude. Nursing plays an essential role in promoting comfort and dignity, the authors conclude, perceived by patients as the fundamental link between technical care and human welcoming in oncological palliative contexts. The study gives end-of-life nursing a patient's-eye measure of what matters most.
openalex-w7220920621:
Joelyson Medeiros Fialho de Oliveira and four colleagues at the State University of Pará profiled how very young children process sights, sounds, touch, and movement, in a 2026 occupational therapy article. Their subjects were children from six months to three years old enrolled in the MATERNAR developmental watch program.

Standard infant and toddler sensory questionnaires showed avoidance, sensitivity, and observation as the most common patterns. Hearing was the most affected sense, followed by touch and oral sensation, with balance and body-position senses also widely altered. Because unusual sensory patterns can already appear in the first years and affect daily play and routines, the authors argue for early screening inside child development programs.
osler-evolution-modern-medicine-1921:
Osler traced the whole story of his field in The Evolution of Modern Medicine. He gave the lectures at Yale in 1913, and the book came out in 1921. From early healing and Greek medicine, he moves through the long centuries. Anatomy, surgery, and the germ theory each get their chapter in the tale.

Osler writes history as a doctor who loved old books and old doctors. His narrative gave modern medical history writing its founding shape. Readers meet the makers of medicine as working people, not statues. The Gutenberg text keeps the lectures in their spoken flow. It remains a fine first history of medicine.
plos-pbio-0020021:
Xuan Wang and James E. Haber studied DNA repair in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. When both strands of DNA break, the cell can fix the gap by copying from a matching strand. A protein called RPA coats loose single strands of DNA during that repair.

The step in focus is strand invasion, when the broken end pushes into the intact copy to start the fix. The authors test what RPA does at that exact moment. Getting this right matters because failed repair can lead to cancer or cell death. Yeast offers a clean test bed for the basic steps. The same core repair tools work in human cells, so the lessons carry over.
plos-pbio-0020321:
Sean R. Collins, Adam Douglass, Ronald D. Vale, and their team watched prion growth in PLOS Biology in 2004. Prions are protein clumps, called amyloids, that grow as more copies of the protein join and fold the same wrong way. In yeast, this growth can be filmed and measured with care.

The team found the clumps grow by adding one protein unit at a time, not by merging smaller clumps. That single detail shapes every model of how prions spread. It rules out some theories and supports others. Amyloid growth also sits behind diseases like Alzheimer's. So a clean growth rule in yeast has reach far beyond the test tube.
plos-pbio-0020421:
Mathias Currat and Laurent Excoffier modeled ancient human mating in PLOS Biology in 2004. As modern humans spread into Europe, they met Neandertals already living there. Whether the two groups mixed has long been debated from fossils and DNA.

Their model shows that even rare mixing would likely have left clear traces in today's DNA, given how the expansion unfolded. Since such traces were then unseen, they argue the two groups did not admix, or mixed far less than some claimed. Modeling like this sets the bar for what counts as evidence. It turns a debate of impressions into a test with numbers that DNA studies can check.
plos-pone-0000021:
Mark Hatherill, Tony Hawkridge, Andrew Whitelaw, and co-authors examined a diagnostic trap in children's lung disease in 2006. Children suspected of pulmonary tuberculosis are often tested by culturing germs from the airway. Not every mycobacterium grown that way is the TB germ: a whole family of non-tuberculous relatives also lives in the environment.

The team isolated those non-tuberculous mycobacteria from children being investigated for TB. Finding them raises hard questions for doctors: is the child infected, merely carrying a harmless germ, or sick with something else? Sorting that out changes treatment, since the drugs and the stakes differ. The study maps how often the confusion arises in real clinics.
plos-pone-0000121:
Rony Zachariah, Anthony David Harries, Marcel Manzi, and colleagues published this health study from rural Malawi in PLOS ONE in 2006. It concerns patients infected with both HIV and tuberculosis who were offered anti-retroviral therapy, the drugs that keep HIV in check. The team measured how many patients accepted the treatment.

Their finding, stated in the title, is blunt: acceptance was low, and the cost of transport to reach care was a key barrier. The paper shows that free medicine alone does not get people treated when a bus fare stands in the way. It remains a clear case study for programs fighting HIV in poor rural regions.
plos-pone-0000221:
Amane Koizumi, Günther Zeck, Yixin Ben, and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It describes organotypic culture of adult mammalian retinas, keeping the light-sensing tissue of the eye alive and working outside the body. The cultured retinas stay physiologically functional, responding much as they would in a living eye.

A working retina in a dish lets researchers test drugs and study vision diseases without whole animals at every step. The authors show their culture method preserves that function. The system is a platform for studying retinal disease and for screening treatments aimed at saving sight.
plos-pone-0000321:
Marylyn M. Addo, Rika Draenert, Almas Rathod, and colleagues published this HIV immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fully differentiated CD8 T effector cells are the most battle-ready killer cells against HIV. The authors report these cells are detectable more often in controlled HIV-1 infection than in progressive infection, where the virus wins.

The contrast suggests that having these mature killers on hand goes with keeping the virus in check. The authors compare patients who control the virus with those who do not. The pattern helps define what a protective immune response against HIV actually looks like, a target for vaccine design.
plos-pone-0000421:
Michael P. Cusack and colleagues used network math to find the amino acids a protein can least afford to lose, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their method needs only the protein's structure. By treating the structure as a network of contacts, they identified critical residues, the positions where change is most likely to break the protein.

Knowing the critical spots in advance guides experiments: those are the positions worth mutating, and the ones where natural variants may cause disease. A method that works from structure alone can scan proteins that have never been studied in the lab. The paper is an early example of network analysis moving into protein biology.
plos-pone-0000521:
Nils Arrigo and Claire Arnold documented escaped grapevines reshaping European landscapes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Many European vineyards grow on rootstocks bred in North America to resist pests; these naturalised Vitis rootstocks have spread into the wild. The team studied the consequences for the native wild grapevine.

Escaped rootstocks can hybridize with wild relatives, diluting the native gene pool, and can also carry diseases. The wild grapevine is itself a relic subspecies worth protecting. The study shows farm technology leaking into ecology. A solution bred for farms becomes a pressure on the crop's wild ancestor.
plos-pone-0000621:
Andres Baena, Alan R. Mootnick, James V. Falvo and their co-authors compared a key immune gene across primates in PLOS ONE in 2007. TNF, short for tumor necrosis factor, is a signaling protein central to the immune response. The promoter, the DNA stretch that switches the TNF gene on, is strongly conserved in mammals and especially in primates.

Small spelling differences in that promoter, called SNPs, drew the team's attention. Their title reports that these promoter patterns mark primate family relationships and trace how innate immunity evolved. Readers interested in both evolution and immunology get a case where one gene's control region tells both stories at once.
plos-pone-0000721:
Frank A. J. L. Scheer, Kenneth P. Wright, Richard E. Kronauer and colleagues tested how far the human body clock can stretch. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study was motivated by Mars: a Martian day, or sol, lasts 24.65 hours. That lies outside the range the human circadian pacemaker can entrain to under typical astronaut lighting. Failing to entrain would scramble sleep and performance.

The authors examine plasticity in the clock's intrinsic period, asking whether the period itself can adapt. If the pacemaker can lengthen its own cycle, mission planners gain a biological solution to the sol problem. The results also matter for shift workers and jet lag on Earth.
plos-pone-0000821:
Lyse A. Norian and Paul M. Allen found that anti-tumor T cells grow up fast inside tumors, but not elsewhere, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Increasing the efficacy of adoptively transferred, tumor-specific T cells is a major goal of immunotherapy, where patients receive lab-grown immune cells. A fuller grasp of the effector phase of T cell responses would clearly help. It must come from the tumor site itself. Most studies instead sample blood or lymphoid organs.

Their title reports rapid maturation of effector T cells in tumors during tumor regression, absent in lymphoid organs. The battlefield changes soldiers faster than the barracks does. Sampling tumors directly could reveal what successful immunotherapy actually looks like.
plos-pone-0000921:
Francesca Gabanella, Matthew Butchbach, Luciano Saieva and co-authors linked faulty particle assembly to severity in spinal muscular atrophy, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The disease weakens motor neurons and is caused by low levels of a protein called SMN. SMN works with partner proteins to assemble small nuclear ribonucleoproteins, machines the cell needs to process its messages.

The team asked whether how badly assembly fails matches how severe the disease is. They also found the defect hits a subset of those particles hardest. A match between a lab defect and real severity supports the idea that failed assembly drives the illness. It also points to where a therapy would need to act.
plos-pone-0001021:
Steven Frank examined the puzzle of robustness in evolution, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Organisms buffer themselves against disturbance in many ways. Repair fixes damage, feedback loops hold body systems at their set points, and chemical filters sort signal from noise.

The puzzle is that strong buffering can also permit maladaptation, hidden flaws that surface later. Frank works through why protection and fragility grow from the same machinery. The paper is theory, aimed at the logic of evolution rather than one species. Its value is a clear frame for cases from drug resistance to genetic disease, where robustness cuts both ways.
plos-pone-0001121:
Jellyfish rarely fossilize well, since their bodies are soft and mostly water. Paulyn Cartwright and co-authors report a striking exception in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They describe jellyfish fossils preserved in unusual detail in Middle Cambrian rocks, from roughly half a billion years ago.

Cnidarians, the group that includes jellyfish, split off early in animal history, so their fossils bear on how animal life first diversified. The authors describe what these specimens preserve and what they show about early jellyfish. The finds also matter because jellyfish remain a major part of ocean plankton today.
plos-pone-0001221:
Notch signaling, a conversation between neighboring cells, decides the fates of cells throughout development. Bon-Kyoung Koo and colleagues examined a protein called Mind bomb-1 in mammalian development, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Notch signaling requires that ligand molecules on one cell be pulled inside it, a step handled by ubiquitin ligase enzymes.

The authors report an obligatory role for Mind bomb-1 in mammalian Notch signaling: without it, the pathway fails. Two families of these ligases, Neuralized and Mind bomb, were known to cooperate in flies. Showing that one is indispensable in mammals sharpens the picture of a fundamental pathway.
plos-pone-0001321:
Salvianolic acid B is one of the most active components of Salvia miltiorrhiza. That plant is a traditional Chinese herbal medicine used for disorders of the brain's blood vessels. Chen-Li Liu and colleagues studied how it protects blood vessel lining cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Hydrogen peroxide, an oxidant, can push endothelial cells into apoptosis, programmed cell death.

The authors report that salvianolic acid B inhibits that peroxide-induced apoptosis through regulating PI3K/Akt signaling, a major survival pathway in cells. The protective effects of the herb were known in practice, but the mechanism was not. Their work connects a traditional remedy to a defined molecular route.
plos-pone-0001421:
Sarah Chapelsky and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a plant compound that may block anthrax toxin. Anthrax germs owe much of their harm to a toxin that weakens host defense. A known effect is the bursting of immune cells in culture. The team tested whether the compound celastrol could stop that bursting.

In mouse immune cells, the compound did hold back toxin driven cell bursting. That marks it as a lead worth more study, not yet a drug. Leads that shield host cells take a path unlike germ killing drugs. They may keep working even when germs resist standard drugs, which keeps this line of work of interest.
plos-pone-0001521:
Clotilde Randriamampita and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a tool to watch T cell signals live. How a T cell tells friend from foe with such speed and care was still debated. Space and time control of signals was thought to be key. The team built a sensor that glows when a core T cell enzyme is active.

With the sensor, they watched the enzyme fire both at the contact point and at the far side of the cell. That far side firing was a surprise. Live sensors like this turn fixed cell views into films. They let labs test signal theories as the acts unfold.
plos-pone-0001621:
Anand Kolatkar, Kevin Kennedy, Dan Halabuk, and their colleagues presented a software tool called C-ME in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. C-ME stands for Collaborative Molecular Modeling Environment. It lets research teams work together in a shared 3D space in real time, even when team members are in different places.

The authors note that big projects spanning many fields now produce data stored in separate places. There is no easy way to view it as a whole. Their tool was built to close that gap for work such as proteome-wide studies, which cover all the proteins in a cell or organism. The full text explains how the tool works, what it can show, and how research and training groups can use it to study molecules together.
plos-pone-0001721:
Ziad Obermeyer, Jesse Abbott-Klafter, and Christopher J. L. Murray assessed the world's main tuberculosis strategy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. DOTS, the WHO strategy built on directly observed treatment, had been running nearly fifteen years, yet tuberculosis stayed a major global health problem. With little hard evidence that DOTS cuts the burden, its future role was under debate.

The authors gathered empirical data on whether DOTS improved case finding or treatment success. The full text gives the countries and data sources, the measures compared, and what improvements, if any, the strategy delivered. An honest audit matters because TB programs worldwide spend heavily on this framework, and policy should follow results, not habit.
plos-pone-0001821:
Ron X. Yu and co-authors presented a method to find direct target genes of transcription factors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A major challenge of the post-genome era is reconstructing regulatory networks from accumulated biological knowledge. Tools for identifying direct targets, genes a factor switches on by binding them, are critical to that effort.

Their approach uses joint sequence and expression likelihood, weighing DNA sequence and activity data together. They applied it to DAF-16, a longevity-linked factor in worms. The full text gives the method and the target lists. Distinguishing direct targets from downstream echoes is what turns a gene list into a wiring diagram.
plos-pone-0001921:
Martin Alphonse and co-authors studied an allergy receptor on a white blood cell type in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The receptor, Fc epsilon RI, binds the antibody IgE and plays a key role in allergic asthma. The team had shown that neutrophils, a front-line immune cell, from people with allergic asthma carry a working form of this receptor.

They then asked what controls how much of the receptor these cells show. Two suspects were in view: contact with allergens across the seasons, and Th-2 signals, the immune messages that drive allergy. Knowing the controls could point to new ways to calm asthma at its source.
plos-pone-0002021:
Pablo Tebas and co-authors studied what happens when HIV treatment is paused, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cost and drug side effects once made CD4-guided pauses look attractive: stop therapy, restart when immune counts fall. The large SMART trial then reported a surprise rise in cardiovascular events after treatment interruption.

The team measured metabolic and immune activation changes during such breaks in chronic HIV infection. Their aim was to show how a pause could raise heart risk. Data of this kind ended the fashion for planned breaks and still warn any strategy that lets the virus rebound.
plos-pone-0002121:
Anna Matynia, Stephan Anagnostaras, Brian Wiltgen, and co-authors reported a mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2008 about the genes behind long-lasting memory. Early steps in forming a memory were known to need genes tied to synapses and to the making of new proteins. Far less was known about the later stages, when memories settle in for the long term.

The team ran a large reverse genetic screen, testing many genes at once to see which ones mice need for remote memory. The screen picked out two genes that play a part in that later stage. The result gives memory research new leads on how the brain keeps old memories alive.
plos-pone-0002221:
Toyoaki Natsume and co-authors studied how fission yeast pass on the special packing of their centromeres, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Centromeres are the chromosome spots where the machinery of cell division grabs hold. Their chromatin, the packing of DNA with protein, is unusual and must be copied exactly each time DNA is replicated.

The team focused on Mcl1, a helper protein for DNA polymerase alpha, the enzyme that starts new DNA strands. They found Mcl1 is required to propagate centromere structures in fission yeast. The result links the basic copying machinery to the survival of the chromosome's most vital landmark.
plos-pone-0002321:
Ran Tao and Wayne Hancock studied why one class of T cells resists a death signal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Nur77 is a nuclear receptor that pushes young T cells to die during the selection that removes self-reactive cells. It may also act in mature T cells out in the body. Regulatory T cells, marked by Foxp3, are the immune system's peacekeepers.

The team reports that these regulatory cells resist Nur77-induced apoptosis, and that the resistance promotes the survival of transplanted organs in their models. If peacekeeper cells are built to survive death signals, boosting that trait might help transplants last without heavy drugs.
plos-pone-0002421:
Bilal, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Erhan Bilal, Raul Rabadan, Gabriela Alexe, among others. Its subject is mitochondrial DNA Haplogroup D4a Is a Marker for Extreme Longevity in Japan. The team reports results from full mitochondrial DNA sequences taken from 112 Japanese semi-supercentenarians.

Each person in that group was aged above 105 years, and the data were combined with published results from older adults. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002521:
Elisaphenko and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Eugeny A. Elisaphenko, Nikolay N. Kolesnikov, Alexander I. Shevchenko, among others. Its subject is a Dual Origin of the Xist Gene from a Protein-Coding Gene and a Set of Transposable Elements. X-chromosome inactivation, which occurs in female eutherian mammals is controlled by a complex X-linked locus termed the X-inactivation center (XIC).

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002621:
In 2008, Eunsoo Kim and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about EEF2 analysis challenges the monophyly of archaeplastida and chromalveolata. Authorship is credited in the record to Eunsoo Kim and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Classification of eukaryotes provides a fundamental phylogenetic framework for ecological, medical, and industrial research. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002721:
Emmanuelle Wilhelm and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of TAF6δ controls apoptosis and gene expression in the absence of p53. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Emmanuelle Wilhelm, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Life and death decisions of metazoan cells hinge on the balance between the expression of pro- versus anti-apoptotic gene products. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002821:
In 2008, Josiah Johnston and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was quantitative image analysis reveals distinct structural transitions during aging in caenorhabditis elegans tissues. The catalog record names Josiah Johnston first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Aging is associated with functional and structural declines in many body systems, even in the absence of underlying disease. A further point appears in the abstract. In particular, skeletal muscles experience severe declines during aging, a phenomenon termed sarcopenia. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002921:
Roger Brookes, Philip Hill, Patrick Owiafe and colleagues tested a candidate tuberculosis vaccine in West Africa in 2008. The vaccine, MVA85A, uses a modified virus to carry antigen 85A from the tuberculosis germ. It had raised strong cellular immune responses in volunteers in the United Kingdom.

The PLOS ONE trial assessed safety and immune response in West African volunteers, a group closer to those most at risk of tuberculosis. Testing in the target region matters, since prior exposure and background infections can change vaccine effects. The study is an early step in judging this vaccine where it is needed most.
plos-pone-0003021:
Wangsheng Zhu, Zhongpeng Fan, Chao Zhang and co-authors mapped a puberty timing locus in mice in 2008. Pubertal timing starts when the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis switches back on, and both genes and environment modulate it. Inbred mouse strains differ in vaginal opening age, suggesting genetic background contributes.

A whole genome scan plus refined congenic strain analysis found a dominant X-linked region controlling that timing, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, locating the region on the X chromosome narrows the gene hunt. The work informs study of early and delayed puberty in mammals generally. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003121:
Marta Mastroianni, Kazuo Watanabe, Travis B. White and colleagues present this 2008 PLOS ONE work on a gene targeting tool drawn from mobile group II introns. These introns can insert themselves at exact sites in DNA by a process called retrohoming. In that process the cut-out intron RNA splices back into a DNA strand and is then copied by a protein the intron itself codes for.

The authors study how these reactions work in eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus. Readers learn the steps that let introns move and settle at chosen DNA sites. The work matters because such systems could be shaped into tools for precise gene targeting.
plos-pone-0003221:
Cristianne R. M. Frazier, Peggy Mason, Xiaoxi Zhuang and colleagues test early sugar exposure in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The cause of the current rise in obesity in western nations is poorly understood but is often attributed to a thrifty genotype, an evolutionary predisposition to store calories in times of plenty. In modern industrial environments, that thrift may backfire.

The authors test whether sucrose exposure in early life alters adult motivation and weight gain, as the title states. Readers see development, not just adult diet, put on trial. Early feeding effects would matter for how childhood nutrition advice is framed.
plos-pone-0003321:
Eric Hatterer, Monique Touret, Marie-Françoise Belin and colleagues track dendritic cells from spinal fluid in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In many neuroinflammatory diseases, dendritic cells build up in several parts of the central nervous system, including the cerebrospinal fluid. Myeloid dendritic cells invading the inflamed central nervous system are thus thought to play a major role. Their role covers both the start and the long course of inflammation.

The title reports that cerebrospinal fluid dendritic cells infiltrate the brain parenchyma and target the cervical lymph nodes when the nervous system is inflamed. Readers follow a route from fluid to brain to lymph node. That route may carry antigens that sustain diseases like multiple sclerosis.
plos-pone-0003421:
Njideka Okubadejo and colleagues screened Parkinson's patients in Nigeria for gene faults in this 2008 study. Most cases in their group seemed sporadic, with no family pattern. Three genes were already known to raise Parkinson's risk elsewhere. The team checked those genes in the Nigerian patients.

The genes were LRRK2, PRKN, and ATXN3. Each has variants that can help trigger the disease. Data from African patients had long been thin in this field. Adding Nigerian results makes the global genetic map of Parkinson's more complete. Genetic risk clearly does not stop at the borders of Europe or North America at all.
plos-pone-0003521:
Lei Wang and co-authors described a new gene shaping rice plants in this 2008 paper. Plant shape, or architecture, limits how much rice a field can yield. The gene, named OsLIC, makes a CCCH-type zinc finger protein. Such proteins can switch other genes on and off.

OsLIC acted through brassinosteroid signaling, a plant hormone pathway. It changed leaf and tiller angles, as its name records. Breeders prize genes that tune plant shape directly. This one offers a handle for higher-yielding rice design. Leaf angle decides how much light a rice plant can catch in a dense field.
plos-pone-0003621:
Keerthi Krishnan, Nathan Salomonis, and Su Guo published this developmental biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It looks at Spt5, a protein that controls how genes are read in cells. The team mapped which genes Spt5 acts on as zebrafish embryos develop.

Their mapping showed Spt5 can both slow down and speed up gene reading in living embryos. Earlier lab work had hinted at this dual role, but its reach in a whole animal was unclear. Finding target genes across the embryo shows Spt5 shapes development in both directions at once.
plos-pone-0003721:
Susan Broughton, Nazif Alic, Cathy Slack, and colleagues published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The insulin signaling pathway shapes both metabolism and lifespan in many animals. Fruit flies have seven insulin-like peptides, called DILPs, each made in set tissues and stages.

The team lowered levels of one peptide, DILP2, in the flies. That change altered the flies' metabolic state while leaving the expected lifespan pattern apart from it. The split shows the other DILPs can back each other up, hiding some effects while revealing others. The work shows one pathway can split its jobs between its parts.
plos-pone-0003821:
Julien Mozziconacci, Linda Sandblad, Malte Wachsmuth, and colleagues published this biophysics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Microtubules are the rails of the cell skeleton, built from pairs of tubulin proteins. With GTP present, purified tubulin dimers assemble into tubes in the test tube, a classic lab system.

The team found the dimers first join into small clusters, called oligomers, before joining the microtubule. That early clustering step changes the picture of how microtubules get built. It gives researchers a new stage to target when modeling or disturbing the cell skeleton.
plos-pone-0003921:
Chikara Kaito, Yosuke Omae, Yasuhiko Matsumoto, and co-authors found a gene that tames a dangerous germ in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Staphylococcus aureus, a common cause of severe infection. Colonies of this germ can spread across soft agar plates. The team compared drug-sensitive and drug-resistant strains for that spreading.

All sensitive strains spread, but most resistant strains carrying SCCmec did not. Within that region they found a gene they named fudoh. The gene curbs both colony spreading and the germ's virulence. Its presence may help explain why some resistant strains behave less aggressively.
plos-pone-0004021:
Nils T. Hagen proposed a fairer way to split authorship credit in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Multi-author papers now dominate science publishing. Credit is often given in full to every coauthor. Or it is split equally, which inflates and flattens real contributions.

Hagen's method allocates credit harmonically by author position. First authors get the largest share, with shares falling by rank. Source-level correction aims to fix biases in citation analysis. Fairer credit would sharpen hiring and funding decisions based on records. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004121:
Joydeep Bhattacharya published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks whether the human brain acts more alike across its parts when a person pictures a scene than when they actually see one. The work draws on an idea from physics: near a sharp change of state, very different systems start to behave in the same shared way.

That shared behaviour is called universality, and it hints that far-apart parts of a system are linked. Bhattacharya tests whether mental imagery pushes brain activity toward that linked, universal state. The paper gives readers a physics-based way to think about how imagining and seeing may rest on the same brain workings.
plos-pone-0004221:
Anjali Nath and colleagues published this heart development study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heart development in the womb is vital. Early embryo loss or malformation has been linked to yolk sac blood vessel defects and congenital heart defects. The molecular pathways behind these human defects remain poorly mapped.

Using proteomics, the survey of a sample's full protein set, the team found a cluster of proteins thrown off balance during cardiovascular development. That cluster points to biomarkers, measurable signs, of congenital heart defects. Catching such defects early, before or just after birth, is the long-term aim of this kind of screen.
plos-pone-0004321:
Vini Pereira, David Enard, and Adam Eyre-Walker published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many genomes contain large numbers of transposable elements, mobile DNA pieces, a few of which are known to regulate gene expression. Recent observations suggest these elements may have played a major role in the evolution of gene expression, since many have landed near genes.

The team measured the effect of transposable element insertions on gene expression evolution in rodents. Their analysis weighs whether the elements merely litter the genome or actively rewire it. The answer shapes how we think genomes invent new regulation.
plos-pone-0004421:
Knowing where in the body a tiny RNA is switched on can reveal what it does. Dong Wang, Ming Lu, Jing Miao, and colleagues built a tool for that job in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tool is called Cepred. It predicts how human microRNAs that sit inside other genes are expressed alongside those host genes.

MicroRNAs are short bits of RNA that tune gene activity, and many are tied to disease. How they are made and turned on is still poorly known, and finding them by lab tests alone is slow. A working prediction tool lets researchers guess the tissues where a microRNA acts, then test the best leads first. That speeds up work on gene control and illness.
plos-pone-0004521:
How fast populations can evolve their way out of climate change is simulated by Mats Bjorklund, Esa Ranta, Veijo Kaitala, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. With the climate shifting, there is urgent need to know whether species can adapt in time. Many traits that matter, like size or timing, are quantitative: they vary by degree and rest on many genes.

The team ran individual-based simulations, following virtual creatures one by one. They varied the shape of the fitness curve, how much of a trait is inherited, and how crowded the population was. Those knobs decide whether a population tracks a moving climate or falls behind. The results help set honest limits on rescue by evolution, which conservation plans must respect.
plos-pone-0004621:
Magnetic pulses can test which brain areas plan a reach, show Pierpaolo Busan, Claudia Barbera, Mauro Semenic, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Planning a reaching movement activates both the superior parietal lobule and the premotor cortex. Their activation seems to take place in parallel, which raises the question of what each area contributes.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation, TMS, briefly disrupts a chosen brain area through the skull. The team applied TMS to the parietal and premotor cortex while people planned reaching movements. By knocking each area off line in turn, they could see which parts of planning suffered. Separating the two areas' jobs helps explain how the brain turns a target in view into an arm movement, and how stroke might break that chain.
plos-pone-0004721:
Wei Sun and colleagues built a model to map DNA stretches that stay free of packing proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2009. These open stretches matter for gene control, since open DNA can be read with more ease. A full map needs each stretch start, end, length, and depth of clearing.

The team used a staged model that splits the genome into open and packed parts. Their method aims for a sharp, genome wide portrait of each open stretch. Sharp maps help find gene switches and the proteins that bind them. They also help compare healthy and diseased cells.
plos-pone-0004821:
Armin Schmitt, Johannes Schuchhardt, and Gudrun Brockmann studied the action of key factors in protein evolution at high temporal resolution, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protein evolution is shaped by conservation of amino acid physicochemical properties and structure of the genetic code. Conservation results from negative selection against proteins with reduced functionality, while codon sequences determine the mutational routes available at each position.

High resolution review separates code effects from selection. Knowing which force dominates informs evolutionary models. It also helps interpret genome variation. Protein histories become more predictable. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004921:
A crawling cell pushes out a flat sheet called a lamellipod. The sheet is a web of actin protein. That web is constantly torn down and rebuilt. Takahiro Tsuji and colleagues timed two rival parts of this turnover. They used single-molecule fluorescence microscopy, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. One part is new web growth by the Arp2/3 complex. The other is web breaking by a protein named AIP1.

AIP1-linked disruption ran about ten times faster than Arp2/3 nucleation. The tearing-down side of the cycle is far quicker than assumed. The result helps settle a debate about how the cell's crawling edge renews itself.
plos-pone-0005021:
Cell division ends with two cells pinching apart. A bridge called the midbody manages the final steps. The midbody had been described only in animals. Laura Eme and colleagues traced its parts across the tree of life. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Other eukaryotes use varied structures for the same final steps.

The team found the midbody's protein machinery is ancient. A complex division apparatus existed in the last common ancestor of eukaryotes. Fungi and plants remodeled that inheritance in their own ways. Cell division's toolkit is far older than assumed. The finding pushes a complex structure back over a billion years.
plos-pone-0005121:
Fins and limbs share ancient blueprints. Small timing changes reshape them during evolution. Koji Sakamoto and colleagues found one such change in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared gene expression during fin development. Their focus was Sonic hedgehog, a key patterning signal. Hox genes control when it switches on.

A heterochronic shift moved the signal's timing. Heterochronic means a change in developmental timing. The shift in Hox-mediated activation led to morphological changes in the fin. Timing is the sculptor here. Evolution remodels bodies by resetting developmental clocks. The work shows that process at the gene level. It connects two famous gene families in one mechanism.
plos-pone-0005221:
Brucellosis is among the most widespread diseases passed from animals to people. Animals are almost the only source of human infection, so testing cattle quickly matters. Bronsvoort and colleagues compared a fast flow test for brucellosis antibodies with the standard lab test in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The work was done in West African zebu cattle, the Bos indicus breed common in the region. The reference test, called cELISA, is accurate but needs a proper lab. A field-ready test that matches it would let vets screen herds on the spot and act sooner.
plos-pone-0005321:
Newborn screening uses dried blood spots to catch metabolic diseases early. The same spots could screen for immune disorders, which number more than a hundred. Janzi and colleagues tested microarray screening for one such disorder, C3 deficiency, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

C3 is a core protein of the complement system, part of early immune defense. Babies missing it face severe infections before anyone suspects an immune fault. A blood-spot microarray test could add immune screening to the panel every newborn already receives. One more test on the same drop of blood costs a lab very little. So a screen that rides on the blood spots already drawn from each newborn is an easy win for child health.
plos-pone-0005421:
John Young, Jan Martel, and co-authors described tiny grains found in blood serum in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Some workers had claimed that such grains were a new form of tiny living bacteria. The authors tested what the grains are made of and how they form.

They showed that the grains form in human and cow serum when calcium or phosphate is added. The grains turned out to be mixed clumps of mineral and protein that can change shape. Their work argues that the grains are not living things, but early stages of mineral build-up in serum.
plos-pone-0005521:
Louise Allan and co-authors followed older people with dementia to study falls, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Falls are a major cause of injury and death in dementia, yet no study had tracked fall risks in this group alone. No proven way to prevent their falls existed either.

The team watched patients over time and recorded who fell and what set them apart. They looked for risks that care staff can change, such as drugs or unsafe routines. Naming those risks is the first step toward trials that can cut falls in dementia care.
plos-pone-0005621:
Lin Han and co-authors studied how DNA looping controls genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Genes are often switched on by proteins that bind DNA far from the gene itself. The DNA bends into a loop so the distant site can reach the gene's start.

The team measured how loop formation depends on the amount of binding protein and on the loop's length. Those two factors set how strongly the gene responds. Exact rules for looping help scientists predict gene behaviour and build genetic circuits that work as designed. Loops also explain how enhancers far away on the DNA can control a gene as if they were close.
plos-pone-0005721:
Olivier Kosmider and colleagues studied in 2009 how a blood hormone switches off a growth receptor in leukemic cells. Their model was a mouse leukemia line stuck at an early red-cell stage, driven by too much of a factor called Spi-1. The hormone erythropoietin normally pushes red cells to mature.

The team found the hormone lowers levels of Kit, the receptor for stem cell factor. A kinase named Lyn helps carry that effect. The finding shows two growth signals trading places as a cell matures. In leukemia, that trade is jammed, and knowing the wiring may suggest ways to free it.
plos-pone-0005821:
Nikolai Khodarev and co-authors reported in 2009 that a signal pathway tied to interferon can, paradoxically, help tumors spread and resist treatment. STAT1 signaling is classically antiviral and tumor-suppressing. But tumors with the pathway stuck on can behave more aggressively.

The team tested whether STAT1 activity amplifies metastatic potential and therapy resistance. Their results supported that darker role in their models. The same pathway can be friend or foe depending on context, a common theme in cancer. Knowing which tumors run it hot may predict which ones need harder treatment.
plos-pone-0005921:
Random ups and downs in protein levels are a fact of cell life. Anatoly Mayburd asked in 2009 whether that noise could help start long-term disease. His PLOS ONE paper argues that chance shifts in gene expression, seen first in nerve precursor cells, may push cells toward a sick state over time.

Mayburd links the same noise to how treatment might work. If random change can tip a cell into disease, then therapy may need to calm the noise, not just fix one gene. The paper offers a frame for thinking about chronic illness that starts from chance events inside cells rather than from clear outside causes.
plos-pone-0006021:
A memory may be stored one tiny spine at a time. Amadou Corera, Guy Doucet and Edward Fon tested that scale of learning in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies long-term potentiation, the lasting boost a synapse gains after strong use, inside single dendritic spines cut off from the rest of the neuron.

Even in isolation, a spine could gain that lasting boost, the title reports. The change runs through NMDA receptors and a rise in AMPA receptors, the standard machinery of this kind of learning. Showing that one spine alone can learn makes the spine the smallest known stage for memory, a fact that guides models of how brains store experience.
plos-pone-0006121:
Schizophrenia disables about one person in a hundred, and its causes run partly in the genes. Jinong Feng, Guihua Sun, Jin Yan and colleagues looked for clues on the X chromosome in 2009.
