Their PLOS ONE paper gathers evidence tying schizophrenia to alterations in microRNAs, tiny gene regulators, including parts of the machinery that processes them, which earlier work had linked to X-linked intellectual disability.

An X-chromosome pattern would help explain the disease's uneven run through families and sexes. MicroRNAs each tune many genes at once, so a few altered ones can bend brain development broadly. The evidence assembled here gives genetics a defined place to dig next in a disease that has resisted simple answers.
plos-pone-0006221:
A gut hormone called GLP-1 helps pancreatic beta cells release insulin when sugar rises. Marie-Line Peyot and colleagues asked whether its signals also steer how beta cells burn fuel, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of rodent cells. GLP-1 and a related drug switch on several known signal pathways in these cells.

The title states the conclusion: those signals do not drive fuel and energy metabolism in the cells. Insulin release and energy burning appear to be run by separate controls. The distinction matters for diabetes drugs based on GLP-1. Sharper mechanism maps help drug makers predict benefits and side effects more accurately.
plos-pone-0006321:
A yeast that causes meningitis in vulnerable patients coats its proteins with sugars as a first decorating step. Sven Willger, Joachim Ernst, and Andrew Alspaugh characterised the PMT gene family behind that step in Cryptococcus neoformans, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. These enzymes add mannose sugars to proteins and form a conserved family with three subfamilies.

Mapping the family's members in this fungus shows which enzymes do the decorating. Protein glycosylation shapes how the fungus grows and interacts with hosts. The characterisation opens targets for antifungal drug design. It also aids comparison with better-studied yeasts.
plos-pone-0006421:
Karl Friston, Jean Daunizeau, and Stefan Kiebel wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE theory paper on how agents learn to act. They ask whether reinforcement learning, where acts are shaped by rewards, is really needed at all. Control theory comes under the same doubt. Their answer rests on a free-energy view of perception.

The authors show that an agent can learn complex, flexible acts by adjusting its inner states to cut surprise. No reward signal has to drive the process. Perception and action become two sides of one self-tuning system. The argument offers a fresh base for thinking about brains and smart machines.
plos-pone-0006521:
Ioannis Stylianou and co-authors described a mutant mouse with a liver-specific defect in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cardiovascular disease is the largest cause of premature death worldwide. Circulating plasma lipid levels are a key risk factor, and scavenger receptor class B member 1 helps control them. The team used ENU mutagenesis, a chemical method, to create point mutations.

One novel mutation caused loss of the receptor in the liver specifically, as their title reports. A liver-only loss lets researchers separate liver roles from effects elsewhere. Such mice are precision tools for lipid research. They may clarify how this receptor protects against heart disease.
plos-pone-0006621:
Enitan Carrol and co-authors tested blood markers of severe bacterial infection in Malawian children in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fast spotting of these infections, and fast use of the right drugs, can cut child deaths by a large share. The team checked the accuracy of five markers in children thought to have severe infections. They weighed how well each marker finds the disease and how well it predicts the outcome.

In clinics with few tools, a cheap blood marker can guide who needs urgent care most. A marker must do both jobs well to earn its place. Their results help hospitals pick markers that work on the ground there. Tests should be proven where they will be used, not just where they were made.
plos-pone-0006721:
Anne-Cécile Huby and co-authors studied kidney damage in mice engineered to overproduce renin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protein leaking into urine marks declining kidney function. It also predicts heart disease risk. The leak is tied to broken slit diaphragms and lost podocyte foot processes. Those structural changes were long considered irreversible.

Podocytes are the cells that wrap kidney filters. The transgenic mice overexpressing renin develop chronic renal disease. The authors examined whether podocyte structure could be restored. They also tracked whether kidney disease improved along with structure. Evidence of repair would challenge the idea that this damage is permanent. It would open new options for treating chronic kidney disease.
plos-pone-0006821:
Clarence C. Gravlee, Amy L. Non, and Connie J. Mulligan studied blood pressure, ancestry, and race in southeastern Puerto Rico in PLOS ONE in 2009. Race in genetics and medicine is a contested topic. Debates weigh genetic against sociocultural explanations for health gaps. Few studies integrate both kinds of evidence. The authors set out to combine them in one population.

They measured genetic ancestry alongside social classification of race. Then they related both to blood pressure inequalities. The design asks whether genes or social labels track health better. Results speak to how medicine should use race at all. The study is a model for separating ancestry from social experience.
plos-pone-0006921:
Laith Yakob and Guiyun Yan published a modelling study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on malaria control. Their subject was integrated vector management, an approach drawing fresh interest at the time. They asked what happens when two tools are combined instead of used alone. The tools were larval habitat source reduction and insecticide-treated bed nets.

The model attacks several points in the malaria transmission cycle at once. Yakob and Yan reasoned that combined pressure might act together and beat single-tool programs. Bed nets alone were then the main intervention in wide use. Their work gives malaria planners a way to test combined strategies before field trials.
plos-pone-0007021:
Joseph Jeffry, Shuang-Quan Yu, Parul Sikand, and colleagues targeted pain fibers in the spinal cord in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic pain is a major clinical problem. Opiates are often the only treatment, yet they bring sedation and dangerous breathing suppression. The team focused on sensory terminals carrying the receptor TRPV1.

They used resiniferatoxin, a powerful TRPV1 activator, delivered to the spinal cord. Silencing just those nerve endings promised pain relief without whole-body drug effects. Long lasting analgesia from one targeted treatment would be a real advance. It could spare patients the daily risks of opioid therapy.
plos-pone-0007121:
Dru Dace, Aslam Khan, Jennifer Stark, and colleagues studied a nerve disease driven by immune cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Demyelinating polyneuropathy strips insulation from nerves. It comes in acute form as Guillain-Barré syndrome, and in chronic forms too. Interleukin-10 is usually classed as an anti-inflammatory signal. Yet it had also been tied to abnormal immune activity.

The team raised IL-10 levels and watched the disease that followed. Excess IL-10 promoted a chronic, macrophage-driven nerve damage. The damage depended on the Fas ligand death pathway. The result warns that a calming signal can harm in the wrong setting.
plos-pone-0007221:
Wayne Dawson and Kenji Yamamoto considered schooling during a fast-spreading epidemic in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Large cities move people quickly through transport networks. An airborne or contact pathogen can ride those routes and spread through a whole population in a short time.

The authors argue that home education may fare best in the right social setting. They point to extended family culture and an aging society as helpful conditions. Their model links daily movement, household structure, and schooling choices. It offers planners another way to think about keeping children learning during a pandemic.
plos-pone-0007321:
Olga Renner, Simone Harsch, Elke Schaeffeler, and colleagues studied a bile acid transporter gene and gallstones in 2009. Gallstone disease, or cholelithiasis, has many causes. Several mechanisms of stone formation had been proposed, including reduced activity of a transporter that reclaims bile acids in the ileum.

That transporter is made by the gene SLC10A2. Earlier work found lower expression of the gene in gallstone carriers. The authors test a variant of SLC10A2 as a risk factor. Their PLOS ONE finding links inherited transporter differences to gallstone formation in patients studied.
plos-pone-0007421: Jessica A. Wray, Mary C. Sugden, Darryl C. Zeldin, and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on an enzyme and a nuclear receptor. The enzyme is CYP2J2, one of the epoxygenases that make signaling fats from arachidonic acid. The receptor is PPAR alpha, a nuclear receptor that controls fat metabolism genes. Their title reports that CYP2J2 activates PPAR alpha in laboratory tests and in living systems, linking fat-derived signals to gene control.
plos-pone-0007521:
Fei Cai and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on carboxysomes, tiny protein compartments inside many bacteria. A carboxysome wraps the carbon-fixing enzyme RubisCO in a thin protein shell. The shell holds carbon dioxide in, giving the enzyme a rich environment to work in. Five-sided proteins sit at the shell's corners, its vertices. The team tested whether those corner pieces are essential to the barrier.

Without the pentameric vertex proteins, the shell could not keep carbon dioxide from leaking. The corners are therefore not decoration; they seal the compartment. That design lesson comes from nature's own carbon-capture device. Engineers hoping to copy carboxysomes now know which parts cannot be skipped. The study also clarifies how a shell built from simple pieces achieves a tight seal. Form and function meet at the corners.
plos-pone-0007621:
Carolyn Riddell and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on insect immunity and the force of matchups. Field work in spineless animals shows the result of an infection hangs on the exact host and parasite pair. That fact clashes with the old view of insect immunity as broad and blunt. The team measured which defenses insects raised across many host-parasite pairs. They asked whether the defenses called up hinge on who is fighting whom.

The pattern was pair by pair. Distinct pairs called up distinct sets of defenses. A blunt alarm would look the same each time; this one did not. Insects, it seems, tune their response more than books once allowed. That tuning reshapes how field scientists model disease in wild insects. It also counts for pest control with living agents, where the matchup decides who wins.
plos-pone-0007721:
Laura Hausmann and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns the barn owl, a bird famed for pinpoint hearing. The owl's face is ringed by a ruff of stiff feathers. That ruff shapes the sound that reaches each ear.

The authors tested the ruff's role by removing it in a virtual model. Without the ruff, the owl's ability to locate sounds dropped. The test shows the facial ruff works like a built-in dish for hearing. It sharpens the cues the owl uses to hunt prey in total darkness.
plos-pone-0007821:
Elisabeth Frank and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It improves protein measurement in mouse models of mental illness. Finding which proteins change in such models is essential for understanding disease. Mass spectrometry is the leading tool for comparing protein levels.

To make comparisons exact, scientists label tissues with heavy isotopes. The team fed mice bacteria enriched with heavy nitrogen, isotope 15N. The novel diet labels the animals' own proteins from within. Their method sharpens proteomic analyses of the brain. Better measurements give psychiatric research a firmer base.
plos-pone-0007921:
William Monahan published a modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It builds a mechanistic model of where species can live as seasons change. Niche theory guides how scientists predict species' responses to climate change. A species' realized niche depends on its neighbors, while its fundamental niche is set by physiology.

Monahan's model starts from that physiology instead of from past sightings. It measures how distributions should shift across seasonal temperature gradients. Models grounded in mechanism can extrapolate to climates never seen before. That is exactly what climate forecasts demand. The work offers conservation a sharper predictive tool.
plos-pone-0008021:
David Gunn and colleagues asked why some women look young for their years, in PLOS ONE in 2009. A vast trade sells creams and treatments on that wish, yet the true drivers of a youthful face were untested. Twins offered a way to split nature from habit.

Comparing twins and other women, the team weighed which face traits set guessed age and how much genes counted against sun, smoke, and other habits. Both sides mattered, but not evenly for every trait. The work gives buyers and makers a sober map of what can, and cannot, be bought in a jar.
plos-pone-0008121:
Kevin Yip and colleagues rebuilt computer gene networks more truly by joining two data kinds in PLOS ONE in 2010. The DREAM3 contest asks teams to infer how genes control each other inside a simulated cell. Two data kinds were on offer: readings from strains with one gene deleted, and readings over time after a push.

Each kind alone left gaps in the map. Joined, they let the team draw the clostest match to the hidden true network in the contest. The lesson is plain for real biology too: kinds of data that seem spare apart can be rich together.
plos-pone-0008221:
Clive Bate and colleagues tested a diabetes drug against prion disease in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Prion diseases turn a normal host protein into a misfolded, harmful form. That harmful form builds up in the brain. Its spread is tied to synapse loss and nerve cell death. Few treatments exist for these fatal diseases.

The drug glimepiride lowered expression of the normal prion protein in their tests. It also prevented formation of the disease form. Cells were protected against prion-mediated toxicity as a result. The findings suggest a common drug class might be worth exploring further.
plos-pone-0008321:
Philip Bejon and colleagues studied malaria and bed nets in children in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Insecticide-treated nets reduce a child's exposure to malaria. Less exposure should cut disease, but may also slow the building of immunity. Long-term data after community-wide net distribution show sustained benefits overall. Common practice, though, varies in who uses nets and when.

The team found that age and net use interact to set risk. Febrile malaria risk depended on both factors together. That nuance matters for targeting protection to the most vulnerable children. It also informs how net programs are evaluated.
plos-pone-0008421:
Long Nam Nguyen, David Trofa, and Joshua D. Nosanchuk studied a fungal pathogen in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Candida parapsilosis is a yeast that infects humans. Its fatty acid synthase is built from two subunits encoded by Fas1 and Fas2. The team deleted the Fas2 genes using a modified genetic technique. The gene proved essential in media lacking fatty acids.

Fatty acid synthase thus impacts the pathobiology of this fungus. It mattered both in vitro and during mammalian infection. An essential enzyme is a candidate drug target. Blocking fat synthesis could weaken a pathogen that resists other drugs.
plos-pone-0008521:
Robert Holman and co-authors survey prion diseases in the United States in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Prion diseases are rare, progressive brain disorders in humans and animals. The most common human form is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, or CJD. It occurs worldwide at low rates. Variant CJD is a newer form linked to animal disease. It emerged as a zoonosis, an infection passed from animals. The team summarize US cases and patterns.

Their survey covers incidence, demographics, and disease forms nationwide. Such surveillance helps detect new clusters or a rise in variant cases. Prion diseases are always fatal, so early detection matters for blood and tissue safety. The paper gives a national baseline for the United States.
plos-pone-0008621:
Annie J. Sasco, Antoine Jaquet, Emilie Boidin, and co-authors published a global health review in PLOS ONE in 2010. Strong drug combinations had begun letting people with HIV live much longer. In wealthy countries, that longer life came with a higher risk of cancer. The authors asked what the same shift would mean for sub-Saharan Africa.

They weighed what was known about cancers tied to AIDS across the region. They also looked ahead, asking how wider drug access and longer lives might change that burden. Cancer care there often starts late, with few tools to treat it. Their review frames planning needs early, before clinics face a wave they cannot handle.
plos-pone-0008721:
Rogério Rosada, Ana Moreira, Fabiani Frantz, and colleagues tested whether prior immunity blunts a lung drug. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drug joins human IL-13 to a weakened bacterial toxin. It aims at cells that drive lung scarring, or fibrosis. Patients may already carry immunity to that toxin from past exposures. Such immunity could disarm the drug before it works.

Mice with immunity to the toxin still gained protection from lung fibrosis. The drug's benefit survived the immune memory against one part. That survival keeps the treatment idea alive for real patients with similar immunity.
plos-pone-0008821:
Yosuke Ichijima, Ken-ichi Yoshioka, Yoshiko Yoshioka, and colleagues linked copy stress in DNA to doubled genomes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early tumor cells gain immortality while their genomes grow unstable. How that instability starts on its own was elusive. Oncogenes can force cells to copy DNA too fast. That rush, called replication stress, leaves lesions behind.

Lesions from copy stress triggered errors during cell division. Some daughter cells ended with twice the normal chromosome set. Tetraploid cells are a known stepping stone to cancer chaos. The route ties a common early stress to genome doubling.
plos-pone-0008921:
Isabelle Mouro-Chanteloup, Sylvie Cochet, Mohamed Chami, and colleagues rebuilt a human ammonia channel inside artificial bubbles. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rh proteins move ammonium across cell membranes throughout the body. The human member RhCG works in kidney and other tissues. Studying a membrane channel in isolation requires a clean setting. Liposomes, tiny fat bubbles, provide exactly that. Purified protein must first be made and kept stable.

Inserted into liposomes, the purified RhCG channel worked. Ammonium crossed the bubble walls through the rebuilt channel. A working rebuild proves the protein alone suffices for transport. The system now allows precise tests of channel mechanics.
plos-pone-0009021:
Anders Larsen and Søren-Peter Olesen mixed two channel versions to copy the heart's real electrical current, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A current called IKr helps reset the heartbeat after each contraction. It flows through channels built from the ERG1 protein. Two forms of that protein, ERG1a and ERG1b, were both suspected contributors.

Natural IKr varies oddly in speed from cell to cell. Expressing the two forms in different ratios reproduced that variety. The blend also changed the shape of the heart cell's electrical cycle. The heart's current, it seems, is a duet rather than a solo.
plos-pone-0009121:
Lorelei Shoemaker and co-authors listed proteins that set young brain progenitors apart from older ones, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brain grows from a mixed pool of neural stem and progenitor cells. The differences inside that pool are poorly charted. Markers distinguishing the cell types would sharpen brain development research.

The team compared proteins in mouse cortical progenitors. Embryonic and postnatal cells carried measurably different protein sets. Some differences likely run migration, growth, or fate choice. A parts list for each age helps labs isolate the cells they need.
plos-pone-0009221:
Jan Spanholtz and co-authors published this cancer therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Natural killer cells are immune cells that can attack tumors. Giving them to patients is a promising extra treatment for many cancers. The catch is numbers: therapy needs huge counts of working cells, grown under clinical rules.

The team built a method to grow them from umbilical cord blood. They started from CD34-positive stem cells found in that blood. Their protocol expanded the killer cells by very large, log-scale amounts while keeping them functional. A reliable supply like this is what adoptive cell therapy needs to reach more patients.
plos-pone-0009321:
Vincent Zijnge and co-authors published this dental study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mouth is coated with biofilms, layered cities of bacteria on the teeth. Those films cause gum disease and tooth decay. They also serve scientists as a handy model for how biofilms grow and resist antibiotics.

The team examined the architecture of oral biofilms on natural teeth. They mapped how the layers are arranged and which bacteria sit where. Structure explains much of a biofilm's toughness, since sheltered cells survive attacks. Knowing the layout of the real thing, on real teeth, grounds the models built in dishes.
plos-pone-0009421:
Danielle Doucet and co-authors published this rat trauma study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Severe injury with heavy bleeding often ends in lung damage and organ failure. A key step is gut injury: starved of blood, the gut leaks and inflames. That gut damage then drives harm to the lungs.

The team tested drugs that activate the estrogen receptor in rats after trauma and hemorrhagic shock. The treatment limited injury to both gut and lung. A hormone-based shield against the cascade could help trauma care, where minutes matter and options are few. The study identifies a pathway worth testing for that protection.
plos-pone-0009521:
Craig Atencio and Christoph Schreiner mapped sound circuits in cat cortex in PLOS ONE in 2010. The primary auditory cortex is the first cortex area to handle sound. Its cells are laid out in columns that run through stacked layers. Signals move both up the columns and across the layers. The team recorded cell activity to trace that flow.

Their map shows how the microcircuit extracts features from sound and passes them on. Different layers play distinct roles in the chain. Knowing the routing helps explain how raw sound becomes a signal the brain can use. It grounds models of hearing in direct measures.
plos-pone-0009621:
Thomas Richardson and co-authors looked at records and extremes in ant colonies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ant societies divide work among many members. Some leave the nest to forage or patrol, while others stay home. The team studied the dynamics of individual activity over time. They asked how record breaking bursts of work arise and fade in such a system.

Patterns in those records matched ideas from the study of other complex systems. Simple rules at the level of one ant can yield rich colony behavior. The work links ant labor to a broader science of extremes and records. It helps explain how a colony stays efficient without any central plan.
plos-pone-0009721:
Trypanosoma cruzi is the parasite that causes Chagas disease in the Americas. Igor Cestari and Marcel Ramirez studied how some strains slip into host cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The parasite spreads to people mainly through biting insects.

The immune system's complement arm should clear the parasite's infective forms from the blood. For resistant strains, that clearance worked poorly, letting the parasites reach cells and invade them. Weak clearance thus helps explain why some strains infect so well. The finding points to an early battle the immune system often loses.
plos-pone-0009821:
Graves' disease is an immune disorder that makes the thyroid gland overactive. Shuang-Xia Zhao and colleagues looked for gene links to the disease in China's Han population. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Han Chinese are the largest ethnic group in China.

The gene they examined is CTLA4, which helps set how active immune cells become. The study tested whether variants in that gene associate with Graves' disease. Immune genes are natural suspects in a disease where immunity attacks the thyroid. Findings in one population help show how widely the link holds.
plos-pone-0009921:
DNA microarrays read thousands of genes at once, but only if their probes are well chosen. Jennifer Mulle and colleagues put probe selection to an empirical test. Their evaluation appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Probes are short oligonucleotide strands fixed to the chip, each matched to one gene. Empirical evaluation means judging choices by real performance, not theory alone. Microarrays were the workhorse of gene studies for a decade. Bad probes blur results and can fake gene activity. The findings help labs design arrays that read genes cleanly. Chips can hold tens of thousands of probes.
plos-pone-0010021:
Rita Pinter and Robert Hindges studied mouse eye development in PLOS ONE in 2010, focusing on small RNA molecules called microRNAs. As eyes grow, nerve fibers from the retina must cross or turn at the optic chiasm, a key choice point. Getting that wiring right is what lets the brain build a proper picture from both eyes.

In mice lacking Dicer, an enzyme needed for microRNAs to work, the team found retinal defects. Fibers also went astray at the chiasm in these mutants. The findings show that fine-tuning by small RNAs is part of how the visual system wires itself.
plos-pone-0010121:
Yukio Yamamoto and co-authors report a 2010 PLOS ONE mouse liver study on how a drug-sensing receptor helps liver tumors grow. Phenobarbital, a seizure drug, promotes liver cancer in mice without damaging DNA directly. It switches on a receptor called CAR, but the growth steps were unknown.

CAR switched on a protective gene, Gadd45b, in livers and tumors. That protein then teamed with CAR to block a death pathway set off by an immune signal, TNF-alpha. Liver cells from mice missing either gene could not be protected. Blocking cell death, the authors propose, is one way CAR lets damaged liver cells survive and form tumors.
plos-pone-0010221:
The authors were María Larriba, Juan Casado-Vela, Natalia Pendás-Franco, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study hunted protein targets of a cancer factor in human colon cancer. The factor, Snail1, drives a change called EMT, where cells loosen and gain invasive traits. Gene studies had listed many Snail1-regulated genes, several tied to tumor spread in different cell types.

Using proteomic analysis, a screen of proteins rather than genes, the team found novel target proteins. Protein-level evidence can catch changes that gene studies miss. Each new target adds to the map of how colon tumors become invasive.
plos-pone-0010321:
Kosuke Tanegashima and co-authors study a signaling protein and body weight in a 2010 PLOS ONE mouse paper. The protein, CXCL14, draws immune cells and was earlier tied to blood sugar control in obese female mice. Its wider role in weight control was explored here in a standard mouse strain.

Mice lacking CXCL14 weighed seven to eleven percent less as adults, in both sexes, mainly because they ate less. Energy use and movement did not rise. In two obese mutant strains, lacking CXCL14 blunted full obesity. Hunger signals in the brain also rose less after fasting, and the mice ate strikingly little in a new cage, hinting at a brain role in feeding.
plos-pone-0010421:
Jérôme Verine and colleagues tested a possible marker for a common kidney cancer in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clear cell renal cancer is the most frequent type of kidney tumor. No specific marker existed to detect or track it. The team had earlier found a gene, angptl4, switched on strongly in these tumors. It responds to low oxygen, a common tumor condition. They asked whether its message RNA could serve as the marker.

A good marker should flag both first tumors and spread ones. It should also appear in samples doctors can actually take. Testing the RNA in patient material was the next step this study took. Kidney cancer found early is far more curable. A reliable marker would change how it is watched and treated.
plos-pone-0010521:
Jan Bressler and colleagues tested whether a fat-linked gene raises diabetes risk differently by ancestry in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variants in the gene FTO track with higher body weight in European groups. One variant also raised diabetes risk when first found in a genome-wide scan. The team used the long-running ARIC study of American adults. They compared effects in white and African-American participants.

The gene's link to weight and diabetes was not the same in both groups. Such differences warn against exporting genetic findings across populations unchecked. They also hint that the gene acts through paths that vary with background and environment. Large mixed cohorts like ARIC are essential for fair genetic medicine. This study uses one to keep conclusions honest.
plos-pone-0010621:
Dorret Boomsma and colleagues estimated how much of adult ADHD is inherited, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most heritability work on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder used children. Far less was known about adults, whose symptoms often persist.

The team scored adults with a standard ADHD index and compared relatives. Genetic factors explained a large share of the differences in scores. Shared childhood surroundings explained much less. The result supports treating adult ADHD as a strongly heritable condition. That shapes how doctors think about family risk, screening, and long-term care for adults.
plos-pone-0010721:
Julia Rausenberger and colleagues built a full model of how a plant light sensor works, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Phytochrome B is a protein that reads red light and steers plant growth. A seedling in shade grows tall and pale; in open light it grows short and green. The sensor's protein dynamics drive that whole-body choice.

Their model links the sensor's slow molecular switching to growth outcomes. It predicts how plants react when light flickers or changes color. Few models in plant science span from single proteins to whole seedlings. A working bridge between those scales can guide crop breeding for dense planting, where shade responses cost yield.
plos-pone-0010821:
John Pisciotta, Yongjin Zou, and Ilia Baskakov measured electric current from cyanobacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cyanobacteria are ancient microbes that capture sunlight and release oxygen. They account for a large share of Earth's photosynthesis. Whether living cells hand off part of that captured energy as current was an open, testable question.

In light, the bacteria produced a measurable electric current. In darkness the current fell away. The flow thus came from photosynthesis itself, not from stored food. Living solar cells remain far weaker than panels. Still, the proof matters: biology can be wired directly. That is a step toward devices that grow their own power source.
plos-pone-0010921:
Alexei Samsonovich and Giorgio Ascoli published this language study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Computers that map word meanings usually place words in spaces with hundreds of dimensions, each tied to a narrow topic, and they often miss that opposites are closely related. The authors built a simpler kind of semantic map using a self-organizing method.

Their low-dimensional map places synonyms near each other and antonyms in an orderly relation, without being told any meanings in advance. Its first three axes came out cleanly interpretable: good versus bad, calm versus excited, and open versus closed. Samsonovich and Ascoli show that a handful of deep dimensions may underlie how minds organize meaning. A compact meaning map could power better automated text analysis and sharpen theories of how people judge words.
plos-pone-0011021:
Peter Loudon, Eric Yager, Debbie Lynch and co-authors published this flu vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recent bird and swine flu outbreaks kept the pandemic threat vivid, and DNA vaccines promise fast manufacture and possibly broader protection. The team tested an H1N1 DNA vaccine shot into the skin of rhesus macaques by a gene gun, with a growth factor added as a booster.

Macaques were immunized three times over sixteen weeks with the vaccine encoding a flu surface protein, with or without GM-CSF, a factor that recruits immune cells. Loudon and colleagues measured responses both in the blood and at mucosal surfaces, where flu first enters. Their work tests whether a skin-delivered DNA vaccine, helped by an immune recruiter, can protect at the respiratory front line as well as systemically, a combination pandemic planning needs.
plos-pone-0011121:
Mancuso, Sammarco and Grabczyk studied a jumping gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. The element, called Tn7, can cut itself from one DNA spot and paste into another. The team asked what kinds of DNA spots it prefers when the DNA folds into a triple strand shape.

Tn7 favored repeated three letter DNA runs when those triple strand forms could arise. Knowing a jumping gene's favorite targets helps predict where it will land. That knowledge is useful for genome science and for designing safer gene tools. It also links DNA shape, not just DNA letters, to where genes move.
plos-pone-0011221:
Polato, Voolstra, Schnetzer and colleagues heated young corals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Larvae of a reef building coral came from several locations. The team exposed them to thermal stress and compared how larvae from each place responded at the gene and survival level.

Responses differed by home location, showing local variation in heat tolerance. That variation is a resource for reef recovery: tougher larvae can seed new reefs. As oceans warm, planting heat tolerant corals gives reefs a better chance. The study helps managers choose source sites for restoration with climate in mind.
plos-pone-0011321:
Curlin, Huang, Lu and colleagues tested gut samples from men in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human adenovirus, a common virus family, was sought in gut samples taken from the men in this study. The team measured how often the virus could be detected there.

Detection was frequent, showing the virus persists in the gut more than expected. That persistence matters for HIV vaccine research, since some HIV vaccine approaches use adenovirus as a carrier. Prior gut exposure could change how such vaccines perform in trials. The finding helps trial designers interpret results in this population.
plos-pone-0011421:
Amir Nia and co-authors showed in 2010 that a gene variant can predict how well a heart rhythm drug works. Flecainide steadies the heart in atrial fibrillation, a common rhythm disorder, yet patients respond unevenly for reasons doctors could not see. The team tested whether variation in the gene for a heart adrenaline receptor explained the difference.

Patients carrying a particular form of the receptor gene responded to the drug differently from those without it. A simple genetic test could therefore help doctors choose who should get this drug and who should try another first. That is the promise of personalized prescribing: less trial and error with drugs that carry real side effects. The study is a step toward heart care in which the prescription is matched to the patient's genes from the start.
plos-pone-0011521:
Eugenia Villa-Cuesta, Brian Sage, and Marc Tatar examined in 2010 how a survival protein keeps being made while fruit flies fast. The protein dFoxO helps cells weather hunger, and fasting normally shuts down most protein production to save energy. The puzzle is how the cell keeps producing this one protector while the general machinery idles.

The answer lies in special landing pads within the protein's own message, internal ribosome entry sites in its head region, which let production continue during fasting. That workaround reveals a priority system: survival instructions jump the queue when food runs out. The mechanism is a neat example of cells planning for hard times inside the design of a single gene. It may also hint at how tumor cells, which often fast in poorly fed tissue, keep their own protectors flowing.
plos-pone-0011621:
Liu Yang and co-authors developed a way to measure cell stress in living tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells react to a build-up of unfolded proteins in a compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum. This unfolded protein response is a key defence and is tied to many human diseases, yet its true level in the body was hard to gauge.

Their method uses a chemical tag that captures a key stress signal, revealing how much strain cells are under in normal conditions. The measurements show how close healthy cells run to their limits. Better measures of this stress should help research on diabetes, liver disease and other linked illnesses.
plos-pone-0011721:
Xuhua Guan and co-authors reviewed three decades of pneumonia research on mainland China, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pneumonia is a leading infectious killer worldwide, but China's share of that burden was unclear, because much of the data sits in Chinese-language journals that international reviews miss.

The team systematically searched both Chinese and English literature from 1985 to 2008 for primary data on pneumonia occurrence and deaths. Combining both sources gives the first clear measure of the disease's toll in China. That baseline is essential for judging vaccines and treatment programmes there.
plos-pone-0011821:
Brandon Beagle and Gail Johnson studied a loose piece of a signal protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Wnt pathway is a master control route that guides cell growth and cell fate, so its output is kept under tight control at many levels. One of its parts is the receptor helper LRP6, which also has an inner piece that can float free in the cell.

The authors tested how that free piece, called LRP6-ICD, changes the work of the TCF/LEF-1 switches that turn Wnt target genes on. The piece tuned those switches, in ways that shifted with context. A loose fragment acting as a dial adds a fresh layer of control to a famous route.
plos-pone-0011921:
Kathryn Butler and co-workers measured in 2010 how burn injury changes the movement of neutrophils, the white blood cells that rush to infections. Severe burns trigger a body-wide inflammatory storm and often end in sepsis. Earlier work had shown that neutrophils from burn patients are worse at homing in on targets.

Using microfluidic devices, tiny channels that steer cells through controlled chemical trails, the team found that burns reduce how fast neutrophils move in the right direction. Slower, less directed cells help explain the infection risk that haunts burn care. The device also offers a compact way to test drugs meant to restore immune cell movement.
plos-pone-0012021:
Joakim Ek and co-workers charted in 2010 how harm spreads through the spinal cord of the rat after a bruise-type injury. The first blow is just the start; a second wave of harm grows for weeks, and the cell steps that drive it are not clear. The team took stock of the wound's size and of how much of each cord tissue was left, from as early as a quarter of an hour to ten weeks on.

That time line shows when the cord's grey core and its white fiber tracts are lost, and where the loss halts. The two tissues do not fail on the same clock. A map with timing tells drug and cell trials when they must act to save each tissue, a point that has sunk more than one past trial.
plos-pone-0012121:
Lin Cui, Kenoki Ohuchida, Kazuhiro Mizumoto, and co-authors compared types of colon cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. They also studied the fibroblasts that grow alongside tumors, since cancer cells do not live alone. One surface marker divides colon cancer cells into two groups, and a second marker picks out a set of tumor-linked fibroblasts the team isolated directly from tissue.

The marked fibroblasts interacted much more strongly with one cancer cell group than with the other. Such pairings may help certain cancer cells grow or spread, fed by the support cells around them. Naming the strongest partnerships points to new places where treatment might cut the tumor off from its helpers.
plos-pone-0012221:
Sangeetha M, Vaijayanti Kale, and Lalita Limaye worked to grow blood stem cells from umbilical cord blood in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cord blood can cure blood diseases through transplant, but one unit holds too few stem cells for many patients. Growing the cells in a dish should fix that, yet the expansion process itself tires the cells out and weakens their later performance.

Adding either of two protective compounds during expansion kept the cells fitter in lab tests and better at settling into recipient mice afterward. Healthier expanded cells could stretch each cord blood unit to treat larger patients. The approach brings cord blood transplants closer to routine use for adults, not just children.
plos-pone-0012321:
Sabine Gollner, Barbara Riemer, Pedro Martínez Arbizu, and co-authors surveyed tiny seafloor animals at a deep-sea vent field in PLOS ONE in 2010. At nine degrees north on the East Pacific Rise, vents pour out fluids ranging from mild to extreme in heat, acidity, and sulfide. The meiofauna, animals smaller than grains of sand, live along that whole gradient in the trough where the vents sit.

Charting which species live at which harshness maps the true limits of animal life. Vent fields are now eyed for mining, so a baseline census tells us what would be lost and which refuges matter. The gradient itself is a natural laboratory for how life responds to worsening chemistry, including an acidifying ocean.
plos-pone-0012421:
Martin Kapun, Viola Nolte, Thomas Flatt and colleagues tested which fruit flies the Drosophila C virus can infect, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The virus is a common pathogen of lab flies and is well studied in two species. In the wild it may meet many hosts, and its true range shapes how it spreads and evolves.

The team exposed several fly species and found that infection success and harm varied widely by host. Some species resisted, while close relatives suffered. Host range data matter for using this virus as a model of insect disease and for judging risks if such viruses were ever used to control pest insects.
plos-pone-0012521:
Ethel Pereira, Nan Liao, Geoff Neale and colleagues studied how cell stress tunes vessel growth factors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When the cell's protein-folding factory, the endoplasmic reticulum, gets overloaded, the unfolded protein response switches on to restore order. Tumors live under such stress and still manage to summon blood vessels, a puzzle the team addressed.

They found the stress response regulates proangiogenic factors at two levels: the genes' transcription and the handling of their messages afterward. Two-level control lets stressed cells fine-tune vessel signals fast. The links may expose weak points where drugs can cut a tumor's blood supply.
plos-pone-0012621:
Rybina and Pasyukova studied a natural gene variant in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. The gene, called Lim3, helps shape nerve cells early in life and matches a human gene pair known as LHX3 and LHX4. It had also been flagged as a gene that may change how long a fly lives.

Their 2010 work shows the variant alters how much Lim3 is switched on, and that this tracks with lifespan. One gene touching both brain growth and ageing makes it a rich case for study. Findings in flies often point to shared controls in other animals.
plos-pone-0012721:
Yue and Chang used DNA parentage tests to study mating in a freshwater shrimp, Caridina ensifera. Genetic parentage tools reveal who really fathers the young in a species. Among the huge crustacean group Malacostraca, mating systems were still mostly unstudied when they wrote in 2010.

Their tests found that females often carry young from several males at once, at high rates. Multiple paternity changes how we think about shrimp breeding and population genetics. It also gives fishery and conservation work a firmer base for this species group.  Field samples from wild shrimp ground the genetics in real mating life.
plos-pone-0012821:
Garcia-Gonzalez, Outeda, Zhou and co-authors showed that two kidney genes are also required to build a healthy placenta. Faults in PKD1 and PKD2 cause the common inherited kidney disease in which cysts grow and kidneys fail. Their 2010 mouse study removed these genes and watched development beyond the kidney.

Embryos lacking them failed to form a normal placenta, the organ that feeds the unborn young. A placenta role widens the known reach of these genes in development. It may also explain some pregnancy losses tied to this gene family.
plos-pone-0335121:
Emanuela H Kang and colleagues used a computer model of a runner stepping on an obstacle to find safer foot placement for high school cross country athletes. Overuse injuries plague young endurance runners. The model varied joint looseness, foot strike position, and ground friction across twenty seven cases, tracking ligament strain millisecond by millisecond with ground forces and muscle action included.

Foot placement dominated strain. Landing toward the inner foot gave the lowest strain in a key ankle ligament, while centre and outer strikes nearly doubled it. Higher friction lowered strain further. Looser joints raised strain in the foot arch band. Inner placement on grippier ground, the authors advise, is a trainable injury guard.
plos-pone-0336321:
Bijaya Niraula and colleagues survey in 2026 women who live in a slum area in a municipality near Kathmandu, Nepal, about care during monthly periods. Several hundred women of reproductive age answered a tested questionnaire chosen through systematic sampling. Questions covered products used, washing, bathing, and social restrictions faced at home and in the community.

About half used disposable pads and many used reusable cloth. Almost all faced some restriction during periods, and more than half felt treated as impure. Schooling and income linked to awareness, while job and ethnic group linked to handwashing. The authors call for better water, toilets, and teaching that tackles stigma.
plos-pone-0343321:
Laure Peyro-Saint-Paul and colleagues surveyed the French public about a delicate ethics question: should people who volunteer for drug trials be paid, and how much? Their 2026 exploratory study gathered sixty-five respondents in clinics and online, presented three fictional trials varying in risk, burden, and personal benefit, and asked what compensation seemed fair.

Three quarters backed payment in principle. The strongest triggers were facing a new experimental drug, invasive procedures, and lost income. Support and suggested amounts rose with burden: highest for a demanding, uncertain trial with some benefit, lowest for an easy one. The survey feeds a larger French project building a decision tool so sponsors and ethics committees price participation fairly without dangling coercive sums.
plos-pone-0344321:
Ginna Patricia Velasco Anacona and colleagues in Colombia studied the genetics of fiber in a wild Andean blueberry in 2026. The fruit, called agraz, is valued for nutrition, but the genes behind its fiber content were almost unknown.

The team measured total, soluble, and insoluble fiber in fruit from many plants, then scanned their DNA for linked spots. They found a set of regions tied to fiber traits, pointing to genes that build and remodel fruit cell walls. One region sat inside a gene from a family that moves sugars. Breeders can use these markers to select plants whose fruit carries more healthy fiber.
plos-pone-0345521:
Berta Munne-Barellas and her team sat down with health staff in Catalonia, Spain. Twenty-one staff took part, from GPs and nurses to birth pros. The talks dug into a hard spot in their work: drugs, shots, and herb cures for women with child or at the breast. Proof is thin there, and rules urge great care.

Each trade met its own snags. GPs and nurses felt short on birth care drills. Birth pros prized close watch when drugs must change. Womb pros feared that some women now shun drugs they need. Flu and cough shots won trust, while the COVID shot still drew doubt. The team backs shared calls and more drills.
plos-pone-0346021:
Habib ur Rehman and two co-authors present new results on fixed points in 2026. A fixed point is a value that a mapping leaves unchanged. Results of this kind help prove that an equation has a solution. They do so even when no formula can produce the solution.

The authors build a four step method for pairs of mappings from a broad class. They prove the steps settle toward a shared fixed point. Worked examples support the proofs. They then apply the method to integral equations in abstract spaces. The scheme gives approximate answers there, not just proof that answers exist.
plos-pone-0346421:
Setting ancient Chinese poems to music revives them, but audiences often feel locked out by unfamiliar settings and history. Zushun Zhang, Panjie Xie, and Jinsong Wang studied concerts built around a historic Wei dynasty music score to measure those barriers, in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

Borrowing a leisure constraints framework, they built a scale of limiting factors and surveyed audiences at three creative concerts. Barriers fell into three families: personal limits like knowledge and confidence, social limits like companions and guidance, and structural limits like venues and scheduling. The families act in sequence, the analysis showed, so removing later barriers fails while early ones stand.
plos-pone-0346921:
Rachel Lara Green and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for filming the electrical conversation between a preschool teacher's brain and a child's during shared tasks. The study uses dual brain recording, called hyperscanning. Teacher and child work on literacy, problem solving, and self-control activities. The tasks are designed to reveal how teachers scaffold. Scaffolding is the moment-by-moment support that builds a child's executive functions.

Researchers will measure how tightly behavior and brain activity synchronize. They will relate synchrony to each partner's own executive skills and intelligence. The child's measured school readiness counts too. Parent-child synchrony is well studied. Teachers, who increasingly share early care worldwide, are not. Findings could shape how preschool teachers are trained to pitch their help.
plos-pone-0347321:
JungHo Jo and co-workers lay out a trial plan for Chuna, a Korean hands-on therapy, in people with longer-lasting low back pain. Chuna treatment is guided by X-ray readings of how the spine sits. Their 2026 protocol describes a randomized trial at two hospitals with forty-six patients whose pain has lasted at least three weeks.

Half will get usual care plus Chuna sessions twice a week for four weeks, shaped to each person's X-ray pattern. The other half will get usual care alone. Pain and daily function will be tracked to three months, along with safety. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet; it sets up the first rigorous test of X-ray-guided Chuna care.
plos-pone-0347921:
Charlotte Morris, Evangelos Kontopantelis, and co-authors examined who actually receives dementia medicines in English primary care. Drugs called cholinesterase inhibitors, plus memantine, are recommended for Alzheimer's disease and some related dementias. Their 2026 study drew on records from nearly fifteen hundred practices, covering more than two hundred forty thousand patients diagnosed between 2006 and 2024.

Only about six in ten patients ever got one of these medicines, and taking both kinds together stayed rare despite guidelines. People in the poorest areas, some ethnic minority groups, and people with learning disabilities were all less likely to be treated. The authors call the gaps unfair and urge better access, since the pattern suggests need alone is not deciding who gets help.
plos-pone-0348021:
Hannah Linney, Ken van Someren, and Sinead Keogh lay out a plan to review research on teenagers' skill at judging health information online. Teens form habits that last into adulthood while swimming in digital health claims, some of them false. Their 2026 protocol describes a scoping review across five databases, screening studies of young people's ability to find, judge, and use online health content.

The review will sort what kinds of studies exist, where they were done, and which skills they measured. Screening follows a standard reporting checklist, with a second reviewer checking part of the records. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. The finished map should show schools and health services where teen digital health skills are least understood.
plos-pone-0348221:
Apisith Saraluck and colleagues studied pelvic organ prolapse, the dropping of pelvic organs common after childbirth. They asked which of its features are tied to two bladder problems: trouble emptying and an overactive bladder that creates sudden urgency. Records came from a university hospital clinic in Thailand covering 2018 to 2020. The comparison covered one hundred fifty-one women with emptying difficulty, one hundred thirty-nine with overactive bladder, and a control group with neither.

Most patients were postmenopausal, had given birth more than once, and were overweight. After statistical adjustment, only specific prolapse traits stayed linked to each bladder problem, while many suspected factors fell away. Knowing which prolapse site and severity drive which symptom helps doctors counsel women and choose between watching, exercises, or surgery with better evidence.
plos-pone-0348521:
Junghoon Kim and colleagues studied a hidden complication of the ports implanted for chemotherapy in colorectal cancer patients: narrowing of the large vein the port feeds into. Among more than fourteen hundred patients whose first port was placed through the right neck vein between 2015 and 2020, follow-up chest scans showed the narrowing in about one in fifteen.

The team used several statistical methods, including survival analysis and a decision-tree method, to find which traits raised the risk. They also checked whether two common cancer drugs changed the odds in patients receiving palliative care. A narrowed vein can swell the arm and complicate treatment, so knowing who is at risk helps doctors choose port sites and watch the right patients with scans.
plos-pone-0349021:
Mingfei Li and Shanshan Huang map what researchers know about anxiety felt by consumers while shopping and spending. Worry tied to buying seems to be rising with climate fears, money strain, and rapid tech change. Their 2026 review gathers sixty articles from major databases and sorts out what sparks such anxiety, what it leads to, and where it sits between the two.

Studies link consumer anxiety to choices, well-being, and buying behavior in many settings, but the work remains scattered. Gaps include how anxiety plays out over time and across cultures. The authors lay out a shared framework and a research agenda. Shops and brands also get practical hints for calming worried customers instead of exploiting them.
plos-pone-0349121:
Alexandra Linz and co-authors built data-driven rules to find Lyme disease cases inside electronic health records. In regions where Lyme is common, fast and accurate case finding would serve clinics and researchers alike. Their 2026 study used records from one health system and tested algorithms built only from structured, easily pulled fields.

Diagnosis codes, laboratory orders and results, demographics, and antibiotic orders all carried signal. A hand-built decision tree performed best. It required a Lyme code, a positive antibody test, and a doxycycline order close in time, in combination. That rule reached solid accuracy with high sensitivity. Linz and colleagues say such simple logic could anchor automated surveillance after wider testing.
plos-pone-0349221:
Kayoko Ito and co-workers follow what shapes saliva flow and the feeling of a dry mouth in healthy young men. Dry mouth can occur even when saliva output looks normal, which makes it tricky to judge. Their 2026 study repeats measures over time in thirty-nine men, tracking room heat and moisture, body water loss, and stress markers in saliva.

Resting saliva flow moved with room temperature, humidity, hydration, and one stress marker. Flow during chewing showed no such links. The dry-mouth feeling itself tied only to one stress marker. Because room conditions shift with the seasons, clinics measuring saliva need to record them. The work also hints that stress plays a quiet part in dry-mouth complaints.
plos-pone-0349621:
Miki Nakamura and colleagues used health checkup records for nearly sixty-five thousand middle-aged adults in Japan's Gunma Prefecture to test how body weight relates to kidney decline. Japan carries one of the world's heaviest dialysis burdens. Checkups from 2018 and 2020 let the team measure whose kidney filtering rate dropped sharply within two years.

The pattern formed a U shape: risk rose at high body mass, as expected with obesity, but also among the underweight, the study's less obvious finding. The analysis accounted for age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, blood sugar, and starting kidney function. Weight advice for kidney protection usually targets heaviness alone; evidence that thinness also carries risk complicates that simple message.
plos-pone-0349721:
Shantengyue Jiang and Mo Zhang offer a 2026 modeling paper on gas moving through hot, cracked coal deep underground. Older work often treated crack roughness in rough terms, which made danger forecasts for mines less useful. Their model links heat, water pressure, rock strain, and crack shape in one system, using a single roughness score to connect surface bumps with how easily gas flows.

Checks against real records from a Liupanshui coal face and from a gas well support the model. Warmer coal and smoother cracks both let gas move faster and raised pressure and ground shift in the tests. Mine teams can use results like these to judge where gas may gather before it becomes a hazard.
plos-pone-0349821:
Pingping Meng and colleagues tested a gene-silencing treatment for the most common kind of hearing loss in mice. Their earlier work showed that a growth factor called neuritin, which supports nerve tissue, falls in the deafened inner ear, and replacing it protected hearing cells. Here they hunted for the tiny RNA switches, microRNAs, that turn neuritin down.

Sequencing the inner ear tissue nominated three microRNAs as the main culprits. Blocking each of them in living mice raised neuritin levels and improved hearing function. With no effective drug yet for sensorineural hearing loss, a treatment that works by releasing a natural protective factor, rather than adding a foreign one, is an appealing direction worth developing.
plos-pone-0350021:
Shubham and Rajan Kumar Pandey modeled how tiny nanosheet transistors behave as their parts shrink toward a few nanometers. These transistors are candidates for future computer chips. The study varied gate length and temperature and tracked electron mobility, band gap, and drive current under different kinds of scattering, the collisions that slow electrons inside a device.

Heat hurt performance most: at high temperatures, phonon scattering cut electron mobility by nearly half and slightly narrowed the band gap. Defects at the oxide surface added tunneling paths that waste current. The results map which effects chip designers must control as gates shrink, and where the smallest designs still deliver strong current.
plos-pone-0350121:
Zoe Sirotiak and Angelique G Brellenthin led talks with adults who live with long COVID. They asked a plain question. Does being active help you, or hurt you? Care teams often urge activity as self-care. But like states can flare with effort. The team held deep talks with thirty-four adults across the United States in 2026.

Near two thirds said activity made them worse. They told of crashes after effort, deep fatigue, and lost skills. A small share, about fifteen in a hundred, felt real gains. They spoke of more energy and a sense of pride. Health scores for the group ran well below US norms. The team says activity plans must fit each person's own limits.
plos-pone-0350221:
Yang Rui and colleagues built a forecasting system for ship paths on inland rivers, with warnings when a ship drifts from its channel. Near river crossing power lines, a drifting ship risks grave harm. Their model stacks time pattern layers, an attention step that weighs speed and heading, and a two way memory unit, trained on real ship tracking data.

Forecast errors fell by roughly a fifth versus strong rival models, and forecast paths hugged real tracks more closely. A layered yaw warning system passed ninety six percent accuracy in typical crossing scenes. River managers could gain earlier, surer warnings to clear ships before they threaten bridges and power lines.
plos-pone-0350821:
Ujin Lee and colleagues studied diet and heart risk in Korean adults. Data came from a national health survey. The years ran from 2016 to 2020. Just over twenty five thousand adults took part. Each adult got a score for a planet friendly diet. That diet favours plants and modest animal foods. Scores were split into four bands.

High scores linked with lower odds of high cholesterol in women. Links also touched belly fat and blood pressure. Some links appeared only in set age groups. No clear links appeared in men. A world diet template may fit Korean food habits unevenly. More work should test the score by sex and age.
plos-pone-0350921:
Carolina Vivas-Valencia and colleagues model where Zimbabwe should place bedside infant HIV test machines to do the most good. Babies born to mothers with HIV need virus testing within weeks, and distant central labs delay answers and treatment. In one southern province, clinics number more than a hundred. There the team linked a detailed child HIV simulation with a placement optimizer. It tested current locations against the best possible ones, for life expectancy and value.

Most existing machines moved to better-chosen clinics in the best layout. A few stayed in place. That layout sharply raised the share of infants getting results within a month. It also raised the share starting treatment within a month. Life expectancy for infected infants rose by more than a year in the best layout. Vivas-Valencia and colleagues argue placement, not just purchase, decides what these machines deliver.
plos-pone-0351221:
Zhiqiang Yang, Jia Liu, and Qingchao Li turned leftover carbon from coal gas waste into a sponge that pulls an antibiotic from water. Antibiotic traces in rivers harm ecosystems and breed resistance. The team treated the carbon with peroxide to add oxygen rich surface groups, then tested how much trimethoprim, a common antibiotic, it could hold.

Treated carbon held about eighty milligrams per gram, well above the untreated form, and worked well in flowing column tests too. Simulations showed stronger surface attraction and more hydrogen bonds after treatment. A waste product becomes a water cleaner here, though real river trials must still prove cost and safety at scale.
plos-pone-0351321:
Sai Sunkara and co-authors stress-tested the electricity grid of the western United States against losing hydropower, which supplies about a quarter of the region's generating capacity. Drought, aging dams, and river rules can all idle hydro plants. The team ran more than sixteen thousand loss scenarios, knocking out hydro across combinations of fourteen river regions, and measured whether the grid could still meet demand.

Some regions punched far above their size: losing their hydro hurt adequacy more than their share of capacity would predict. Losses in paired regions could also compound each other. Tree-based analysis picked out the critical combinations. For grid planners facing a drier West, the study names the basins where backup power, transmission, or water agreements buy the most safety per dollar.
plos-pone-0351421:
Xuemei Xu and four colleagues study how live-streamed selling builds trust in an unlikely product, durian, in this 2026 marketing study. Durian is expensive, perishable, and famously pungent, so buying it unseen from a phone stream is a leap of faith. The researchers interviewed buyers of durian sold through Douyin livestreams, then surveyed more than four hundred verified purchasers to test what drove their buying.

Four features of the streaming scene stood out: visual signs of freshness, the streamer's expertise, real-time interaction, and a wish to support rural farmers. Freshness cues and expertise built trust, which in turn drove impulse buying. Interaction and farmer support worked differently, by making the experience enjoyable; the good feeling of helping farmers itself acted as a pleasure that encouraged purchase. The authors offer the model to regional farm brands going digital.
plos-pone-0352021:
Muhammad Farooq and co-authors propose in 2026 a blockchain system to track sugarcane from field to factory and rebuild trust among farmers, traders, and officials. Hidden dealings and fake shortages cut farmer earnings and strain national economies in their account. Their design uses smart contracts, a dedicated digital token for payments, and a decentralised file system for private records.

Tests reported faster block handling, higher transaction capacity, and lower costs than rival supply chain projects they compared. A public coin launch is suggested to fund the system long term. The work is a design and test study, not a report of a live national rollout.
plos-pone-0352121:
Heydarpour, Mokhtari, and Dehnavi modeled vaccine supply networks with many products and storage needs in a 2026 study. Vaccines differ in dose schedules and cold demands, from ordinary fridges to ultra-cold freezers. Their math model places distribution centers, assigns vaccines, and sets storage across three tiers, aiming for no shortages at injection sites.

A tailored genetic search solved large cases nearly as well as exact methods that are far slower. Planning many vaccines together, rather than one campaign at a time, matches how real programs run year-round. The model can help health ministries place cold storage where it prevents the most missed vaccinations.
plos-pone-0352321:
Hanji Chen and seven colleagues test a combined therapy for stroke recovery in this 2026 pilot trial. The patients had suffered intracerebral haemorrhage, bleeding inside the brain. Weak legs are a common lasting problem. One group received ear-based vagus nerve stimulation plus repetitive facilitative exercise. The control group got sham stimulation with the same exercise. Sixty patients were split evenly between the arms.

After six weeks, both groups walked and moved better than at the start. Leg function scores, walking category, and stride length all improved. The real-stimulation group improved significantly more on every headline measure. Gait analysis also captured better hip motion in that group. Because the trial was small, the authors frame it as a pilot. The gains justify a larger trial of pairing nerve stimulation with guided exercise.
plos-pone-0352421:
Jiadong Yu, Denitsa Bekerian, and Radhika Khandelwal model why people followed health guidance while information sources fought for their trust. Their 2026 study reanalyses survey data from seven hundred forty-two American adults. During COVID-19, official channels competed with social media and peer networks. The authors traced how each diet of information shaped risk perception, political belief, and conspiracy thinking. Those in turn drove intentions to wear masks and accept vaccination.

Formal sources pushed toward protection. Relying on government sites and mainstream news raised perceived severity and cut conspiracy belief. Both fed stronger protective intentions. Informal sources pulled the other way, softening severity and hardening conspiracies. Perceived severity sat at the model's centre, moving mask use directly and vaccination indirectly. Masking and vaccinating also clustered as one general protective stance. Information strategy, the study implies, is health policy by other means.
plos-pone-0353021:
Qian Wu led a team of six authors reviewing AI for a puzzling lung pattern, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The pattern, called PRISm, shows a preserved ratio with impaired spirometry readings, a gray zone in lung testing. Clinicians disagree on what it means and who needs follow-up, so AI tools have been proposed to help.

Wu's review gathered those AI applications and judged where the evidence stands. It maps where algorithms genuinely aid reading of lung tests, and where claims outrun proof. That candor helps doctors decide what to trust now and what to await. It also tells developers which gaps, such as wider patient testing, they must fill before clinics should rely on their tools.
plos-pone-0353121:
Thirada Srinil and colleagues run in 2026 a blinded trial for people having keyhole shoulder surgery, comparing two drugs added to a nerve block near the neck. One added drug was a sedative type agent given at a high dose, and the other was a steroid. Neither patients nor assessors knew which was used, and pain relief time was the main measure.

Both mixes gave similar time before pain returned, though the sedative mix kept feeling and movement blocked a bit longer. Pain scores, extra painkillers, and satisfaction matched. Low blood pressure, slow heart rate, and sleepiness occurred more often with the sedative mix, but all passed without intensive care.
plos-pone-0353521:
Anan Jarab and seven colleagues check how well heart-attack survivors at an outpatient clinic control their 'bad' cholesterol, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Keeping LDL cholesterol low after a heart attack is one of the surest ways to prevent the next one. A research pharmacist extracted records for two hundred and fifty-five patients and measured their beliefs about medicines and how faithfully they took them.

More than three quarters had uncontrolled LDL — a worrying miss rate. Smoking, uncontrolled blood pressure, and taking beta-blocker medicines each came with higher odds of poor control. The authors argue clinics should pair prescriptions with smoking-cessation help and tighter blood-pressure management rather than simply adding more cholesterol drugs.
plos-pone-0353621:
Long and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, hunt for genes that help cervical cancer resist cisplatin, a widely used chemotherapy drug. Drug resistance is a major reason treatment fails. Their search through large cancer data sets singled out a gene called SPP1, which was turned up in tumor tissue.

Tests in cancer cells showed SPP1 levels were higher still in cells that had learned to resist cisplatin. Turning SPP1 down slowed cell growth, raised cell death, and made the drug work better. Turning it up did the opposite. The gene's effects ran in part through a second gene, KRAS: adjusting KRAS partly undid what SPP1 did to drug response. The authors propose that blocking the SPP1 to KRAS path could help restore the power of chemotherapy. The evidence so far comes from data sets and cells, not patients.
plos-pone-0353721:
Muhammad Hussien and three colleagues survey Egyptian farming households on whether failing land pushes people to move away, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Salt creeping into soil is shrinking harvests across Egypt. Nearly eighteen hundred respondents answered questions on land condition, income, and migration wishes, and the team modelled the answers through a theory of how people weigh threats and their ability to respond.

More than a third had seen their land's productivity fall within a decade, and over a fifth were actively seeking to relocate, mostly to Cairo or abroad. Surprisingly, older people and women showed strong migration intent, against the usual stereotype of the young male migrant. The authors urge land-restoration policies that treat staying as a real option.
plos-pone-0354021:
Hamed Nejat, Jason Sherfey, and André Bastos introduce in 2026 an evolutionary method for tuning spiking brain models that aim to explain how the brain predicts incoming signals. Such models can produce real brain rhythms, but setting their many connection values by hand is slow. Their genetic search adjusts values automatically against goals such as firing rates and the balance between fast and slower rhythms.

Tests moved from simple cases to recordings from monkey visual cortex, where the method reproduced recorded rhythm patterns tied to prediction. A second neuron model gave similar success, showing the search is not tied to one setup. The authors frame it as a tool, not proof of the theory.
plos-pone-0354121:
Peixue Liu and coauthors published a 2026 computer vision paper in PLOS ONE on clearing haze from satellite images. Haze dulls the images that land-use mapping and change detection depend on, washing out detail and color. Their network, DEMANet, processes the image through three shrinking stages: early layers use a dual-path module to protect fine detail. Deep layers use two-level attention to grasp the whole scene and haze pattern. A cross-stage module uses edges and color differences to locate haze and ferry detail between stages.

On widely used public remote sensing datasets, the network beat existing dehazing algorithms while keeping intricate detail and faithful color. The authors attribute the gains to the division of labor: local branches guard texture, attention guards global consistency, and the haze-guided links stop information leaking away during reconstruction. Cleaner satellite imagery feeds directly into better environmental monitoring and land management.
plos-pone-0354521:
Rebecca Muñiz and co-authors used oysters from the Texas Gulf Coast as early warning sensors for plastic pollution. Oysters filter feed, so microplastics collect in their tissues. Their 2026 study sampled sixty oysters at two field sites and compared them with oysters held two weeks in clean water.

Field oysters carried many plastic fibres, mostly polyethylene, in gills and digestive glands. Clean-water oysters held notably smaller particles, supporting the warning idea. Tissue checks showed raised markers of protein damage and shifted antioxidant defences where plastics were present. Muñiz and colleagues propose oyster chemistry as a cheap sentinel for coastal contamination before wider harm shows.
plos-pone-0354721:
Sudip Saha and four colleagues published this 2026 engineering paper on predicting how much working life a machine has left. Their model pairs convolutional layers, which spot local wear patterns, with memory networks that follow slow decline over time. It was tested on construction machines, steel casting equipment, and lithium batteries.

The combined model beat rival methods on all three data sets, cutting prediction error notably against older approaches. Light retraining helped it move between machine types. Saha presents the single framework as a practical base for maintenance planning across very different industries.
plos-pone-0354821:
Linyao Peng led a team of six authors on this 2026 study replacing hand counting with computer vision in worm reproduction tests. The tiny nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is a workhorse of aging and genetics research, but each mother can leave over a hundred offspring to count. They trained recent YOLO image models on nearly ten thousand brood photos.

The best model counted viable offspring with high accuracy against human counts, cutting months of microscope work to about two hours on a home graphics card. Peng shares the pipeline so other labs can adapt it to new image collections.
plos-pone-0354921:
Junkang Ren and three colleagues present a deep learning system for reverse-engineering how computer protocols behave, in this 2026 paper. Security analysts often face private or undocumented protocols and must infer their internal state machines, the rules for which message can follow which, from observed traffic alone. Their framework pairs a sequence model called Mamba with a graph learning method.

The system first extracts deep features from message exchanges, builds an initial map of protocol states, then merges redundant states in a data-driven way rather than by fixed rules. Tested on five protocols, from web and email traffic to industrial control protocols, it recovered state machine structures accurately and predicted behavior better than mainstream alternatives. Removing either main component hurt performance, confirming both contribute. The authors offer it as a sharper tool for protocol analysis and security testing.
plos-pone-0355221:
Ashwini Kumar and co-authors design in 2026 a compact four part antenna shaped with a spider like pattern for advanced fifth generation wireless use. Multiple antennas working together need to stay small, cover a wide band, and avoid interfering with each other. Learning methods helped tune the design, with one method giving the most accurate predictions.

A built sample matched the design goals, covering a broad range of frequencies below the higher bands with good gain and strong separation between parts. Standard checks for linked antenna performance passed. The authors present the antenna as a candidate for future fast wireless gear, including early sixth generation work.
plos-pone-0355621:
Wondaya Fenta Zewdia and co-authors modelled home birth and under-five child death together in Ethiopia. Both outcomes remain common and may share roots, so studying them jointly sharpens the picture. Their 2026 analysis used a national mini survey of more than five thousand women with a birth history.

About half of the women had delivered at home, and about one in twenty reported losing a child under five. The two outcomes were significantly linked: home delivery came with more than double the odds of a child death experience. Schooling, wealth, pregnancy care, and media exposure lowered both risks, while rural living raised them. The authors urge combined action on access, education, and care visits.
plos-pone-0355721:
Dorcas Kalaba and co-authors reviewed outcomes for drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment across Zambia over five years. Success rates sat below the global target, and national evidence on who fares worst was thin. Their 2026 study drew programme records for more than twelve hundred patients treated in all ten provinces.

About two thirds of patients finished with a favourable outcome. Normal body weight more than doubled the odds of success compared with underweight patients. Two provinces, Muchinga and Western, showed markedly lower success odds than the rest. Kalaba and colleagues argue food support and province-targeted fixes are essential if Zambia is to close its resistant-TB outcome gap.
plos-pone-0356421:
Mairobys Socorro and three colleagues set up a goat model for studying jaw joint degeneration, in this 2026 paper. The temporomandibular joint, which hinges the jaw, can develop osteoarthritis, but its cartilage is a fibrous type unlike that in knees.
