Therapies therefore need testing in a large animal with a similar joint. The team surgically created two kinds of bone-and-cartilage defects in the goat jaw joint and compared how they healed.

Neither defect type healed properly over two months: the holes filled with fibrous tissue and rough new bone at the edges, with no new cartilage, and the surrounding cartilage showed arthritic changes. Because both behaved alike, the authors favor the tunnel-style defect, which spares the joint disc and needs less surgical disturbance while producing larger defects. The model gives regenerative medicine a realistic testbed for future jaw therapies.
plos-pone-0356621:
Sancho Pedro Xavier led a team of eight authors who used machine learning on cancer records from Mato Grosso, Brazil, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. They linked the state cancer registry with death records for women diagnosed with breast cancer. The aim was to predict which women face the highest risk of dying.

Xavier's models sorted patients by risk and pointed to the factors that drive that risk. In a state with vast distances and limited clinics, such sorting can help direct scarce follow-up care to the women who need it most. The study also shows what linked public records, handled with care, can teach a health system about its own gaps.
plos-pone-0356721:
Gary Duclos led a large team, including the EUROBACT-2 Study Group, examining steroid use in sepsis, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Whether steroids help sepsis patients is one of intensive care's fiercest debates. The team studied patients whose sepsis came with bloodstream infections picked up in hospital, and linked hydrocortisone use to their outcomes.

Duclos's ancillary analysis uses a large existing cohort, adding real-world nuance to trial evidence. It asks when steroids help and when they harm, a question bedside doctors face nightly. Hospital-acquired infections are among the hardest sepsis cases, so evidence in exactly this group is valuable. The study will not end the debate, but it sharpens it with data from real wards.
plos-pone-0356821:
Mahmoud S Abdallah, Rania Mahafdeh, and Rima Hisham Shakhatreh tested one simple idea. Could a single short training session improve how Jordan's local pharmacists handle asthma? Their 2026 study enrolled 110 licensed pharmacists. It measured their asthma knowledge, attitudes, and inhaler technique. Then came a two-hour session based on treatment guidelines. Two weeks later, the team measured everything again.

Scores rose across the board after training. The gains covered knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported practice with both common inhaler types. Pharmacists with higher pharmacy degrees started ahead of those with first degrees. Pharmacists are often the health workers asthma patients can reach most easily. So the study supports brief, focused refreshers as a cheap way to lift day-to-day asthma care.
plos-pone-0357021:
Chetwynd Osborne, D Huy Dang, Soyini Mc Pherson, and Shaun A Watmough traced mercury through the forests and streams of Guyana. Mercury is the toxic metal released by small-scale gold mining. The team compared its ratio to carbon in leaves, litter, soil, water, and sediment. The comparison set was twenty-five studies worldwide. Their 2026 study used carbon as the yardstick because mercury rides on carbon through ecosystems.

The pattern of movement matched the global picture. Mercury builds as leaves fall and decay, then travels toward streams. But near Guyanese mines the ratios ran far above world averages. That confirms heavy local loading from the air. The comparison also suggests wetlands worldwide quietly feed mercury into surface waters. It is a route managers of mining regions should watch.
plos-pone-0357821:
Francesca Genovese, Martina Fanghella, Corrado Sinigaglia, and Guido Barchiesi revisit a basic question about how people copy each other, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Watching someone move tends to prime the same movement in the observer, a reflex called automatic imitation. One leading theory says the reflex is learned, built from paired seeing and doing. If so, training people to respond against what they see should weaken it.

The team measured the reflex before and after such counter training at several time points, expecting it to fade if learned pairings drive it. It did not fade significantly at any tested point. That stubbornness challenges the learning account, at least in its current form, and pushes the debate toward mechanisms that training alone cannot rewrite. The study is a useful reminder that a tidy theory of imitation still faces contrary evidence.
plos-pone-0357921:
Müfide Arzu Özkarafakılı and three colleagues studied a hidden burden of lung disease in women, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease steals breath over years, and intimacy often suffers quietly alongside. The team measured sexual dysfunction in women with COPD and linked it to how heavy their overall symptom burden is.

Özkarafakılı's study brings a cost of lung disease into the clinical conversation where it belongs. Doctors rarely ask, and patients rarely raise it, so the problem stays untreated. Evidence of a link with symptom burden gives clinicians a reason to ask and a guide to who may need help most. Quality of life in chronic disease includes private life, and this work insists on counting it.
plos-pone-0358221: Kang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a trial on cleaner air for children with asthma. The AIRVAC study will test home ventilation and air cleaners in four parallel groups. Families are assigned at random in this controlled trial. Home air is one asthma trigger parents can change, so a four-way test can show which fix, or pair of fixes, truly helps.
plos-pone-0358321:
Debbie Johnson led a team of eight authors who studied NHS staff in England after pregnancy or newborn loss at work, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Midwives, nurses, and doctors who care for grieving parents carry their own grief, often with little support. The team used a qualitative approach, listening closely to staff accounts.

Johnson's group recorded what staff say helps, such as peer support, time to recover, and simple acknowledgment, and what is missing. Those findings give hospital leaders concrete steps rather than vague calls for resilience. Services that support their own carers protect both staff retention and the quality of care that bereaved families receive at their worst moments.
plos-pone-0359321: Jiang and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on guessing body poses in 3D from images. Their framework, HADD, is aware of body hierarchy and splits the pose into parts before cleaning the result. A denoising step works over space and time at once. Better pose tracking helps animation, sports analysis, and robots that need to follow human movement safely.
plos-pone-0359421: Chen and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on predicting where vocational college graduates will work. Their model uses the XGBoost method, tuned by a search method called TPE. It aims for fine-grained guesses about each student's employment destination. Colleges in China could use such forecasts to guide career advice and to show how well their programs place students.
pmc-13197621:
Lingling Song and colleagues report a 2026 study on how a parasite harms the eye. Toxoplasma gondii infects about a third of the world's people. In the eye it can threaten sight, yet how it drives damage was unclear.

Infection pushed eye surface cells toward a state change linked to scarring and invasion, in both lab cells and mouse eyes. A parasite protein called ROP16 drove that shift by switching on two host signal paths. Parasites lacking the protein caused less change, while extra protein caused more. Blocking either signal path eased the cell shift and eye damage in mice. The paths are promising drug targets for this infection.
pmc-13201721:
Changing a single building block in a huge protein machine is technically hard, and a 2026 methods article authored by Adel Beghiah offers a workaround. The research article presents plasmid sub-fragmentation, a way to perform site-directed mutagenesis on large multi-subunit protein complexes by splitting their genes into short, manageable pieces.

The authors demonstrated the method on the genes for the E coli Complex I, a large respiratory enzyme. They divided a 15.1 kilobase sequence into twenty fragments of about nine hundred bases, mutated them with ordinary polymerases, and reassembled the pieces accurately. The approach promises easier functional studies of other large protein complexes with repeated subunits.
pmc-13202421:
A wound dressing that fights germs and reports wound acidity by changing color is presented in a 2026 materials study authored by Miaoshen Kou. The research article builds a hydrogel from silk fibroin and hyaluronic acid, using one plant-derived molecule, rhein, to supply every active function.

Laboratory tests showed the gel killed more than ninety-four percent of three bacterial types, including drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, in the reported assays. It also scavenged free radicals strongly and kept cultured cells healthy under the tested conditions. Its color shifted distinctly across the acidity range typical of wounds, which would let clinicians read wound status visually without separate sensors or electronics.
pmc-13203721:
Barley hay could replace poor-quality roughage in sheep diets, and a 2026 feeding study headed by Xiaoyuan Wang measures the trade-offs. The research article feeds forty-five young sheep diets in which barley hay replaces a quarter, half, three quarters, or all of their usual roughage, then tracks rumen fermentation and blood markers.

Barley hay encouraged fiber-degrading microbes in the rumen, which improved feed digestion in the flock. Blood tests also showed higher concentrations of protective immune proteins in the hay-fed animals. Although switching feed caused minor short-term stress signals, the full replacement diet performed best overall, and the authors recommend barley hay as a practical primary roughage.
pmc-13220121:
Joe Bradley and co-authors report a 2026 physics study on how to measure the tiny particles in milk. Milk holds fat drops and much smaller protein clusters called casein micelles, and most sizing tools cannot tell the two apart.

The team combined two methods on homogenised milk, meaning milk treated so the fat stays evenly mixed. A microscopy method tracked particle motion in the liquid, while a frozen-sample imaging method cut and viewed thin layers directly. Together they showed two overlapping size groups without first separating the milk. The authors note that different tools rarely give the same answer, so using both gives a fuller picture.
pmc-13235921:
Cheng and colleagues study how business analytics students engage with AI-supported learning. AI tools are now woven into coursework, yet little work has asked what keeps students using them over a whole course. The team treats AI use as part of the course itself, not a one-off choice to try a new gadget.

They ask how students' views of AI-supported learning shape their wish to keep using it. They then link that wish to interest in the subject and to plans for a career using analytics. The chain matters for teachers: a tool students abandon early cannot deepen interest, while one they value may steer both grades and ambitions.
pmc-13240921:
Ratsavong's team in Vientiane asked why toddlers stay underfed where food is at hand in Laos's capital. 333 mother-child pairs filled out a structured survey. 47 caregivers also gave in-depth interviews. Two districts, one urban and one peri-urban, were covered.

About 27 percent of children under two were stunted, with low weight near fourteen percent. What set thriving children apart was not food access alone. Parents who gathered feeding advice from varied sources, and turned knowledge into daily practice, had better-fed children. The team advises hands-on, show-how feeding outreach for urban and peri-urban families in Laos.
pmc-13241521:
Pasvolsky and colleagues at MD Anderson report outcomes for older myeloma patients treated with a four-drug induction and stem cell transplant. Landmark trials of daratumumab-based D-VRD therapy excluded patients over seventy. The team reviewed one hundred twenty-five newly diagnosed patients treated between 2021 and 2024. Twenty-seven were aged seventy or older, with a median age of seventy-four.

Older patients often received gentler conditioning and lower lenalidomide doses than younger ones. Even so, response depth matched: nearly every older patient reached a very good partial response or better after transplant. No transplant-related deaths occurred in either group. Two-year survival was similar across ages, supporting transplant-based therapy for fit older adults.
pmc-13242121:
Stahl and colleagues at Ulm traced gut microbiome aging back to the immune system's own stem cells. Young recipient mice were rebuilt with either young or old blood stem cells. Their gut immunity then aged according to the donor, not the host. Fecal sequencing and blood vitamin levels completed the picture.

Old stem cells reproduced mucosal immune aging, with naïve T cells vanishing from the gut wall. The microbiome shifted, losing bacteria tied to vitamin B6 production. Blood B6 levels duly fell in the aged-immune animals. Stahl proposes an immune-microbiome-vitamin axis behind some aging changes.
pmc-13243321:
Mitsuaki Hirai and colleagues asked health workers how a water and sanitation improvement program actually landed in Zimbabwean facilities. Their qualitative study appeared in Discover Public Health in 2026. The WASH FIT program ran in one hundred facilities from 2021 to 2023, aiming to cut infections tied to poor water, toilets, and hygiene. The team interviewed facility staff and government officers across four provinces about their experience of the rollout.

Staff judged the tool practical and credited it with better services, happier patients and workers, and higher use of care. The constraints were concrete: too little money, missing supplies, and not enough staff time or skills. Training had not always been deep enough for teams to make the method their own. The authors argue ownership at facility level decides whether gains survive. Steady financing and fuller training are their two headline recommendations.
pmc-13245821:
Raja presents five clinical cases in this 2026 Cureus case series, all married women with years of bodily complaints such as pain, stomach trouble, dizziness, fatigue, panic, and broken sleep. Repeated scans and specialist visits had found little to explain their symptoms, and most had seen several doctors before reaching psychiatric care.

In long assessment sessions, including couple discussions led jointly by male and female psychiatrists, another story emerged: emotional loneliness, feeling unheard by their husbands, lost physical and emotional intimacy. Sexual concerns they had felt too ashamed to raise. Raja argues that careful, sensitive psychiatric interviewing can surface such hidden distress, while noting five cases cannot prove cause and effect.
pmc-13246921:
Vilela, Gomes-Andrade, and Silva review the cancer tubulin code in this 2026 Cancer Metastasis Reviews article. Microtubules, the cell's internal rails and division machinery, are built from tubulin proteins that come in many versions, and chemical tags added after assembly fine-tune their behavior. That variety, the tubulin code, differs between tumors and shapes how cancer cells divide, move, and spread.

Standard chemotherapy drugs that attack microtubules, such as taxanes, often fail through resistance, and no validated test predicts who will respond. The authors argue the code itself could become that test, marking prognosis and likely drug response, and that enzymes writing or erasing the tags are promising drug targets. They also warn that antibody tools for measuring the code need rigorous validation first.
pmc-13248421:
Peppler and colleagues studied how German nursing teams handle growing diversity, in a 2026 BMC Nursing paper. Hospitals and care homes increasingly recruit nurses abroad, mixing languages, training, and customs on one ward. Rather than study the newcomers alone, the team watched how whole receiving teams work with difference day by day.

Across six teams, the researchers logged two hundred three hours of observation plus interviews and group talks. Three patterns emerged: teams that treat diversity as routine, teams in active transition, and teams where friction builds around boundaries and competence. Managers, the authors argue, must match support to each pattern instead of using one fix for all.
pmc-13248521:
Brown and Shandas modeled future heat illness across the United States in this 2026 GeoHealth study. Hospital visits surge during extreme heat, yet how weather, housing, health, and income combine to drive those surges is poorly mapped. The authors built a system dynamics simulation covering the fifty-three largest metropolitan areas and their climate regions.

The model projects illness counts and costs through 2040 under lower and higher emissions paths. Results diverged by region, shaped by changing heat patterns and by where vulnerable groups live. The authors argue the approach lets officials test interventions at specific points in the chain, and time regional responses before heat waves arrive.
pmc-13249921:
Girasol and a Brazilian team simulated therapy lasers traveling through human skin, in a 2026 Lasers in Medical Science study. Using optical properties measured from real skin samples, they ran Monte Carlo simulations, a photon-by-photon lottery, for three common treatment wavelengths. Beam width and beam spread were measured from actual devices rather than assumed, then fed into a voxel model of tissue.

All three wavelengths faded with depth in similar fashion over the first millimeters. Beam width mattered most: wider beams lowered the surface peak but carried more light to depth at the same total power. Realistic beam spread barely changed anything in contact use, while exaggerated spread wasted light sideways. The results guide dose planning for light therapy.
pmc-13250221:
Ayele and a large team track severe bleeding around childbirth across two hundred four countries and territories. Their 2026 BMJ Open analysis draws on Global Burden of Disease data from 2000 to 2021, with projections forward to 2050. Maternal haemorrhage remains one of the deadliest risks of pregnancy worldwide.

Global rates of cases, deaths, and lost healthy years all fell across the two decades studied. The burden stayed heavily concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, where rates in the west ran hundreds of times higher than in Western Europe. High-income Asia Pacific and Australasia recorded the lowest figures of all. Forecasts show further improvement by 2050, but the authors urge targeted local action because national gaps remain wide.
pmc-13250321:
Preethika Murugesan and Manimaran R report an easily missed diagnosis in this 2026 case report. A 22-year-old man came in with an upward curve of the penis that had bothered him since his teens, and standard checks, including a camera look inside the urine tube, were normal.

During corrective surgery, leaking gel revealed a hidden side channel in the urine tube that tests had missed. The team repaired it with a three-layer flap of nearby skin while also straightening the curve, and recovery went smoothly with good function and appearance. Old records suggested a childhood repair as the likely cause. The authors urge careful checks during surgery itself.
pmc-13251521:
Kadyan and co-authors show that a mother's fat choices during pregnancy and nursing shape her pups' guts and brains into adulthood. Their 2026 Gut Microbes study fed mice diets rich in saturated fat, omega-6, or omega-3 oils, then switched all offspring to a Western-style diet for ten weeks. Only the early-life window differed between the groups.

Pups of omega-3 fed mothers kept leaner bodies, healthier gut linings, and far less low-grade inflammation along the gut-blood-brain route. Their brains showed stronger synaptic plasticity signals, quieter inflammation, and lipid profiles tied to membrane health. Omega-6 also left lasting microbiome marks, distinct from saturated fat. The authors frame maternal omega-3 as long-term neuroprotection delivered through the gut-brain-immune axis.
pmc-13251821:
Adithya Sarma and colleagues rescue forgotten social memories in mice in this 2026 neuroscience study. Remembering who you have met matters for social life, and losing sleep right after a meeting can wipe that recognition away.

Using a new test, the team showed mice can tell apart several past meetings held in the same place on different days. Sleep loss after meeting blocked the memory from settling. An approved drug given during sleep loss protected it, and given just before testing it briefly restored access. Shining light on the tagged memory cells in the brain also brought the memory back, pointing to a recall failure rather than a lost trace.
pmc-13252821:
Shiqiong Yan and colleagues review machine learning for predicting bleeding during surgery in this 2026 paper. Bleeding mid-operation threatens patient safety, and prediction models are multiplying, but their quality and readiness for wards were unclear.

Searching seven databases to April 2025, the team kept 23 studies with sample sizes from 48 to over 48,000. Tree-based models were the most common, and accuracy varied widely. Feeding models both records and images helped. Only six studies tested their model on outside patients, and accuracy often fell sharply there. Every study carried a high risk of bias by a standard tool, so the authors urge stricter building and reporting.
pmc-13253921:
Aiman Waheed and colleagues sequence a drug-resistant bacterium in a 2026 study from Peshawar, Pakistan. The isolate came from a urinary tract infection and belongs to Klebsiella quasipneumoniae, a germ easily confused with a close relative. It resisted many drug classes, including colistin, a last-line antibiotic, but stayed sensitive to a few others.

Whole-genome sequencing found resistance genes on its chromosome, not on plasmids, plus many mutations tied to resistance. Genes for attachment and iron uptake were also present, matching a classic, not hyper-virulent, type. The authors stress better species naming and wider genome checks, while noting one isolate cannot show regional patterns.
pmc-13254321:
Mohamed Ismail, Assem Hassan, and Osama Shehata test concrete wear in cold weather in a 2026 study. Abrasion, surface wearing away, matters for bridge decks, highways, and runways in cold regions. The team tested self-consolidating and normal concrete mixes at four temperatures, from plus 20 down to minus 20 degrees Celsius.

Mixes with metakaolin or silica fume gave the highest strength and wear resistance, while fly ash performed poorest. Normal concrete beat self-consolidating mixes at all temperatures. Colder temperatures raised both strength and wear resistance across mixes, and cutting binder content caused the largest losses.
pmc-13255221:
Pfisterer-Heise and colleagues built a core outcome set for research on centralizing hospital services into fewer, higher-volume units. Because studies measure different outcomes, their results resist comparison. The team combined a systematic review, focus groups with patient representatives, interviews with medical societies and insurers, and a survey of researchers, all based in Germany.

A longlist of outcomes went through two Delphi rounds judged against a strict agreement threshold. The final set contains twenty-seven outcomes spanning every domain of an established taxonomy, with nine addressing quality of care. The authors say future centralization studies should report across these domains, though agreed measurement instruments still need work.
pmc-13255421:
Jinghang Yu and colleagues ask whether an extra thigh-bone cut is needed in hip surgery for young children in a 2026 study. Walking-age children with developmental hip dysplasia often get open reduction plus socket reshaping, sometimes with a femoral osteotomy added. The team compared 52 children, 59 hips in total, treated with or without the extra cut.

After roughly three and a half years, socket angle gains and hip growth measures were statistically the same in both groups. The authors conclude the femoral cut is unnecessary for children with dislocation grades up to the third level when the other two steps are done.
pmc-13255521:
Merve Koseoglu and co-authors use machine learning to predict dental student grades in a 2026 study. Schools hold rich pre-university data on students, from exam scores to family background, but rarely use it to forecast success. The team gathered 96 records on dentistry graduates, including high school grades, entrance exam scores, and parent education and income.

Entrance exam scores and rankings predicted later grades better than traits like hometown, gender, or school type. The best models explained at least 74 percent of grade variation and sorted course grades with over 70 percent accuracy. The authors say such models can flag students who may need support early.
pmc-13255921:
Pingbo Yin and colleagues study how the frontal cortex handles opposite tasks in a 2026 neuroscience paper. Two groups of female ferrets learned sound tasks with reversed rules, so the same sound meant opposite actions and rewards. The team recorded single brain cells and field signals in the frontal cortex during the tasks.

Surprisingly, cell responses looked similar across the opposite tasks. Responses were stronger and longer for target sounds, which signal a change of action, than for reference sounds. Activity fell into three dynamic profiles from separate cell clusters. The authors propose the frontal cortex holds an abstract code of task structure, sent onward to deeper brain areas.
pmc-13258121:
Emad Hafaf and colleagues present a 2026 study of stockout risk in supply chains, meaning the risk that needed stock runs out. Their framework tests whether longer lead time, the wait between ordering and delivery, causes stockouts. It mixes causal inference methods, which aim to isolate cause and effect, with machine learning prediction and time series forecasting. The data covered 20,000 supply chain incidents.

Propensity score matching gave the most credible causal estimate, an average treatment effect of 0.882, confirming a strong link between lead time and stockout risk. An instrumental variable test gave a weaker, non-significant result, which the authors blame on a weak instrument. Random Forest and LightGBM models predicted best among the machine learning methods. A moving average forecast tracked stockout patterns over time with a score of 0.883.
pmc-13259621:

Precision improves over conventional therapy in these designs. Stable colonization, immune reactions, factory-scale production, and missing rules still stand between prototypes and patients, the authors caution.
pmc-13260021:

The devices were fitted in one general dental practice and followed for up to thirty years. In total, 196 prostheses and 563 abutment teeth, the natural teeth that anchor them, were observed. Mean follow-up was 14.07 years, with a maximum of 31.66 years, and survival was analyzed by standard time-to-event methods.

Devices replacing eleven or more teeth performed worst, while one classification group performed best.
pmc-13260921:

pmc-13262421:
Benito Baldauf and co-authors track infections from implanted heart devices in Germany in a 2026 journal article. These devices treat faulty heart rhythms but can become infected at the device pocket or along their wires, causing a serious heart infection. Pocket infections occurred in 1.91 percent, and wire-linked heart infection in 0.82 percent. pmc-13263021:

Shorter reported breaks oddly tracked with lower risk, which the authors say needs better measurement in future work.
pmc-13263121:
Chang Gyo Jung and colleagues map soil genes that drive nutrient breakdown across the continental United States in a 2026 journal article. Soil microbes release enzymes that free carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus from organic matter. pmc-13263221:

The authors supplied raw data, but review raised further concerns. As a result, the journal and publisher judged the article's results no longer reliable and retracted it. pmc-13264021:
Kanoko Yoshida and colleagues connect a mitochondrial enzyme's failure to how the placenta is built in pregnancies with high blood pressure. pmc-13264921:

Thinking skills are tested with two standard tools, and surveys cover mood, sleep, balance confidence, and diet. Data gathering was due to finish in April 2026. The team hopes to show how lifestyle shifts across menopause shape inflammation, belly fat, and brain health.
pmc-13267821:

Of them, 66 developed massive ascites and 166 did not.

The team built a nomogram, a scoring chart, from these four. It sorted patients with strong accuracy and stayed well calibrated under repeat testing. Benefit checks suggested the chart helps real decisions across a wide risk range. The authors offer it for tailoring care after surgery.
pmc-13267921:
Xiaoyu Feng, Jianmei Gong, and Shuangying Ma wrote a 2026 review drawing together interview studies on living with lymphedema after gynecological cancer. Lymphedema is lasting swelling, often in the legs, after lymph nodes are removed or damaged. The team searched ten databases up to February 2026 for studies reporting patients' own experiences.

Second, patients understand and adapt to the condition in widely different ways. Third, support needs span medical care, information, and emotional help. The reviewers rated confidence in the combined findings as moderate. They urge fuller support and wider research coverage.
pmc-13269121:
Marcel Krumrein and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on tiny light guides built into silicon carbide, a hard crystal used in electronics. Inside the crystal sit color centers, flaws that can hold and read out quantum information, meaning data stored in single particles. The team added a mirror to boost the light signal.

Their mirror reflected over 80 percent of light at its peak, across a wide range of colors. At very cold temperatures, the centers gave about 104,000 light counts per second in standard tests. A second checking method raised that to about 125,000 counts. The authors calculate that such rates could allow a correct single reading more than 98 percent of the time.
pmc-13269321:
Danwei Yang and David D Kim published a journal article in 2026 on heart and metabolic diseases and quality of life in the United States. They tracked how much each condition lowered self-rated health from 2001 to 2022. Six conditions were compared, including stroke, diabetes, and obesity.

National survey data on adults showed overall quality of life rising after a low in 2012. Stroke lowered it most, followed by heart disease and then diabetes. The losses tied to diabetes and heart disease shrank steadily over the two decades. The loss tied to obesity, by contrast, grew after 2012. The authors argue that health values used in policy studies need updating over time, not one fixed figure.
pmc-13269521:
Jay J W Han and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 following up patients after belly hernia repair with a muscle-release technique. Surgeons measured the force needed to pull the wall tissues together before and during repair. The question was whether leftover tension predicted later problems.

Median closing force was 4 pounds, down from 11 pounds at the start. Only one hernia returned, a rate of 1.4 percent among those checked in person. No tension measure was linked to hernia return, wound problems, or patient-reported pain and quality of life.
pmc-13269921:

Drug blockade of the same guard cut tumor burden in aggressive mouse models and in mini-tumors grown from patient tissue. A cross-cancer analysis linked the death program to Ras pathway activity and interferon signatures. The authors present the alarm program as a treatment opening in this cancer.
pmc-13270021:

One patient score averaged 72.8 after repair against 46.5 after removal in the comparison reported. The authors title repair as the superior option at five years and beyond.
pmc-13270221:

pmc-13271921:

Anlotinib is a multi-target drug that blocks blood vessel growth signals. Patients had already failed at least two prior drug regimens, leaving few options.

Median time without progression was 6.3 months and median survival 8.4 months. Tumours with an inflamed immune profile, marked by a PD-L1 score and more killer T cells, responded better.
pmc-13272621:

Gracia argues that rates stay high, progress has stalled, and some advanced, gender-equal countries show oddly high levels. Prevention work also seems not to reach younger people well, he says. pmc-13272921:

At a low dose, the guard effect reached mostly 80 percent. More of the salt worked better, while more heat worked against it. Surface tests showed a guard layer on the steel, and computer work supported a mixed binding mode. Tests also probed harm to a germ that attacks steel, suggesting a dual-purpose guard for harsh settings.
pmc-13273421:
Lidia Gazzola leads a 2026 multicentre survey of how acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections are managed in Italy. These common infections range from cellulitis to major abscesses and carry clinical and organizational burden. A 107-item questionnaire went to nine expert Italian centers, with one senior specialist replying for each.

Practice varied widely in organization and care pathways, the survey found. Infectious disease specialists were central, but round-the-clock availability was limited, and access to microbiology and wound care varied. Monitoring and cost evaluation were inconsistent.
pmc-13273521:
Yu-Sun Guo leads a 2026 case report of a sacral nerve implant that pushed out through the skin twice in a patient doing heavy labor. Sacral neuromodulation treats overactive bladder, urine retention, and fecal incontinence with an implanted pulse generator. Extrusion is uncommon but can cause severe complications and loss of benefit.

At seven months there was no recurrence. The authors also reviewed nine related cases, summarizing triggers and best treatment, and stress strict limits on activity after surgery.
pmc-13273721:

Patients often paid high costs or reached care too late. The review projects rising demand as populations age. It urges stronger primary care and fairer funding. Coordinated regional action is presented as the path to better heart health.
pmc-13274921:

pmc-13276821:

Mutations tied to drug resistance were pinpointed along the way.
pmc-13278021:

A blood-based check could make repeated monitoring easier, the authors propose.
pmc-13279921:

Drug ideas that guard power cores to block the death blend close the review.
pmc-13280221:

pmc-13281321:

pmc-13281421:

The author urges action on food, care access, and mother schooling.
pmc-13281821:

pmc-13282321:

pmc-13283121:

The authors offer the model as a design aid for engineers who build smart sensor systems for harsh settings.
pmc-13283421:

pmc-13283921:

pmc-13284421:

The authors propose a shared sweet-spot map, while noting more testing is still needed.
pmc-13285221:

pmc-13285621:

pmc-13285921:

pmc-13286221:

pmc-13286521:

pmc-13287121:

pmc-13288721:
Kaisa Kujansivu and co-authors profile chat clinic users in Finland in 2026. Their study uses linked national records. Years ran from January 2022 to February 2025. The set held 1,599,588 residents. Eight service counties fed the data. Older, poor, and jobless groups got close looks.

pmc-13289021:
Rebecca K Kelly and colleagues study heart risk by wealth and sex in the UK. Their 2026 study uses UK Biobank data. It holds 500,769 adults with one risk read. Wealth was split by a town score. Women made up 54.4 percent of the group.

pmc-13289221:

No factor showed a clear link with problematic use in the pooled results so far. pmc-13289921:

Trend modeling then tested whether slopes diverged with time.
pmc-13290121:

The real stimulation group finished fastest and showed stronger activation in key leg and trunk muscles, plus greater co-activation and coupling between muscle pairs. Li and Sheng propose stimulation as a short pre-competition priming tool.
pmc-13290521:
Different ball sports sharpen different corners of children's thinking, Tongyan Zhang and colleagues find in a 2026 network meta-analysis. They pooled randomized trials in children and adolescents to compare how football, tennis, table tennis, and other ball games affect executive function subdomains.

Twelve studies covering five sports entered the network. Football ranked best for the accuracy of inhibitory control, while tennis led for reaction time and table tennis for reaction time in cognitive flexibility tasks. Working memory accuracy, oddly, ranked highest under control conditions rather than any sport. Zhang and colleagues caution that several rankings flipped when the analysis was limited to typically developing children, and with thin, mixed evidence the domain-by-domain verdicts should be read as provisional.
pmc-13290721:
Plant essential oils attack gum-disease bacteria on several fronts at once, Yan Huang and colleagues summarize in a 2026 review of alternatives for periodontitis care. With standard drugs facing resistance, the review gathers what is known about oils' antibacterial strength and how they work.

Many oils suppressed key plaque pathogens, including Porphyromonas gingivalis, often at minimum inhibitory concentrations below 100 μg/mL, and some blocked biofilm formation at even lower doses. Their weapons include tearing bacterial membranes, jamming metabolism, switching off virulence genes, and interrupting quorum sensing. Single components such as carvacrol, thymol, and eugenol carry much of the punch, and carriers like nanoemulsions and liposomes can steady the oils and deliver them better. The authors flag poor water solubility, leftover toxicity, and instability as the work that remains.
pmc-13290821:
Adding a diode laser to scraping improves inflamed gums around dental implants, Akif Nalbant and colleagues report in a clinical study from 2026. Peri-implantitis threatens implant survival, and the team tested whether a 940 nm laser, alone or combined with mechanical cleaning, beats cleaning alone on clinical signs and a fluid biomarker.

Thirty-nine patients split into debridement-only, laser-only, and combined groups, with pocket depth, attachment level, plaque and gum indices, and fluid volume checked at baseline and weeks 4 and 12. Every group improved, but the combined group cut plaque and gum inflammation most, with the largest numerical gains elsewhere too. The biomarker S100A8, however, did not move significantly in any group. Nalbant and colleagues endorse the combination for calming inflammation while doubting the marker's short-term sensitivity.
pmc-13291021:
Robots placed in older people’s homes might flag who needs depression care, according to a 2026 real-world study led by Han Wool Jung. Participants used a social robot called Hyodol, which asked daily health questions, held free conversations, and logged how people touched and used its content.

Data came from 215 community-dwelling older adults, split into a 2024 training group of 170 and a 2025 test group of 45, with depression judged by surveys and expert video consultations. A random forest model caught most people who were symptomatic and most who needed referral, though it also raised many false alarms. Quiz use, chat frequency, meal regularity, and physical contact with the robot ranked among the strongest signals.
pmc-13291221:
Deep space travel strains the heart in ways still unclear. Agnieszka Brojakowska leads a 2026 review of heart risks for Moon and Mars crews. Space flight brings weightlessness and strong radiation. Long trips add isolation, poor sleep, and scant medical help.

Known effects include rhythm faults and stiffer blood vessels. Control of blood pressure by nerves also shifts. A body-wide inflammatory state may develop. What these changes mean over years away from Earth is unknown. Particle radiation from deep space adds new danger. The review gathers all known risks in one place. Planners can use it to design safeguards for long missions.
pmc-13291321:
New brain cells in mice may soften social rank fights. Birte Doludda leads a 2026 study of female mouse groups. Genes and homes were held the same across groups. Yet each mouse still acted as an individual.

Groups mixed normal mice with mice lacking new neurons. A tracking system watched them for three months. Stable rank orders formed in all groups. Mice without new neurons grew more rank-bound over time. They also took higher ranks than normal cage mates. Social rank in normal mice tracked new cell counts. Flexible social skills may need fresh neurons. Flat groups may rest on that flexibility.
pmc-13292321:
Kim L Vockert and co-authors run a 2026 five-year imaging follow-up of people with inherited nerve diseases, hunting for measures that track slow decline. Fourteen patients with genetically confirmed Charcot-Marie-Tooth types and related conditions received muscle MRI of the legs and high-resolution nerve ultrasound twice, about 4.75 years apart. Clinical scores, strength, sensation, and nerve conduction studies ran alongside.

Clinical examination scores worsened significantly, driven by motor symptoms, yet nerve conduction and MRI muscle volume barely budged. One MRI measure, normalized signal intensity in the lateral calf muscle, rose clearly and matched fat fraction readings, exposing creeping fat replacement. The ultrasound pattern score also climbed in demyelinating forms and tracked with slower conduction speeds. The authors nominate fat fraction and the ultrasound score as trial-ready progression markers.
pmc-13293121:
Andrew A Davinack and co-authors introduce, in 2026, a free Python package that turns genetic distance data into smooth maps. Standard population genetics often forces data into set groups, which can hide steady shifts across a landscape.

The package, called pygenoscape, takes distance tables or aligned DNA and blends embedding, map projection, gap filling, and interactive viewing in one workflow. Trials used genome data from an invasive bumblebee and DNA from a marine worm, matching earlier findings in both. Tests with made-up data also rebuilt known patterns, such as slow drift with distance and sharp breaks at barriers. Anyone can install it from PyPI.
pmc-13293721:
Linqin Xie and colleagues make, in a 2026 study, a foam dressing loaded with copper-bearing bioactive glass for chronic diabetic wounds. Such wounds need dressings that soak up fluid, kill germs, and actively support tissue repair at the same time.

The foam soaked liquid well, let vapor pass at a fit rate, and held its strength in tests. Copper glass gave germ killing above 99% against two common bacteria, values the authors report, and boosted growth of vessel lining cells. In diabetic rats, the dressing sped wound closure with more vessel growth and collagen than shop dressings. Physical and biological gains came in one product.
pmc-13293921:
Jintao Zhu and colleagues test age-friendly room design with virtual reality in a 2026 framework study. Interviews with 50 older adults named seven design features, including ceiling height, openness, daylight, and noise. Those ideas became variables in 18 virtual scenes tried by 40 older participants, whose skin conductance, heart rate, and mood scores were recorded.

Early results link daylight strength, noise level, and openness to short-term body and mood responses. The authors warn that repeated measures and a screening design make the work exploratory only, fit for forming hypotheses rather than proof. Still, the participatory tuning method offers a practical way to test rooms before building.
pmc-13294921:
Dong Gao and colleagues predict coal self-heating risk when oxygen is scarce in a 2026 study. Coal left in worked-out mine areas can slowly oxidise, build heat, and catch fire. Oxygen levels there fall well below normal air, changing how different coal ranks behave.

Three coal types, from lignite to fat coal, were heated at oxygen levels from 18 percent down to 3 percent. Higher rank coals reacted less readily, while falling oxygen slowed weight loss but raised the energy barrier for reaction. Heat release peaked at a different oxygen level for each coal. Grouping methods then sorted conditions into risk and no-risk classes for practical mine warnings.
pmc-13295421:
Silvana Aparecida de Souza and colleagues review plant-based insecticides and bee safety in a 2026 article. Botanical sprays are often sold as gentle on nature and people, but proof about pollinators is thin. Harm can hide below death, in changed behaviour, growth, or breeding.

Most safety testing still uses honey bees alone in lab settings, missing stingless bees, bumblebees, and solitary species entirely. Effects on foraging and colony upkeep may matter as much as outright kills for farm pollination. The authors call for testing that spans bee diversity and realistic field exposure, so natural labels rest on evidence rather than assumption.
pmc-13295921:
Upeka Senanayake, Phoebe Aubugeau-Williams and Gemma Barnard evaluate, in 2026, debrief support for junior children's cancer doctors after a patient dies. The work is rewarding yet draining, and one centre had set up private debrief sessions led by a pastoral doctor.

Local and national surveys of trainees and new consultants found universal agreement that the role takes an emotional toll, with varied effects on wellbeing. Respondents valued regular wellbeing sessions offered by their trusts. The evaluation supports structured debriefing as part of wider efforts to curb burnout and keep staff in post.
pmc-13296621:
Liu Wen and colleagues map, in 2026, nurse-led diet advice for bowel problems after rectal cancer surgery that spares the sphincter. Searching four databases to May 2025, they find just five small studies, mostly pilot trials, testing such programmes.

Advice covered fibre management, food diaries, symptom-tailored changes and fibre supplements, sometimes alone and sometimes inside wider nurse care. Benefit varied across studies, and timing and delivery differed a lot. The authors call for standard, evidence-based programmes and for research on remote and more precise nurse-led diet support after rectal surgery.
pmc-13297921:
Three immune molecules may help read a tumor's prognosis and likely drug response across many cancers, propose Christos Panagiotis Rigopoulos and co-authors in a 2026 data study. They profiled CD70, CD80, and TIGIT through cancer genome data spanning gene expression, methylation, mutations, and single-cell records.

All three molecules were widely misregulated, with joint overexpression standing out in clear-cell kidney cancer. Higher levels tracked with advanced stage and worse survival in selected cancers, including uveal melanoma and kidney tumors. Expression also lined up with immune cell mixes, TIGIT marking T-cell-inflamed tumors, and with sensitivity to several anticancer drugs in cell lines. The authors present the trio as candidate biomarkers for precision immunotherapy.
pmc-13299321:
A mint-family plant's scent repels a disease-carrying mosquito, and Jinfeng Xiong with co-authors traced the molecular handshake behind the effect in a 2026 study. They distilled Mosla chinensis leaf oil, identified its main components, and tested them on Culex quinquefasciatus.

The oil strongly repelled the mosquitoes. Two odorant-binding proteins from the insect bound five oil components tightly, including citronellal, citronellol, and geraniol, and a blend of the five also repelled well in behavior tests. Docking and mutation experiments pinpointed two amino acid positions, Phe123 and Gln77, as key contact points. The authors propose the blend as a candidate natural repellent.
pmc-13299821:
Ant communities inside farm-country forest fragments answer to the landscape around them, not just the fragment itself, find Helivelton H M Araújo and colleagues in a 2026 field study from Brazil's Cerrado. Using baited traps, they sampled ground-dwelling and tree-dwelling ants across fragments and compared richness and composition with fragment structure.

Community makeup shifted significantly under the study conditions, and the signal pointed beyond fragment-level traits to the surrounding agricultural matrix. Because ants carry out many ecological jobs, from seed dispersal to predation, altered communities imply altered ecosystem processes. The authors endorse ants as cheap, fast bioindicators for judging fragment quality in converted landscapes.
pmc-13301921:
Predicting which proteins a fungus ships out in tiny vesicles can be done from sequence alone, João Neves-da-Rocha and colleagues show in a 2026 computational study of Mucor circinelloides. The fungus matters twice over: it causes dangerous mucormycosis in vulnerable patients and yields useful enzymes for industry. The team first catalogued its full secreted protein set in silico.

A random forest trained on trusted vesicle datasets from other organisms then sorted the fungal proteins for vesicle cargo. The predicted vesicle proteome echoed patterns seen in human vesicles, suggesting the model reads real sorting signals. Carbohydrate-cutting enzymes featured richly in the secretome, feeding both the virulence and the biotechnology sides of the story.
pmc-13302021:
Friendly fungi can guard picked tomatoes against rot, Lobna Hajji-Hedfi and colleagues show in a 2026 biocontrol study. Local strains of three Trichoderma species faced two rot fungi, Alternaria alternata and Curvularia spicifera, in dishes and on fruit. The team also checked growth-boosting traits and the chemistry of treated fruit.

Two species led the pack, shrinking Alternaria sores on fruit by roughly half and Curvularia sores by similar margins. Both made the plant hormone IAA and freed phosphate from soil compounds, though none fixed nitrogen. Treated seedlings grew better and fruit stayed firmer with less cell damage, making the case for living storage guards.
pmc-13304021:
Ke Xie and co-authors compare soil microbes under tree plantations on the Yellow River floodplain in western Shandong, China, in a 2026 field study. Planted forests aid land recovery there, yet what shapes their underground microbe communities is unclear.

Four stand types mixed or grew alone two tree species, poplar, willow, and black locust. Gene sequencing mapped bacteria and fungi alongside soil chemistry. Mixed poplar and locust soil held the richest bacteria, while mixed willow and poplar soil held the richest fungi. Soil carbon, nitrogen, acidity, and moisture best explained community shifts between stands.
pmc-13304421:
Qing Li and co-authors test rare earth additions to marine steel in a 2026 corrosion study. Low-alloy steel dominates sea engineering, yet salt air eats it fast, shortening service life and risking major failures.

Steels with varied lanthanum and cerium doses were melted, rolled, and put through lab cycles mimicking tropical sea air. Electric tests and rust analysis tracked the damage. Both additions improved even corrosion resistance, and the richest mix cut corrosion current by roughly one third. The rust layer grew denser and more stable, with fewer cracks and pores to let attack continue.
pmc-13305521:
Cátia Moreira de Carvalho leads a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of programs that fight false information to curb violent extremism. False stories now spread faster and wider, feeding division and possibly easing paths into radical groups.

The planned review will gather programs that reduce or counter exposure to misleading, false, or harmful information and measure effects on extremist attitudes and behavior. Studies of many designs and settings will be combined, gaps mapped, and strong practices extracted. Results aim to give policy makers, teachers, and practitioners workable steps against harmful narratives.
pmc-13307621:
Dimitrios Kouroupis and co-authors review in 2026 tiny parcels called exosomes that stem cells release, and their promise for easing pain from worn joints. Knee osteoarthritis touches about 500 million people worldwide, and pain plus stiffness drive much of the burden for those who live with it.

Joint fat and lining tissue feed swelling and send pain signals through agents such as substance P and CGRP. Exosomes can carry calming signals into that setting without placing live cells in the joint. The review weighs how such parcels might quiet nerve driven swelling and protect joint balance, while noting that dose, targeting, and proof in patients still need much more work.
pmc-13308321:
Altynshash Rakhat and Gulzhanat Aimagambetova pool in 2026 studies of self taken urine and vaginal samples for high risk HPV, a cause of cervical cancer. Their search covered four databases for work from 2015 to 2025 and drew 22 studies with more than 9000 people in total.

Vaginal self samples caught 91.3 percent of true cases and cleared 86.9 percent of true non cases in the pooled figures. Urine samples scored lower on both counts, yet they stay a kind option for women who skip clinic checks. DNA based tests beat RNA based ones, and warm storage hurt urine results. Self sampling could widen screening where clinic access is thin.
pmc-13308721:
Huiyun Fan and co-authors measure in 2026 calprotectin, a swelling linked protein, in people with HIV at two stages and in healthy controls in Chengdu. Groups held 15 patients with AIDS, 15 with silent infection, and 10 controls, with blood, stool, and gut lining samples from each.

Blood and stool levels ran high in both infected groups and peaked in the AIDS group in this small set. Gut lining scores rose with the protein signal, and both tracked against falling CD4 counts in mirror form. Blood and stool tests thus offer a needle free way to gauge gut swelling and immune wear, which could steer daily care for patients.
pmc-13310721:
Yujie Guan and colleagues map links between looks based worry and mental health in teens with curved spines in a 2026 study. Young people with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis often feel anxious about appearance and fear harsh judgment. Past work looked at single traits, not how traits connect as a web.

The group surveyed 349 patients aged 10 to 18 years at a hospital in northeast China. Worry about lacking good looks sat at the center of the web. Control of feelings acted as the main bridge between risk traits and helpful traits like support and strength. Guiding care toward looks worry and feeling control may help most.
pmc-13311021:
Qian Yang and colleagues study sleep quality among troops posted at high altitude in a 2026 survey. Thin air and long stays disturb sleep, which can hurt health and duty fitness. Added oxygen and trips down to low land may help or harm, so their joint roles were tested.

A poll covered 1,316 troops in high regions with a standard sleep score. Longer total stays and more frequent returns to low land linked to worse sleep scores. More frequent and longer oxygen use linked to better scores. The worst pattern paired long stays with short oxygen sessions and frequent returns. Steady oxygen plans may guard sleep best.
pmc-13311321:
Yuriko Kiriya and co-authors offer a 2026 case of heart sac removal aided by a microwave device in IgG4-related constrictive pericarditis. The stiff, scarred sac squeezed the heart, and dense sticking made surgery risky.

The patient was a 79-year-old man with repeat heart failure from the condition. Surgeons worked off the heart pump and used the Acrosurg microwave tool to cut the sac widely while sparing the phrenic nerves. No heat injury, rhythm trouble, or nerve palsy followed. His heart output rose and vein pressure settled, with no return of disease and no steroids needed.
pmc-13311621:
Bettina Schwind and co-authors lay out a 2026 study protocol, GiveCare, on fair end-of-life care in Switzerland across gender and diversity lines. Palliative care is among the least equal areas of health care.

The project runs four linked parts. A national survey gauges how aware palliative staff are of gender and diversity issues. Close field study in two specialist wards follows patient and family journeys. Network analysis and event modeling in Zurich map how care paths tangle across settings. Findings feed teaching, policy, and practice, with knowledge shared throughout rather than only at the end.
pmc-13312021:
Venetia Koidou and co-authors describe, in a 2026 methods study, a lab test built to measure double-stranded RNA pesticides in soil and in lab preparations. These sprays use RNA interference to silence a chosen gene in a pest, but until now there was no standard way to track how much of them remains in the environment.

Working with a 297-base-pair RNA aimed at the Colorado potato beetle, the team tuned a reverse-transcription PCR assay. Enzyme treatment sharpened the test's specificity, while a chitosan coating lowered sensitivity yet helped the RNA persist longer in soil. Because the RNA sticks fast to soil particles, the method recovers both loose and bound fractions, and matched calibration let them measure it in three soils of differing acidity. The workflow gives regulators a way to monitor these new pesticides.
pmc-13312721:
Bahar Hassantabar and colleagues survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how mothers in Tehran decide to stop breastfeeding entirely, what methods they use, and where they turn for support. Stopping altogether is a distinct step from adding complementary foods, and evidence on the decision process in lower-income settings has been thin.

An online survey run through 28 public health centers gathered 420 mothers of healthy children aged six months to under four years. Stopping was mostly the mother's own choice, reported by 86.4 percent of respondents, and over half finished between 18 and 24 months. Traditional discouragement practices were common: 41.2 percent used bitter or sticky substances on the breast, and 32.9 percent used medicines without prescription, while only about a third consulted professional sources. The authors organize the influences through a social ecological lens.
pmc-13313021:
Ziyi Wang and colleagues compare, in a 2026 prospective observational study, long versus standard courses of dual antiplatelet therapy after coronary stenting in patients whose blood still shows high inflammatory risk. A C-reactive protein level of 2 milligrams per liter or more marks this group as prone to further ischemic events, yet the best length of blood-thinning treatment for them was unsettled.

At Fuwai Hospital, 2,440 patients, 69.5 percent of the cohort, stayed on dual therapy past twelve months. Three years out, their combined rate of death, heart attack, stent thrombosis, and stroke was 1.5 percent against 4.2 percent for the conventional group in the reported analysis, with net adverse events also lower. Serious bleeding did not differ significantly between the strategies. The authors conclude that, in inflamed high-risk patients, longer therapy buys protection without a bleeding penalty.
pmc-13314521:
Jiuli Zhao and colleagues test how heart rate skews heart function readings in small animals in their 2026 study. Ultrasound checks under anesthesia drive most rodent heart research, yet the rate itself can shift the numbers, blurring comparisons between healthy and failing hearts.

The team made heart failure in rats by tying a heart artery. The model group held 11 rats and the control group held 11 too, as counted in the report, and both were checked at days 7 and 28. Mice got a two-hit model of failure with kept ejection fraction, using a nitric oxide blocker plus a high-fat diet. By varying anesthesia depth, they set different heart rates and read function at each load. The aim was to name safe rate windows for fair measures, so labs can trust their ultrasound data.
pmc-13316621:
Olyad Erba Urgessa and colleagues mined, in a 2026 computer study, bacterial genomes from horse feces for phytase enzymes that could free locked-up phosphorus in animal feed. Phytic acid in grain blocks nutrition for chickens, pigs, and fish, and better enzymes would cut waste.

Screening 162 genomes yielded 69 distinct candidate enzymes in two families, spread across familiar gut bacteria. Scoring of predicted traits picked a few standouts, and shape modeling plus docking tests ranked how tightly each grips phytic acid. One candidate bound most strongly. Safety screens flagged possible risk factors in some sources, so the authors warn that lab and animal tests must come before any feed use.
pmc-13318821:
Yue Sun and co-authors report a 2026 cross-sectional study of meaning, emptiness, and depression in Chinese teenagers. Students at one senior high school completed standard questionnaires in May 2022. Scales measured depression, presence and search for meaning, and feelings of emptiness. The authors tested how these inner states connect.

In total, 2,230 students were included in the analysis. Depression was classified in 726 students, or 32.6 percent of the sample. Depressed students reported more emptiness and less felt meaning. Correlation between depression and presence of meaning reached r = −0.46 in their data. Emptiness and low presence of meaning each predicted depression status. Searching for meaning did not predict it. A combined model reached an AUC of 0.74 for screening.
pmc-13318921:
Angela Clemens and co-authors report a 2026 methods study on monitoring transplanted hearts in mice. Feeling the graft beat by hand is the usual check, but it says little about immune attack strength. Results also vary between operators. The team tested ultrasound imaging against palpation.

Mismatched donor hearts were transplanted into recipient abdomens. Ultrasound judged rejection more accurately than hand palpation. Motion-mode changes also matched the size of the anti-donor T cell response. Immune tests timed by imaging gave cleaner readouts than fixed time points. The authors argue imaging should replace touch for rejection calls. That change would improve reproducibility and the value of this widely used model.
pmc-13319721:
Jie Yu and co-authors build tiny copper based capsules for cancer immune care in a 2026 study of tumors that hide from the immune system. Many tumors block immune attack by keeping warning signals weak. Their capsules aim to start a chain where copper stress inside tumor cells spills cell DNA, which then trips a strong alarm path in the cell.

The capsules free their load in the sour fluid around tumors, and a second metal in the mix boosts the alarm signal while also lighting up scans so dosing can be timed. A drug that blocks a growth path is packed in to stop tumors from dodging the stress. In a mouse tumor model the chain woke immune cells, shrank tumors, and slowed spread.
pmc-13320021:
Jack H Ratliff and co-authors study a fat handling protein in lung immune cells in a 2026 mouse study tied to chronic lung disease. Lung guard cells must eat dead cells and calm swelling for lungs to heal, and in this disease that clean up falters. Past gene work flagged the protein as low in patients, so mice lacking it were tested after germ or sterile lung insults.

Guard cells without the protein ate far fewer dead cells and took in and burned less fat for fuel. Their power houses slowed, waste products piled up, and gene access shifted toward stress pathways. Without the protein the cells never switched into repair mode. Raising its levels may help lungs settle after swelling.
pmc-13320421:
Mina Owrang reviews gut microbe products and immune balance in a 2026 narrative review covering live germs, dead germ brews, and paired mixes. The gut microbe crowd talks to the immune system in ways that shape health and disease far past the gut. Many gains once tied to live helpful germs in fact flow from the compounds those germs make. That fact has swung focus toward their brews and toward mixes that pair germs with their food.

Proof for live germ effects on immunity runs deep, while proof for brews and mixes stays thinner and still grows. How each class calms or wakes immune arms, and where they may beat live germs on safety or shelf life, is mapped from the past literature. Sharper trials could turn these tools into real care options.
pmc-13320521:
Pu Liang and co-authors reflect on the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in a 2026 perspective. The prize went jointly to Mary E. Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell, and Shimon Sakaguchi for work on how the immune system tolerates the body's own tissues. Their findings centred on regulatory T cells, a group that calms immune attacks.

Older teaching stressed a central check in the thymus that removes self-reactive cells early in life. The laureates showed a second, outer system also matters, since some risky cells escape the first check. Regulatory T cells police those cells in the tissues and help explain why severe self-attack is rare. The piece traces how that view of tolerance grew.
pmc-13322921:
Vahid Akbari and a large team build a blood immune encyclopedia called HuBIE, reported in 2026, covering T-cell and B-cell receptors in infection and cancer. The resource holds repertoire data from 2,614 samples taken from 1,941 participants, including bloodstream infections, several cancers and controls, with repeat samples for many people.

Using a Roche targeted sequencing platform, the team read heavy chains for T-cell receptors and antibodies in all participants at once. Analyses cover repertoire diversity, gene use, chain shares and CDR3 features. Small cohorts, narrow diversity and uneven lab methods have held this field back, and the authors offer HuBIE as a shared base for diagnostic, prognostic and treatment work.
pmc-13323821:
Jin Young Hong and co-authors review devil's claw for musculoskeletal pain against standard anti-inflammatory drugs, in a 2026 structured narrative review. The plant Harpagophytum procumbens is a traditional remedy whose use grows as long-term NSAID harms to gut, heart and kidneys limit care.

Lab work suggests its key compound harpagoside can damp inflammatory paths such as COX-2, NF-kB, cytokines and oxidative signals, though that proof is indirect. Clinical studies, mostly in osteoarthritis and low back pain, hint at symptom relief for some patients, yet trials are small, formulas and doses vary and follow-up is short. The authors judge NSAIDs still far better proven, with devil's claw generally well tolerated.
pmc-13324221:
Anas M Barabrah and co-authors pool 218 cases of heart chamber clots in Behcet's disease, in a 2026 systematic review of case reports and cohort studies to December 2024. This rare autoimmune disease can clot inside the heart, with high illness and death risk.

Cases clustered in young men from historic Silk Road regions, and the clot was the first sign of Behcet's in over half the cases in their count. Fever, breathlessness and coughing blood were common, and the right heart chambers were hit most. Steroids, immune suppressants and anticoagulants formed the main treatment, with full resolution in about two thirds of treated cases. Surgery carried high recurrence and death rates, so the authors favour medical care first.
pmc-13325321:
Yaqi Zhu and colleagues report four beef tapeworm cases in Hunan Province in a 2026 case report. Taenia saginata spreads through raw or undercooked beef, and Hunan is not a usual hotspot for the parasite.

Cases surfaced in 2023 and 2025, and worm segment checks plus PCR sequencing confirmed the species. Every patient had eaten raw or undercooked beef at mid-to-high-end restaurants, and some were healthcare workers. Cases clustered within households, hinting at shared meals as the source. The authors urge stronger food safety teaching, tighter meat inspection, and clear public warnings about raw beef dishes, even in regions where the worm is rare.
pmc-13325421:
Tomislav Bracanović argues that parts of AI ethics overreact to new technology for evolved mental reasons in a 2026 essay. The field has grown fast, and many papers treat broad AI trends as urgent moral threats.

Three habits from Stone Age psychology anchor his case: seeing agency where none exists, moralizing charged scenes too fast, and spreading moral alarms widely. Fresh technology, moral shock value, and career rewards for finding new problems all feed those habits. Even training in ethics shields experts only weakly from such bias. The essay builds a framework of testable claims about why some worries swell beyond the real risk of present systems.
pmc-13327021:
Soon Kyu Lee and co-authors present a 2026 case report about a liver lump that looked like cancer on scans. A 74-year-old man with metabolic and alcohol-related liver disease had a 5.3 cm nodule found on ultrasound. Blood tumor markers were normal, yet scan features met top-level criteria for liver cancer.

Surgeons removed the left half of the liver, both to treat the lesion and to learn what it was. Under the microscope the growth held spindle-shaped cells, and staining for c-KIT and CD34 showed it was a gastrointestinal stromal tumor starting in the liver, not liver cancer. He then took imatinib and stayed free of recurrence, a reminder that look-alike lesions need tissue proof.
pmc-13327921:
Lei Zhang and co-authors tune a seaweed gel dressing so its calcium speeds wound repair in a 2026 study. Alginate gels form when calcium links their chains, and the same calcium can steer cell behavior. Gels were made with calcium chloride at 20, 50, 100, and 200 mM and tested for strength, calcium release, and cell response.

The 100 mM recipe balanced firmness with bioactivity best, driving fibroblasts to multiply, move, and lay down matrix in dishes. On full-thickness skin wounds in rats, that gel sped closure and tissue regrowth, and gene profiling showed calcium signaling switched on in fibroblasts. Dose of the cross-linking ion, not just the gel itself, is the design lever.
pmc-13328021:
Yanhui Wang and co-authors sort children with appendicitis into inflammation types in a 2026 cohort study. Single blood markers miss how varied the body's response can be, so the team applied latent class analysis to nine indicators in 402 children who had keyhole appendix removal. Learning models then forecast complications after surgery.

Three types appeared: low inflammation at 29.4 percent, moderate at 40.8 percent, and high at 29.9 percent of the group, differing in markers, perforation, stay length, and complications, which hit 17.4 percent overall. Perforation alone independently predicted trouble, with an odds ratio of 3.03 in their model, while the XGBoost model forecast complications with an AUC of 0.911 on held-back cases. Phenotype plus algorithm could guide watch intensity.
pmc-13330521:
Lee Wha Gwon and a large team improve twin prime editing for large genome changes in a 2026 study. Twin editing uses two editor complexes with matching guide RNAs to write bigger changes. The team reworked the editor by adding a La domain and tuned the guides, then tested the system in human-derived cell lines.

Editing efficiency rose by a fold gain of 1.75 in the reported results, without more stray cuts or faulty edits. The system placed a green marker gene of about 2.8 kb at target sites. It also removed the expanded repeat tract in the ATXN3 gene in a cell model of spinocerebellar ataxia type 3. Simpler guide design may widen use in research and therapy.
pmc-13331221:
Ismail Aslam, Masood Sadiq, and Asma Aslam review artificial intelligence in brain tumour diagnosis and surgery planning in a 2026 article. Searches of two databases covered peer-reviewed English work from 2015 to 2025 on learning systems, image traits, and planning tools for neurosurgery.

Learning systems have sharpened tumour spotting, sorting, and outlining on scans, the review finds. Image trait methods can guess molecular type without tissue sampling. Planning uses span brain shift models, fibre maps, live tissue checks, and smart navigation. Hurdles include scarce data, opaque logic, mixed datasets, and approval and setup needs. Firm prospective proof must come before safe wide use, the authors conclude.
pmc-13331421:
Shahad Al Jebeli and colleagues review clot removal for stroke in pregnancy in a 2026 article. Pregnancy raises stroke risk through heart, vessel, and clotting shifts, yet treatment proof is thin. Searches of four databases to May 2024 followed standard review rules, taking any study design that reported such cases.

From 785 first records, 16 studies with 26 cases in total met the rules in the reported flow. Mean mother age was 32.6 years in the pooled cases. Strokes split most between the first and third thirds of pregnancy. Techniques mixed stent retrievers and suction, alone or with clot drugs. Mother function, vessel reopening, harms, and baby outcomes were charted for each case.
pmc-13334121:
Wafaa A Mohamed and co-authors gauged the accuracy of custom-made titanium plates for repositioning the upper jaw in a 2026 surgery study. Computer planning promises precise orthognathic surgery, but the plan must survive transfer into the operating room.

Ten patients had digital simulation, and their cutting guides and customized plates were designed and built by computer, replacing the classic splint. After surgery, the team overlaid actual jaw positions on the virtual plan and took shifts in three directions plus rotations. No landmark differed by much between plan and outcome across the sagittal, coronal, and axial planes. The largest wobble showed at the posterior nasal spine in the axial plane, at 1.7 mm of deviation. The results support splint-free, plate-guided jaw surgery.
pmc-13336021:
Jianhua Wang and co-authors foretold a giant light-to-current effect in atom-thin ferroelectric metals in a 2026 computing physics study. Materials that are simultaneously ferroelectric and metallic are rare, and their switchable polarity could control electron topology.

First-principles math and symmetry analysis picked three candidate monolayers, the XO family with X as niobium, tantalum, or rhodium, each with notable out-of-plane polarization and only modest switching barriers. Rhodium oxide's polarization of 5.68 picocoulombs per meter exceeds most known two-dimensional ferroelectric metals. The layers also host protected Weyl points and edge states, making them topological semimetals. Their broken symmetry and topology yield a large bulk photovoltaic effect, which doping and strain can enlarge further, pointing to solar and sensing uses.
pmc-13336421:
Oscar O'Dwyer Lancaster-Jones and co-authors set quality benchmarks for blood vessel tissue assembled by sound in a 2026 tissue study. Acoustic handling can pattern cells without touching them, but nobody had defined how good the patterning must be for complex tissues to form.

The team made sound-patterned 3D vascular tissues and followed them for seven days. The tissues built their own vessel networks, secreted their own matrix, and shifted angiogenic gene activity in response to the acoustic patterning. Most tellingly, the quality of cell alignment tracked positively with the vascular structure that followed, so pattern quality predicts tissue growth. The method gives bioengineers measurable requirements, spanning biological and physical parameters, before acoustic assembly can be trusted for medical use.
pmc-13337821:
Gaiyan Du, Ping Zhang, and Qiaojun Liu sort pregnant women with hepatitis B by knowledge patterns in a 2026 study. Passing the virus to the baby remains a worry despite good prevention tools. Education helps, but treating all women as alike can hide groups with stubborn false beliefs.

Survey data from 203 women in Taiyuan from 2020 to 2022 were reanalyzed with latent class methods. Two groups appeared: a large low-error group and a smaller group at 9.8 percent that knew true spread routes yet also believed casual myths such as spread through food in the reported profile. That smaller group was younger and needs targeted teaching.
pmc-13338821:
Ferhat Bozkurt and colleagues review fifteen years of skin squamous cell cancer cases in a 2026 single-center study. This common skin cancer can return or spread, and reliable warning signs guide follow-up intensity. Records covered surgically treated primary lesions from 2008 to 2022.

A total of 428 lesions entered the analysis, with average patient age 71.5 years as reported. Local return occurred in 4.5 percent of cases, spread to nodes in 4.7 percent, and distant spread in 1.9 percent in the reported counts. Larger tumors, especially above 3 cm, returned and spread more often. Poor cell grading also raised risk, supporting closer watch for big, poorly graded tumors.
pmc-13339621:
Tyler W. Hines and colleagues squeeze a terbium crystal to force a rare oxidation state in a 2026 study. Terbium normally sits at +3, and +4 chemistry is sparse. Crystals of a cesium terbium chromate were pressed in a diamond cell to gigapascal levels.

Color shifted from yellow toward dark red and black under pressure as reported. X-ray absorption spectra gained a second edge feature near 7528 eV starting at 19.62 GPa in the reported measurements, the signature of Tb4+. Diffraction, Raman, and light spectra tracked the change. Pressure thus opens a new route to tetravalent terbium chemistry.
pmc-13341421:
Liver involvement in Prader-Willi syndrome is examined through new lab models by Romar Guintu Dabban and colleagues in a 2026 review. The genetic disorder pairs extreme obesity with oddly mild insulin resistance and fewer liver complications than expected.

Faulty fat storage and burning in fat cells appear to shift lipid burden toward the liver, and blood profiling shows a distinct pattern of altered phospholipids. Fatty liver disease stays comparatively uncommon. The authors highlight stem-cell-derived liver-like cells and organoids as tools that carry patient-specific gene regulation, letting researchers connect molecular defects to whole-body metabolism in this rare condition.
pmc-13341521:
Immune checkpoint drugs appear usable in people with HIV and cancer, in a 2026 retrospective study by Xiaola Xue and colleagues. Ninety patients treated with PD-1 inhibitors between January 2022 and December 2024 were enrolled, including some with very low CD4 counts or detectable virus.

After matching, 56 patients were compared across HIV-positive and HIV-negative groups. Response and disease control rates were comparable, with the HIV-positive group at 16.2% response, and side effect profiles were tracked alongside survival. Data on this population have been scarce because trials often exclude them. Real-world evidence of this kind helps oncologists weigh treatment for a group long left out.
pmc-13341721:
Sleep protects rosacea patients from acne while sunscreen may aggravate it, in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Shiyu He and colleagues. Questionnaires on lifestyle, skincare, and diet covered 300 rosacea patients, and regression models hunted factors tied to also having acne.
