Acne appeared in 30.33% of these patients versus 14.83% in the general population. Enough sleep lowered odds (OR 0.738), with a smooth dose-response as sleep lengthened. Sunscreen use raised odds notably (OR 2.602). The counterintuitive sunscreen signal may reflect product choice or skin sensitivity rather than sun protection itself, but it gives dermatologists a concrete habit to ask about.
pmc-13343221:
Rose-Marie Lindkvist, Anders Håkansson, and Lars Garpenhag study the ethics of routine violence risk screening in Swedish emergency psychiatry in 2026. Two units in Malmö introduced the V-RISK-10 screening tool, and the authors interviewed developers and staff about whether general screening feels ethically acceptable in daily care.

Six interviewees welcomed the tool's promise of uniform and fair judgments, yet worried about accuracy, how scores get read, and how results turn into risk management steps. Acceptability, they found, rests on balancing personal and shared interests. Screening can fit staff values, the authors conclude, if knowledge spreads well and clear rules govern how scores are used.
pmc-13345821:
Tuba Eda Arpa Zemzemoğlu and co-authors tune a gentler juice process for broccoli in 2026, pairing heat with ultrasound. Standard pasteurization drains the drink's phenolics and antioxidants, so the team optimized thermosonication with response surface methods checked against two swarm algorithms.

Best settings landed at 40 degrees for 6.75 minutes at about 64 percent amplitude, holding strong agreement across all three optimization routes. Treated juice kept more phenolics, chlorophyll, and vitamin C than pasteurized juice, led by gallic acid and naringin. Simulated digestion then recovered 30.45 percent of phenolics from the treated juice against 26.22 percent for pasteurized, meaning more of the good compounds survive to be absorbed.
pmc-13349921:
Yafei Ge and Ting Gao reviewed the complement system in preeclampsia in 2026. They argue it helps explain why this pregnancy disorder takes such varied forms. Preeclampsia is a major cause of illness and death for mothers and babies worldwide.

Complement is part of the immune defence system. It must stay tightly controlled for a healthy placenta to form. The authors describe distinct patterns by subtype. One pathway dominates in early disease driven by placental failure. Another runs at a low level with metabolic disease. Faulty control defines a severe group that overlaps with vessel clotting disorders. Matching these patterns to subtypes could guide targeted care instead of one-size treatment.
pmc-13350021:
Joanna Konkol and fellow authors pooled research in a 2026 meta-analysis on poverty and death risk in people with diabetes. Nineteen studies reporting income, education, job, or area deprivation links to death were gathered from four databases through September 2025.

Low social and economic standing came with 67 percent higher odds of death from any cause, and the pattern held across each separate measure. Study results varied greatly, yet removing any single study barely moved the total. The finding underlines that diabetes outcomes depend on more than medicine: money, schooling, and housing shape who lives longest with the disease.
pmc-13350321:
Reto Engeli and colleagues studied babies who had heart surgery before six weeks of age in a 2026 Swiss registry analysis of 240 infants operated between 2020 and 2024. The question was how often a heart-lung machine, ECMO, was needed around surgery and what it meant for survival and development at one year.

Overall one-year mortality was 5.8 percent. ECMO supported 34 babies, whose mortality reached 29.4 percent against 1.9 percent for the rest. Development was scored with standard infant scales for thinking, language, and movement. The stark gap marks ECMO babies as a group needing close follow-up, even though the machine itself may reflect illness severity.
pmc-13353821:
Gabriela Fioranelli leads a 2026 scoping review of reporting gaps in the BREAST-Q outcome survey. The tested tool measures satisfaction and quality of life after breast surgery, but reporting habits vary worldwide. Five sources were searched from January 1, 2009 to September 16, 2022, and 307 of 6,921 records qualified.

Studies covered reconstruction after mastectomy plus cosmetic enlargement and reduction, grouped for contrast. Most-reported domains in both groups were satisfaction with breasts, at 91.21 percent and 96.36 percent, plus mental-social and sexual well-being. The weighted global mean score ran higher in cosmetic patients, at 81.99 versus 74.49 in the reconstruction group. Uneven domain use limits fair contrast across studies.
pmc-13355321:
Yongsheng Chen writes a 2026 commentary on a design idea for cheaper organic solar cells. Light, bendy solar films could be made cheaply with simple materials, but those materials twist into many shapes, which disorders them and weakens power output. Costly ring-fused materials avoid this but are hard to make at scale.

A study he discusses borrowed a lesson from protein folding: cut the number of shapes a molecule can take, a measure called conformational entropy. The tuned molecule settled into one flat shape, packed neatly, and hit a record efficiency near 19 percent for its class, at a far lower cost. Chen presents the measure as a guide for future solar materials.
pmc-13358621:
Eduardo de Souza M Fernandes and Orlando Jorge M Torres wrote a 2026 letter on a major trial of pancreas surgery. The trial, called MAPLE-PD, compared two ways to remove the head of the pancreas in patients with pancreatic cancer. One way starts at the gut's main artery and isolates the tumor early, aiming to stop cancer cells from spreading during surgery.

The trial found that this artery-first method did not improve survival. Fernandes and Torres weigh what the result means for a technique that many Japanese centers treat as standard. Their letter helps surgeons judge where the method still earns its place, such as checking artery involvement early.
pmc-13358821:
Xiao Sun and co-authors map how lung cancer spreads to chest lymph nodes in a 2026 study. Node spread decides how much tissue surgeons should clear. The team paid special attention to subsolid nodules, tumors that look partly hazy on scans and often act less aggressively than solid ones.

They reviewed 6,273 patients treated from 2014 to 2018 and charted spread by tumor site and stage. Spread followed the lung lobe in a regular pattern, more so in early lesions. In small hazy nodules with little solid core, spread was almost nil, under one percent. Such maps can help surgeons clear enough nodes without over-cutting low-risk patients.
pmc-13359521:
Russell J. Diefenbach and co-authors test a two-in-one blood test for cancer in a 2026 study. Tumors shed DNA into the blood, and reading it can reveal both gene mutations and chemical methylation tags that mark cancer. The Avida Duo assay reads both from one sample of this floating DNA. The team checked its performance in patients with advanced melanoma.

Using plasma from two separate patient groups, they tuned the workflow for steadier output and sharper mutation detection. Methylation results matched a rival established assay closely. A single sensitive test for both signal types could simplify how doctors detect cancer, track it, and pick treatment.
pmc-13359721:
Anh Duc Vu and co-authors review a versatile protein in a 2026 paper. RNF126 is an enzyme that tags other proteins with ubiquitin, a small label that can order a protein's destruction or change its job. Working with helper proteins, it clears misplaced and misfolded proteins, keeping the cell's protein stock healthy. It also helps repair damaged DNA through several partners.

Beyond housekeeping, the protein supports embryo growth and male fertility, and many cancers exploit it to grow faster. The review gathers these roles and the tumor-driving tricks the protein performs. Such a hub, with one clear working part, draws interest as a possible drug target.
pmc-13359921:
Zaher Merhi studies sugar-damaged proteins and ovarian insulin resistance in a 2026 paper. Women with polycystic ovary syndrome often show high levels of advanced glycation end products, compounds formed when sugar sticks to proteins. These build up in the ovaries and may disturb insulin signaling in the cells that nurse the egg. Merhi tested that idea in human cumulus granulosa cells from IVF patients.

Cells fed the glycated protein raised the gene for its receptor more than threefold and the gene for an insulin signaling protein, IRS-1, more than fourfold. The results support the theory that these compounds help drive ovarian insulin resistance in the syndrome.
pmc-13360021:
João Rocha-Gomes and co-authors review the economics of a harsh cancer group in a 2026 paper. Biliary tract cancers are uncommon, aggressive, and usually found late. New immune and targeted drugs have widened choices but raised costs. The team gathered the published economic evidence: studies of value for money, illness costs, and resource use.

Twenty studies qualified. Older chemotherapy plans looked better value in several settings, while most immune combinations and targeted drugs exceeded local value thresholds at current prices. Real-world care proved heavy on hospitals, above all in later treatment lines. Evidence on prevention and screening was thin, the review notes.
pmc-13361321:
Fuge Cai and co-authors mapped the genetics of rice grain clarity in a 2026 study. How clear a rice grain looks drives buyer preference and price, yet its genetic basis was poorly known. The team grew 450 rice varieties in two places and scored their grain transparency. A genome-wide scan tied the trait to spots across nearly all rice chromosomes.

Nineteen regions linked to clarity were found, and four showed up in both growing places. Two steady regions sat right at known grain shape genes, GS3 and GW5. For one new region, the team narrowed the search to a short DNA stretch and named candidate genes, including an F-box protein gene. Breeders can use these markers to select rice that looks better in the bag.
pmc-13361721:
Lattawat Eauchai and co-authors review vision-language models in medical diagnosis in a 2026 paper. These AI systems read both images and clinical text at once, much as a doctor does. The review asks whether this dual input truly improves diagnosis over single-input models. It also weighs how the tools perform alone versus as helpers to physicians.

Across studies, multimodal models beat models using only text or only images. Doctors assisted by such a system reached higher diagnostic accuracy than doctors without it. But proof for the models as standalone diagnosticians conflicts between studies. The authors advise building AI as a co-pilot that backs human judgment, easing fatigue and cutting mental load rather than replacing doctors.
pmc-13362521:
Charalampos Voros and a large team offer a 2026 review on the immune balance inside the ovarian follicle, the small sac where an egg matures. They focus on the PD-1 and PD-L1 pair, a brake system that keeps immune cells from attacking the body's own tissue. The authors argue this brake may shield the growing egg from swelling and immune stress during its development.

If that shield slips, they suggest, egg quality and embryo growth could suffer, which may matter in conditions like endometriosis and in cases where IVF fails without a clear cause. The idea is fresh and largely untested in the follicle. The review lays out the logic and points to studies that could confirm or refute it.
pmc-13362921:
Dilara Tüfek Öztan and colleagues present a 2026 study on intensive care planning after major lung surgery for cancer. Care level is usually set before the operation, yet events during surgery often change what a patient needs. The team screened 1,060 patients at one center and focused on 159 who had a written plan for intensive care watch after surgery, then checked who actually went there.

Fewer than a third of the planned patients used intensive care in the end. Long operations and problems during surgery were the strongest signs of real need. A model that adds surgery events beat a plan based on pre-surgery facts alone. The authors argue for a second triage check right after the operation to place patients more fairly.
pmc-13365221:
Miguel Padilha and co-workers test in 2026 a drug named anle138b in cell and mouse models of Huntington disease, a gene ill that wastes the brain and has no cure. The drug reshapes harm clumps of the ill protein. Treated brain cells made few clumps and took less harm.

Mice on the drug by mouth showed late clump build, less brain waste, calm swell, and betters steps and life span. Brain marks and nerve links lost in the ill came part way back. Human stem cells from patients also clumped less. No harm shows in well mice, a hope for trials.
pmc-13367921:
Rexford Gyamfi leads a team that polls in 2026 fresh stroke kin in Ghana on what they know of high blood press, the top stroke risk. Near five hundred folks from ten care sites take a 14 part test at sign up to a phone aid trial. Scores run mid, with wide spread.

School rank lifts scores most: each school tier adds more than a point. Faith group and a stroke weight score pull scores down, while body weight adds a trace. The gaps tell phone aid teams where to aim press teach for stroke kin.
pmc-13372821:
Maria Clara Fagundes Lucio and co-authors summed up exercise trials for weak muscles of age in a 2026 review. Weak, thin muscles raise falls, need for help, and death risk in old age. The team searched eight data banks for trials up to May 2025, with no bar on tongue or year.

Trials were scored for care of method, and results were pooled with set math. Muscle mass, grip and leg strength, walk skill, life quality, and death were the points tracked. Trial types still vary a lot, so pooled means need care. The sum-up helps clinics pick the drill types with the best proof so far.
pmc-13374821:
Colin Jones and Ambalangodage C. Jayasuriya sum up six gene bone ills in a 2026 review. Each ill is rare, but each can shape a whole life of pain, breaks, and care. The search held peer work from 2020 to the end of 2025, and 36 studies made the cut.

For each ill the review logs cause, signs, film traits, tests, and care. New care in test is logged too, like a growth drug bid for brittle bone ill and gene hush care for a joint ill. Sound sum-ups help rare ill teams share craft across clinics that may see one case in years.
pmc-13378021:
Aso Navaee and co-authors made a copper frame by spark craft in a 2026 study. The frame links copper to a glow coal ring, a type prized for light and charge acts. Their way runs a two-pole spark in a bath for 150 minutes at a set push.

The made stuff was checked, then tried as a light-aid to split water for its fuel gas. It woke at a low push and gave more flow as the push grew. No salt bath was in the test, a hard mode it still won in. Spark ways may build next frames and films with less fuss than heat ways.
pmc-13379721:
Canthiya and colleagues interviewed pre-medical students in 2026 about how they form views of what medical school admission demands. The process is widely seen as grueling, and beliefs about it can push students toward extreme steps and burnout. Twelve students recruited through online forums and personal contacts described how their views formed and steered their choices.

Four themes emerged from the interviews. Formal and informal sources together shape how students read the process, and many begin early, polished self-presentation to match a felt sense of rivalry. Students test, adjust, and rethink their approach in cycles, slowly building an image of the ideal applicant. A lasting tension runs through the accounts between being genuine and giving the system what it seems to want. The authors urge clearer outreach from medical schools to break echo chambers and ease needless strain.
pmc-13380521:
Deya AlWady and co-authors wrote a 2026 systematic review on choosing back surgery when a worn, curved spine also narrows the spinal canal. Surgeons may relieve pressure alone or also fuse the spine for stability. The size of the curve, measured as the Cobb angle, informs that choice but does not settle it alone.

The team searched major medical databases for adult surgical studies that reported curve size before surgery and outcomes afterwards. Mixed patient groups were excluded unless the relevant patients could be separated. Because the studies differed, results were combined in narrative form. The review aims to show how curve size should be weighed alongside symptoms and other factors.
pmc-13384721:
Frederick F. Strale and co-authors compare SPSS 31.0 with GPT-5.5 across common statistical procedures in a 2026 study. Fourteen analyses, from simple descriptions to multi-way variance models, were run on real datasets drawn from published papers. Prompts for the AI model were copied in with the original variable names intact.

Most descriptive and inferential results agreed closely between the two tools, the team reports. Some notable mismatches did appear, though the summary leaves their exact pattern to the full results. The study adds a fresh replication check on whether newer language models can match trusted software for research statistics.
pmc-13390221:
Mingqian Yu leads a 2026 study of how vision prescriptions change over time after orbital decompression surgery for thyroid eye disease. The operation relieves pressure by expanding the eye socket, but moving the eyeball can also shift focus.

Following 57 eyes from 46 patients with moderate-to-severe disease, the team tracked eyelid position, refraction, eye length, and corneal shape and stiffness, and compared paths across surgical techniques. Eye length configuration and globe position played the dominant role in prescription change, with technique and corneal behaviour adding smaller effects. Eye surgeons gain predictors they can check before surgery to warn patients whose glasses prescription is most likely to change afterwards.
pmc-13392521:
Yi Tai, Zhihao Chen, Yuping Zhu, and Weidong Han survey GLUT1, the transporter that carries glucose into most cells and across the barrier guarding the brain. Having too little working GLUT1 from birth causes a severe syndrome in which the brain runs short of fuel. Having too much, driven by cancer signals, feeds tumour growth through the glucose-hungry pattern known as the Warburg effect.

Blocking the transporter everywhere harms healthy tissue, and tumours adapt, so older drug plans stalled. The review charts newer tactics meant to hit cancer cells only. Among them are sugar-coated carriers that smuggle cargo inside, tools that tag the transporter for destruction, and immune cells reworked to thrive in glucose-poor tumour surroundings. Framing GLUT1 as the hub of a suppressive tumour setting, the authors map routes toward sharper metabolic cancer therapy.
pmc-13392621:
Tran Thi Thao, Nguyen Tran Phuoc Chien, and Tran Ngoc Bich ran a forward-looking survey of liver and bile disease in dogs seen at a university clinic in southern Vietnam during 2025. From well over a thousand visits, one hundred eleven dogs met the entry signs for closer checks, and sixty-three had confirmed problems on ultrasound. Blood tests accompanied the scans in every enrolled dog.

Older age, obesity, and being underweight all raised the odds of abnormal scans, as did exotic breed status. Hepatitis was the commonest pattern, followed by fatty liver change and cirrhosis. Among hepatitis cases sent for infection testing, more than half carried an infectious agent, most often germs spread by biting insects. Dogs with fatty livers showed a different picture, which the authors use to argue for routine infection screening alongside imaging.
pmc-13393321:
Masahiro Ishikane and five colleagues ran a randomised crossover trial testing whether a large language model speeds the tedious data extraction behind evidence reviews for emerging infections. At Japan's national reference centre, five seasoned reviewers pulled set items from mpox articles twice over, once helped by OpenAI's o3 model producing set summaries and once reading PDFs by hand. Twenty task-level checks were completed.

Assisted extraction averaged about eight minutes faster per article, near a quarter saving, with accuracy at one hundred percent either way and no adverse events. The time gap did not reach the bar for statistical proof, and its confidence interval crossed zero, so the authors stay cautious. Still, they argue the practical value for rapid evidence gathering during outbreaks looks real as tools and prompting improve.
pmc-13394021:
Hasegawa and team examine, in 2026, regional gaps in Japanese gut surgery using the National Clinical Database, which captures over 95 percent of operations across Japan. They tracked three major ones from 2013 to 2023: colectomy, gastrectomy, and pancreaticoduodenectomy, a complex surgery on the pancreas and nearby organs. The team compared prefectures by population density and measured case volumes, surgeon numbers, and cases per surgeon.

The registry held 955,168 colectomies, 514,155 gastrectomies, and 126,008 pancreaticoduodenectomies across the decade studied. Colectomy and pancreaticoduodenectomy volumes rose even as surgeon numbers fell, pushing more work onto each surgeon. Gastrectomy volume declined across Japan over the same period. By 2023, workload per surgeon had largely converged across dense and sparse regions. One concern stands out: surgeons with at least 20 years of experience are disproportionately concentrated in low-density areas, leaving rural surgical care dependent on senior doctors nearing retirement.
pmc-13395321:
Farhana Ahamed Shanila leads a 2026 trial on salt levels for giant freshwater prawns. Salt shapes shell shedding, growth, and stress in shellfish. Young prawns lived for 56 days in water from fresh to mildly salty, across five set levels. The team weighed growth, feed use, and survival, and read gene activity for stress, immunity, and shell work.

Prawns grew best at a low salt level, three parts per thousand. Feed use, body condition, and survival also peaked there. Genes for shell shedding woke up, stress genes quieted, and immune genes rose. Fitted curves put the ideal near that same low level. The authors back mild salt for prawn farms seeking faster growth.
pmc-13395421:
Yi Huang, Wei Li, and Mohammed Misbah Ul Haq catalogue, in 2026, harms linked to camrelizumab, a cancer immune drug. Reports came from a world safety database covering 2019 to 2025, plus published case reports. Six hundred and one database reports were logged, almost all from Asian patients and mostly men. Eighty case patients from China added detail.

Blood and skin harms led the list, from marrow suppression to rash and a drug-typical growth of tiny skin vessels. Grave events included heart muscle swelling and a blistering skin emergency. Harms struck at a median of eight weeks but could arrive far later. The authors urge early spotting and steroid care for immune harms.
pmc-13395521:
Adam Swanson and co-authors report, in 2026, a gut drug that cleared a severe bowel standstill in a young man with liver failure. Ileus, where the bowel stops moving, plagues critical care and resists standard steps. The 28-year-old had decompensated alcoholic hepatitis and brain fog from liver failure. His small and large bowel both stalled despite usual care.

The team tried prucalopride, a drug that wakes a serotonin receiver to drive gut motion. The bowel soon restarted, and scans and symptoms improved in step. The drug is cleared for long-term constipation, not for this crisis use. The authors call for trials to test safety and gain in like patients.
pmc-13395821:
Enoch A. Appathurai and co-authors survey, in 2026, work-related aches among Australian optometrists. Eye doctors spend long hours bent over lamps and lenses. An online survey in two states drew 119 replies. Most reported neck, shoulder, or lower back discomfort, with neck pain scoring worst.

Repeated tasks, still poses, and awkward angles were blamed most. Lamp work at the slit lamp stirred pain most often. Only one fifth knew their workplace safety rules, and almost none had employer training on injury cuts. Aches spilled into work quality and home life, replies said. The authors call for posture training, safety rules, and better gear in clinics.
pmc-13395921:
Fangquan Chen and seven colleagues published a 2026 review on how cancer cells control acidity in separate compartments, and whether changing that balance could help treat tumors. Healthy cells keep their inner fluid near neutral, but cancer cells keep theirs mildly alkaline while the space around them turns sour.

The authors sort findings by compartment, covering the tumor surroundings, the cell interior, and small inner structures such as lysosomes. Forcing these spaces to become more alkaline can upset ion balance, damage organelles, and trigger a form of cell death called alkaliptosis. They also weigh immune effects and warn that benefits depend heavily on tumor type, so gains in the lab may not carry into care.
pmc-13396221:
Ning Liu and co-authors engineered a ceramic that stores an unusually large amount of energy for use in capacitors, and report it in 2026. Capacitors release power far faster than batteries, which suits advanced electronics, but they usually hold too little energy per volume to take on bigger jobs.

The team used a high-entropy recipe, mixing many different metal ions into a sodium niobate base so the crystal's neat order breaks down. What remains is a tangle of thread-like polar regions only a few nanometers wide. That tangled state lets the material take a strong charge without locking it in place, so more of the stored energy can be recovered when the capacitor discharges.
pmc-13396521:
Xueyao Chen and co-authors worked out the maths of electric fields under Arctic-style seas, where a layer of ice caps the water, in a 2026 paper. Ships and underwater targets carry electric signatures, and knowing how those fields spread through layered water helps others detect and locate them.

Their model stacks four layers: air, sea ice, seawater, and seabed. Starting from the equation for a steady field, they used a repeated image method to reach an exact formula for field strength inside the seawater. That method mirrors the current source across each boundary in turn. A numerical model built on small volume cells checked the formula, giving engineers a tested tool for ice-covered waters.
pmc-13397521:
Published in 2026 with no author named, the study asks whether nicotine from vapes and other non-tobacco sources harms healing after body contouring surgery. Smoking is long known to slow wound repair, but the risk from nicotine alone has drawn far less study. Contouring lifts and shifts large areas of skin, so blood flow matters a great deal.

Records from the TriNetX network covered adults having operations such as tummy tucks, fat removal, breast lifts and skin trimming. Patients with nicotine dependence from non-tobacco products were matched against similar patients without it. The team then compared wound problems and other bad outcomes after surgery, testing whether nicotine by itself carries the same danger as smoke.
pmc-13398521:
Xinhang Zheng and colleagues find a self-limiting switch inside a rice immune receptor. Their 2026 study works on SDS2, a surface receptor kinase found only in grasses, which governs cell death and defence in rice. Immune receptors must fire fast yet shut down before their own response harms the plant, and the balancing wiring was largely unknown.

One spot, Thr671, works as the switch: adding a phosphate there starts signalling but also tags the receptor for destruction by the ligase SPL11. A phosphatase named SIPP1 removes the tag and stabilises the receptor, until a rival, SIPP2, pushes it aside and lets destruction proceed. The three-part module keeps rice immunity poised between readiness and restraint.
pmc-13398921:
Roland Kotolloshi and co-authors test a drug that breaks a growth-signal partnership inside bladder cancer cells. Their 2026 study targets the β-catenin/BCL9 complex, part of the Wnt pathway that drives many cancers. Bladder cancer is the commonest urinary tract malignancy, yet its progression machinery still hides drug-worthy weak points.

The partner protein BCL9L pushed bladder cells to grow and invade, and silencing its sibling BCL9 slowed growth, movement and invasion too. The inhibitor ZW4864 shut down a subset of Wnt target genes and curbed cell proliferation in the experiments. Jamming this one protein handshake, the authors argue, could become a bladder cancer strategy distinct from broader Wnt blockade.
pmc-13399121:
Vytautas Kučikas and co-authors present a laboratory device in 2026 for watching blood vessel calcification develop over time. Their miniaturized flow chip grows a thin layer of vascular smooth muscle cells, pumps liquid past them to mimic blood flow shear, and allows detailed three-dimensional imaging through multiphoton microscopy. Vessel wall calcification drives much cardiovascular disease, yet it has been hard to model under realistic flow.

As a test case, the team grew smooth muscle cells in a fibrin gel on a textile scaffold and perfused it with a calcifying medium for four days. Without added magnesium, mineral deposits covered the construct by day two, though the cells stayed alive. With magnesium added, calcium phosphate built up far more slowly, matching magnesium's known power to block crystal growth. The authors offer the platform for therapy screening and for studies needing flow plus repeated imaging.
pmc-13399221:
Kiany Miranda and co-authors tested capsinoids, the mild compounds from sweet peppers sold as fat-burning supplements, in obese rats for a 2026 study. The team wanted to know what long-term capsinoid treatment does to the heart, while their cardiac effects remain unclear. Male Wistar rats were fed either a standard diet or a fat-rich diet for 19 weeks.

The animals were then regrouped into control, obese, and obese-plus-capsinoid groups, the last receiving capsinoids by oral gavage at 10 milligrams per kilogram. Obese rats carried more fat than controls, and capsinoids did not reduce that fat or improve the metabolic and lipid changes of obesity. Heart size did not differ between groups. The treated obese rats, though, showed a reduced shortening fraction, a sign of weaker heart-muscle contraction. The authors conclude capsinoids failed to help metabolism here and harmed heart muscle function.
pmc-13399421:
Raquel Brito Elmescany and co-authors set out to examine how the brain's electrical activity relates to slow motor reactions in older women with differing degrees of sarcopenia, in a 2026 study. Sarcopenia is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Reaction time lengthens with age, and some of that slowing happens in the brain rather than the muscles. The authors reasoned that women with more advanced muscle loss might show distinct patterns on the electroencephalogram, the scalp recording of brain waves.

Earlier evidence builds the case. Meta-analyses of motor tasks show older participants responding more slowly, less precisely, or both. Postmenopausal hormone changes accelerate muscle quality loss in women, especially in the legs. Against that backdrop, the study compares electroencephalogram measures across women grouped by sarcopenia severity while they perform reaction tasks. The aim is to separate the brain's share of slowness from the muscles' share.
pmc-13399721:
Antti Palomäki leads a Finnish team that asked whether gout adds stroke risk on top of atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 nationwide cohort study. The FinACAF registry linkage captured every patient diagnosed with atrial fibrillation in Finland between 2007 and 2018, some 229,565 people, and followed them for a mean of four years.

Gout appeared in 6,910 patients, 3.0 percent of the cohort, and 16,296 ischemic strokes occurred during follow-up. Patients with gout suffered strokes at higher rates: the incidence rate ratio was 1.35 before adjustment and 1.12 after. Among patients who had both conditions, time spent on urate-lowering therapy came with a stroke rate about 30 percent lower in the reported models. Crude stroke rates in untreated gout patients climbed with the standard risk score. The authors argue gout deserves a place in stroke risk thinking for fibrillation patients, not least because it can be treated.
pmc-13400721:
Alessia Canevotti and colleagues analyze, in 2026, a DNA-unwinding factor called HLTF across human cancer cohorts, asking whether it suppresses or promotes tumors. Evidence pointed both ways. The team combined gene activity with mutation, copy number and methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas to untangle the contradiction.

Distinct regulatory setups appeared in different cancers, shaped by gene dosage changes and loss-of-function events. Methylation at both nearby and distant control regions helped set HLTF activity in each context. Several tumor-specific patterns tied HLTF changes to patient outcomes, supporting its promise as a biomarker. The work argues that HLTF role depends on the molecular setting, not a fixed label.
pmc-13400921:
Jungkyung Min and colleagues interview, in 2026, rural partners about adapting a smartphone program that teaches ear acupressure self-care for chronic muscle and joint pain. Rural areas have more such pain and fewer services. Ear point acupressure is a needle-free technique patients can apply themselves, but the app version was not designed for rural users.

Six focus groups gathered 24 participants across South Carolina and Texas in late 2024. Four themes emerged, starting with trust: building credibility in rural communities, offering meaningful incentives and fielding well-trained staff. Partners also stressed explaining the value of acupressure clearly, with detailed guidance and motivational messaging. The regional sample limits generalizability, the authors note.
pmc-13401321:
Markus Magerl and co-authors studied how doctors and patients talk about long-term preventive care and shared choices in hereditary angioedema. The condition causes swelling attacks under the skin or in internal tissues that are hard to predict. Better preventive drugs exist, yet complete control stays hard to reach.

The German study interviewed ten health professionals who manage the condition, watched them run simulated patient consultations, and interviewed eight patients for thirty minutes each. In the simulated visits, most professionals recommended long-term prophylaxis when attacks were frequent. Quality of life had to suffer badly too. The interviews showed how clinicians usually open the prophylaxis conversation. They also surfaced barriers that block shared decisions and treatment starts, plus strategies meant to beat them.
pmc-13401521:
S Nithyapriya and co-authors are the subject of a 2026 retraction note in Microbial Ecology. It withdraws their 2024 paper on purifying desferrioxamine B from Pseudomonas fluorescens and using it to boost peanut growth and nutrient uptake. The journal's editor-in-chief retracted the article after multiple concerns surfaced.

The note lists specific problems. The structure drawn in Figure 7 and labelled desferrioxamine B is actually ferrichrome. The data do not support identifying the siderophore as desferrioxamine B, and a statement about centrifuging at 1,000 rpm is wrong. Carbon-13 data in Figure 6 lack assignments. The claimed benefit to plant growth was judged unconvincing, and the authors could not give a satisfactory explanation, so confidence in the article was lost. Six authors disagree with the retraction; Najla A Alshaikh did not respond to the publisher.
pmc-13402621:
Seyedmojtaba Seyedraoufi, Mari Bergstøl Gornitzka, and Andreas Lossius present GATHeR, an open-source tool that rebuilds full paired antibody recipes from single-cell RNA sequencing reads. Antibody genes are sparse in naive and memory B cells, so older methods often stop before the constant region, blurring which subclass or allele a cell carries. GATHeR assembles heavy and light chains together and stretches the reads into the constant region.

That extension lets the tool assign subclass and allele with confidence and tell surface receptors apart from secreted antibodies by their membrane anchor parts. It also catches splice variants in naive and memory cells, including heavy-chain transcripts still holding introns. Benchmarks against existing methods favored GATHeR, with the widest gains exactly where data run thinnest. The tool handles Smart-seq2, Smart-seq3, and 10x Genomics libraries.
pmc-13403621:
Huanglin Huo and co-authors published corrections in 2026 to their study of a propolis gel meant to speed healing of diabetic wounds. Three figures in the printed version held faults found after release. One panel used the wrong image for a gel strength, and another panel mixed up its image too.

A time label in one chart read 12 hours where 24 hours was correct. A size figure in a third chart was also wrong. The notice supplies fixed versions of all three figures. The team states the fixes came from assembly slips and leave the data reading and main findings unchanged.
pmc-13405121:
Pau Pons-Gomila and colleagues measure training loads in women's basketball over a season, reporting in 2026. Fourteen players wore local positioning trackers and heart rate monitors for 22 weeks. Sessions were sorted by purpose, from unopposed drills to full games.

Small-sided games produced higher values than competitive formats on nearly every measure, including distance, accelerations, jumps and player load. Only time at high heart rate failed to follow that pattern in the reported results. Court space size added a second layer to the comparisons. Linear mixed models handled repeated measures across the season. Coaches can use the contrasts to dose drills deliberately rather than assume games are always the hardest work.
pmc-13406121:
Akshai Mansingh reviews twenty-five years of a needle procedure for trigger finger, in a 2026 single-surgeon series. A trigger finger catches or locks because its tendon sheath narrows. Releasing it through the skin with a wide needle can be done in an office visit.

The series covers 863 fingers in 551 patients with moderate to severe triggering. Women were affected three times as often as men, and the thumb was the commonest site. About a third of patients had several fingers involved, and the dominant hand was strongly favoured. Jobs with repetitive hand use and diabetes showed no notable link. No complications were reported, leading the author to recommend the method as first-line care.
pmc-13407121:
Cynthia Angeline and colleagues studied toddlers in Bandung District, Indonesia, in 2026, linking parenting style, anaemia, and early development. Their clinic-based survey covered 193 children aged 6 to 59 months seen in February and March 2026, with blood tests for haemoglobin, a parenting questionnaire, and a developmental screening tool.

Anaemia affected 20.2 percent of the children, concentrated in those under two years. Permissive parenting, where limits are loosely set, was far more common among anaemic children and came with roughly tenfold odds of anaemia after adjustment. Anaemic children in turn faced much higher odds of developmental delay. The authors argue that anaemia programmes should add parent education and early screening to the usual nutrition focus, especially before age two.
pmc-13407321:
Salman Soltani and colleagues report a 2026 randomised trial from an Iranian urology emergency service: could a heart drug placed under the tongue help men void again after a blocked bladder? All 80 men, aged 50 or over, had a first episode of acute urinary retention from an enlarged prostate and received catheter drainage plus standard prostate medicines.

Half also took daily isosorbide dinitrate for 21 days. After catheter removal, half the added-drug group passed the voiding trial, versus 22.5 percent on standard care alone, and leftover urine volumes fell further in the combined group. Prostate marker levels stayed steady and no serious side effects appeared. Adjusted analysis confirmed the added drug independently predicted success, making it a candidate adjunct worth wider testing.
pmc-13407821:
Fatma Abdul EL Hak and co-authors turn, in 2026, stale bread into a high-yield broth for growing bacterial cellulose, a flexible material for medicine and industry. Costly standard media block large-scale production, so the team fermented a cellulose-making bacterium in hydrolysate from bread waste broken down by another microbe, then tuned the recipe with statistics.

Screening singled out glycerol and ethanol additions, warmth near 28 degrees, mildly acidic conditions, and a young starter culture as key levers. A formal tuning design then refined the mix. The result was striking: 39 grams of dry cellulose per litre in under six days, far above the 4 to 15 grams typical of waste-based systems. The material also came out more porous, with larger pores and lower crystallinity, traits suited to drug delivery, wound care, and filtration.
pmc-13408821:
Louise Kelly-Hope and co-authors test in 2026 whether a thermal camera can help map dengue risk across Nepal's three ecological belts. Dengue mosquitoes breed in household containers, and the water temperature inside those containers decides how fast they develop. The pilot study catalogued breeding sites, measured water chemistry, and compared camera readings with an ordinary thermometer from the Terai lowlands to the mountains.

Plastic containers, metal items, and tyres were the common nurseries, and both dengue vector species turned up in most locations. The camera agreed reasonably with the thermometer, reading about a degree lower and drifting at high temperatures. Breeding water mostly sat in the mosquitoes' preferred warm range and ran about four degrees hotter in the Terai than in the hills. The team judges thermal imaging feasible for rapid habitat surveys.
pmc-13409721:
Fengqin Tang and co-workers report in 2026 on beads that pull phosphate out of water and later give it back slowly. Their material joins a zirconium, magnesium, and iron layered mineral with two soft polymers to form small hydrogel spheres. Too much phosphate in lakes and streams feeds algal blooms, so a bead that can be scooped out has clear appeal.

Tests with microscopes, spectra, and surface measures showed how the spheres were built and what their outer layer held. The beads took up about 51 milligrams of phosphate per gram at most. Uptake stayed strong even when chloride, nitrate, and carbonate were present in the water. Once loaded, the spheres let phosphate leak out slowly, which points toward reuse as a gentle plant feed.
pmc-13409921:
Xingbao Feng and co-workers ask in 2026 which plant feeds make black soldier fly larvae grow best. These larvae turn cheap feed into protein and fat that can go into animal rations. The team fed groups on diets built mainly from soybean flour or from cottonseed meal.

Diets were tuned to cut the plant compounds that can slow larval growth. Larvae were weighed and checked for protein and fat content as they grew. Gut microbes were also profiled to see whether they help larvae cope with those harsh plant compounds. Results point to a feed recipe that yields larvae rich in protein and fat. The gut findings add evidence on how microbes soften the load of plant defenses.
pmc-13410821:
Rongrong Hu and co-workers measure in 2026 how long electron and hole spins hold their state inside perovskite crystals, a trait prized for quantum devices. These crystals mix two organic cations with lead and iodine, and they shine brightly while hosting lively spins. Optical resonance methods let the team read spin behavior directly.

Several distinct spin groups appeared, with electrons and holes showing quite different magnetic fingerprints, which points to varied trapping spots in the crystal. Best spin lifetimes reached two milliseconds at cold temperatures, long for such materials. Random fields from nearby atomic nuclei set the pace of spin loss. Weak trapping of charges helps explain the pattern, backing these crystals as quantum platforms.
pmc-13411821:
Li and colleagues offer a way to extract measures from an MRI scan. The method uses a neural network that learns a scan as a function rather than crunching voxels one by one. The scan type, IVIM, separates water diffusion from blood microflow without dyes, but fitting is noise prone and ignores neighboring tissue. Their 2026 method works in two stages. A first network cleans the signal. A second fits the IVIM values, guided by coordinates and 3D patches.

On brain data the method's errors in tumor regions undercut every rival tested. On a breast imaging challenge set of one hundred cases, its error for the blood flow fraction fell by over half against a network baseline. In glioblastoma scans it gave the most repeatable readings, key for tracking treatment response. Steadier numbers from noisy scans, the authors argue, are what this technique needs to earn a clinical place.
pmc-13412221:
Haile and co-authors report, in 2026, a newborn whose head mass was confidently expected to be an encephalocele, a sac of brain tissue herniating through a skull defect. It proved after surgery to be a mature teratoma, a germ cell tumor containing developed tissues. Intracranial teratomas account for less than 1 percent of brain tumors and usually sit midline in the pineal or suprasellar regions; the occipital location here is uncommon.

Prenatal imaging had shown the midline occipital protrusion plus a nodule of about 5 millimeters, and the favored diagnosis was encephalocele. Surgery within the first week of life found the mass hanging from a narrow stalk through a calvarial defect of roughly 3 to 4 millimeters below the torcula, with no dural communication. Pathology confirmed mature teratoma. At 8 months of age the infant showed no sign of recurrence. The authors urge a differential for congenital cranial masses despite suggestive imaging.
pmc-13413321:
Jenny Patricia Muñoz-Lombo and co-authors chart in 2026 how yeast blood infections changed after the pandemic at a large teaching hospital in Colombia. Their chart review covered adults with candidemia in 2022 and 2023. Labs named the yeast species and tested drug response in close to 3,500 blood cultures. Cases ran at just over one per thousand hospital stays, and near six per thousand in intensive care.

Yeasts other than Candida albicans caused 61.5 percent of the 109 cases found. Candida tropicalis and Candida parapsilosis led the list. Nearly three in ten parapsilosis samples shrugged off fluconazole, the main drug used against them. More than half the patients died. Those seen by an infection expert lived more often, so the authors press for expert input and stronger labs.
pmc-13415521:
Athanasios Tsanas and co-authors follow forty-five workers aged fifty to sixty-six for a year, in a 2026 study linking work, sleep, and wellbeing. Participants across several sectors filed weekly and monthly reports on job stress, workplace wellbeing, general wellbeing, and sleep quality. Wrist sensors recorded movement across three long windows.

The dataset gathered 1,901 report entries and 5,258 days of sensor data. Job stress answers tied very strongly to both wellbeing and sleep scores. Sensor analysis exposed disturbed sleep and frequent awakenings in most participants. Sleep features from sensors also predicted wellbeing scores, adding information beyond self reports. Pairing both sources could feed personal health monitoring for older workers.
pmc-13415721:
Maxime M. E. Brandts and colleagues run a randomized trial on delaying early morning swim training, in 2026. Twenty-seven national level swimmers, average age near sixteen, attended two eight day camps with morning sessions at seven or nine o'clock. Sleep was tracked by wrist sensors and diaries, recovery by questionnaire, and performance by timed swims.

Later starts gave a full extra hour of sleep per night on average, a clear statistical effect. Recovery scores did not improve significantly despite the longer sleep. Timed swims over one hundred and eight hundred meters also stayed unchanged. Mediation checks found no chain from sleep to recovery to performance in this short camp setting.
pmc-13417021:
Yingsong Yuan and Yang Gu present a case of a rare benign bone tumour that broke after first surgery, in a 2026 report. The tumour, a liposclerosing myxofibrous tumour, grew in the lower thigh bone of a 38 year old man. First treatment scraped it out, filled the space with synthetic graft, and added a plate.

A minor fall 25 days later fractured the weakened bone through the treated area. Revision surgery cleared the graft, packed the space with bone from the patient's own hip crest, and fixed a stable plate. The fracture healed, pain resolved, and function recovered well. The case guides salvage after early failure.
pmc-13418121:
Varun Chauhan and co-authors test what a fungal enzyme does to the safety of plant phenols from biomass, in a 2026 laboratory study. Four phenols, including vanillin and ferulic acid, were treated with laccase, an enzyme fungi use to alter such compounds. Treated and untreated versions were compared on human lung fibroblast cells.

Untreated phenols at rising doses harmed cells and raised oxidative damage markers while draining protective antioxidants. Enzyme treated versions kept cells healthier in shape and activity, with less fat oxidation damage and better antioxidant levels. Several analysis methods confirmed treated and untreated groups behaved distinctly. Fungal conversion may soften phenol toxicity for industry.
pmc-13418221:
Kirill Markin and colleagues set out a trial protocol for a phone and web app that guides lithium dosing, published in 2026. Lithium remains a first line bipolar treatment, yet use is falling because blood monitoring is demanding. The app combines model based dose prediction, statistical refinement from measured levels, reminders, and clinician dashboards.

The open trial will enrol 210 adults starting lithium for bipolar or schizoaffective disorder, half with app support and half with standard care. The main outcome combines stopping lithium, toxicity admission, and unplanned mood crisis care over 12 months. Mood, functioning, quality of life, and lab monitoring adherence are also tracked.
pmc-13418421:
Xiao Yang and co-authors measure a fat signalling molecule and its receptors in major depression, in a 2026 biomarker study. Diagnosis still rests on subjective judgement, so blood markers are sought. Fifty six patients were treated for eight weeks and compared with 42 healthy controls, with depression rated on two standard scales.

At baseline, the molecule S1P and receptors S1PR1 and S1PR3 all ran high in patients, strikingly so in women for the receptors. Levels fell toward normal with treatment. Starting S1P predicted how much symptoms improved, and the three marker panel separated patients from controls with high accuracy. Personalised psychiatry may benefit.
pmc-13418521:
Junting Wang and colleagues propose a corrected way to measure interactions between brain connections themselves, in a 2026 methods paper. Standard edge connectivity compares how pairs of brain links fluctuate together, yet it folds in average levels that bias the result when the real interest is covariation. Their centred version removes that bias, with theory showing it settles to the truth as data grow.

A testing framework controls false discoveries across many edge pairs, and a thresholded version works when brain regions outnumber scans. Simulations and a real scan club dataset validated performance. Sharper edge statistics could refine brain network maps used in research.
pmc-13419321:
Ngo Cheung asks whether depression and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, usually treated as unrelated, share a weak point at the synapse. Low mood appears in a sizable minority of ALS patients and can arrive early in the disease. Cheung reworked gene-level association results for both conditions across brain tissues, guided by pathways nominated in rescue work with a vitamin-related compound.

The strongest exploratory signal for depression sat in the synaptic vesicle cycle, the loop that loads and releases chemical messengers. Its combined score reached 3.41 in the cross-tissue screen, though the range around it stayed wide. A shared pruning model is proposed, with immune cells trimming synapses in both diseases. The author stresses that every test here is exploratory, a map for later proof rather than proof itself.
pmc-13420321:
Menchions and Angert ran a lab experiment in 2026 on two floating water plants and climate-driven range shifts. The team grew eight types of the resident duckweed Lemna minor with a low dose of the shifting competitor Spirodela polyrhiza. After fourteen weeks they checked growth, survival of types, and dormant buds called turions.

The resident plant showed subtle but real change after meeting the competitor. Types that grew faster were favoured, and the plants also shifted traits without gene change, a response called plasticity. When the competitor later met these changed resident populations, it produced more turions, its dormant survival buds. Whether that means weaker or stronger resistance from the resident depends on how turions drive long-term growth. The authors conclude that even sparse newcomers can push resident species to evolve quickly.
pmc-13421221:
Achille and colleagues reviewed in 2026 factors that predict the course of multiple sclerosis that starts in childhood. This paediatric-onset form makes up a small share of all cases and behaves differently from adult-onset disease. The review separates three questions often mixed together: who develops the disease, who converts after a first attack, and who gains disability after diagnosis.

The most repeatable prognostic signs were early inflammation activity, such as frequent relapses in the first two years. Lesions in the brainstem or spinal cord, growth in lesion counts on scans, and a blood marker called neurofilament light chain also predicted worse course. Delayed treatment predicted worse outcomes, while early use of strong therapies predicted better ones. The authors stress that no validated prediction score exists yet for these children.
pmc-13421321: Leukemia has retracted a 2023 paper by Mazzera and colleagues on drug response in a hard-to-treat form of leukemia. The work claimed that MEK1/2 enzymes shape how tumour cells answer arsenic trioxide. After publication, readers flagged likeness between blots in two figures. The authors checked their data. They found that a number of blots had been picked in error for the figures. All living authors back the withdrawal. The team plans to send a revised version for fresh review.
pmc-13421921:
Radka Pecková leads an eight-author team testing rainforest plants against a gut parasite, in a 2026 study guided by watching orangutans. Sumatran orangutans eat certain plants that seem to lower their parasite loads — behaviour read as self-medication — and the team chose sixteen Indonesian species on that basis.

Extracts made with three solvents were incubated with Giardia intestinalis, a common cause of diarrhoeal disease, in laboratory plates. Every plant showed some killing or growth-blocking activity against the parasite's swimming form, benchmarked against the standard drug metronidazole. Eight species had never been tested for any biological activity before, as far as the authors know. The results support the self-medication interpretation and nominate candidates for alternative antigiardial treatments.
pmc-13422921:
Kevin Moncion leads a twenty-two-author team setting out, in a 2026 protocol, the PROTECT trial: whether intensive exercise soon after stroke can shield the brain from cognitive decline. Up to half of survivors show cognitive impairment within six months, and a fifth develop dementia within five years, while the early months may be the brain's most responsive window.

Participants in the subacute phase are randomised to twelve weeks of combined aerobic and resistance training at moderate-to-high intensity, or to a gentle exercise comparison. Cognition is the main outcome, joined by brain imaging and blood markers of dementia risk, with follow-up to a year. The design is Bayesian and adaptive, allowing the trial to learn as it recruits.
pmc-13423721:
Ali Amr and seven co-authors issue a correction to their 2024 study of cardiac myosin inhibitors for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a thickened-heart condition, in a large single-centre cohort. Errors had crept into Table 1 of the original article, and the notice supplies the corrected table in full, with an apology for the mistake.

The repaired table sets out the entry rules of two landmark trials of the drug mavacamten, EXPLORER-HCM and SEQUOIA-HCM. Criteria include an age of at least 18 and a wall thickness of 15 millimetres or more. A peak outflow gradient of at least 50 millimetres of mercury also counts, while recent fainting or dangerous rhythms exclude patients. The authors state the fix changes neither results nor conclusions.
pmc-13424021:
Nicola Davide Cavallo and seven colleagues ask whether the wiring pattern of the resting brain predicts how young adults handle social norms. Twenty-eight healthy volunteers underwent detailed psychological testing, covering general cognition, empathy, reading others' minds, and norm processing, plus high-density scalp recordings while resting with eyes closed.

From the recordings the team built connectivity networks for each brain rhythm and measured how clustered and how integrated each network was. Only the personal, internal side of norm processing tracked with wiring: higher scores came with looser clustering and longer paths between regions, chiefly in the theta and alpha bands. Other social skills showed no such link, suggesting norm internalisation has its own network signature.
pmc-13424121:
Gulinigaer Taxi and eleven colleagues fine-tune nitrogen feeding for alfalfa grown between jujube trees in an arid oasis farming system. Alfalfa fixes its own nitrogen, yet the best added dose for this intercrop was unknown. The team compared four rates from zero to 240 kilograms per hectare. They measured leaf gas exchange, light use, yield, and feed quality.

The middle dose, 160 kilograms per hectare, won clearly. At early flowering it lifted photosynthesis by about 31% and 43% in the first and second cuts, and fresh yield rose by up to about 46% over unfertilised plots. Protein content also gained, by about 10% in the second cut. Yield tracked closely with leaf photosynthesis measures, supporting the middle dose as the local recommendation.
pmc-13424321:
Ilya Belevich heads a seventeen-author study showing that intestinal stem cells aim their internal shipping department, the Golgi apparatus, toward the neighbour cells that feed them signals. In the small intestine, stem cells sit beside Paneth cells of the niche, and the team asked whether stem cells arrange themselves to listen better.

They do: the Golgi splits into several stacks and turns sideways toward the Paneth cells, speeding delivery of signal receptors to the right surface. A scaffolding protein, Akap9, is required for the arrangement and for normal renewal. In aged stem cells Akap9 falls, the Golgi loses its aim, and the cells stop responding to niche cues, a tidy mechanism for age-related decline in gut renewal.
pmc-13424421:
David Mens and seven colleagues build a machine-learning model to predict, before treatment, which locally advanced rectal cancers will vanish completely under chemoradiation, sparing some patients major surgery. Their preliminary INTERCEPTOR model trained on 238 patients treated between 2004 and 2018 at a major referral centre, all of whom had radiation with capecitabine followed by full rectal removal.

Only thirty patients, 12.6%, achieved a complete response. The count of suspicious lymph nodes on scans was the strongest single predictor, yet on its own separated patients weakly, with a discrimination score of 0.65. Explanation tools ranked the clinical features for the full model. The authors present the work as a first step toward decision support.
pmc-13424521:
Luo and Cao introduce a simple metabolic score in this 2026 study of hypertension risk, built from three routine measurements: triglycerides, total cholesterol, and body weight, combined into a single index. They tested it in 5,731 middle-aged and older adults from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing using three complementary designs.

Cross-sectionally, each unit rise in the log-transformed index carried 43 percent higher odds of hypertension in adjusted analysis. Prospectively, among people free of hypertension at baseline and followed a median of twelve years, the index predicted new cases with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.16 per unit in the model. Trajectory analysis sorted people into low, moderate, and high long-term patterns with graded risk: the high group carried 69 percent higher odds than the low group. The authors propose the index for cheap early risk stratification.
pmc-13424821:
Brendan Parnell and five colleagues report a rare and dangerous complication of hip replacement: a channel opening between the bowel and the new joint. Their patient was a 65-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer. She had earlier undergone total pelvic exenteration and heated chemotherapy inside the abdomen. She then received a hip replacement for dead bone in the femoral head.

After surgery she showed body-wide infection signs, and joint cultures grew gut organisms, a strong hint of bowel communication. Scans revealed gas tracking from pelvis to hip, and reoperation confirmed small bowel stuck to the pelvic wall with graft material poking into it. Treatment combined bowel removal, mesh repair, repeated joint washouts, and prolonged antibiotics, coordinated across specialties.
pmc-13425021:
Fandresena Arilala Sendrasoa and three colleagues study how acne damages quality of life in Antananarivo, Madagascar, and which factors deepen the harm. Their letter reports a cross-sectional study run from June to October 2023. Participants came from two pools: dermatology clinic patients at the university hospital and people with acne met in a large city market.

Those with other visible skin conditions or pregnancy were excluded so acne's effect stood alone. Quality-of-life damage tracked with having consulted a dermatologist, with stress, with acne scarring, and with severe grades on a standard acne scale. Background details from age and schooling to economic level were recorded. The authors argue that rating the psychological side of acne would improve everyday care.
pmc-13425821:
Yang Li and colleagues synthesized evidence linking chronic kidney disease with hearing loss in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Kidney disease, defined by damage or filtration below 60 units for at least three months, now affects a median 9.5 percent of people globally by recent estimates cited in the review. Pooling prior studies, the authors conclude kidney disease raises hearing loss risk overall.

Risk appeared higher in Asian populations, especially China, in men more than women, and in patients aged 45 to 64 years. Clinicians caring for kidney patients gain a reason to ask about hearing and arrange testing earlier.
pmc-13426021:
Yihun Mulugeta Alemu and colleagues pooled studies that compare heart disease risk scores worked out with and without blood tests. Non-laboratory scores use simple measures such as age, weight, and blood pressure, while laboratory scores add cholesterol and other blood results.

The review covered 33 studies with 243,587 people and nine different risk equations from many countries. The two score types tracked each other very closely, with a pooled correlation of 0.954 on a scale where one means perfect match. Agreement on who counts as high risk was solid but not complete, and scores matched better in richer countries. Alemu cautions that close tracking is not proof of equal accuracy, so each setting should test and tune the simpler scores.
pmc-13426321:
Weinberg and colleagues report an unusual die-off in 2026 among Egyptian fruit bats in northern Cyprus, an isolated population of conservation concern. From January to June 2025, the island's wildlife hospital admitted twelve bats. That is nearly as many as in the previous eight years combined, and most arrived near death and died within a day.

Over half the admitted bats had pus-filled skin lesions and abscesses. Lab cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus, a common bacterium, from lesions and tissue, and the strains stayed sensitive to tested antibiotics. Roost surveys in early 2026 then found steep declines: colonies of hundreds had shrunk to single digits, and some roosts stood empty. No storm, food shortage, or human disturbance explained it, so the authors urge monitoring, gene sequencing, and toxin screening.
pmc-13426421:
Satoshi Oikawa and colleagues identify a transport protein that switches on during fasting and moves fuel into mitochondria, the cell's energy hubs. The carrier, called SLC25A34, sits in the inner wall of mitochondria in hard-working muscle.

Lab tests with rebuilt membranes showed the carrier imports a fuel molecule named PEP into the mitochondrial core. Without it, muscle cells under food shortage could not burn the amino acid glutamine well, though sugar use stayed normal. Mice lacking the carrier in muscle broke down fewer amino acids during fasting, and those amino acids piled up. The pile-up wrongly switched on a growth signal, leaving the muscle enlarged and diseased, Oikawa reports.
pmc-13427421:
Zhi-Jin Zhang and colleagues forecast epilepsy prevalence in poorer countries to 2050 in a 2026 modeling study using Global Burden of Disease 2023 data. Their hybrid framework blends a deep neural network with transformer architecture alongside Poisson regression and ARIMA time series models. Projections split idiopathic and secondary epilepsy by age, sex, year, and income level from 2024 onward.

Decomposition analysis separates how much future growth comes from population change versus true rate change. Health planners in low- and middle-income countries, where epilepsy burden concentrates, gain numbers for budgeting clinics, medicines, and specialist training decades ahead. Counts by age, by sex, and by wealth of land let chiefs see where need will grow most and where funds should go in the years to come.
pmc-13427721:
Yang and colleagues release SuperWing in 2026, an open dataset built to train machine learning models that predict airflow over three-dimensional aircraft wings. It holds 4,239 wing shapes and 28,856 detailed flow simulations computed with standard engineering solvers. Shapes vary along the span in airfoil profile, twist, and upward angle, rather than being small tweaks of one baseline wing. Conditions span the normal flight range of speeds and attack angles.

Two state-of-the-art transformer models trained on the data predicted surface flow accurately, missing drag by only two and a half drag counts on unseen wings. Models pre-trained on SuperWing also transferred without retraining to complex standard test wings used by German and NASA benchmarks. The authors argue such diverse shared data is the missing ingredient for general-purpose aerodynamic design tools that can answer in seconds instead of hours of simulation.
pmc-13427821:
Harjeet Kaur and colleagues show, in a 2026 field study, that when farmers sow sweet sorghum changes how badly stem borers attack it. The borer Chilo partellus is a caterpillar that tunnels into stems and cuts yield. Four sorghum types, two known as tolerant and two as sensitive, were sown on three dates across the 2024 monsoon season in India. Plant chemistry, photosynthesis, and pest damage were all measured.

Sowing a month late raised average infestation from about 42 percent to about 69 percent. Tolerant types kept photosynthesis steady and built tougher, more fibrous stems. Sensitive types instead packed leaves with sugars and proteins that feed borers. Early sowing pushed the plant's carbon toward defense rather than pest food. Growers gain a timing lever that costs nothing extra.
pmc-13428421:
Mueller and colleagues surveyed palliative care consultation teams in German hospitals in 2026 about how they recommend strong opioids, the backbone drugs for pain and breathlessness at the end of life. Ward teams lean on these specialist services when symptoms are complex. The online survey asked about indications and drug choices.

Thirty-nine teams replied, split between university and general hospitals. Every team endorsed strong opioids for cancer pain and cancer-related breathlessness. Agreement thinned for non-cancer disease: lung and heart breathlessness won wide support, but non-cancer pain convinced only about half. Hydromorphone and morphine were the workhorse drugs named by most services, while fentanyl, oxycodone, and buprenorphine use varied widely. The authors read the spread as differing clinical judgment and call for research and clearer guidance on opioid use beyond cancer.
pmc-13428721:
Lesan and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare case of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia that faded on its own after an infection, without the chemotherapy nearly all patients need at diagnosis. This leukemia is the most common blood cancer of childhood and far rarer in adults. Spontaneous remission is documented only in scattered cases, and what drives it is poorly understood.

The team describes the course of the illness, the remission that followed the infection episode, and the later relapse. At relapse, the cancer cells carried changes in PAX5, a gene that guides B-cell development. The authors lay out the genetic findings in detail, since chromosome changes in such vanishing acts may hint at how the immune system briefly gained the upper hand.
pmc-13429121:
Sukrisman and colleagues tracked immune cell changes in 2026 in Indonesian patients with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. This cancer of white blood cells is often treated with chemotherapy plus rituximab, a drug that targets B cells. The team measured lymphocyte, CD4, and CD8 cell counts before treatment and after the third cycle in 71 patients.

Patients on rituximab regimens ended with far lower CD4 counts than the smaller group on chemotherapy alone. CD4 cells are helper immune cells that coordinate defence against germs. Their share fell while the CD8 share rose, so the balance ratio between them dropped. Inside the rituximab group, all three cell counts fell, while the control group largely kept its CD4 counts. The authors urge routine immune monitoring for these patients.
pmc-13429921:
Chenyi Zhang, Weijian Zhu, Bo Li, and Ping Hong measure, in a 2026 wind tunnel study, how air drag on a basketball changes with wear, pressure, and angle. Ball flight decides passes and shots, yet basic drag data for basketballs were scarce. The team varied surface roughness and wear, inflation pressure, and yaw angle, the tilt between the ball's axis and its flight path. Drag was tracked across a range of flight speeds.

Drag fell as speed rose, then leveled off, sliding from roughly a half to roughly a third on the standard coefficient scale. Softer, underinflated balls dragged slightly more. A yaw angle of zero gave the least drag, as symmetry suggests. Rough surfaces hurt at low speed yet helped at high speed. A mild drag crisis, a sudden dip known from other ball sports, appeared in every setup. Trajectory modelers gain real numbers.
pmc-13430021:
Galina Semenova and colleagues design, in a 2026 study, combination attacks for prostate cancer that no longer answers hormone therapy. Antibody-drug conjugates deliver a poison directly to cancer cells through a surface marker, yet alone they rarely hold this cancer for long. The team first mapped which of three known surface markers appear together on real patient tumors. They then screened drug payloads, alone and paired, across prostate cancer cell lines of different types.

DNA-damaging payloads paired strongly with a drug that blocks BCL-XL, a protein cancer cells use to avoid suicide. Together they fired the cell's built-in death pathway. Three custom conjugates, one per marker, each gained power from the pairing, and losing the p53 gene changed responses in telling ways. In mice, a clinical-stage conjugate plus the blocker shrank tumors more than either alone.
pmc-13430421:
Juliette J Rubin and co-authors raised Morpho helenor butterflies under three heat settings to test how warmth during growth shapes wing shine. Their 2026 report compares a normal tropical setting, a cooler one, and a hot one meant to mimic a warmer future climate. The team guessed that the hot setting would dull the bright blue shine the most.

Wings from the hot setting did lose brightness, and their color shifted enough that birds and other butterflies would see a clear difference. For some bird viewers, the shine vanished in full. Closer study tied the shift to a smaller gap between tiny structures on the wing scales, which also made each scale more narrow. Cool growth left the wings much like the tropical group.
pmc-13431021:
Marine Hubert and colleagues describe the study protocol for ELUZO, a One Health project working with rural communities in Senegal and Burkina Faso. One Health joins human, animal, and environmental health, and ELUZO targets diseases that jump from animals to people.

Small livestock farming feeds many families there but can spread such diseases where water and sanitation are poor. The project centres women, who do much of the small animal care yet are often overlooked in planning. Baseline data were gathered with tools designed alongside community members, mixing surveys with other methods. Those findings shaped local interventions, which the team will now run and assess, alongside training in One Health and gender equity.
pmc-13431721:
Bergès and partners across countries gathered 13 new patients with harmful variants in PUS7. The gene's enzyme performs pseudouridylation, a chemical tweak that steadies RNA strands. Earlier reports on 16 patients had linked PUS7 faults to marked slow growth and small head size. They also linked them to intellectual disability and behavior problems, including self-injury and aggression.

The new cohort carries 15 new variants. They were found by matching families and doctors through GeneMatcher, a matching service for rare diseases. Together with the earlier cases, these patients widen the known range of PUS7-related disorder beyond the first reports. The authors use the enlarged series to sharpen genotype-phenotype links. They match certain variant types to certain feature patterns in the combined data. They argue the refined picture should improve diagnosis and advice. It should also improve day-to-day healthcare for patients and their families.
pmc-13432221:
Mariasilvia Guardiani and co-authors tracked immune wear in people with HIV in 2026 who switched to long-acting shots of two virus drugs, set against peers who stayed on daily pills by choice. Even with good virus control, HIV leaves a slow burn of immune stir and cell aging. A past herpes virus that many carry may feed that burn.

Thirty-seven switchers gave blood across a year and a half of shots. Their helper cell counts held steady while killer cell counts fell late in the course. Signs of immune stir dropped at set weeks, and aging marks fell in both cell sets. Nine pill peers showed a near-mirror drift in cell counts. The team also weighed virus-specific immune replies from the herpes partner to see how they track cell wear.
pmc-13433621:
Megan J Moran and co-authors rebuilt a family health program in 2026 with rural Colorado locals, aimed at teens at risk for sugar disease and heart faults. Deep habit and life-style care trims those risks, yet rural teens can rarely reach such care, and stock plans fit farm life poorly. The rebuild weighs old walls built by unfair systems.

The plan draws whole families in, with a bent toward low-pay homes, Spanish-first parents, and groups long pushed to the edge. A sturdy build frame with a fairness lens steered the work. Long fact hunts came first, then rounds of tweaks with more checks. Reach and warmth faced grades through forms, head counts at meets, and group talks with rural families of teens aged eleven to nineteen.
pmc-13434421:
Flavia Constantinescu and coauthors film a gene silencing protein at work in living cells in 2026. The protein, SMCHD1, helps switch off one X chromosome in female cells. Faults in its gene cause a muscle wasting disease and a rare face and nose condition.

Single molecule movies show a partner protein brings SMCHD1 to marked spots on the genome. A fuel burning part of SMCHD1 must work for it to gather at the right spots. Disease linked changes sped up gathering or packed the X more tightly. The films explain how dose and timing shape gene silence.
pmc-13435121:
Lulu Xue and coauthors grow tiny organic crystals that lase with blue light in 2026. The gain material forms hexagon cavities on its own from solution, yet uneven sides leak light and dull the beam. Tuning the air above the solution plus the mix strength yields near perfect hexagons.

Even sides trap light far better inside the cavity. Lasing starts at low pump power, with a line width of just 0.2 nanometers. Shrinking the hexagon down gives single mode output. Size and shape both answer to the growth recipe. Small, cheap lasers for optical chips look more practical.
pmc-13435821:
Panizzutti and a large team grow brain-like networks from bipolar disorder patients' cells in this 2026 study. Stem cells reprogrammed from blood retain each donor's genetics, letting researchers study living human brain cells in a dish. The team built cortical networks from twelve people with bipolar disorder. Twelve people without any mental health history served as the comparison. The networks mix neurons and astrocytes. The team then sequenced all active genes in the cultures.

The bipolar networks showed 191 enriched gene pathways, and most of them, 171, were turned down rather than up in the patient-derived cultures. About a tenth of the pathways involved the immune system, and the authors dug into the Toll-like receptor signaling pathway, which senses infection and damage, finding it downregulated. They interpret the pattern as profound immune dysregulation inside the brain cells themselves, not just in the body.
pmc-13435921:
Evaborhene and colleagues analyzed in 2026 the explosive 2025 mpox outbreak in Sierra Leone and its risk for the wider Mano River Union of West African states. Cases passed 4,400 within six months, the largest documented burden in the region, spreading through heterosexual networks in dense cities such as Freetown. The surge broke prior assumptions about how mpox behaves in West Africa.

The authors trace the failures that fed it: slow detection, weak testing, stigma, and missing links to sexual health services, all worsened by cross-border movement.
