Vaccine supply lagged badly, with only about 43,000 people dosed, which they blame on dependence on outside makers and global financing gaps. They call for targeted vaccination, testing closer to communities, mpox care folded into sexual health programs, and investment in African vaccine manufacturing.
pmc-13436921:
Guan Lyu and coauthors test blood DNA profiling to foretell cancer in uncertain breast lumps in 2026. The set holds 212 patients with BI-RADS 4 nodules treated from 2020 to 2024. Surgery results split them into 128 benign and eighty four malignant cases for the check.

Blood DNA levels and mutation burden ran higher in the malignant group. A composite gene score also split the groups cleanly. Mutations in BRCA1, TP53, ESR1, and ERBB2 showed more in malignant cases. Some promoter signals ran lower in cancer, a pattern the team flags as distinct. A blood test before surgery could sharpen who needs aggressive workup.
pmc-13438421:
Shuijuan Zou, Ying Wang, and Yinmei Fu pooled trials of digital help in the delivery room, from virtual reality headsets that soothe labor pain to AI that helps read fetal heart traces. Pain and anxiety shape how a birth is remembered, and drug-free options are in demand. Their 2026 review searched four databases through March 2026, keeping six randomized trials with 492 women.

Four trials with 362 women could be merged, and they favored the technology clearly. Pain intensity fell by a large margin against routine care, and anxiety fell by even more. Two further trials pointed the same way without joining the pool. Bias risk rated moderate, and results varied widely, which the authors say should cool any rush. Their verdict is hopeful and hedged: digital support looks like a real comfort tool for labor, but larger trials must confirm the size of the relief.
pmc-13439421:
Zimu Li and colleagues copy the brick-and-mortar layout of pearl shell to build a shield that cools gear while blunting impacts, reporting in 2026. Outdoor electronics face a double bind: they overheat under sun, yet they also need cushioning from blows. Their layered composite steers heat sideways far better than through its thickness, reflects nearly all sunlight, and radiates heat to the sky efficiently. Dynamic links inside make the material stiffen under sudden hits while staying workable otherwise.

Test panels shrugged off an hour under a very hot flame without burning. They stopped a projectile moving at fifty metres per second in trials. A sandwich version cooled a hot device by more than twenty degrees and soaked up nearly all impact energy. Spent material could be recycled in a loop with little loss of performance, and life-cycle checks showed a light footprint.
pmc-13439921:
Malaiwong and co-authors refine a visual method for inserting genes into the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. Their 2026 paper presents FLInt 2.0, an upgrade of a technique that uses CRISPR cutting at glowing landmark genes to signal successful transgene insertion. The first version produced many false positives, forcing laborious screening of candidate worms.

The new strategy cuts the fluorescent landing sites so that failed repair events mostly keep their glow, while true insertions lose it. Molecular checks confirmed that non-glowing second-generation animals more reliably carried stable, multi-copy insertions. The team also found DNA shape matters: straight DNA pieces formed arrays and inserted more robustly than other forms. A follow-up cutting step can then tune expression levels of the inserted genes, reducing screening work and raising throughput for worm genetics.
pmc-13441121:
Yue Zhang and colleagues review circular RNAs floating in blood as tools for finding and fighting cancer, writing in 2026. Circular RNAs are RNA loops with no loose ends, a shape that shrugs off the enzymes that chew ordinary RNA. That toughness lets them linger in tissues and circulation, where their levels shift with tumour presence and stage. They steer cell behaviour by interacting with small RNAs, proteins, and DNA, sometimes feeding tumours and sometimes restraining them.

Patterns that specific make the loops attractive as biomarkers for early detection, prognosis, and predicting treatment response. The review gathers the main laboratory methods for measuring circulating loops, from sequencing to targeted amplification. Hurdles between bench promise and clinic use receive frank treatment, including standardisation of sampling and assay design. The authors cast standardised detection as the gate through which this biomarker class must pass.
pmc-13441721:
Fangyu Xu argues that two rare melanomas of the female genital tract should stop being lumped together, in a 2026 review. Vulvar and vaginal melanomas are usually grouped as one vulvovaginal disease because both are rare and evidence is thin. Xu gathers clinical, tissue, and biological observations suggesting the sites behave as distinct diseases. Vulvar tumours arise in a skin-to-mucosa transition zone and partly resemble skin melanoma, while vaginal tumours fit the mucosal melanoma pattern more consistently.

Those roots shape how each presents, spreads through lymph channels, and answers to surgery and systemic therapy. Vaginal disease is often found late because early symptoms hide, and local control is hard, driving a particularly poor outlook. Vulvar disease spans a broader spectrum needing subsite-aware reading. Xu urges site-aware design in research, surgical planning, and drug strategy for both.
pmc-13441921:
Xiaoxiang Zhu and colleagues separate carbohydrate quality from quantity in lung cancer risk, following a large screening cohort in a 2026 study. Diet's role in lung cancer is gaining attention, yet carb debates usually fix on amount. The cohort drew 101,755 participants from the PLCO cancer screening trial. A carbohydrate quality index graded fibre, grain wholeness, and sugar type, while a low-carb score captured quantity restriction.

Across nearly nine hundred thousand person-years, 1,706 lung cancers appeared. Higher quality scores tracked with steadily lower risk, with the top quarter showing roughly a quarter less risk than the bottom quarter after full adjustment. Quantity scores showed no significant link once confounders were weighed. The quality pattern bent rather than running straight, and it survived repeated sensitivity checks, including models with heavier smoking adjustment. The authors argue that what kind of carbohydrate people eat matters more than how much.
pmc-13444121:
Yuxuan Feng and colleagues build a live-animal RNA tagging method, 5FU-seq, in a 2026 paper. A tagged feed base, 5-fluorouridine, slips into fresh RNA, which lets teams catch gene activity as it happens. Past tags worked mostly in dishes, with weaker uptake and reach.

Their tag entered RNA at higher rates and caught a broader span of messages with finer feel. In mouse brains it exposed stimulus-tied gene webs and a dynamic Nrf2 program during anesthesia-linked sleep loss. A bred mouse line adds cell-type tags in place, so gene maps and enhancer maps come from the same tissue. Checks against sorted-cell RNA and open-chromatin reads held up. The authors offer the kit for tissue-wide time maps.
pmc-13445521:
Minoo Aryanpour and colleagues ask what shapes a woman's plan to seek cervical cancer screening, using two classic behavior models at once, in a 2026 survey from Iran. Screening can prevent most cases of the disease, yet uptake in Iran stays low. The study group was female teachers, a group with wide reach into families and schools.

Two hundred teachers in Karaj filled a tested survey in 2023, and path analysis linked their answers into one model. The model accounted for near half of the spread in screening plans. A sense of personal control led the links, followed by felt benefits, social norms, and attitude, while felt barriers pulled plans down. Knowledge fed attitude and control, so the authors aim programs at control, benefits, and norms.
pmc-13446021:
Belarra and colleagues investigate 3D-printing materials for breast imaging test objects in this 2026 study. Anthropomorphic phantoms, models that mimic the body, let clinics check mammography quality, but printed plastics must weaken X-rays exactly as breast tissue does. The team printed step wedges from five base polymers in nineteen color variants, since colorants are dopants that might alter attenuation, and scanned them on a clinical system.

Color variants of the same polymer differed noticeably in attenuation, especially for standard mammography, and the differences shrank as thickness grew across the tested range. Tomosynthesis scans showed less variability between variants. The team matched the prints against commercial reference materials. Specific PLA variants best mimicked fully glandular tissue. White ABS best imitated fatty tissue. Attenuation sat within a few percent of the references.
pmc-13447421:
Yi Zhou and co-authors map spread to an often-overlooked neck node region in papillary thyroid cancer in a 2026 single-centre study. Nodes in the carotid triangle, a neck area beside major blood vessels, are frequently skipped during side neck clearance. How often cancer reaches them, and by which routes, was poorly defined despite clear surgical stakes.

Four hundred ten neck dissections in three hundred eighty patients were analysed by neck side. Spread to the triangle appeared in over four in ten dissected sides. Larger tumours, a tall tumour shape and upper tumour position each raised risk, while lower tumours lowered it. Triangle-positive necks carried heavier spread elsewhere too. Route analysis suggested upper tumours reach the area sideways, while middle tumours climb from the central neck, guiding more complete surgery.
pmc-13447621:
Liufeng Qin, Yuanqian Yao and Jianlin Lv profile a mitochondrial carrier gene across cancers in 2026 database work with lab validation. The gene helps govern oxidative metabolism inside mitochondria, the cell power units, yet its cancer-wide pattern was largely unmapped. A broad scan could reveal whether it marks prognosis or offers a drug target shared across tumour types.

Public multi-layer datasets were mined for gene activity, survival links, immune features and related pathways. The gene ran high in nearly all cancers studied and marked worse prognosis where raised. Its levels tied to immune cell entry, checkpoint molecules, mutation load and RNA modification patterns across tumours. Silencing the gene in two liver cancer cell lines sharply slowed their growth, supporting a tumour-promoting role and biomarker potential.
pmc-13448721:
Horacio Duarte and colleagues model in 2026 whether long-acting injectable HIV treatment could protect babies in Kenya when standard therapy fails. Their simulation follows pregnant and breastfeeding women on first-line dolutegravir treatment who still carry detectable virus. One strategy adds injectable cabotegravir with rilpivirine as a second-line option, with viral load checks every six months.

In the model, women waited over eight months on average between detectable virus and switching, and only a small share ever switched. Even so, the injectable strategy cut mother-to-child transmission by 1.2 percent in newly diagnosed women and 4.2 percent in women already in care. With three-monthly monitoring and full switching, those gains rose to 4.0 and 11.5 percent, showing that speed of switching drives the benefit.
pmc-13448821:
Chengyong Jiang and colleagues map in 2026 a small brain circuit that lets mice move their eyes during dream sleep yet also helps end that sleep stage. During rapid eye movement sleep, most muscles switch off while the eyes keep darting. The team focused on cholinergic neurons in the oculomotor nucleus, long suspected of driving those eye movements.

They found two distinct subsets doing separate jobs. One group projects to a midbrain region called the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray. It ramped up before each dream episode ended, and switching it on with light cut the episode short without stopping eye movements. A second group, projecting to the eye muscles, reliably triggered eye movements without disturbing sleep state. Two genetically distinct upstream cell types in the nucleus papilio coordinate these parallel functions.
pmc-13448921:
Golestan Salimbeigi and co-authors combine in 2026 statistical design and machine learning to tune synthetic membranes that imitate the lung's basement membrane. Their electrospun mats blend two degradable polymers, PCL and PLGA, into fine fibers meant to be soft yet strong enough to flex with breathing-like motion. A response surface design first mapped how spinning settings shape fiber diameter, stiffness, strength, and stretch.

The statistical model predicted a best membrane with fibers about 0.386 micrometers wide, and bench checks landed within ten percent of every prediction. Machine learning then widened the search. A CatBoost model best recovered the polymer recipe from desired properties, while an XGBoost surrogate found a candidate mix scoring higher on combined desirability than the bench-confirmed design. The authors present the pairing as a way to shortlist spinning recipes before spending laboratory time.
pmc-13450621:
Azadeh Ghiasvand, Masoud Rezaei, and Shahab Naghdi set out in 2026 a greener way to pull chitin from shrimp shell waste. Pacific white shrimp plants throw away half or more of each animal as shells, heads, and tails. Those shells hold chitin, a useful chain sugar for food, drug, and material trades, yet the standard pull uses harsh acids and bases.

The new route uses deep eutectic solvents, a class of mild mixed liquids, paired with ultrasound-made tiny bubbles. The pairing aims to free chitin while cutting the harm and waste of the old bath method. The authors frame shell waste as a resource that can raise farm income and ease strain on coastal waters at once.
pmc-13451921:
Bo Fu and co-authors model in 2026 a hidden cost of farming's answer to climate-driven crop losses: clearing new land. When yields fall, growers can plow fresh ground to make up the gap. The team coupled a climate-yield emulator with a world assessment model to trace that answer under two futures.

Under a mid-range future, world cropland grows by about eight percent, mostly over forests, grasslands, and pastures. A hotter, looser future makes the spread near five times larger and adds warming of its own. Even with better farm methods and new tech in the mix, land clearing stays a likely answer. The authors urge holding heat down to guard both food and wild land.
pmc-13452021:
Zhu and colleagues study a small RNA that is overproduced in both Down syndrome and Alzheimer's disease in this 2026 paper. The RNA, miR155, sits on chromosome 21, so people with Down syndrome carry an extra copy, and it is also elevated in Alzheimer's brains. The team worked with human stem-cell-derived brain cells. They also used cortical organoids and Alzheimer's model mice. They deleted or boosted miR155 to see what it does in neurons.

Deleting miR155 made neural stem cells multiply more and generate more GABAergic interneurons, the brain's main inhibitory cells, while boosting it had the opposite effect. In mice, deletion likewise expanded the hippocampal stem cell pool and increased those interneurons. The authors suggest miR155, already known for driving inflammation in immune cells, also shapes brain development and could be a treatment target.
pmc-13452321:
Soggia and colleagues reported a 2026 case of diabetes mimicking a stroke. Diabetic striatopathy is a rare harm from very high blood sugar. It usually causes jerky, uncontrolled movements on one side of the body. Their patient showed weakness instead, with no jerky movements at all.

The patient, a 52-year-old woman, arrived with left-side weakness and sky-high blood sugar. Her brain scan showed a faint pale patch where stroke would also appear. Closer measures proved the patch differed from healthy tissue on the other side. Once sugar levels settled, her strength returned within one week. A scan one year later looked normal again, backing the diabetes cause. Her case shows that blood sugar checks belong in every workup for sudden one-sided weakness.
pmc-13453021:
Zahra Montaseri, Maryam Montaseri, Mohammad Ekrahi, and Mohammadreza Eskandari Kooshkeghazi report a rare case where brucellosis, an infection caught from animals, hid behind stomach complaints. Their 2026 case report follows a 20 year old woman in Fars Province, Iran, with six months of nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, and loss of appetite. She had lost 10 kilograms yet had no fever, joint pain, or night sweats.

A scope exam found mild esophagus irritation and an inflamed, eroded stomach lining, while tests for the usual stomach microbe came back negative. A careful history then surfaced the clue: she had drunk unpasteurized sheep colostrum, the first milk after lambing. Blood tests and a gene test confirmed brucellosis, and standard treatment cleared her symptoms fully over a year of follow up. The authors urge doctors in regions where the disease is common to keep it in mind for stubborn stomach cases.
pmc-13453121:
Emma O'Lone and Patrick B Mark argue that heart failure events in dialysis trials need sharper, shared judging rules. Their 2026 commentary notes that heart failure itself has grown harder to pin down, with guidelines now splitting it by ejection fraction, the share of blood the heart pumps out. Major kidney trials have each defined a hospital stay for heart failure in their own way.

The piece lines up those rival definitions side by side, covering symptoms, blood markers, and scan findings that trials require. Some trials demand a stay of 24 hours plus hard proof, while others set lower or different bars. Such drift adds noise that can hide a real treatment effect or fake one. The authors push for careful event judging, called adjudication, so dialysis trials give a cleaner signal for patients and doctors.
pmc-13453721:
Yuqing Zhang, Shumin Nie, and Xiaoli Ren sort dental implant patients into pain and anxiety response types across surgery. Their 2026 study tracks 204 outpatients at five points around their implant work, scoring pain and anxiety on simple line scales. The aim is early sorting of patients who will struggle, so nurses can tailor care.

Two clear types emerged. About 64.2 percent stayed low key, while 35.8 percent ran hot, with anxiety high before surgery and pain peaking during it and six hours after. A dental anxiety score, a more complex operation, and coming alone each raised the odds of the hot type. Smoking, by surprise, lowered those odds. The authors back early screening on these three flags so staff can add support where it counts most.
pmc-13455221:
Demeester and team studied how the KickAsh! smoking prevention program played out in eight Flemish youth social work groups. Its effectiveness trial had found no real impact on smoking starting among at-risk adolescents. They held seven focus groups with 52 adolescents. They also interviewed eight youth workers delivering the intervention.

Seven themes organized the findings, from how participants perceived the program to the decisive importance of adaptability in materials and delivery. Youth workers' own smoking status, skills, and motivation visibly shaped how sessions landed with the teenagers in their charge. Organizational structure and context further bent implementation, which varied substantially from site to site in the cross-case comparison. The authors argue this strong context dependency likely explains the flat effectiveness results, while noting unmeasured gains such as raised awareness that the trial's endpoints missed entirely.
pmc-13455421:
Patricia Hewston and colleagues tested whether a dance program built for older adults could be delivered by video call into people's homes. Their 2026 trial, called GERAS DANCE, was designed with geriatric and rehabilitation specialists for adults aged 60 and older who wanted better brain health or mobility. The question was practical: would home delivery prove feasible, acceptable, and safe enough to justify a larger trial?

Fifty older adults were assigned by chance to the dance group or to usual care, with live one-hour classes held twice a week for six weeks. The retention rate reached 84 percent, and participants attended about 78 percent of classes on average. Ninety percent rated the program good to excellent, 93 percent found the challenge level right, and no program-related injuries or harms were reported.
pmc-13455621:
Basabi Bagchi and co-authors investigate why the strength of cytoplasmic incompatibility, a reproductive manipulation by Wolbachia bacteria, changes with temperature. Infected males effectively sterilise matings with uninfected females, a trick now used to suppress disease-carrying mosquitoes. Their 2026 study measures eight Wolbachia strains in fruit flies across four temperatures.

Four of the eight strains showed temperature-sensitive incompatibility. The team measured development time, bacterial and virus densities, and activity of cifB, the gene that induces incompatibility. In two of the three strains active at several temperatures, cifB activity was higher at the temperature giving stronger incompatibility, while bacterial density in the testes did not predict strength. Transcript levels also stayed independent of bacterial and virus counts. The authors conclude temperature shapes the symbiosis at several levels, and cifB transcription explains only part of the variation.
pmc-13456921:
Márcio Flávio Moura de Araújo and nine colleagues ran, in a 2026 pilot trial, a test of green coffee capsules boosted with magnesium in women with type 2 diabetes. Forty-eight women were split evenly between the real capsules and a placebo for twelve weeks, with neither side knowing which. Feasibility, meaning whether women would stay in and take the capsules, was the main question.

About 83 percent finished the study, and capsule taking ran above 82 percent, so the protocol proved workable. Blood sugar measures wobbled in both groups without a consistent edge for the real capsules. Triglycerides and a sugar-fat index drifted down numerically in the treated group, while uric acid rose and fell in both. The authors stress that a pilot of this size cannot settle benefit. Its value is proving the design, so a larger trial can test the early hints properly.
pmc-13457121:
Qi Gan, Kaide Xia, and Xiuju Yang chart, in a 2026 national study, cancer deaths in the United States where the death certificate also recorded severe protein-energy malnutrition. Malnutrition worsens cancer care yet often goes unnoted. Using the federal multiple-cause database, the team counted such deaths from 1999 to 2024 for everyone aged fifteen and over.

Annual counts climbed from about five thousand to over eighteen thousand. The age-adjusted rate more than doubled, reaching about 5.3 deaths per hundred thousand people. Malnutrition's share of all cancer deaths rose from under one percent to nearly three. The trend bent at joinpoints in 2006 and 2013, falling first, then flattening, then climbing steeply. Rates in 2024 ran highest in men, in Black Americans, and in those over sixty-five. Digestive cancers carried the largest burden. The authors cannot tell better recording from true growth, and they say the gap itself deserves attention.
pmc-13457621: Coexisting PTEN and SDHB mutations — in a pediatric patient with PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome, in a case report. Yaqin Zhang, Sooyeon Lee, Justin P. Annes, and others report the case. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is a genetic case. It doubles mutations in one child.
pmc-13458621: Endometriomas sclerosed with ethanol — improving in vitro fertilization pregnancy results, in a chance-picked medical trial. Leila Shahsavari, Vajihe Hazari, Ashraf Aleyasin, and others run the trial. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is reproductive care. It shrinks endometriomas to boost IVF success.
pmc-13458821:
Ralph J Mobbs wrote this 2026 editorial marking ten years of the Journal of Spine Surgery and the award of its first journal impact factor. The journal reached a 2025 CiteScore of 2.6 and an impact factor of 2.3, figures the editor treats as milestones rather than the point of publishing. Mobbs uses the moment to ask what a journal should give its field, and looks back at the articles that shaped the decade.

He singles out three most-cited papers. They include a 2015 review comparing lumbar fusion techniques from the inaugural issue, a review of trends in spinal fusion use, and a synthesis of complications in front-of-neck spine surgery. Each, he argues, gives surgeons help with decisions. He also recalls the journal's 2020 series on endoscopic spine surgery, published when many surgeons saw endoscopy as a niche tool. The editorial closes by looking toward the journal's next phase of growth.
pmc-13458921:
Haochang Hu and Xianbao Liu wrote a 2026 commentary comparing balloon-expandable and self-expanding valves in women with small aortic annuli during transcatheter aortic valve replacement. A small annulus, often defined below 430 square millimeters, occurs most often in women. It raises concern about a prosthesis that fits the patient poorly and about pressure gradients staying high.

The writers weigh randomized evidence favoring self-expanding valves on blood-flow measures against seven-year registry results in 1,827 women from Japan's OCEAN-TAVI registry. After matching, balloon-expandable valves left smaller openings yet were linked with lower death and stroke rates, while heart failure admissions matched. Because the registry was observational, the commentary urges cautious reading and longer follow-up.
pmc-13459121:
Zhiliang Li and colleagues review in 2026 how tertiary lymphoid structures, immune clusters that form inside tumors, affect drug resistance in colorectal cancer. Unlike normal lymph organs, these structures arise within the tumor's surroundings and can prime immune cells on the spot. The review covers their cell makeup, stages of maturity, uneven placement in primary and spread tumors, and links with patient outcomes.

Signals that build these structures include chemokines, tumor necrosis factor family members, and interactions with gut microbes. Early experimental strategies try to grow them deliberately, using immune-stimulating drugs, nano-sized vaccines, or focused radiation schedules. The aim is to turn quiet tumors responsive and rescue treatments that resistance had blunted. Clinical proof, the authors note, is still developing.
pmc-13459321:
Ping Xie and co-authors report the first human trial of an iron loaded carbon nanoparticle injection designed to revive drug sensitivity in resistant solid tumors. The particles, injected directly into tumors, flood cancer cells with iron to trigger ferroptosis, a rust like form of cell death that resistant cells usually evade. Their 2026 cohort analysis covers nineteen heavily pretreated patients in a phase I trial. It tracks safety, imaging changes, tumor growth rates, and survival after treatment.

The injections proved acceptably safe and consistently hollowed out tumors from the center, producing marked internal necrosis on scans even when overall shrinkage looked minimal by standard criteria. Four patients, about a fifth of the cohort, with ovarian, pancreatic, vulvar, and thyroid cancers survived roughly twenty nine to thirty six months afterward. Strikingly, those four regained responses to chemotherapy or targeted drugs that had previously stopped working for them.
pmc-13460021:
Yang Yang and co-authors explored why older Chinese adults living in the United Kingdom exercise less than guidelines advise, interviewing them about what blocks and what enables activity. Their 2026 study ran sixteen interviews with twenty seven self identified Chinese residents over sixty, recruited by convenience sampling. Transcripts were mapped against the COM-B framework, which sorts influences into ability, chances, and drive. Participants ranged from fully active to inactive by World Health Organization standards.

Barriers clustered on every side of the framework. Poor health, pain, and low energy limited ability, alongside weak knowledge of activity guidelines and low confidence in how to work out safely. Social chances were thin: many lacked workout partners or community support for activity. Drive suffered when workouts felt culturally unfamiliar or pointless against chronic conditions. Facilitators mirrored the barriers, pointing to group based, culturally familiar activities with social support as the most promising design.
pmc-13461321:
Kartali and colleagues presented in 2026 Cardio-FL, a smartphone system for spotting heart rhythm faults outside clinics while keeping heart data private. Wearable ECG sensors and phone cameras can track rhythm at home, but a usable system must handle messy real-world signals, guard sensitive data, adapt to each user, and limit false alarms. Their prototype streams ECG from a chest wearable to an Android app for on-device analysis.

Kartali's model is tiny, with only about five and a half thousand parameters, and sorts beats into normal, early upper-chamber, and early lower-chamber types. The phone's camera adds a pulse check after alerts. Learning adapts on the device itself using unlabelled beats, and updates are shared in a federated way, meaning data stay on phones while model gains are pooled. Activity sensing gates when recording and training run, to save power and cut noise.
pmc-13461421:
Qiming Zhao and colleagues tested whether a combined inflammation-metabolic index predicts new heart disease in rectal cancer survivors. The index, CTI, merges C-reactive protein, triglycerides, and glucose into one score of body-wide inflammatory and metabolic strain.

The main cohort held 1,160 survivors from a Chinese hospital, with 1,752 UK Biobank survivors as an outside check. Each standard-step rise in CTI came with 18 percent higher odds of new heart disease after full adjustment. Risk climbed in a near-straight line and concentrated in the top quarter of scores, above all in younger, non-hypertensive survivors. In the UK cohort the link faded to nothing after adjustment, Zhao notes, so the index fits high-burden clinic settings best.
pmc-13461521:
Sidneva, Lobanova, and Vysotskaya presented in 2026 a way to design story-based tasks that show whether preschool children truly use counting, not just recite it. Many young children can count formally yet never use counting as a tool inside other activities. The team set five design principles for narrative tasks and built a battery that sorts counting mastery into formal, reasonable, and functional levels.

Sidneva piloted the battery on 56 older preschoolers, about 69 months old on average. Scores fell in a clear staircase from the formal level to the reasonable and then the functional level. Formal and reasonable scores tracked executive skills such as working memory and self-control, as expected. Functional scores did not, which hints that using counting inside a story task leans on different mechanisms. The authors say purpose-built stories are needed to test real use, though more validation is required.
pmc-13461621:
Huang and co-authors pooled a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing ultrasound with plain X-ray for spotting signs of necrotizing enterocolitis in newborns. That disease inflames and can kill sections of a baby's intestine, so early imaging signs matter greatly. Six databases were searched for studies comparing the two scans head to head.

Twenty studies covering 1,793 newborns with confirmed or suspected disease entered the pooled analysis Huang led. Ultrasound found gas in the portal vein, a danger sign, more than twice as often in odds terms as X-ray did. Ultrasound also trended ahead on gas within the bowel wall, while X-ray trended ahead on free air and bowel widening without reaching significance. The authors suggest combining both scans for earlier recognition and tracking of the disease.
pmc-13461821:
Zhang, Zhang, and Liu reported a 2026 case report of a newborn boy with cblC-type methylmalonic acidemia combined with high homocysteine, an inherited fault in handling vitamin B12. The disease blocks normal processing of certain amino acids and fats. From birth the baby fed poorly, responded weakly, and had floppy muscles and muted reflexes.

Blood screening showed raised homocysteine and a pattern of carnitine markers pointing to the disorder, and urine carried extra methylmalonic acid. Brain imaging lit up in two deep structures called the globus pallidus on both sides. Genetic testing found two faulty copies of the MMACHC gene, one from each parent, confirming the diagnosis. The authors urge metabolic screening for any newborn with unexplained feeding trouble and abnormal tone.
pmc-13462121:
Man Gao leads a 2026 study of a mitochondrial protein, METTL17, in stomach cancer, formally gastric cancer. Stomach cancer is widespread and carries a poor outlook. METTL17 belongs to a family of proteins that tag other molecules. It had been shown to drive colorectal and mouth cancers. Its role here was unexplored. The team measured it in tissue and cells, then raised and lowered its levels in tests.

It ran high in stomach tumors, and high levels went with worse patient outlook. Lowering METTL17 slowed cell growth, movement, and invasion, and weakened tumor formation in mice. Raising it did the opposite. Protein surveys showed how it works: METTL17 holds down a protein, GSK-3beta, which restrains a growth pathway, Wnt/beta-catenin. With the brake weakened, the pathway switches on and fuels the cancer. The authors present METTL17 as a drug target for stomach cancer, pending checks.
pmc-13462221:
Shalini Gakhar and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how generative AI could turn farm science into advice fitted to each rice farm in India. Agriculture produces oceans of data, yet farmers rarely get guidance shaped to their plot. Old expert systems gave stiff, general answers. Newer language models can reason and handle images, and rice-specific versions trained on science texts make fewer errors.

The strongest designs pair a language model with a knowledge graph, a structured web of facts that grounds answers, and with crop growth simulators. Satellite, drone, and phone images with vision models could give near-instant diagnosis for small farms. The authors are clear about the conditions. Connectivity gaps must close, farmers' data rights must be protected, and a human adviser must stay in the loop. Only then can such tools make precision farming fairer rather than a privilege of large farms.
pmc-13462321:
Ame Stephanie Ayemere and Jeanny B Aragon-Ching discuss, in a 2026 commentary, estradiol skin patches as an alternative way to lower testosterone in advanced prostate cancer. Standard hormone treatment uses injections crushing both testosterone and estrogen, bringing bone loss, fractures, hot flashes, and muscle wasting. An older oral estrogen worked, yet raised clot risks by passing through the liver. Patches bypass the liver, keeping estrogen's benefits without that risk.

The commentary covers a randomized trial in 1,360 men treated between 2007 and 2022, which compared patches against injections. The question was whether patches controlled cancer as well, measured by time free of spread or death. Cancer control proved no worse with patches. Side effects differed: fewer problems tied to estrogen loss, yet more breast growth in men and more patch-related skin trouble. The authors present patches as an option whose trade-offs suit some patients better than others.
pmc-13462921:
Suhail Sayed and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a scoring chart to predict dangerously low blood calcium after parathyroid surgery in patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism. The condition, where overactive parathyroid glands follow severe kidney disease, is treated by removing all four glands and reimplanting a fragment. Severe calcium drops strike a quarter to a half of patients, driven by hormone loss and hungry bones soaking up minerals.

The study gathered 227 patients treated at two centers between 2019 and 2024, all on intensive calcium plans after surgery. Just under half developed severe low calcium by the study's definition. A screening method picked four predictors from data available before surgery, including age and two blood measures taken a month ahead, phosphate and an enzyme, alkaline phosphatase. Repeated internal resampling corrected the model's optimism. The authors offer the chart for risk planning around surgery, while noting it needs validation at other centers.
pmc-13463321:
Zufiria-Gerbolés and colleagues mapped in 2026 the wiring of the locus coeruleus, a tiny brain stem hub. The hub sprays a wake chemical through the brain, and stacks Alzheimer's tau first. Two scan banks fed the work. The team traced the hub's white tract links and weighed them by age and ill.

The tracts sort in a top to base plan no one had shown in man. Some link shifts come with plain age, some with the ill alone. Link shifts tracked gene maps, mind scores, and tau in a memory zone. The team built a gap mark for stray links. In sound folk at high risk, a wide gap went with slow tau growth.
pmc-13463521:
Park and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a handheld six-lead heart tracing device can stand in for the standard twelve-lead electrocardiogram. Their patients all had rhythm disorders. In a single hospital, both tracings were recorded at the same time. Patients were tested lying down and sitting up. A heart rhythm specialist, blinded to the source, then read each pair.

The team analyzed 229 usable paired recordings. The handheld device matched the standard machine's rhythm diagnosis in about 99 of every 100 cases. That held in both postures. Each time, it missed one case of atrial flutter by calling it atrial fibrillation. Measured intervals differed only slightly, with most gaps under 20 thousandths of a second. Heart rates were nearly identical. Agreement slipped to about 97 in 100 when postures were mismatched between devices. Timing and posture, the authors conclude, clearly matter.
pmc-13464321:
Li and co-authors asked in 2026 whether the retina can forecast depression. The retina is the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye. It grows from the same tissue as the brain and can be photographed noninvasively. UK Biobank scans from 36,220 adults aged 40 to 70 supplied the data. Six retinal layers were measured. New diagnoses of depression and anxiety were tracked over a median follow-up beyond twelve years.

During that time, 1,340 participants developed depression and 1,373 developed anxiety. Each standard-step thickening of the ganglion cell layer came with about eight percent lower depression risk. That layer carries visual signals toward the brain. Greater overall macular thickness came with about nine percent lower risk, even after full adjustment. The protection looked stronger in women. No retinal measure predicted anxiety once other factors were counted. Eye scans might one day help flag people deserving closer mental-health watching.
pmc-13465721:
Sunggyun Park, Kyoungbo Kim, and Jung-Sook Ha compare two lab methods for measuring how much of a blood sample carries the JAK2 V617F mutation, in a 2026 study. That measurement guides care in a group of blood cancers that lack the Philadelphia chromosome change. Both methods ran on leftover DNA from 76 mutation-positive patient samples. Detection limits sat close together, slightly favoring the digital test, which also varied less between repeats, above all at low mutation levels where precision matters most. Straight-line accuracy was strong for both. The authors also checked how mutation levels related to routine blood counts and diagnosis groups.
pmc-13466421:
Tianqi Cao, Hongyu Cui, Junyi Liu, and Chuanhui Zhang dope a cobalt oxide catalyst with rare earth elements to speed oxygen reactions in rechargeable zinc-air batteries, in a 2026 study. Both oxygen uptake and oxygen release at the air electrode run sluggishly, which holds the battery type back. A citric acid gel method produced equal-share doping with four different lanthanides for comparison.

The samarium version won, showing the smallest voltage gap between the two reactions and a clean four-electron pathway. Doping warped the crystal lattice, opened oxygen vacancies, and shifted the balance between cobalt charge states. The authors tie those structural facts to performance, building a structure-activity map for later catalyst design.
pmc-13466721:
Muhammed Dogukan Aksu and co-authors chart the genomic landscape of colorectal cancers carrying mutations in ERBB2, the gene for the HER2 growth receptor. Their 2026 analysis compares these mutated tumours with cancers where the gene is instead amplified, meaning copied many times.

Drawing on the cBioPortal database, the team analysed 4,348 patients and found driver mutations in 95 and amplifications in 87. Mutated tumours were enriched for KRAS alterations and for microsatellite instability, a marker of faulty DNA repair, and tended to sit on the right side of the colon with high mutation counts. Amplified tumours favoured the left side, avoided KRAS mutations, and often carried TP53 alterations. Clustering confirmed the two groups are distinct, which the authors say supports different treatment strategies for each.
pmc-13467521:
Mehtap Ertekin and Salih Gozmen compare in 2026 the sleep of children treated for leukemia or lymphoma with that of similar children seen for harmless blood conditions. Sleep problems are now recognized as part of good supportive cancer care, yet their pattern in this group is poorly described. The study enrolled 54 young patients and 56 comparison children of similar age and sex, using a standard parent questionnaire on children sleep habits.

Patients scored worse overall on sleep disturbance, averaging 53.56 points against 49.07 for the comparison group. The clearest gaps appeared in sleep anxiety and parasomnias, unusual behaviors during sleep, while sleep duration barely differed. Within the patient group, the authors modeled recent hospital stays and steroid treatment, both common in cancer care, as possible drivers. The results argue for routine sleep screening during treatment.
pmc-13467821:
Huang and colleagues quantify how frailty drives hospital costs and stay length for older patients having colorectal cancer surgery, in a 2026 multicenter study. Frailty means reduced physical reserve from aging. The team analyzed 4,936 patients aged 60 or older who had elective surgery between 2014 and 2024. They then decomposed the frailty effect to see how much ran through other illnesses the patients had, and how much through complications arising after the operation.

Frail patients faced higher odds of expensive admissions, with an odds ratio of 1.274 in the adjusted model. Their odds of adverse events were far higher still, at an odds ratio of 3.317 against non-frail patients in the same analysis. Stays also ran longer for frail patients. Existing comorbidity burden explained 28.6 percent of the frailty-linked cost difference, the decomposition showed. Postoperative complications explained only 3.8 percent of the stay difference and not significantly. Huang urges frailty screening before elective cancer surgery.
pmc-13468021:
Nuria Aide López Hernández and colleagues compare in 2026 two remote sensing routes for scheduling irrigation in forage maize: satellite images and drone flights. Both feed a vegetation index that tracks crop greenness, which the team converted into crop water-use coefficients during the 2023 season and then tested in real fields in 2024. Two maize hybrids were grown under farmer practice, satellite-guided watering, and drone-guided watering.

The drone model fit the water-use data more tightly, with an R-squared of 0.9414 against 0.8278 for the satellite. pmc-13468121:
Danila Maltsev and colleagues make silk fibroin gels in 2026 that change color when squeezed, pointing toward soft mechanical sensors. Higher starting protein levels gave stiffer gels that stayed stable in water, with a uniform network of physical crosslinks.

The resulting blue gel blushed red under compression. A biodegradable, silk-based material that visibly reports force could serve in wearables, wound dressings, or soft robotics.
pmc-13468321:
Muhammad Tayyab Noman and co-authors examine in 2026 the fiber-matrix interface in polymer composites, the thin boundary where load passes from resin into reinforcing fibers and where performance is often decided. Many surface treatments improve the interface on paper, yet those gains do not reliably become stronger finished parts. The review connects surface chemistry, interphase structure, nano-scale modification, and processing conditions into one account of load transfer and damage growth.

Reported gains are checked against real structural results, exposing limits from poor particle dispersion, resin flow behavior, processing defects, and scale-up trouble. The authors propose a multiscale framework to carry interface design from chemistry to factory floor, a bridge the field has lacked.
pmc-13468521:
Xiaobing Hu and co-authors review in 2026 the circadian clock of cyanobacteria, the simplest organisms known to keep true daily time. The cyanobacterial system matters beyond microbiology: it proved a clock can be pure protein chemistry, and it remains the test bed for understanding how all circadian clocks stay robust yet adjustable. The authors also look ahead to engineering timing into industrial microbes.
pmc-13468721:
Wei Gao and colleagues build in 2026 a shore-based instrument that watches river carbon almost continuously, filling a gap between sparse satellite passes and finicky underwater sensors. Their ground hyperspectral system photographs the water surface with three miniature spectrometers. It measures the light coming off the water, the sky, and the incoming sunlight, deriving the water reflectance every ten seconds at best.

The unit runs on solar power, reports over a 4G link, and covers wavelengths from 400 to 900 nanometers at one-nanometer resolution, allowing long solo deployments. Models for dissolved and particulate organic carbon were built and checked against 90 paired water samples taken in place. Rivers carry a major, poorly counted share of the global carbon budget, and a cheap always-on watcher at a riverbank could tighten those numbers.
pmc-13469021:
Dotan and colleagues build a fishing platform for antibodies against targets hidden inside tumour cells. In a mouse breast cancer model engineered to make a glowing intracellular protein, tumour growth triggered a class-switched B-cell response against that hidden antigen. The selected hybridomas kept both surface receptors and secreted antibodies, enabling efficient selection. The resulting monoclonal antibodies recognised native intracellular targets that conventional screens missed. Given system-wide, one antibody slowed growth of early established tumours. The team also demonstrated the approach with human B cells from tonsils and blood, supporting translational use.
pmc-13470521:
Sato and colleagues in Japan told in 2026 of six hip swaps redone with a graft trick that packs crushed donor bone round a fresh stem. The classic form of the trick glues the stem with cement. Patients bore full weight from the first day.

Stems sank a hair, just over a millimeter, well shy of worry marks. Scans showed new bone growth in all six, and one deep scan showed bone fused to the stem.
pmc-13470721: changed starch coaxes more oil from stubborn carbonate reservoirs. Lorraine de Araujo, Luciana Sodre, Danielle Franco, and others test flooding good use in the lab. The 2026 Europe PMC paper tests healing and composition changes. It optimizes removal methods practically. Energy production benefits a lot. Innovation unlocks resources. good use matters.
pmc-13471421:
Trabelsi-Mescheloff and co-authors present a faster version of a peptide docking program. pmc-13471521:
Huang and Lin built a bedside risk model to flag severe psittacosis, the pneumonia caught from birds, using two ordinary blood tests. Lung scans followed a set rhythm, peaking in severity at two weeks with a median total CT score of 7 before gradually clearing. With only 36 patients, the authors frame the model as hypothesis-generating and warn against clinical use until larger prospective studies confirm it.
pmc-13473721:
Ciancio and colleagues in the United States read in 2026 the charts of 107 child kidney swaps done at their hub since 2014. All had no stent left in the new urine pipe. Snags were rare: four children in all had one, a rate under four in a hundred. Just three needed a fresh operation to fix theirs. Two snags were blocks high in the pipe, and one was a low block from stones. No child leaked urine at all in the first year, the snag stents are most meant to stop. The authors call the stent free way safe for child swaps.
pmc-13475521:
Julia Hawthorne and co-authors review calcium use in 2026 during resuscitation for heart arrest inside hospitals. Calcium was long given for its hoped heart-boosting effect, despite thin proof. pmc-13476621:
Yi Chen and co-authors show in 2026 that a tag system for proteins is required to build kidneys before birth. pmc-13478521:
Alwabli presents a task offloading strategy in 2026 for the Internet of Vehicles, where connected cars generate computing jobs too heavy to run on board. Against nine rival methods, from simple rules to rival learning systems, the strategy posted low average delay and low energy use in the simulations run. It also achieved a high task success rate and settled into stable behavior faster than the competing approaches tested alongside it. Tuning the balance between delay and energy shifted the system between safety-style services, which prize speed, and tolerant services that prize saving power, which the author frames as sustainability.
pmc-13479221:
Jeremy Howick and colleagues present a 2026 proposal for a model of empathic leadership aimed at crises in modern management. Business writing celebrates empathic leadership, yet two gaps persist. The authors argue this sequence can guide leaders facing staff burnout, conflict, and rapid change. A defined model also lets organizations train the skill deliberately instead of treating it as a personality trait. The paper offers the model as both an explanation of good crisis leadership and a teaching foundation.
pmc-13479621:
Tina Nanyangwe-Moyo, Laura J. Rosa Pereira, and Mathieu Jean-Patrick Poirier published a 2025 evaluation of how well tobacco control research handles gender. Forty of the forty-three studies did identify specific target groups and their challenges, a stronger showing than the authors' framing might suggest. pmc-13480921:
Ren and colleagues set side by side in 2026 three decades of ischemic stroke data for China and the United States. Rates of living with past stroke rose in both. Raw case loads will still swell by 2035 in both lands, as crowds age. The authors urge more stroke proofing and care funds.
pmc-13482621:
Barre and Mohamud survey Mogadishu households in 2026 on what would make them pay for renewable energy, modeling the decision with the theory of planned behavior.
