His ideas seeded two movements: New Thought took them up gladly, and Christian Science grew from soil he tilled. Dresser published the manuscripts to fix Quimby's place as the source. Readers meet here the rough, earnest notes of a pioneer whose influence ran far beyond his lifetime.
russell-analysis-mind-1921:
Bertrand Russell published The Analysis of Mind in 1921, a set of lectures on psychology and philosophy. Russell defends neutral monism, the view that mind and matter share one basic stuff. Sensations and images, arranged in different ways, make both minds and physical things. He draws on the behaviorism of Watson and the work of William James.

Chapters treat desire, memory, belief, and consciousness itself. Russell doubts that consciousness is a special inner light. The book became a landmark of early philosophy of mind. Its plain style suits general readers. Later philosophy of psychology still starts debates from its positions.
rutherford-harp-of-god-1921:
Joseph Franklin Rutherford, the Judge who led the Bible Students after Russell's death, published The Harp of God in 1921. The book offers proof of a Creator and of his plan for mankind in catechism form. It became the Jehovah's Witnesses' first great textbook.

Questions and answers walk the student through creation, the fall, the ransom, and the coming kingdom on earth. Rutherford plays the Bible as a harp of ten strings, each string a doctrine sounding in harmony with the rest. Millions of copies went out as the movement's chief tool for teaching new believers.
sapir-language-1921:
Edward Sapir was a scholar of speech who studied the Native languages of North America and taught at Ottawa and Chicago. His 1921 book Language is a plain introduction to how speech works and changes. Sapir had already spent years writing down grammars of tongues few outsiders had studied. It remains one of the most loved books in its field.

Sapir covers sound patterns, grammar, word building, and the slow drift of languages over time. He shows how speech shapes thought without trapping it, an idea later linked to his name and Benjamin Whorf's. Students still read him for his clear style and his feel for language as art.
sawyer-wonderfull-discoverie-edmonton-16:
Elizabeth Sawyer kept a poor home at Edmonton, north of London. The Wonderfull Discoverie of Elizabeth Sawyer, printed in 1621, tells how she came to be hanged as a witch. Her case grew out of quarrels, a curse, and a neighbor's death.

The pamphlet mixes her confession with stern moral warnings, as Stuart crime print often did. It asks readers to see God's hand and the Devil's snares in a poor woman's fall. Within the year, her story reached the stage as The Witch of Edmonton. That play kept her name alive long after the gallows.
say-letters-to-malthus-1821:
Jean-Baptiste Say wrote his Letters to Malthus on the great question of gluts, and John Richter's English translation appeared in 1821. The two economists were friends who disagreed in public. Malthus feared that a whole economy could produce more than it could sell, leaving workers idle; Say denied the possibility.

Say argues that production itself creates the income with which goods are bought, so a general glut cannot last. Particular goods can overflow a market, he grants, but the cure is more production of what is wanted, not less of everything. Malthus answered in kind, and the friendly fight shaped the classical creed for decades. The letters are courteous, clear, and sharp at once. Economists still argue the ground these two friends staked out in 1821.
say-treatise-prinsep-1821:
Jean-Baptiste Say was a French writer on trade whose Treatise on Political Economy first appeared in 1803. This English version, translated by Prinsep, was published in 1821 and carried his ideas across the Atlantic. Say wrote in the line of Adam Smith but with his own sharp twists.

The book is famous for Say's Law, the claim that making goods itself creates the means to buy them, so supply creates its own demand. Say also gives the entrepreneur, the risk-taking organizer of production, a central place in economic life. For decades his treatise served as the continent's leading guide to the subject.
shahnama-warner-vol-8-1921:
Volume 8 of the Warner Shahnama appeared in 1921, the eighth of nine volumes. Arthur and Edmond Warner had begun their English Book of Kings in 1905. Firdausi's Persian epic, which they translated, ends with the fall of the Sasanian Empire to Arab armies.

This volume brings the story near that end, through the last shahs and the invasions that broke their power. Persian tradition tells these events with grief and pride, honoring rulers who lost an empire. The translation keeps the poem's couplets in English verse where it can. Readers approaching the final volume can feel the weight of a thousand years of kings passing into memory.
shankara-vivekachudamani-madhavananda-19:
Shankara, the eighth-century teacher of Advaita Vedanta, wrote the Vivekachudamani, the Crest-Jewel of Discrimination, as a manual for seekers. Swami Madhavananda's 1921 translation comes from the Advaita Ashrama, the order's publishing house. The poem is the beloved handbook of its school.

In verse dialogue, Shankara teaches the student to split the real from the unreal until the self stands clear as pure awareness. Body, mind, and world are coverings; Brahman alone, he argues, is finally true. Generations of Hindu students have learned their first Vedanta from these verses, often by heart. The translation keeps the verses' direct, questioning music as far as English allows.
shelley-adonais-1821:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Adonais in 1821 after learning that John Keats had died in Rome at twenty-five. Shelley blamed harsh reviewers for hastening Keats's death, fairly or not. The poem appeared in Pisa that same year, in the form of a classical pastoral elegy.

Shelley mourns Adonais, his name for Keats, through shepherds, dreams, and the figures of other poets. Grief slowly turns to triumph as he argues that the dead poet's spirit joins nature and outlives his enemies. The famous lines call life a dome of many-colored glass that stains eternity. Adonais is often ranked as Shelley's greatest short poem and one of the finest elegies in English.
spr-proceedings-vol31-1921:
Parts seventy nine through eighty one and an appendix make volume thirty one, dated 1921. The SPR is now a veteran body, near forty years from its founding. Its journal keeps the founding mix of experiment, case, and criticism. Trance mediumship still supplies the longest reports.

New sittings test fresh mediums under the old safeguards. Telepathy work continues, scored with the care of long practice. Spontaneous cases arrive from a public schooled by war to ask such questions. Volume thirty one sustains the primary archive into the 1920s. Its pages show a field both older and no nearer settlement. The open file remains the society's gift.
the-return-of-sherlock-holmes-pg221: This edition of Doyle's Return gathers Holmes' resurrection cases. The detective lives. The Tower library holds the full text. It returned a sleuth. Death cheated. Cases solved. Fans cheered. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
tischner-telepathie-hellsehen-1921:
Rudolf Tischner gave his land its first full study in Ueber Telepathie und Hellsehen, out in German in 1921. The name means on thought leaps and far sight. Tischner was a healer in Munich. He ran his own tests with cards, draws, and hid marks, then weighed the hits gainst the odds that mere chance could give the same sums.

His prose is strict, calm, and free of cult zeal. The book founds the field's line in the German tongue. Fans there cite it as their charter. Its care set a bar for all who came next.
tob-0021:
Thecla, a young woman of Iconium, hears Paul preach and leaves her fiance and family to follow the apostle. The Acts of Paul and Thecla tells her story, and early Christians cherished it for centuries. This entry draws on a verified pre-1930 public-domain edition.

Condemned to beasts and fire, Thecla escapes again and again, and in the arena she baptizes herself in a tank of water. Some church fathers condemned the tale; many believers read it as a call to courage. Thecla became a famous saint, with shrines across the Christian East. Her story remains early Christianity's boldest tale of a woman apostle.
tob-0121:
Ignatius Donnelly was a lawmaker and writer from Minnesota. His 1882 bestseller Atlantis: The Antediluvian World said the lost isle was real. It sank in one great flood, he held, and its heirs seeded all the peoples of the earth. Each flood tale in the world, for him, told of that one drowning.

He piles up rocks, myths, like words, and old authors in a bold, sure case. Scholars scoffed, but the crowds bought the book. It built the whole modern craze for Atlantis on its own. As false history it is a wild, fun read, and its mark lies on a century of lost land tales.
tob-10221:
William James delivered the lectures that became The Varieties of Religious Experience in 1902. A psychologist and philosopher, James studied religion as lived experience rather than doctrine. He drew on hundreds of firsthand accounts, letters, diaries, and autobiographies from people of many backgrounds.

Chapters sort conversion, mysticism, saintliness, and prayer, asking what these states do for the people who have them. James takes extreme cases seriously without mocking or simply believing them. The result helped found the psychology of religion. Readers still use his test: judge religious experience by its fruits in a life, not only by its claims.
tob-10521:
Three Initiates, a pen name most now link to the New Thought writer William Walker Atkinson, put out The Kybalion in 1908. The short book claims to teach the old Hermetic lore of Egypt and Greece. It sums that lore up in seven rules said to govern all things.

The rules are mind, matching, shaking, the pull of opposites, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender. As above, so below is the key line. Was the lore truly old, or new work in old dress? That fight still goes on. True or not, the book has shaped a whole age of occult thought.
tob-4021:
Books Three and Four of Locke's Essay, gathered in volume two, turn from the origin of ideas to language and to knowledge itself. Book Three asks how words hook onto ideas, and how badly they can mislead when they do not. Book Four asks what we can truly claim to know, and with what certainty.

Locke's famous distinction between primary qualities, like solidity, and secondary qualities, like color, stands here, along with his degrees of knowledge and his defense of probability where proof runs out. The volume completes empiricism's founding document. Paired with volume one, it shows a philosophy trying to be honest about the limits of the human mind.
un-ga-res-21: Judges of the International Court of Justice had been picked, and Resolution 21 of the General Assembly, passed on 10 February 1946, hurries the court into life. The Secretary-General must call its first meeting at The Hague as soon as it can be arranged. The Carnegie Foundation, which owns the Peace Palace there, had agreed to talks on the terms for the court's use of the building. A secretary and stopgap staff would help the court until it named its own registrar.
un-ga-res-a-69-21:
Staff work for the Palestinian cause is renewed in Resolution A/69/21, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Assembly had read the yearly report of its Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People. That committee has tracked the question since 1977, with the help of a small UN unit, the Division for Palestinian Rights.

The text notes with thanks the work of the Secretary-General under the last vote on the point. It holds that the division's staff support lets the committee carry out its task in full. That support, it says, keeps world eyes on the question of Palestine and on the urgent need for a just peace.
un-ga-res-es-10-21:
The General Assembly, not the Security Council, adopted Resolution ES-10/21 in October 2023. It came at the Assembly's tenth emergency special session. The war in Gaza had begun after the attack of 7 October 2023. The Assembly voiced grave concern at the worsening situation in the occupied Palestinian territory.

The resolution condemned all violence against Palestinian and Israeli civilians. It called for an immediate, durable, and sustained humanitarian truce, leading to a halt to the fighting. All parties were told to obey international humanitarian and human rights law. Civilians and civilian objects had to be protected. Aid, supplies, and basic services had to reach everyone in need in the Gaza Strip. The text also restated the duty to respect the Geneva Conventions in all circumstances. Because it is an Assembly text, its call carried political weight rather than binding orders.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The General Assembly adopted Resolution 21 on 10 February 1946, at the twenty-eighth plenary meeting. It arranged the first meeting of the International Court of Justice. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to call the Court together at The Hague as soon as its judges were elected. He was to name a temporary secretary and staff. He was to open talks with the Carnegie Foundation on the terms for the Court's use of rooms in the Peace Palace.

General Assembly resolution 69/21 (2014) concerns the Division for Palestinian Rights of the Secretariat, the office that supports the Assembly's Palestinian rights committee. The Assembly judges the Division's work useful and helpful and asks the Secretary-General to keep funding it. Its tasks include watching developments and holding international meetings. They include running the 'Question of Palestine' website and its information system, and publishing materials. They include training Palestinian government staff. They include holding the annual exhibit for the International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People on 29 November.

Resolution ES-10/21 was adopted by the General Assembly at its tenth emergency special session in October 2023. Its title is Protection of civilians and upholding legal and humanitarian obligations. It answered the sharp rise in violence from 7 October 2023 and the fast worsening crisis in the Gaza Strip and the rest of the occupied Palestinian territory.

The Assembly called for an immediate, durable, and lasting humanitarian truce leading to an end to the fighting. It demanded full respect for the laws of war. It demanded steady delivery of water, food, medicine, fuel, and power to civilians in Gaza. It also demanded access for aid agencies and the release of civilians held captive. It demanded no forced transfer of the Palestinian population.
un-sc-res-121: Japan applied to join the United Nations. Resolution 121 records the Council's answer. The Council adopted it on 12 December 1956. No member dissented. The meeting was the Council's 756th. The text is a single formal step. The Council states that it examined Japan's application. It recommends that the General Assembly admit Japan to membership.
un-sc-res-1321:
Sierra Leone's peace remained fragile in the autumn of 2000. On 20 September 2000 the Security Council extended its mission there, UNAMSIL. The new term ran until 31 December 2000. The Council also set a deadline for itself. It would review the situation again no later than 31 October. Earlier resolutions had built the mission up after rebels seized peacekeepers that spring.

The short extension kept United Nations troops in place through the year-end. It bought time to judge whether the ceasefire could hold. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. Sierra Leone's war, fought over government control and diamonds, still had more than a year to run.
un-sc-res-1421: Dated 2002 in the catalog, Resolution 1421 records formal action by the United Nations Security Council. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1521:
Liberia's civil war drives Resolution 1521, the Council's sanctions text for that country. Guns from the war had spread across West Africa, and thousands of people had died. Even with fighting over, the Council kept strict limits in place.

The measures target the trade that fed the war, above all Liberian timber and rough diamonds, along with arms sales and travel by listed figures. Panels of experts were to watch for cheating and report back. For readers, the text shows how the Council uses trade bans to keep a fragile peace from collapsing.
un-sc-res-1621:
MONUC gained election reinforcements on 6 September 2005. Congo's transition rested on the Global and All Inclusive Agreement signed at Pretoria in 2002. Elections were the base for lasting peace and the rule of law, the Council stressed. Transitional bodies had to hold free, fair, and peaceful polls and keep the electoral commission's timetable. Armed groups in the east still threatened the vote.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council approved the Secretary-General's recommendations and concept of operations for the elections. It authorized a temporary rise in MONUC's strength of 841 personnel, soldiers and police, to help secure the polls. The extra deployment would end by 1 July 2006 at the latest, and its short-term character was underlined. MONUC was encouraged, within its means, to give the electoral process its full support. The Council stayed actively seized. The boost covered the run-up to polling day.
un-sc-res-1721:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1721, adopted on 1 November 2006. Elections could not be held on time, and the transition period had expired the day before. The African Union had ruled on how the country should be run until a vote was possible. The crisis kept causing large-scale suffering and displacement.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backs the African Union plan in full. The president stays as head of state for one final transition of at most twelve months. The prime minister also stays, barred from running in the coming election. He gains full powers to deliver the road map, including command over the security forces. Elections must happen by 31 October 2007.
un-sc-res-1821:
The Golan Heights force closed out 2008 with a routine renewal. On 27 June 2008 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 31 December 2008. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission that month. The Council welcomed the force's work on staff conduct rules. UNDOF enforced the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse. Its members had to meet the United Nations code of conduct in full.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. A closing report was due at the term's end. It would cover events and steps taken toward 338. UNDOF's patrols kept the separation zone quiet. That calm had held, with rare breaks, since the force arrived in 1974.
un-sc-res-1921:
Nepal is the subject of Resolution 1921 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 12 May 2010. A ten-year civil war had ended there in 2006. The United Nations Mission in Nepal, called UNMIN, watched over arms and fighters after the war.

The text renews the mission's mandate until 15 September 2010, at the Nepali government's request. It notes worry that parties had not yet agreed on a new constitution. It calls on the government and the Maoists to set a clear plan for former fighters. The mission was told to prepare its withdrawal by the same date.
un-sc-res-21:
Trust rule over the Pacific islands once held by Japan was set in Security Council Resolution 21, passed on 2 April 1947. The Charter's trusteeship system could take in lands held under old League mandates. The islands north of the equator had been given to Japan by the League in 1920. Japan, beaten in the war, no longer held any sway in them.

The Council approves the terms of trust for the islands as a strategic area, a class of trust land watched by the Council itself, not by the Assembly. The United States would run the islands under those terms. The trust lasted till the islands chose their own paths, most as free states in the 1980s and 1990s. The catalog year of 1921 is wrong.
un-sc-res-221:
Oil tankers bound for Beira, with fuel for Rhodesia's illegal regime, drew a rare call to action at sea on 9 April 1966. One tanker had already arrived at Beira, in Portuguese Mozambique. Another was on its way. A pipeline ran from Beira to Southern Rhodesia. The Council had already ordered states to cut the regime off from oil. Resolution 221 answers those reports.

The Council decided that the situation was a threat to the peace. Portugal was told not to let oil be pumped through the pipeline to Rhodesia, nor to accept oil at Beira meant for Rhodesia. All states had to divert any of their own ships believed to be carrying such oil. Britain was called on to stop suspect tankers from reaching Beira, by force if needed. It could arrest and hold the tanker named in the text after unloading.
un-sc-res-321:
Portugal's attack on a Senegalese border post was condemned on 23 October 1972. Senegal's complaint told of regular Portuguese troops striking the post at Nianao on 12 October 1972. Earlier Council texts, from 178 (1963) to 302 (1971), had condemned Portuguese violence in Senegal again and again. Lisbon refused to comply with any of them. Incidents along the borders of Guinea-Bissau, Angola, and Mozambique kept growing.

The Council condemned the frontier violation and the attack on Nianao. It recalled resolution 294 (1971) on Portuguese acts of violence and destruction. Portugal was told to stop at once, and for good, every act of violence and destruction against Senegal. Lisbon also had to respect self-determination and independence for the peoples of its territories, as the 1960 declaration set out. The Council declared that if Portugal failed to comply, it would meet to weigh other steps.
un-sc-res-421:
South Africa's mandatory arms embargo gained its watchdog on 9 December 1977. Resolution 418 (1977), passed that November, had judged South Africa's arms build-up a threat to the peace. It banned arms sales to Pretoria under Chapter VII. The Council now judged that the ban needed machinery to check its progress. The Secretary-General already owed a report on the embargo's working.

The Council set up a committee of all its members under rule 28 of its rules. The committee would examine the Secretary-General's report on the embargo. It would study ways to make the mandatory ban bite harder and advise the Council. It would seek from every state fresh word on the steps taken to apply resolution 418. All states were called to cooperate with the committee in full and supply the facts it sought. The Secretary-General had to give the committee every help it needed.
un-sc-res-721:
Fighting in Yugoslavia deepened in the autumn of 1991. The parties had signed a ceasefire deal in Geneva on 23 November. The Secretary-General's personal envoy had carried that agreement to the Council. On 27 November 1991 the Council backed his warning to the parties. A peacekeeping operation, he had said, could not be deployed without full respect for the Geneva deal.

The Council also restated its arms embargo from resolution 713. It deplored the heavy loss of life and wide damage in the fighting. Neighboring states felt the effects as well. The Council stayed seized of the matter until a peaceful solution came. The envoy's warning framed the mission that followed months later.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 121 was adopted unanimously on 12 December 1956. It recommends to the General Assembly that Japan be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The Council had examined Japan's application. Its file before the Council included documents from 1952 and from the autumn of 1956. Acting on a membership application is one of the few steps the Charter reserves to the Council and the Assembly together. No state can join the United Nations without a Council recommendation first.

Sierra Leone's battered UN mission gained a short lifeline in 2000. On 20 September, the Council adopted Resolution 1321. The force, UNAMSIL, had been built in 1999 to back a peace deal. That spring, rebels had seized hundreds of its peacekeepers as hostages. Fresh troops and reviews had followed in August and early September.

Three short lines do the work here. The mandate runs to 31 December 2000. The Council will review the state of play by the end of October. It stays seized of the matter in the meantime. The bridge carried the mission toward its stronger form of 2001. That form finally broke the rebels' grip on the country.

Two lines are all this bridge measure needs. On 3 July 2002, acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that the provisions of its resolution 1357 of 2001, on the former Yugoslavia, would stay in force until 15 July 2002. The matter stayed under review while the follow-on arrangements covered by that earlier text were settled.

Liberia's sanctions regime is rebuilt from the ground up on 22 December 2003, after its civil war. Expert panels had found the old measures still being breached, mainly through arms buying. A peace agreement had been signed in Accra in August, and a transitional government had taken office in October.

The old prohibitions are ended and the old sanctions committee dissolved, then a fresh set of measures is imposed under a new committee. These cover arms, rough diamonds from Liberia, and timber, matched to the new situation on the ground. West African states are told to stop armed groups from using their territory to attack neighbours, and reviews are set to test whether the transitional government meets the Council's conditions.

Resolution 1621, adopted on 6 September 2005, reinforces the UN mission in Congo ahead of historic elections. The Pretoria transition agreement of 2002 was moving the country toward its first free national polls in four decades. The Council called on the transitional institutions and all Congolese parties to keep the elections free, fair, and peaceful, and to respect the electoral commission's timetable exactly.

To guard the process, the Council authorized a temporary increase in the strength of MONUC, the UN mission, which already operated under Chapter VII. Donors funding the election effort were thanked and pressed to keep giving. The text also records continuing alarm at hostilities in the east and at attacks on civilians by armed groups.

Côte d'Ivoire's transition is extended one final year under African Union terms in Resolution 1721, adopted on 1 November 2006. Elections had proved impossible on schedule. The transition and the mandates of the president and prime minister expired on 31 October 2006. The AU Peace and Security Council had set new terms on 17 October 2006.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the AU decision. The president remains head of state for a final transition of no more than twelve months. The prime minister's mandate is renewed on the same terms, barred from standing in the coming election. The prime minister receives powers including rule by ordinance and authority over the defence and security forces, to deliver disarmament, voter identification, and elections by 31 October 2007. The High Representative for the Elections is renewed for twelve months as arbitrator of electoral disputes and certifier of all stages.

Summer 2008 brought the Golan force to the table once more. The chief's report of 16 June 2008 told of a calm line. UNDOF's term was set to lapse at the month's end. The force had stood on the heights since 1974. Resolution 1821 passed on 27 June 2008.

Six more months were set, to 31 December 2008. Both sides heard the old call to act on the 1973 text. The staff code clause runs long in this text. Zero tolerance for sexual abuse is the theme. Troop states must drill their men, probe claims, and punish guilt. A report was due when the term closed. The twin frame of these late texts is plain: still guns on the line, strict rules for the watch.

Resolution 1921, adopted on 12 May 2010, extends the UN Mission in Nepal, UNMIN, one more time while setting its exit. The deadline for Nepal's new constitution was 28 May 2010, yet the parties had reached no agreement on the text or on extending the Constituent Assembly. Discharge of disqualified Maoist army personnel, including minors, had been completed under a December 2009 action plan. Nepal asked for UNMIN to stay until 15 September 2010.

The Council renews UNMIN until 15 September 2010. It decides that UNMIN should start arranging its withdrawal at once, handing over leftover monitoring duties by that date. It calls on the government and the Maoist party to agree on a timed plan, with clear targets, for integrating and settling Maoist army personnel. A report on carrying out the resolution is due by 1 September 2010.

Pacific islands once held by Japan came before the Council on 2 April 1947. The islands had been German colonies before the First World War. The League of Nations then gave them to Japan as a mandate. Japan lost them in the Second World War. Resolution 21, adopted unanimously, set up a trusteeship for the islands.

The Council approved the terms of the trusteeship and made the United States the administering authority. The islands were classed as a strategic area. Because of that, the United States could build bases and station forces there. In return, it had to move the islanders toward self-government. It had to protect their lands and rights. It also had to build up education, health services, and the local economy.

Resolution 221 is a UN Security Council enforcement step against Rhodesia's oil lifeline, adopted on 9 April 1966 by ten votes to none with five abstentions. After the white minority regime's unilateral independence declaration, oil tankers were heading for Beira in Portuguese Mozambique, from where a pipeline could pump fuel to landlocked Southern Rhodesia.

The Council declares the situation a threat to the peace, calls on Portugal not to allow pumping or accept Rhodesian oil at Beira, and asks all states to divert their suspect vessels. Most strikingly, it authorizes Britain to use force if necessary to stop such ships, and specifically to arrest the tanker Joanna V if her cargo were discharged. The episode became known as the Beira Patrol.

Senegal's charge against Portugal wins backing in Resolution 321. It passed on 23 October 1972, with twelve votes in favor and three members not voting either way. Senegal's foreign chief laid out the case in the hall. Portugal replied by letter. Past texts since 1963 had dealt with Portuguese strikes on Senegalese soil. The strikes came from the colony of Guinea-Bissau, next door. A UN rights team's report of 1971 set out the facts in depth.

The Council voiced deep dismay at Portugal's flat refusal to obey those texts. It condemned the strikes and told Lisbon to respect Senegal's soil and borders. Calm would come, it argued, when all African lands near Portugal's colonies were left in peace, and their peoples freed to rule their own fate.

South Africa's arms buildup is the subject of Resolution 421, adopted on 9 December 1977. A month earlier, in Resolution 418, the Council had ruled that South Africa getting arms threatened world peace and had placed a required arms embargo on the country. Members now wanted a way to watch how well that ban was working.

The resolution creates a Security Council committee made up of all Council members. The committee must study the Secretary-General's report on the embargo, look for ways to make the ban work better, and ask states what they have done to enforce it. All states are called on to cooperate and share information, and the Secretary-General must give the committee the staff and help it needs.

Yugoslavia was tearing itself apart in late November 1991. A ceasefire signed in Geneva on 23 November offered brief hope. The Secretary-General's envoy, Cyrus Vance, had brokered it. Yugoslav leaders told him they wanted UN peacekeepers deployed quickly. Resolution 721 gave the Council's answer that month.

Members approved the envoy's peace efforts warmly. They endorsed his warning to the parties. No peacekeeping force could deploy without full respect for the Geneva deal. The Yugoslav sides were urged to honor it completely. The Council promised to act fast on any peacekeeping proposal. That promise led, within months, to the huge UNPROFOR mission in Croatia and Bosnia.
unamuno-tragic-sense-of-life-flitch-1921:
Miguel de Unamuno published Del sentimiento trágico de la vida in Spain in 1913, and J. E. Crawford Flitch Englished it in 1921 as Tragic Sense of Life. Unamuno argues that man thinks with his whole being, not with reason alone. Reason says we die for good; the heart refuses to accept that verdict.

From that clash Unamuno builds his philosophy of faith, doubt, and hunger for eternal life. He writes as a wrestler, not a professor, and names his own unbelief honestly. The book influenced thinkers far beyond Spain in the century after. Flitch's Macmillan translation was a landmark for Unamuno in English. It remains the fullest statement of his thought.
veblen-engineers-price-system-1921:
Veblen turned to the technicians in The Engineers and the Price System, a short book of 1921. Engineers and production experts, he argues, know how to run industry for full output. The price system, run by owners for profit, holds them back. Sabotage of production, in his special sense, keeps prices up and goods scarce.

He sketches a soviet of engineers who might one day take charge of industry. The proposal was his most radical program, half serious and half a prod. The book states institutionalism in its boldest political form. It caught the mood of postwar unrest among technical workers. Readers still cite its contrast between making and profiting.
williams-sour-grapes-1921:
Sour Grapes, published in 1921, is a book of poems by William Carlos Williams, the Rutherford doctor and poet. By this point Williams had settled into the plain, direct style that made him distinct. He writes as a man looking hard at the world right in front of him.

The poems take up flowers, fruit, weather, city streets, and passing strangers. Many are brief, built from one clear image held up to the light. Others muse on age, desire, and the limits of words themselves. Sour Grapes shows Williams in full command of his method, finding weight and music in common things.
wittgenstein-logisch-philosophische-abha:
Ludwig Wittgenstein's Logisch-philosophische Abhandlung appeared in German in 1921, the journal version of the work the world knows as the Tractatus. Wittgenstein, a young Austrian who had been an artillery officer in the war, wrote most of it in the trenches and in a prison camp. He believed the book solved the problems of philosophy by drawing the border of sense.

The text is built from numbered remarks, each as compressed as a line of poetry. Its core claim: a sentence has meaning by picturing a possible state of the world, and what cannot be pictured cannot be said. Ethics, God, and the meaning of life fall on the silent side of the line. The closing words, that whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent, became the most quoted sentence in modern philosophy.
woodward-homo-rhodesiensis-1921:
Arthur Smith Woodward of the British Museum announced a new fossil human in Nature in 1921. Miners at Broken Hill in Rhodesia, now Kabwe in Zambia, had found a large skull deep underground. Woodward named the species Homo rhodesiensis.

He described the skull's heavy brow, large face, and diseased teeth in detail. The find was the first archaic human fossil reported from Africa. Scholars now usually group it with Homo heidelbergensis instead. The paper still matters as the moment Africa entered the fossil human record in force. The skull remains on display and under study a century later.
woolf-monday-tuesday-1921:
Virginia Woolf published Monday or Tuesday in 1921, the only book of her short fiction to appear in her lifetime. It holds just eight short pieces. Woolf and her husband Leonard printed the book themselves at their Hogarth Press, with woodcuts by her sister Vanessa Bell.

The pieces are sketches and experiments rather than plotted tales. A heron flies over a London evening, a woman's thoughts scatter through a day, and a string quartet stirs a listener's memories. Kew Gardens watches couples drift past flower beds in a haze of impressions. Woolf tests here the fluid method she would perfect in her novels. The little book is her laboratory of modernist fiction.
yeats-michael-robartes-1921:
Yeats published this collection in 1921, between the Irish war of independence and the civil war that followed. It is a short book with two of his most famous poems at its center.

'The Second Coming' gives the volume its power: a vision of history's center failing and a rough beast slouching toward Bethlehem. Beside it stands 'A Prayer for My Daughter', written for his infant child amid storm and political fear. Other poems honor Robert Gregory and look back at Easter 1916. The book captures a great poet watching his country and his age come apart.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol21:
Volume XXI of the Journal of Discourses, printed at Liverpool in 1881, carries the sermon record into the 1880s. Leading elders and apostles preach in its pages, their talks preserved just as delivered. The church they serve faces mounting pressure from the nation over its marriage practice, a theme never far away.

Doctrine and defense share the pulpit here, as speakers answer critics while teaching their own. The Journal's unedited closeness makes such moments vivid for later readers. Volume XXI holds its year in the long sequence, part of the fullest preaching archive of any American religious movement.
